My hon. friend from Lafontaine (Mr. Lachance) supported by an hon. member opposite gave proper reasons, in my view, why the name of Lapointe should be retained. Despite what the sponsor of the bill had to say, I believe this riding was named after a great Canadian statesman, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. The hon. member in introducing this bill told us, as far as I can gather, that the main reason for seeking a change was that all the other candidates and party leaders except himself had promised the name would be changed. In view of what happened in that riding during the election I would imagine that the hon. member, who of course was successful, would be superstitious enough to be reluctant to have the name altered in any way.
I am opposing a change in name for three reasons. First, as I said, I believe this riding was named for a great French Canadian, Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, a statesman who made an outstanding contribution to the public life of this country. I am sure this view will be shared by those of my colleagues, and others, who come from the province of Quebec and who would, I am sure, be unhappy to see the name of this gentleman taken from its present place. I could speak at length about the contribution made to Canadian public life by Mr. Lapointe but I do not think this is the occasion on which to do so. But I think it would be wrong for us to make any effort to change the name of a riding which was, I am sure, called after this great French Canadian statesman.
My second reason for opposing this bill is the fact that we recently set up a redistribution commission to bring about necessary changes in the constituencies of this country. In these circumstances I think it would be premature to make any effort to change even the name of a constituency. I do not think there is any good reason for the request contained in this bill. From rumours most of us have heard it seems every riding in the

Representation Act
country will undergo at least minor changes and it is almost inconceivable that the riding of Lapointe will be an exception.
My third reason for opposing any change is this: I believe that before we can accept a proposal of this kind, logical reasons must be advanced in its favour. I do not think such reasons have been advanced on this occasion. The hon. member said this change had been promised, but advanced very little by way of further justification. I would point out that any change of this kind is bound to result in some confusion. Difficulties are bound to arise when anything of this nature is done. For these reasons I have to oppose this measure.

We cannot help but ask ourselves this question. Why has the Prime Minister gambled so frivolously with the time of parliament and with the will of the Canadian people by taking the time that has been asked of parliament for the consideration of a measure for which there is widespread lack of support throughout the country? I have not heard a single person say that he is in favour of the new design submitted to parliament by the committee which was set up by the House of Commons. Search out the newspapers. How few or non-existent are the expressions of the Canadian people endorsing this design which has been brought forward by the members of the committee. Search out the problems which face the people in all parts of the country today and ask yourselves whether the priority placed on the measure is a priority which is justified in view of these problems, which are before the Canadian people.
Therefore for those reasons, while this debate has its deplorable aspects, nevertheless in the face of the tactics employed by the Prime Minister the official opposition has no other course than to take the action we are taking at the present time. The Prime Minister and hon. gentlemen opposite cannot afford to think they can hide behind the rules of parliament even in this debate or in any other debate in the House of Commons. What the government is asking is for the careless acceptance of this proposal, not for a

I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there are other things the government could do not only in that old province of Quebec but in other areas of Canada where attention is needed that would be of far greater moment than the measure now before us. I want to say also that if the Prime Minister and the government think that by the passage of this measure they can possibly slough off the electorate of the province of Quebec with the thought that they have done something for them, when the real and major issues at stake in that province have been left untouched, then I think they are acting most unwisely. They are acting in a way that is detrimental to the future of the nation and to national unity itself.
This flag that we are asked to endorse, which we on this side of the house say should be put before the Canadian people in a plebiscite along with other designs; this measure that the Prime Minister wants to push through parliament, could well become the symbol of discontent more than any other flag Canadians have ever had in the past if little or nothing is done to meet the everyday problems that face Canadians not only in the province of Quebec but in the other provinces as well. When we consider that the Prime Minister has already told the people of Canada that he is making the gesture of giving them a flag, while at the same time he brings before parliament another measure enabling him to say that the union jack will continue to fly to represent our connection with the commonwealth, what a hollow gesture this is. We heard from the ranks of the Liberal party a very profound and courageous speech by the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), a real contribution to a debate of an extremely serious character.
Now, I thought there would be some support from the Liberal party for the proposal now before the house. It makes for a debate when opposing views are presented in this cham-

ber. That is the purpose of debating. We are putting forward our case; the other side should be putting forward their case, if they have one. It makes it very difficult when members on the government side do not enter into the debate. Obviously they have no interest in this matter; they are fainthearted with regard to the flag now proposed, or else they hesitate to put on the sackcloth and ashes and tell us they were all wrong six months ago when they were talking about the three maple leaf flag with the blue border.
I intend in the course of this debate to put forward two reasons why this matter should be referred to the people. But I propose, in leading up to those reasons, to deal with matters which have been mentioned by the hon. member for Leeds and the hon. member for Villeneuve, because those gentlemen have presented a point of view to which I am opposed, and in the course of this debate I think I am justified in drawing attention to their remarks and giving an answer to them. I also hope to deal with other matters, all leading up to the two main points I intend to make during the course of this debate. I appreciate the nature of the ground rules which have been staked out. All I ask is the same privilege that was extended to the hon. member for Leeds, the hon. member for Terrebonne, the hon. member for Villeneuve and various hon. members who touched on other matters rather than the question of a plebiscite; and I hope I shall not be asked to use the word "plebiscite" in every other sentence.
In the speech he made to the house the hon. member for Leeds once again brought us information which I consider to be inaccurate. I refer to his interpretation of the proclamation of 1921, which he uses as a basis for advocating the adoption of the proposed flag now before us, the flag with the white centre and red borders having a red maple leaf superimposed in the centre, as recommended by the committee. I dealt with this subject when I was speaking in August, but apparently I did not convince the hon. member for Leeds, who has repeated in this house the argument he used on that occasion. Consequently I must again draw the attention of the house to the fact that I believe the hon. member for Leeds and others, including the hon. member for Danforth, have been misled by the interpretation given to the royal proclamation of 1921.
They have stated here that the national colours are red and white, and I say they have no evidence that such national colours were 20220-688

ever established. I said in August and I say again now that the committee which drew up the proclamation of 1921 and delivered it to the government of that day said nothing in its brochure, which was published later, about the establishment of national colours. No reference was made to them in subsequent brochures until the one published in March of this year under the present Liberal government. The others said nothing about Canada's national colours being red and white. I say the information supplied to us to the contrary is misinformation and should be rejected.
My second point is this, and I reiterate it because of the statements which have been made with regard to the coats of arms as determined in 1921. The only maple leaf which was coloured in red was the maple leaf resting in the paw of the hon. and it was put there for the express purpose of commemorating Canada's sacrifice in the first world war. It represented Canada's losses in that war; 60,000 Canadian young men lost their lives in that struggle. That is why the red maple leaf was incorporated in the coat of arms. I argued in August, and I do again, that having used a red maple leaf for this purpose it is disgraceful to abandon it now and use it for some other purpose, as has been done in the revised coat of arms and as is being done in this proposed new flag. The red maple leaf on the coat of arms represents the sacrifice of the first world war. Is this Liberal government going to wipe that out and forget about it? I say, no.

And it should not appear on the flag of Canada, a red maple leaf. We should go back to what it was originally, a green maple leaf as was determined in the proclamation of 1921; because in that proclamation the red maple leaf was mentioned and given its proper heraldic term, gules, and the three maple leaves were given their term "proper" which means "in their natural state" which means green.
The coat of arms was revised a few years later. I say it was improperly revised, and that our government was misled by that revision and that a correction should be made. I say that the red maple leaf should not be used on a flag of Canada; that the red maple leaf represents the blood sacrifice of Canadians in the first world war, and it should be retained for that purpose. If the Liberal party intend to wipe that out, let them conduct another revision of the Canadian coat

of arms from which this flag is being drawn -the references are always to that. If this message could only get across to the people of Canada-and this is why we suggest referring this question to the people of Canada-* we believe they would reject the proposed new flag because it improperly uses the red maple leaf.
This committee was set up after a rather lengthy debate in the House of Commons in the expectation that some solution would be found, through the work of the committee, that would be acceptable to the house, to parliament and to the people of Canada. I commend the committee for its diligent work. I regret to say that the committee failed in its task because it did not come up with a solution that is satisfactory. I have given one reason why their solution is unsatisfactory. We had hoped that some compromise might be effected during the work of that committee. The stand taken by our party in the debate in August and September was very largely this. We wished to retain the Canadian red ensign, modified, if you like, in the fly, replacing the coat of arms with the maple leaf, adding the fleur-de-lis and recognizing the history and traditions of our country, which would constitute a distinctive and acceptable Canadian flag.
When the committee met I entertained some hope-not very much-that the committee would bring forward a design somewhat along that line. I had hoped that the committee would start with the design approved by the parliamentary committee of 1946, which voted 23 to 1 for a modified Canadian red ensign, with the shield removed and a golden maple leaf placed in the fly. I thought the committee, starting from that point, would perhaps add the fleur-de-lis; because I have always thought-and this is where I have been mistaken, as I have discovered from the debate in the house during August, September and this month-that the fleur-de-lis should have more prominence on our flag than it has just in the coat of arms. I will point out where I have been mistaken in that belief as I proceed with what I have to say.
The committee, which started off with great expectations, ended in failure; and it ended in failure because the Liberal members on that committee did not apparently deal with anything in the nature of a compromise in which our history and traditions would be recognized, because they rejected any reference to our past and rejected the flag which was brought in with the blare of trumpets last May by the Prime Minister. They threw

out the three maple leaf flag with the blue borders and substituted the white flag with a red maple leaf and red borders.
Where was the compromise? There was no meeting of minds with regard to the position put forward by the Conservative party, and we represent quite a number of people in Canada; it runs into millions. Why could there not be a meeting of minds? We have had pointed out to us that the Conservative members on that committee endeavoured to bring about a compromise by superimposing on the red and white flag the union jack in one corner and the fleur-de-lis in the other. Quite frankly I did not think that was a very attractive design, but it was a sincere effort to bring together opposing points of view. But the committee rejected that design and insisted on bringing before us a new design, falsely called a design based on Canada's alleged national colours.

In so far as the second question is concerned the hon. member, drawing from his knowledge of heraldry-perhaps I can assist him in this-has reached the conclusion that because the mantle under the helmet is described as being red and white, that this constitutes the national colours of Canada. I say there is no authority for that statement. I suggest to him that he produce the evidence from the books of heraldry to show that they constitute the national colours. They may constitute the colours of the monarch whose helmet is there, but not necessarily the colours of this country. If he will examine the coat of arms for Australia and the coat of arms for New Zealand, he will see that there is no mention of national colours in their coats of arms. As I pointed out earlier

today, the committee that sat on this problem in 1921, and to whom the hon. member paid tribute, as I do, said nothing in their descriptive booklet with regard to Canada's determining at that time that her national colours would be red and white. Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time I have risen to participate in this debate. If there are those who do not wish to participate in it, that is their privilege. I have spoken now at least four times, but only twice in this year. The other occasions on which I spoke were January 21, 1962 and November 21, 1962 which, by a peculiar coincidence was just 41 years after the date on which King George V is purported to have wanted to incorporate, as the Canadian flag, the three maple leaf design, which has been now abandoned. The three maple leaf design certainly had some merit. I suppose most of the designs which came before the flag committee had some merit.
When the flag committee was established I hoped, as I presume most of us did, that they would be able to come up with a proper decision which would be acceptable to everybody in this house. I, for one, did not want the matter decided that way. I think the matter should be decided by parliament if it is possible. I believe this is our job and this is the reason we were sent here. We were given a mandate by the people, not necessarily or only to fulfil election promises because we live in a dynamic society, a changing world. In any event, the people who voted for me expected me to put what talents I have to work to solve the problems of the day as they arise. Some people are saying, therefore, that we have no right to decide this matter by means of a plebiscite; that we should decide it in parliament. I rather supported this view up until the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and his government made it impossible for me to vote freely in this house. They forced us all to take a partisan attitude. A free debate would have permitted us at least to instruct each other, if not provide us with better ideas on how to act like gentlemen and on how the people in our own districts feel.
This is what I have done. I challenge anyone to say this is not so. I hear remarks in the corner to the effect that I have spoken four times already and this will be another

Canadian Flag
empty contribution. Hon. members should at least do me justice by reading what I have said before they condemn me. These four speeches were as long as I am permitted under the rules. I stated what I sincerely felt. No one could construe from my words that I had anything but the greatest respect for that other great race of people, the other partner in confederation, for whom I have great admiration and affection. What do I get? When I get on my feet I get abuse, hisses and catcalls. If any member doubts my word, he has only to read Hansard. I do not want to name the man who said these things, but at one point he went so far as to say I would be rubbed out. Those are the exact words. His name does not appear on this page of Hansard to which I shall refer. I do not know if he was not identified or if he was talking behind his hands so that the Hansard reporter could not get his name; but I know who he was. I am not going to say who he was, but his exact words can be found at page 6938 of Hansard for August 17, and they were, "We will rub you off." By no stretch of the imagination can anybody take any meaning from that other than it is the language of the underworld. I hope the hon. member did not mean it. I hope he was not speaking for any group of people when he said that. I spoke from my heart and in my speech there was not one word which anybody could say was narrow-minded, controversial and so partisan that I should have been subjected to that type of abuse.
The only reason I mention this today is because the same type of remark is being made, and I do not think it is the type of remark that will keep partisanship down. I have been trained to control my temper. Perhaps at times I may sound a little warmed up but I shall never get to the point where I threaten the life or safety of another hon. member of the house.
I expected at the time that, after seeing it in Hansard, the hon. member might deny it because it is the kind of talk Canadians dislike. By rights we could have asked the Speaker to have him removed from the house. The fact that such a threat is made under the protection of parliament does not add any lustre to it.

Mr. Speaker, if I have gone a little beyond the bounds it is because I am trying to show that if this type of attitude persists in parliament and creates the kind of atmosphere we have, then the press and T.V. commentators can assume we have lost our heads and are no longer fit to make a proper decision on this subject.
I started out by saying 1 wanted parliament to decide this question, but how can it when threats are made on a person's life? I hear groans opposite, but I point out that that remark has never been removed from Hansard and is to be found at page 6938.
Only one man on the opposite side got up on his feet and gave his true and unchanging attitude to this whole matter, the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan). He made a courageous speech and I can only assume he must speak for the Liberal party because they have not repudiated or refuted him. No hon. member on the other side got up and took exception to what he said. I believe it is the duty of hon. members not only to oppose arguments put forward by the opposite side of the house but also to qualify such definite statements as appear to be entirely in opposition to the stand taken by one's own party. In the absence of that I can only assume the hon. member has the approbation of most of the members in his party. If the rest of them do not agree then they must be 100 per cent behind the three maple leaf flag which was originally introduced and upon which the Prime Minister said the government would stand or fall. Then he said there would be a free vote, but the ink was hardly dry on Hansard before he returned with a different proposition, a double flag for Canada.
If there was an election promise that we were to be seized of this question and had to decide it before going home for Christmas, why did the government not stand behind its pledge to have one flag for Canada, one flag for one nation? It was a courageous act on the Prime Minister's part to introduce a motion on the flag issue, but it was not particularly courageous on his part to back down almost immediately, and to continue to back down until now we have reached the position where a flag recommended by a parliamentary committee is before us, a flag originally proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), a single maple leaf flag.
You may argue all you like about the colour, and design but to my way of thinking this decision to abandon the three maple leaves and adopt one maple leaf was nothing

but a political gimmick. Those who staked their political future on the three maple leaves back in May have forgotten them completely. They now say they believe in a gentlemanly compromise, but it is hard for me to believe this is a gentlemanly compromise.
It is hard for me to believe that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), who was the spiritual mother of the three maple leaf flag, could be convinced by a short argument in a plugged committee-plugged in the sense that there were more government members on it than we had on it-that he should abandon the child of his own imagination. I can only assume he was told to do so. I know he is a man of great courage and conviction, but I cannot understand why he did not stand up like the hon. member for York-Humber and fight this thing to the bitter end.

No, I do not think anything I said suggested that at all. 1 am talking about why I insist on a plebiscite, because parliament has made a political football out of this thing. The question has gone beyond that of design. We have made a political football of this, perhaps on all sides. I am not accusing the government alone of doing this. We have been driven into a corner where we are perhaps putting up too strong an argument for a particular design which we happen to prefer, but I certainly do not see anything wrong in my standing on my feet and saying I prefer one particular design, or in the hon. member for Leeds supporting his spiritual child. No one would criticize him for doing that. In fact this is all so reasonable that a member of his own party agrees with me.
But when the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) says, "I will have anything that is not British," surely this is a partisan point of view. Why not something that is partly British? I do not object to any design which may have some connection with the French race, whether remote or not. Personally, if I had to design a flag-and I know a little about heraldry-I would like to see the union jack quartered with the lily banner of France. This would represent the marriage of two nations and would be correct in heraldry.
Canadian Flag
It would designate the differing points of view and loyalties but show them co-operating together.
I hope my contribution to this debate has been positive. I have tried to find the proper compromise. At no time have I said I want to ram the union jack, or any other design, down hon. members' throats. I believe in democratic free speech. I believe in it to such an extent that I did not make a point of it when a threat was made against me. I thought the important thing here was to decide, if we could, on some compromise- if we must. I do not think any member of the Conservative party has said: We must have the red ensign and that alone. If we were rabid about our British connection, surely we would make no objection about having the double submission to parliament. I want one flag for one nation. I had hoped we could reach agreement by compromise on such a flag. If we had started with a clean slate and kept it out of politics and if the Prime Minister had not risked the life of his government on it, we might now have something like the lilied banner of France, and the union jack quartered in our national flag.
Some day Canada may be a republic; I do not know. We may be moving in that direction. If such should be the will of Canada as a free democracy, I suppose I must accept it. I am not a great royalist, but I still believe there are many ways in which the British commonwealth is of great help to Canada. I think the monarch as referee under our parliamentary system is still essential to proper debate, to British justice and to that loyalty which unites us all in one big, happy family. There were many people in Quebec who went out, perhaps to jeer the Queen as she passed. But when they saw the cultured woman who went by, in all her majesty and simplicity, a woman who speaks the two languages, English and French, as well as any member of this house, they began to change their minds and were even proud of her. And all I want to do, is to present my attitude toward democracy and co-operation in such a way that members will perhaps be proud of me. I mean by this that I love the French nation. I am trying to learn the language so as to be able to speak to Canadians of French origin in their own tongue.

speechtext:
The people of my riding want a plebiscite and I would be delinquent in my duty if I did not tell the members of this house how they feel. That is, surely, my first, second, third, fourth, and every other duty, namely to do what the people back home want me to do. That is why they sent me here and

that is what I have to do. This is why I have no difficulty whatever controlling my temper; I will stand here and represent them no matter what is said. They want a plebiscite. They want a chance to express their opinions because-and I think I can say this quite properly-they think we have abdicated our position here; they can have no faith in any decision we may reach, now, in the House of Commons on this subject.
As to whether or not we are engaged in a filibuster, let me say this: On September 8 we had a vote in this house as to whether or not we should end the flag debate and get along with more important matters. The Liberal party voted 100 per cent to carry on the debate. Apparently they did not want to carry it on themselves; they wanted to hear us. Well, we are doing what this house voted to do; we are carrying on the debate. And I think the debate could soon be put into its proper perspective if we were to vote on whether or not we should hold a plebiscite.
There are arguments that a plebiscite should not be held because that is not the Canadian way of doing things. I remember the last plebiscite. It was during the war and a plebiscite was taken to decide whether or not individual Canadian citizens should be forced to bear arms in the service of their country. The questions on that plebiscite were worded in such a way that they were difficult to understand and interpret. It may well be argued that if a plebiscite is hard to understand and if its results may be misconstrued it has serious defects. But I am convinced that plebiscites are not without value and that they are legitimate and normal when a parliament has got itself into a position where it cannot carry out its duty properly. I am convinced we are in that position today and that it is my plain duty to vote so as to give the people a chance to get us out of the unholy mess we are in. The people have their ideas. They want to be heard and I believe they have the right to be heard. They have asked me as their representative, as their member from Athabasca, to make their views known in no uncertain terms, because they agree with the fourth estate and the representatives of other news media in what they say to the effect that we have not done a very good job here in parliament on the flag.
I do not intend to accuse members of being partisan in anything they have said or done since the start of this debate. I do not believe in accusing other people. I believe that if you accuse other people of being crooked,

the accusation carries within it an indication of your own character. I would advise the people who accuse me to read my speeches and see whether I am a narrow Anglo-Saxon. They might even look into the latter statement more closely. I have in my constituency people of other origins, and sometimes from people of those other origins I get letters saying: Why do not the two great founding races, so-called, get together on this question and behave like gentlemen? Our native people say: We kept our side of the treaty, why don't you keep yours? They were promised conditions in which to live superior to those they had. They were men of honour, and they expected to be dealing with men of honour.
The position taken by our own French speaking members is often regarded by members of the opposition as a horrible example of disunity within this party. I can give an explanation of this. It is not possible to expect unanimity, even on such a matter as a plebiscite, because in our party we are individuals, each and every one of us. Our leader has been accused by people outside the party, of trying to ram this plebiscite idea down our throats. I believe the idea of a plebiscite is very largely backed by the members of our party, although we are not unanimous. It would be strange if 95 men at any time- if they were men of thought and courage- were able to say they were absolutely unanimous and could find no reason for difference. If this was human nature, if this was the Canadian way and we could expect 20 million people to be unanimous, why would we need this institution? Surely it is to decide whether a question such as the holding of a plebiscite can be resolved here like gentlemen, having free speech and tolerance one for another.
I repeat again, Mr. Speaker, because I do not think it can be repeated too often in this atmosphere, that I do not deny to people of French origin or people who merely live in Quebec, perhaps, their full opinion on this matter. I do not object to any symbol which they may want incorporated in their flag. The only reason I have stood up for the red ensign myself is because since a child I have considered it my flag. Since 1921 it has in fact been our legal flag, and is until parliament decides to the contrary. Since 1944 it has been confirmed, and was confirmed by a Liberal government at that time who thought that perhaps Canada was not mature enough to accept the responsibility for changing its flag and perhaps putting on that flag something entirely new. There are arguments 20220-689i
Canadian Flag
in favour of that point of view. I do not object to giving the people of Canada the opportunity to remove the union jack or any part of it from our flag; I merely make my own contribution and say that I like the union jack, and I know why-because it stands for British justice. Is it strange that a man like myself, who spent 23 years in the mounted police, should have some respect for that flag which flies every day outside our detachments? It is a lifelong habit of respect, if nothing else. But I do not expect everybody to respect that flag; all members of this house were not mounted policemen. We do not have unity even in the army on this subject; there are many servicemen who do not want to retain the red ensign. They have the right to get up and say so, if that is their opinion. And many of them are of British origin.
If you read all the speeches in Hansard, Mr. Speaker, on this subject I think you will find that most of those which have come from this side of the house have been reasonable, well thought out, factual and even unimpassioned. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am sometimes surprised at the restraint with which we accept the barbs; I am surprised at the way we accept hisses and catcalls when saying merely that we like the flag under which we serve.
Surely it is not strange that men should stand up and say, "I respect this flag because I served under it". I wonder what citizen of the United States would even dare get up and say, "Let's pull down old glory". We are a very tolerant people; we allow people to get up and say, "Get rid of it and everything British, regardless". That was said in this chamber this afternoon. I have not said, "Let's shoot them. Let's take them out and hang them", or that sort of thing. A member has a perfect right to say that he wants no part of this flag to be retained as a symbol; but I would object very strongly if, having voted on the matter and having decided on one particular design, he said he was no longer going to be loyal to that flag and serve under it. The hon. member has not said that and I am not accusing him of it. Surely we have a right to stand up and put forward our views in connection with those things we love dearly. I do not only love things that are of Anglo-Saxon origin, but I love things of French origin; their literature, songs and the people themselves. There are times when I wonder whether this feeling is mutual. I do not like to wonder about these things; I do not want ever to wonder whether we are a united nation. But people talk that way

Canadian Flag
sometimes. I like to hope it is only because they are taking things a little too seriously; that their passions are aroused by things said over here, or things which they think have been said over here. These things do make people angry.
I believe I am making my point, Mr. Speaker, that in this atmosphere we cannot decide this matter like gentlemen and therefore we should let the people decide what they want in this regard, who after all are a little more removed and can be more dispassionate than we in this house. The people should be given the opportunity to make their views known in this matter. There are objections to this course being followed. It is said that we cannot put this problem to the people in a reasonable manner. I think we can. I do not think there is any haste in this matter. I do not see any reason why, even though the government has in the past committed itself to something-I think they committed themselves to a foolish promise-they cannot withdraw this matter. I would admire them more if they withdrew as gracefully as they can and said, "Really there is no haste. We made our promise to bring this subject forward and intended to dispose of it in parliament; but we have got to the point where we cannot". I do not think we can, and therefore I believe the only solution is to send it to the people. I do not think it is beyond our legal brains to draw up a plebiscite that would be fair and would allow everybody to vote on this question. I do not think it would be very difficult to decide upon one of a number of designs in this manner. I would suggest that the most important thing to be decided is whether or not we are going to have the red ensign or some modification thereof, or a complete denial of that type of flag. If that is what the Canadian people want, what is wrong with there being two votes on the question. We could get rid of the first question first and then decide, if we can, between the three maple leaf design, the one maple leaf design, or four, five or six designs. At this juncture I do not think it is a question of design. I do not believe this is bothering most of us. It is a question of method; it is a question of whether we can make a rational decision of some kind with a gun at our heads- economic, perhaps.
I do not believe most of us are here to earn a living. It is a tough way to earn a living, if that is what it is. Some of us like home life. So don't use that kind of economic gun, because it doesn't work. Some of us

would come here for nothing; some of us would pay to come here and have the privilege of putting forward the views of our people at home. Men on both sides of the house have paid; members of the Liberal party in this house have served their country with great distinction and great personal sacrifice, perhaps even to the point of death. How much their services in this house have contributed to their early death, I do not know; but these people did make great contributions. I am not going to say-and never will-that because a man sits on the opposite side of the house he has no contribution to make; and I hope there are men over there-in fact, I know there are-who will not write me off as nothing but a partisan, because I am not.
If a plebiscite is put to the people, the three maple leaf design may well be resurrected, and if the people of Canada vote for that flag, I will do the same as the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) and serve under it. He and I served under the old flag and I am certain we will do it again. I know it is that kind of thing that will bring us out of this difficulty. Let us have some of this spirit now, and co-operate; let us admit that we are in a boghole and resolve this difficulty. Let us admit that we have called each other too many names and have been impatient with each other. I hope that my speech today will induce members to let bygones be bygones so that we may have a free vote, a vote free of political pressures of any kind. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that is what we came here for. This would be far and away better than holding a plebiscite. However, I do not think there are ten men in this chamber who believe we can decide this question here fairly and squarely, because it has already gone too far. I accept responsibility in this regard. On behalf of myself and my party I do not say the fault rests with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). It certainly does not. I share the responsibility with him. I am not speaking for the rest of my party but I am speaking of my impressions from what the rest of my party have done when this matter has been discussed-unless they have had secret meetings which I have not heard about. The Leader of the Opposition has merely been expressing the feelings of our party arrived at in a democratic way; we are democratic in our party and in our country. There are times when we have to take a stand somewhere, especially when we have this political and economic gun put to our heads. We are forced into a corner in

which we have to make decisions that perhaps would not be made if people had the courage of the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan). I am quite sure he made his decision all on his own. It is a mistake, to my mind, for the rest of the Liberals to be silent and to suggest that the whole case has been made for their flag. If I were the hon. member for Leeds I would be disappointed if my colleagues did not rise and speak in the debate in this house. They knew they would be here, because they planned it. They had no legislation or anything else-

but since I am asked to make a speech, I shall cut it down to five words: I am against a plebiscite.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened with keen interest and attention, and despite the absence of many, to the many speeches which have been made on this issue. At the outset of my remarks may I point out that in a democratic country we cannot all be of the one opinion, and I am in favour of a plebiscite on this issue. I think that if the entire population of this great country of ours had the opportunity to voice their views and opinions there would be a greater degree of unity and satisfaction than would be the case if a flag is selected by this house and forced on the people. Regardless of the fact that this choice may be the flag which becomes the flag of Canada, it will not be the flag of the majority. I am not of the opinion that questions such as this should be decided by 265 representatives in this house. I agree, as do many others, that in most cases that is right; and the position is stated by Mr. Bruce West much better than I could state it.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question. Does he not think that decision by parliament is the traditional British way to decide things; and is he not a strong supporter of British traditions? I believe he is.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am just going to explain that, Mr. Speaker. The selection of a flag is different from many other questions, in fact from all of them. There are no experts or specialists who can select or determine what should be the flag of this country. I should like to quote Mr. Bruce West, who says this:
All I can say is that we did not introduce this contentious question into our country's affairs. It was introduced by the advocates of the new flag. Let them demand a new flag if they choose to do so. This is their right, as citizens of this country. But when some of us object to this proposal, let the blame for spreading disunity fall upon the heads of those who introduced the proposal, not upon those who exercise their right to oppose it.
Much has been said about how undesirable it would be to hold a nation-wide referendum on the flag question, on grounds that the ordinary man in the street should be content to leave this matter in the hands of his elected representatives. Ordinarily, I would agree with this theory.
That answers the point made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). Mr. West continues:
But not in the case of the proposed new flag. For one thing, every Canadian is fully qualified to make a decision on this particular matter.

In fact, I'd like to see even the children have a chance to express their views. Second, I do not believe that in the case of the flag our members of parliament are actually representatives of our people in the broad sense although they are, of course, in the legal one. You know and I know that the cards in this important game are politically stacked in Ottawa in such a way at this time that the true wishes of the people have become greatly obscured.
I have read that because it is a very good editorial. I have said that I am in favour of a plebiscite. I am happy to have this opportunity to voice my view and the views of many of my constituents and many other people, groups, organizations and individuals, many from a great distance, who have written me letters and who have sent me petitions. They are deeply concerned regarding the heritage and traditions of our country.
At the outset I want to go on record that the whole flag issue is, as I said when I spoke on August 25, a very important one though not one of immediate urgency. Decades have come and gone and Canada has gone forward. So let us, I suggest, lay a proper foundation for the selection of what touches on the very soul of our nation. I am more and more convinced that the only way this nation can have any reasonable degree of unanimity in a problem as emotional as this one is by a plebiscite.
It has been suggested that the reason for bringing about a new flag is to have a purely Canadian flag for the nation. If this is so, then it must be one that is the choice of the people. What other way can we get the democratic opinion of our entire population than by giving them the opportunity to voice their views in a plebiscite?
The navy has always had its own flag, the white ensign. The R.C.A.F. has had its flag with the blue background, and the army has used the red ensign. All these flags have one thing in common, the union jack in the upper quarter. Over the years these flags have come to mean much to those who have served in the forces and have therefore become part of our heritage and the focal point in rallying the nation in times of emergency. I say that a plebiscite would be most fair to those gallant men and women who have served this country, in that it would give them the opportunity to voice their own likes or dislikes. To prevent this now would seem to me to strike at the very foundation of our nation and discount entirely our past heritage. It would mean that we would be turning our backs on the many glorious

sacrifices made in the past that have built up this country to where it stands among the nations of the world today.
These sacrifices were not made by one ethnic group alone but by individuals of all groups who had come to regard Canada as their homeland. As a Canadian I am proud of this heritage and these sacrifices, and I see no legitimate reason for tossing them out without giving all our people the chance to voice their views in respect of this important matter.
In this fast changing world, Mr. Speaker, are we trying to establish a new Canada today, something which began in 1964 and which posterity will look upon as dating from 1964? Yes, Mr. Speaker, a plebiscite is what thousands of Canadians want. We have been made aware of this through the petitions which have been addressed to the house, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the members of his cabinet and to individual representatives of the different ridings. The people feel it is their democratic right to have the right to decide on their nation's emblem.
I further realize that feelings in regard to this important issue are mixed, but to what extent is one of the things that I think is unknown. They are mixed and we cannot be sure as to the situation. We do not know whether 30, 40, 50 or 60 per cent, or what percentage, hold a particular view; but if a plebiscite is held it will establish to what degree and satisfy all.
There are many besides those who have spoken in this house who have endorsed a plebiscite and the democratic right and privilege of the people of the country to voice their opinion. I should like to quote from The Legionary of July, 1964:
The Legionary therefore takes what is probably the last opportunity available to make one more appeal to the Prime Minister to let the people of Canada decide this crucial question. We do so because we earnestly believe a national plebiscite is by far the most clearcut way of settling the problem once and for all, and because we sincerely believe it is the only means of avoiding, so far as it is possible to do so, making it a partisan issue. Even if a "free" vote of M.P.'s and senators were allowed there would be a natural tendency, human nature being what it is, for government supporters to vote for the government's own design, and it is far from certain that a parliamentary vote on an issue of this nature would accurately reflect the feelings of the whole people of Canada.
As we said in our May issue: "In a free democratic country, where public opinion is neither regimented nor suppressed, instances occur when the people are stirred to the innermost depths of heart and soul. Then it is that government by the people, for the people, is given true effect by a
Canadian Flag
national vote on the issue at stake, and on that only."
The Legionary believes that the flag question is such an issue and again strongly urges the Prime Minister to let the Canadian people decide it, one way or another, through a national plebiscite. It is the most democratic way of solving this problem. It is the only way to ascertain what the people really want. And the request for a plebiscite is sure to be warmly supported by all Canadians of good will and moderation because, no matter what the result, if the issue were settled by a parliamentary vote only, grave doubts would arise in the minds of a great many citizens that it represented the will of the people. These doubts would linger on for many years and would remain a serious obstacle to the attainment of national unity.
So please, Mr. Prime Minister, let the people decide. It would be a statesmanlike solution and might well be a nation-saving move.
Now, those are the sentiments of the Legion which has, I suppose, upwards of a quarter of a million members. Many of their comrades who served in the war paid the supreme sacrifice and are not here to tell their story. I said before, and I repeat, I feel the government got off to a wrong start by introducing a definite design. This contention has been borne out by the report of the flag committee. The committee voted 100 per cent against the proposed three leaf flag. Surely, Mr. Speaker, when an issue tugs at the very soul of a nation great care should be taken in arriving at a solution. Each citizen should be given the democratic opportunity to express his or her opinion. In my opinion, if this were done it would do a great deal to curtail much of the controversy which the choice of a flag has created and bring about a greater degree of unity in our country, which the fathers of confederation endeavoured to create by binding us together in one great family.
I say, give the people a voice. They will remember our great inheritance. By the same token, we are the custodians of a sacred trust. Let us remember the religious emblem which permeated the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II. Let us recall the significant reply given by Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, the then prime minister of Canada, when he was asked why the new Queen had been proclaimed in Ottawa as the defender of the faith. He said that this was a Christian country. As a Christian country, I believe the majority of the people wish to retain the emphasis of the cross in our national flag. The cross is primarily the symbol of the Prince of Peace, the Saviour of the world. Every city, town and village throughout Canada has a church building upon which there

Canadian Flag
is a cross as a symbol of worship and racial tolerance.
Like many hon. members who have already spoken in this debate, I have received many letters and petitions from individuals and organizations throughout the country concerning the way in which the flag should be selected. Since I have received many petitions, I should like to quote from just a couple. First, I should like to quote a short portion of a petition coming from my own constituency of Lanark, which I have the honour and privilege of representing:
We, the voters of Lanark county, go on record as being opposed to the proposed new flag-or a new maple leaf flag to replace the red ensign. Every Canadian should be given the right to vote on this vital matter by means of a national plebiscite.
I said before, Mr. Speaker, and I say again, there are no experts in this matter of deciding a flag; there are no specialists in this field. It is purely a matter of emotion and sentiment. It is for this reason I am so definite and strong in my conviction that the only equitable way of bringing about maximum unity is to allow the people to go to the polls and decide by means of a plebiscite.
I should like to quote now from a letter from the Canadian Corps Association which, on many occasions, has been in favour of the red ensign. I quote:
The comments of our Prime Minister that those who support the retention of the Canadian red ensign are endeavouring to pressure the government into an election have been made by him to simply confuse the flag issue. It is not the supporters of the present Canadian national flag who have been pushing this flag issue to the priority decision position that it has at this date reached in parliament, but it is the Prime Minister's personal endeavour to place his flag design on the flag poles of this country that has resulted in this issue reaching such controversial prominence. With such divided opinion throughout Canada on the flag question, we cannot understand why Mr. Pearson will not allow the people of Canada the opportunity to choose between the Canadian red ensign and his new suggested maple leaf choice.
It is true that the government is elected by the people to change or set policies from time to time with regard to the conduct of this country's business, i.e. Canada's pension plan, income tax rates, baby bonus, agricultural policies, national defence policies, immigration policies, etc. However, the changing of Canada's national flag cannot possibly be classed in the above general business procedures of our country. We, as Canadians, do not feel that we want Canada's national flag to be changed from time to time at the whim of the various governments. Does our Prime Minister not realize that millions of citizens living in Canada today of voting age will still be alive for another 50 or 60 years, and therefore why should 265 members of parliament whose average years in office are approximately 15 to 20 years, choose the flag which all Canadians would then be expected

to respect during their entire lifetime? This is the reason why a plebiscite on the flag question is most necessary...
We would also like to point out in this letter, that the Canadian Corps Association, dominion command, considers the advice of the Prime Minister that a referendum on the flag would cost over $10 million is again simply another smokescreen in the flag question. Those who support the retention of the present Canadian national flag have not urged that the flag plebiscite need be conducted immediately-
-we do not wish to see our government waste money either, for it is the people of Canada who supply the money. The flag question ballot could be placed in with the regular voting ballots in the next scheduled general election of this country, and there most certainly is no need of either an election to be called, nor a $10 million immediate referendum when the question can be placed before the voters of this country, when the next regular general election is scheduled, and in the meantime the present national flag should be flown as it has been for the past many years until the people of Canada signify to the contrary.
Our organization fully realizes that there are many important national problems before the present members of the House of Commons that should most definitely take precedence over the flag question, and again we reiterate that it is not the supporters of the retention of the Canadian red ensign as Canada's national flag who are forcing this issue to the foreground in parliament.
In conclusion, I would like to mention that for the past half a century or more, this country's prime ministers and members of parliament have always indicated that Canada's veterans' views were respected statements by citizens who had served their country well in war, and were continuing to serve it loyally in peace through the welfare and service work of their organizations. During the past few weeks because of our present Prime Minister's open-combat attitude against the veterans organizations' views on the flag question, politicians, newspapers and general citizens have openly ridiculed the ex-servicemen who down through the years since 1900 have served Canada both at home and abroad. This type of criticism by those particularly in government authority has damaged the prestige and character of "service organizations" and we trust that it was never the intention of our present government to do so.
That is signed by the president of the Canadian Corps Association. As mentioned in that letter, there is no rush.
Much discussion has been given by many concerning the design of a flag, as though we never had one. It is strange that we should exist as a nation for nearly 100 years, sending our representatives to all corners of the earth, with our armed forces serving on every continent and recognized as Canadians wherever they have gone, yet our present government has wasted valuable time stirring up discord and resentment in every part of Canada.
Distinction is something that is earned. Culture is something that time creates. You do not build culture trying to destroy another, or denying that it exists. You give free

vent to all worth-while cultural influences. Surely it is not wrong to look back over our shoulders at yesterday. The fact that we are still predominantly British and French in outlook is what really makes us Canadians. If we forget sentiment and abandon tradition we may court extinction rather than distinction. We cannot live in the past, but we can live by it. A country which does not honour its past has no future.
This is no time for party politics. We should rise above it. The democratic world is watching. This is a matter in which history is being made, and some day a boy may ask his father to tell him the story of our flag and the father should be able to say, "Son, it was our finest hour." Let us see that our efforts are such that the generations to come will be able to say, "Son, it was our finest hour."

If the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) would listen for a moment he might learn something. It is unlikely that he will do so but it is a suggestion he might follow. I am speaking on the amendment which in effect proposes a plebiscite on the question of the national flag.
At the outset let me say that I am strongly opposed to the principle of a plebiscite-

speechtext: I hear applause from the other side, Mr. Speaker. speechtext: What about the political considerations?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Responding to the interjection from the other side may I say the
Canadian Flag
political considerations are entirely from those on that side.
In conveying to hon. members my conviction against the principle of a plebiscite when it is up to parliament, the governing body, to accept the responsibility, I would like to relate that when I was in local government in British Columbia, before I became a member of this house, on many occasions I decried the provincial legislation in that province which required consent of the people-in effect a plebiscite-when in my opinion the local body of government should have had the responsibility or right of decision. Yet in spite of my strong aversion to the principle of a plebiscite, I nevertheless feel there are valid arguments for supporting the proposal at this time.
The mere fact that, in spite of my convictions as to the principle of a plebiscite, I have arrived at my present position must surely indicate-at least it does to me-that we have arrived at a sorry state when we have to resort to this measure. If the whole issue of a flag had been approached in a different manner the question of a plebiscite would never have arisen. For example, if the same approach was taken by the present government as was taken in 1945-46, I doubt if this question would ever have occurred to anyone in the house.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They never had a
decision.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hear from the other side, from some person who is afraid to stand up and make a speech, that there was no decision. There was a very clear decision from the special joint committee of 1945-46; but the difference in procedure at that time and today was this, that in 1945 the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons was set up to propose a national flag for Canada and it was not told in advance that this or that flag for the preference of the government or the prime minister.
The committee entered upon that debate with a completely open mind. No instruction was given to them as to what they might or might not do. As a result of this approach the 1945 committee came up with a recommendation. As a matter of interest only, the recommendation happened to be the Canadian red ensign with the shield replaced by a maple leaf. The pertinent point is that the committee came up with a recommendation based on a vote of 23 to 1.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Fourteen to nothing.

Canadian Flag

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That vote of 14 to
nothing was, of course, the committee's vote against the flag proposed by your Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
It is unfortunate that after the committee reported in 1946 the government of the day neglected to take action. But the fact remains that if the flag question with which we have been dealing had been approached in the same manner, and if the government had proposed the adoption of the report, there would certainly have been the odd person here and there who would raise objection, but generally speaking there was a consensus. To me, the question of the flag is akin to certain matters which are defined in the British North America Act. In other words, I feel that questions such as the flag should be treated as constitutional amendments, and that only when there is general consensus among the major groups within Canada should a change be made. If this question had been approached as it was in 1945 and had the report been acted upon by the government, then the question of the plebiscite would not have arisen. As it is, the manner in which the government opened this flag question has created difficulty and disunity. I intend to quote from certain newspapers across the country to substantiate my contention that the manner in which this question was raised has resulted in disunity. Because of the disunity which has been created it becomes necessary, unfortunately, to proceed with a plebiscite as the only way out of the dilemma in which we find ourselves.
There are one or two alternatives and if the government were to accept them a plebiscite would not be necessary. However, I doubt whether the government will accept these alternatives; I will come to them later. On the basis that the government is determined to pursue its present course I believe a plebiscite is the way out, because this government is creating and compounding disunity.
In support of my contention that the government's approach to the flag question is creating disunity I would quote from the Victoria Daily Colonist of May 29, 1964 which says, referring to the proposed change in the flag:
Such attempts were resisted by Mr. King and Mr. St. Laurent but their successor, Mr. Pearson, is now leading the attack on the pretext of unifying the country.
Why the change? It doesn't require much insight to realize that Mr. Pearson is after additional seats in the House of Commons and thinks this is one way he can get them.
No matter what his scheme there can be no doubt that the Pearson way of handling the flag issue has caused bitterness that goes very deep; that it is bound to weaken the country; and

that it will not satisfy those who have been and still are shouting for a nation made up of a partnership of states.
Certainly, Mr. Pearson has no right to expect that his arrogant action will be applauded or accepted by millions of his fellow Canadians.
Perhaps I can relate my personal impression of this disunifying action. What has disturbed me more than anything else, and I speak with the utmost sincerity, is the reaction which has been created, certainly in British Columbia. I agree that most of this reaction is not justified. But it exists and it makes the necessary reconciliation very difficult. This reaction has been caused by the manner in which the Prime Minister and the government have treated this question of the flag-a very emotional one. Incidentally, I may say that those who are interested may read the speech I made in this house during the previous debate. I come from an area which is probably one of the most pro-red ensign parts of the country, but I have been most conciliatory. As a matter of fact, I have been blamed by many people in my riding for being too much so. I read from an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of June 16, 1964, of which this is the opening paragraph:
Prime Minister Lester Pearson's claim that he has pressed the issue of a national flag at this time to promote national unity is now no more than a bad joke-a sick joke. It is painfully apparent that he has succeeded only in encouraging disunity.
The first point I am trying to make in justification of the holding of a plebiscite is that the present course of the government is continuing to create disunity and that, therefore, a plebiscite would be the least objectionable course open to us. I wish to quote an editorial which appeared in the Vancouver Province of October 31, 1964. These opening paragraphs refer to the flag debate creating disunity:
Undue prolongation of the flag debate. ...would bring about a general election which would be fought on the French-English issue, would set province against province, group against group and would jeopardize confederation.
The foolish tragedy of all this is that the whole flag argument is a phony, politically-manufactured issue of relatively little importance compared with the urgent and important agenda confronting parliament. And yet it has been allowed to stalemate the nation's business and threaten a minor civil war.
Mr. Diefenbaker and those who support retention of the red ensign are told they will destroy Canada if they don't knuckle down to Mr. Pearson's new flag. They are warned that on them rests the onus of responsibility.

This is an enormous distortion that should not be allowed to hide the truth. And the truth is that the ugly, nonsensical dilemma in which Canada finds itself is the direct result of pathetically inept leadership on the part of Prime Minister Pearson and his little coterie of brain trusters.
If the Prime Minister has an ounce of statesmanship he will recognize the danger of his foolish flag policy and withdraw his flag proposals until times are more propitious.
I have shown that the procedure adopted by the government in regard to this flag question has tended to create disunity. May I digress by saying that in my opinion the right in Canada to hold a plebiscite is not reflected only by our statutes, but by the British North America Act. It is reflected also in the minds of people. I think the most unfortunate part of this flag debacle is the fact that in the minds of people, particularly those in western Canada, there has been created a suspicion which will take a long time to overcome. It must be overcome, and I believe that every member from those parts of Canada is duty bound to try to overcome it. But the fact is that this suspicion has been created and it has tended to destroy the mental attitude of the people toward understanding our difficulties in Canada.
I now come, Mr. Speaker, to the way in which the flag question was handled by the flag committee set up during this session. At the time the flag committee was set up- I believe that was on September 10-I think there was a genuine desire in all parts of the house to arrive at some compromise conclusion that would have been satisfactory or at least reasonably acceptable to most groups across Canada. To my mind that feeling was very obvious from speaking to members on both sides of the house. I believe that if the feeling which was prevalent at that time had prevailed when the committee was considering this question-I hope I am not wrong in saying this-they might have come up with a conclusion which would have been reasonably acceptable to all groups within Canada. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Prime Minister perhaps largely because of mis judgment, in his statements immediately after the flag committee was set up tended to prejudice the chance of the committee's arriving at a near-unanimous and acceptable report.

speechtext:
I am giving my reasons for believing that the present and past procedures of the government make it necessary or advisable to have a plebiscite. According to the transcript of the program "Conversation
Canadian Flag
with the Prime Minister", on Sunday, September 13, 1964-that was just three days after the flag committee had been set up-the Prime Minister was asked a question by Mr. DePoe. This is the question:
Just time for one more quick question-perhaps a very quick answer, sir. Are we going to have a new flag by Christmas?
The Prime Minister: We are going to have a new flag by Christmas. It's going to be a distinctive national flag and it will be based on this historic and proud emblem of Canada, the maple leaf.
I was watching television at that time. I believe the committee had been set up on the previous Thursday, and I was most hopeful when it was set up that an acceptable conclusion would arise out of the committee; but when I heard the Prime Minister on that Sunday night I said to my wife, "There isn't a hope". Mr. Speaker, whether or not the Prime Minister meant that, in my opinion those statements of his made it extremely difficult for the members of the flag committee to go into the committee with a completely open mind and a sincere wish to arrive at an acceptable compromise.
I should now like to quote from the Victoria Daily Times of September 17. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that the Victoria Daily Times is a good newspaper but it is not one that has been renowned for its support of our party. In this article, written by Mr. Frank Rutter, it is said:
Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson Wednesday night brushed aside any question of a personal compromise on his new Canadian flag.
A crowd of 750 people who came to shake his hand at a coffee reception held by the Liberal party cheered wildly as Mr. Pearson rededicated himself to his maple leaf design.
He made it clear that he expects the House of Commons special committee to approve and the house itself to adopt the recommendation without further fuss.
I maintain that with a committee operating under those circumstances, whether or not its members did in fact make the sincerest effort to arrive at a compromise, in view of those remarks of the Prime Minister in advance of the committee meetings it certainly made any recommendation of the committee suspect in the minds of a great number of people.
Another reason I say a plebiscite should be held is this. I believe the flag committee could very easily have arrived at a recommendation which might have been accepted by this house with no or with very limited debate. I say this of my personal knowledge, Mr. Speaker. I believe that one of the flags considered by the committee would have been acceptable to members on both sides of this

Canadian Flag
house if there had been no debate or argument as to the design subsequently. I refer now to one of the three final flag designs to which the committee had boiled down all the designs. As the house knows, the committee divided all the designs they had received into three groups. The first group was based on the single maple leaf, the second group was based on the three maple leaves, and the third group were those that contained the union jack and/or the fleur-de-lis. From each of these groups the committee selected one as the best design.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that if a design had been selected such as I am going to describe, the question of a plebiscite would never have arisen. To repeat, I maintain that if the design I shall describe had been selected, the question of a plebiscite would not be before us today. This particular design, for the record, is exactly the same as the one finally selected-that is, the red maple leaf on a centre white background and a red border at each end-except that there are two small additions. In one red column there is a small union jack, and in the other red column a small, equally sized square with three fleur-de-lis in it. As soon as the committee report was filed, I believe on November 29, I became curious as to what this flag looked like. I happened to get a copy of the flag and it immediately seemed to me that this was a perfect solution. This design had many advantages. In the first place, it was not a political flag; it was not a flag proposed by the Conservative party, or any other political party. It was apparently a design of the experts on the flag committee. That design has as its central motif a maple leaf; it is a maple leaf flag.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order. In spite of the suggestion made by the hon. member to the effect that what he is now saying is relevant to the question before the house, the Chair has very serious doubts about it and it seems the hon. member is now discussing the question of the work done by the committee. He says that if the committee had reached a different conclusion or had made a different recommendation, then a plebiscite would not have been necessary. To my mind this is rather far fetched in the line of relevancy. I would ask him to relate the argument he is now proposing to the Chair to the subject matter under discussion.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may eliminate my references to the findings of

the committee, I am trying to state the case that under certain circumstances I for one would not support a plebiscite, but that under the circumstances which prevail I would support it. I am trying to describe these circumstances which do prevail, and one of the factors which make up the circumstances is that I believe there is a design which might be acceptable, which would therefore eliminate the necessity for a plebiscite. This particular design I have described could, I believe, be acceptable to members on both sides of the house, and I hope I am not too optimistic when I appeal to the Prime Minister and to hon. members opposite to take another look at the question of design. A design which met the requirements of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition would surely eliminate the need for a plebiscite.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we are not very far from arriving at such a design. To me, the whole question whether we should have a plebiscite or should not is not necessarily one which the people have the right to determine. I believe that if the members of this house came to a consensus on a selected design and there was no major group in the house which took strong exception to it, then I for one would not for a moment consider the necessity for or advisability of a plebiscite. I think the whole question boils down to the selection of an acceptable design.
There is at the moment an amendment before the house, and on the basis of the present amendment I could not within the rules move another amendment which would bring about what I have in mind, which is reconsideration by the committee of a design which might be acceptable to groups in all parts of the house. Such a design, of course, would eliminate the necessity for debate. I would go as far as to say that if such design were agreed upon by even the two major parties I would, under those circumstances, support the government if it were to invoke closure in order to bring about a design which is acceptable to the majority of the groups within Canada. I do not know whether it is too late to do this. I do not know whether the positions of the various parties have hardened too much. But I would make an appeal to the members on the other side of the house. I have spoken to many members from all parts of the house, and I must say I had hoped that we might reach agreement in spite of the recommendations of this committee. I have spoken to individual members on an individual basis, and they agree with me that possibly there is a design which would be generally accept-

able and which would eliminate all necessity for extensive debate, and certainly obviate any stipulation that there be a plebiscite on the flag question.
With regret, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I must now support the proposal for a plebiscite in spite of the fact, as I have pointed out, that I am strongly averse to the principle involved. As to what should be covered by a plebiscite, that is another point; but if this question were referred to a committee, I would hope that the committee would come up with two designs, and I do not think the red ensign should be one of them.
If this question were to be covered by a plebiscite, I think the designs which the committee should come up with are these. First of all, the committee grouped some flag designs into three kinds. I say that the committee should consider two groups of various designs. Everyone seems to be agreed that a new flag should be based on the maple leaf, which would be its main motif. Then the committee could recommend that two flags be submitted to the people from which they could choose. The first flag should be based on the maple leaf but carry no symbols of our heritage, our traditions or our past-as the present one recommended by the committee. The second one should be a design something of the order of the one I have described. It too should be a maple leaf design but should carry something of our history and of our past. I know from what some of my colleagues who are French speaking have told me that they are not anxious to have the fleur-de-lis on the flag. But let me tell them that the people in the west consider that the contribution made by our French speaking colleagues is a most important one and they would like to see some indication on the flag of the major contribution they made to Canada.
May I call it six o'clock?
