speechtext: Order. I might mention to the hon. member that this is the second time in the course of his remarks he has offended against one of the rules of the house that requires members not to reflect on votes of the house. So I would ask him not to refer in this particular way to the vote which was taken earlier in this debate.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I accept your ruling. Sometimes it is difficult to stick to the rules in the face of provocation.
I want to conclude briefly the remarks I was making before six o'clock. I said that I was opposed in principle to a plebiscite but that the circumstances were such that I thought a plebiscite was the only course open to the house in view of the situation to which the government had brought us. I still think at this late stage that although positions have hardened, particularly the position on the government side, there is room for manoeuvre, room to arrive at a conclusion which might eliminate the necessity of what I consider would be an unfortunate plebiscite. I say that because if we did have a plebiscite, no matter what its terms might be, it would tend to continue and perhaps even deepen the disunity that has been caused by the raising of this question. But at least after a plebiscite I believe the people would accept the decision that might be made, whatever it might be. But if the decision is to be made on the basis of the present course of the government, then, Mr. Speaker, judging by what a great many people in my area have told me, it will take a long time, a generation or more, for those people who feel so strongly about the flag that they considered was our flag, to overcome the feeling that something has been taken away from them, something which they have revered, something they thought was an essential part of Canada as they saw it.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, unless the government is prepared either to postpone the flag issue or unless they wish to consider a further referral to the committee so that the committee can come up with a proposal

Canadian Flag
that will be acceptable generally to the various groups within Canada, I maintain that the only alternative, and a regrettable one, is to refer the question of a flag for the decision of the people of Canada, and in my opinion the decision should be made simpler by having two designs submitted to the people.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to be brief. I did not intend to speak in this debate, but since the last flag debate I have had so many letters and so many comments on the way this matter has been conducted in the house that I am almost forced to say a few words.
On Armistice day, when I watched the parade with the four red ensigns being carried at the front, I felt sad and with heavy heart I said to myself: Is this going to be the last time we will see our grand old flag being used on Armistice day? I was standing in front of the west block and a gentleman and his wife came along. The Canadian red ensign was flying side by side with the stars and stripes. This man spoke to me and he said, "Why do the people of Canada want to throw away the red ensign?" He looked with pride at his American flag. He reached over and stretched it out and stretched out the red ensign and his wife took a picture. He said, "I want this picture for fear the red ensign will not be seen flying again beside our stars and stripes."
I was in St. Catharines over the week end. Having been born near the water, I love boats. On the prairies we do not see many boats and I spent a lot of time at the Welland canal watching the boats of almost every nation in the world go through the locks. On their masts they all flew the Canadian red ensign along with the flag of their own nation. As to the ships that were coal burners or diesel types, the white in the flags they were flying had become dirty, but the Canadian red ensign stood out with its loud colours. It is a very picturesque sight.
While I was standing there talking to some people, one man said to me, "You know, the Canadian red ensign looks great on those ships." I said, "Yes". He said, "Why are the people in Ottawa trying to throw it away?" He did not know I was a member of parliament or that I Was standing up for it. He gave me quite a talk on his feelings about throwing away our heritage, all our
[Mr. Chatterton.l
past experience, for a flag with none of our traditional symbols on it.
These are just a few of the comments I wished to make on some matters that have been brought to my attention since the flag debate took place a few weeks ago. I am still getting quite a few letters. Here is one from the Canadian Corps Association, which reads in part as follows:
The Canadian Corps Association, dominion command, at this time reiterates that no change in Canada's present national flag should be made unless the government is so instructed by the citizens of Canada by means of a plebiscite vote held in conjunction with Canada's next general election.
I do not know why those sitting on your right, Mr. Speaker, are so afraid to let the people decide. I believe this is the fair method. We are down here to make rules and laws, but I do not believe a minority should decide on an issue upon which the people of Canada are so divided. I am one of those who are willing to go along with the opinion of the majority after the people of Canada decide. If it is the majority wish to have a distinctive Canadian flag, I would go along with that. I was born in Canada and spent my whole life here. I was not overseas in the first world war, but as a boy of 16 I offered my services and was led by the Canadian red ensign. I was proud to be one who marched behind it.
I said my remarks would be brief, Mr. Speaker, but I felt that because of the way things have been handled in this parliament this issue should be decided by the people. If they choose the red ensign, that is O.K. If they choose a distinctive Canadian flag, that is fine. I cannot see any of the traditional symbols of Canada on the flag that has been proposed. As I have said, I just wanted to make a few comments on these matters. I am still receiving letters about the flag. I have received 154 letters from my constituency and 152 of them have asked me to stand up for the red ensign. Oh, yes, I received one letter from a man I know very well. He said, "why should we worship England all our lives?" I answered that letter and I suggested that regardless of the flag upon which we decided, he would not be satisfied unless it had the hammer and sickle on it. I also received a letter from a 15 year old school boy. He did not say what kind of a flag he wanted, he just wanted a change. The other 152 letters asked me to stand up for the red ensign and to bring this issue before the people of Canada.

I hear a few railbirds down there, Mr. Speaker, but they do not say much. I am sorry I do not speak French, and your speeches are not worth the bother of putting on earphones.
With these few remarks, I will resume my seat, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, did not intend to take part in this debate. I took 20 minutes of the time of this house during the last debate, and I do not regret it. I tried my best not to say anything that would provoke anyone else. I have sat in as many parliaments as any man in this house except one. In the 25 years I have been here, I have never sat in a worse conducted parliament; I can say that truthfully. I am not referring to the Speaker or the Deputy Speaker. They have had an impossible job, and for the life of me I do not know how they control themselves. It is ridiculous, the things they have had to put up with, and mostly from members on the government side. We on this side know enough to keep our mouths shut and remain quiet when there is someone speaking from the other side. Apparently all hon. members opposite want to do is make interjections to try to confuse the person who has the floor.
I have a few things I want to say and because I have only a few things I wrote them out during the supper hour. I am one of those who has to either speak without notes or follow my notes closely. I do not want anybody razzing me about reading my speech. I am not going to read it all, but if I have to throw it away it will be all the worse for you. As I see it, there is only one excuse for bringing the flag resolution before the house and that is the lack of preparedness on the part of the government to introduce other important legislation. I could add that the legislation which has been introduced was withdrawn and redrafted before it even had a change of being passed by parliament. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) used the flag issue to stifle parliament for his own selfish, personal advantage. He used the flag issue also to kill time in order to get more important legislation ready to bring before the house. What an excuse that is. It has cost the Canadian taxpayers millions of dollars. If I were the Prime Minister of Canada and responsible for introducing a controversial subject such as the flag, I would at least be in my place in the house to hear what members had to say about it.
Canadian Flag
I have a clipping here from a newspaper that is very favourable to the government. I would not quote from any other newspaper because I want to be very fair to them. This comes from the Winnipeg Tribune.
There was nothing wrong with Prime Minister Pearson's speech to the Royal Canadian Legion except its object.
He chose this occasion to haul down the red ensign.
The speech was in reality a declaration of Liberal government intent. At the same time it was an attempt to justify a new emblem on the grounds of national unity. The case was unconvincing.
Prior to his visit to Winnipeg, Mr. Pearson had let it be known that his government would stand or fall on the flag issue. It is the government which has selected this particular time to force a showdown.
It is this newspaper's opinion that the timing of this flag proposal is bad. If the main purpose is to consolidate unity it is a peculiar approach for, as witnessed at the Legion meeting, the dominant reaction is disunity. Unfortunately, too, the Prime Minister's approach leaves little ground for thoughtful consideration. He asks, in effect, for a surrender of what is known for something unknown. He entertains a mystique about the price of unity which he is unable to articulate.
In addition to poor timing, the method of introducing the design was odd. In Ottawa last week a high level press conference made it clear that the Pearson government would stand or fall on the new flag. The following day in the Commons Mr. Pearson said that a new design had not been decided upon. At the Legion meeting on Sunday, he left the impression that only the maple leaf motif was firm. Yet the next day Mr. Pearson unveiled his choice at a press conference.
Just how much the cabinet was apprised in advance of all this is unknown. But certainly parliament has been kept completely in the dark.
I might mention at this point that the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) made a statement in the house to the effect that this subject was never brought up in the Liberal caucus, and nobody knew anything about it except a few at the top levels of government.
In attempting to force an absolute decision in this ill-defined region, the Prime Minister has created a maelstrom. It is true that he has attempted to reduce the problem to straight political terms but unfortunately this does not provide the flexible basis required.
He has placed himself and his government on the record to introduce a new flag. He has rejected the proposal for a national plebiscite and insists that the issue must be decided on a free vote in the Commons. But then he has also added that the result would be interpreted by his government as a vote of confidence.
In other words he is prepared to fight an election on the issue. He is willing to jeopardize national unity in the hope of political advantage but he is unwilling to seek an expression of opinion in a plebiscite in which the issue would be the flag, not seats in parliament.
This places the M.P.'s in a position where they no longer will be truly free to exercise their

Canadian Flag
judgment on the merits of a flag. Instead they will have to weigh the significance of the consequences, a government defeat and, even worse, an election to be fought on the design of a flag.
Such an unpleasant encounter could scarcely be an ingredient of unity. It would also be mischievous and perhaps seriously harmful, for surely the problems of this country cannot be resolved in the flag alone.

Mr. Speaker, on two other occasions I have spoken on a resolution on the flag, or on one of the amendments. On June 20 I did my level best to try to plead with the house that we in Canada must always remember we are a country of minorities. I tried to remind the members that we should be an example to all the new countries of the world where several languages and several races have to get along within the same geographical boundaries.
On that occasion I reminded the house that most of us in Canada do not favour the technique of the plebiscite. It is foreign to the system of parliamentary responsibility we have learned to trust, but I pointed out that there are certain occasions which touch the heart and affect the rights of minorities when we have to consider whether we should use the plebiscite technique or not.
In that speech of June 20 I reluctantly supported a plebiscite, on the grounds that looking back at the last plebiscite we had during the war, on the conscription issue, the speeches made in the house on that occasion contained all the arguments that could be used against holding a plebiscite; yet a plebiscite was held, and when it was finished Canadians found it easier to accept the will of the majority than they did in 1917 in the first world war when conscription was imposed by parliament. When the rights of the individual are affected, when matters close to the conscience are affected, there is sometimes a place for the plebiscite. That was the burden of my remarks on June 20, though I did not succeed in making many converts.
I want to remind the house of what I said on that occasion. All the veterans of our country have asked for, through majority votes in their Legions, is that a plebiscite be held. They have promised if a plebiscite is held to honour any flag which the majority may choose. What more can you ask of them?

The same is true of the other organizations. I would point out that if the government turns down the formal request of the official organization of most of our veterans it has done something which everyone of us in Canada will live to regret. Surely after what they have done they deserve our best consideration.
In the second place I want to remind the house that according to Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, speaking in this house as prime minister, by a single resolution here in parliament the guarantees to the French language could be taken away. I suggest that if we set a precedent in this debate by taking away an emblem of a minority culture, we are setting a precedent for things to happen in the future when passions are aroused which will tend to break this country apart. I say this slowly and deliberately with no sense of malice whatsoever. If someone moved a resolution in this house to take away the rights accorded to one of the founding races of this country I would expect every person on the Conservative side to fight as long as they could within the rules to protect the rights of that group. This is what is happening today.
I do not know what percentage of the people of this country wish to retain on the flag an emblem of their tradition and their past. I do not really know, but I am aware that.it is sizeable. Certainly if one third of the people of this country want to have something of the union jack as a reminder of their great history, their rights must be considered if we wish to maintain this country as a democratic country of minorities. Rightly or wrongly the flag is one of the symbols of one of the founding races of this country. As I said earlier, this speech of mine on June 20 did not make much of an impression across the way. But on August 20 I tried again and this time, in the middle of that long debate, I asked that this question be considered by a committee. I laid down four basic principles which could, I thought, have united this house and the whole country behind the work of that committee. These principles were apparently not considered by the government. It was not until after the long Labour week end, after a motion on the Thursday by the New Democratic party that the debate be adjourned so that the house could go on to more important business; it was not until the Tuesday after the week end, when the Creditiste members had come back from the rural seats and said they wanted to adjourn
Canadian Flag
the debate because the people demanded it, that the government, saved by a narrow squeak, realized that every opposition party was united behind the idea of sending this matter to a committee. It was only after 22 days of debate that they let the question go before the committee. Did they consider the four basic principles which were laid down by the opposition-and I was speaking on behalf of the opposition that night?
What were those four principles? First, that in a matter such as the flag we should all strive, regardless of whether we are Conservative or Liberal, to start off with the largest possible percentage of the people behind it. That was the first principle. It was wrong to take a personal flag, a party flag, and force it on parliament saying: If you do not accept it there will be an election. We fought against that blackmail, and with the help of all the opposition parties we forced the government to place this question before a committee, after 22 days of the time of this house had been wasted in discussion. I say this loudly and clearly, Mr. Speaker, because I believe you know we are speaking from the heart on this subject on this side of the house. It would make no difference to us if all the people of Canada were to turn against us as long as we remain faithful to what we consider to be the right. It is not a question of counting noses in this house or even across the country. Above all our party divisions the people sometimes expect that we should, on certain occasions, stand up in this house and say what we think as individuals. This is what I am trying to do.
What was the second principle I enunciated at that time? It was that on any flag the symbols and the background of the two founding groups should be there in equal parts, neither superior and neither inferior. I said this not because I was unaware that our country today is a multiracial country but because I thought it is recognized that certain understandings were reached in the early days which we must honour today. The flag now put forward ignores this fundamental principle.
Third, I said there should be something on the flag to represent the humility which any country should have if it hopes to have a future. And the only way I knew for us to do that was to put something of religious significance on the flag. Because of the faith which is accepted by the vast majority of people in the western world, the only thing we know as a generally accepted emblem of religious significance is the cross-and I say this without

wishing to assert the superiority of the Christian faith over other faiths. But in the flag of Canada should be expressed that humility, that acceptance of the fact that there is a greater power than ourselves.

I do not know whether you will rule me out of order, Mr. Speaker, but before you take any action in this regard, what I want to discuss now is the type of things which the committee should recommend as matters to be dealt with on a plebiscite which will make sense. We have already suggested to the house that the plebiscite should contain four choices. Obviously with the three maple leaf flag shot down in flames the proposed committee flag will have to be left as one of the choices on a plebiscite. Because of the strong emotional feelings for the red ensign, that will have to be left off. Therefore I am going to propose

Canadian Flag
at this time, as a suggestion from an individual member of the opposition and not from a party, that there is still one chance for us to come out of this matter united. I suggest we realize the strength of feeling behind the traditional, distinctive national flag we now have, but at the same time realize the strength of feeling which would be created by a brand new flag. My suggestion is that we get down to basics and realize that most people in this country are not ashamed of their past, be they English or French. We would all like to have on our flag our own symbols. If the union jack is not acceptable because it is an indication of subservience to a colonial structure, let us take off the union jack the two crosses, one white the other red; one standing for the cross of St. Louis which was flown on the ships in which Jacques Cartier landed here in 1534, and the other the cross of St. George which was the standard of John Cabot when he landed here. I know that many French Canadians do not regard John Cabot as the equal of Jacques Cartier, but that is a small consideration in the achievement of unity. I know that the Scots, the Irish, yes and the Welsh, will feel a little unhappy that their symbols have been removed. But for the sake of unity I suggest that if we had the two flags of the two founding races, the two crosses, we would have both insignia that I and my party want to see.
I think that if there was a willingness in this house to reach some sort of compromise instead of complete division, and we could get 80 to 90 per cent of the members together-and they could come together on this -if the government still wanted to fight for a maple leaf flag I am sure that not one of us would oppose the emblem of the maple leaf centred on the two crosses. I ask every member if he is willing to sell the democratic rights of his constituents down the river of political expediency over the flag issue by denying them the privilege of expressing their individual opinions. How often we have heard that we, the elected representatives, even though nearly all of us were elected by a minority vote, should not hesitate to take the responsibility of selecting a flag for all future generations, and at the same time discarding without the expressed wish of the people that which has been our national flag for most of the time since the birth of our nation. With this attitude I most heartily disagree.
What is the compelling urgency about settling such an emotional issue? Most people never heard of the flag issue during the last election and they certainly did not mark their ballots to decide the issue. They voted to send representatives to the House of Commons to carry out legislative duties on behalf of their constituents. I feel that a national flag certainly does not fall into that category. It is an emotional issue, Mr. Speaker, that should be held over until the next election when a plebiscite could be conducted by means of a transferable ballot.
Why the urgency? During the last world war we were faced with the possibility of conscription. The prime minister of that day, in his wisdom, would not undertake conscription without a plebiscite. If ever there was urgency for a decision, Mr. Speaker, it certainly was during that time of war. We all hear expressions of opinion from across the country, and particularly from our constituents. We see the results of polls being conducted, but they are not always reliable. I know the majority of Canadians want a plebiscite held. Recently I listened to a radio broadcast in which the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) participated. I note he is back in the house and he may be able

to correct me if I misinterpret his remarks. He was being interviewed with regard to the flag, and what did he say? The words he used were to this effect: I do not know if the majority of the people in my constituency would be in favour of the suggested design, but I do know they want to see the matter settled.
Of course, the people of Canada are sick and tired of the way the flag issue is being handled. I am, too. However, I was interested in hearing the member for Medicine Hat admit he did not know how the majority of his constituents felt about this design. If this be true, perhaps under those circumstances he would agree that the only way he could find out would be to support the amendment to hold a plebiscite. I believe this applies to every constituency in Canada. After the people decided, they could forever hold their peace. Why all the urgency, Mr. Speaker? Why all the unnecessary delay of important business when the amendment could be passed so that we could get ahead with those matters which were promised in the speech from the throne, such as the labour code and other unfinished business? Incidentally the flag was never mentioned in the speech from the throne. Suddenly we were faced with a demand for a flag by July 1; then again for the Queen's visit, and now we are supposed to have a flag by Christmas. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the decision on a new flag must be left to a plebiscite. It is too important to do anything else.
It is not too late for the government to listen to reason. I hope they will listen to reason. The present adamant program is so destructive of our national unity that it is doing damage beyond repair. The obliteration of our national symbols, which most Canadians cherish, is destructive in the extreme and cannot be creative of national unity. The only feature of this government's obsession to force a flag on Canadians that could be helpful eventually would be to make future generations flag conscious. This discussion has awakened the people to the real significance of something we have accepted as a matter of course. We have neglected to impress upon our rising generation, as well as upon our adult generations, the true significance of these symbols.
What does history really mean to our country? It has been said, unthinkingly I hope, that people could not care less about a flag. They say that any old rag will do. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this signifies nothing
Canadian Flag
more nor less than complete ignorance of the real significance of our most important emblem. We should learn from this experience the importance of educating our young people with regard to such matters. We could well follow the example of our United States friends along this line. As the Prime Minister said in the house, this is a serious, a solemn and an historic occasion. Yes, Mr. Speaker, it is indeed just that. It is an historic occasion, and I hope the record will show that we acted with forethought and wisdom; that we did not allow ourselves to become an arrogant dictatorship, but we chose the method of true democracy. We referred the matter, not hurriedly, not impetuously with political bias, but with careful instruction to the people so that they could properly exercise their thoughtful judgment in choosing what our national flag must be for all generations to come.
It is said that the majority of the committee made a recommendation which should be acceptable. It is my impression that the majority of Canadians are concerned and do not find this design acceptable. I could be wrong, but 1 am agreeable to leaving the decision to a plebiscite and I will abide by the decision of the majority. The report of the committee set up in 1945 was approved by a majority of 95 per cent. The report of this recent committee was approved by only 70 per cent. Prime minister Mackenzie King, in his political wisdom could see that a decision supported by even 95 per cent could cause serious national disunity, so he never presented the report to the Commons. During the following 11 years no other Liberal government would dare subject the country to such a division. The 1945 report never reached the Commons.
I most urgently suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it would be the part of great wisdom if this report could be withdrawn and either forgotten or have the matter left to a plebiscite as suggested by the amendment. If this were done, it would have a double barreled effect. First, it would remove a most dangerous, divisive subject from the political arena. Second, it would also allow us to get ahead with more important legislation, which would be in the best interests of the country. What is of secondary importance is that it would allow parliament to have a long overdue recess, so that we could return to our constituencies and clear our brains of the cobwebs everybody has been collecting in the house. We could then return to our duties here, better informed and more refreshed to

Canadian Flag
continue with our responsibilities. If this session represents the "continuing diversity" which was mentioned in the speech from the throne in 1963, we have sure had it. Ambiguities of this kind have certainly not been constructive or in the best interests of our country.
If the decision in 1946 was to drop the flag issue-a wise decision I know-probably by reversing the figures 46 to 64, the same decision today could be one of the greatest wisdom. Failing this, a plebiscite is the only sensible answer. However, it would seem that the government has developed a complete mental block regarding the issue. Its obsession to have a new flag regardless of the consequences has created a psychiatric problem in the House of Commons.
It would seem from the way the flag issue has been brought in and out of the house-consuming about one tenth of our time that could be given to important legislation-that it is brought in and not purely to gum up the works, and also to make those of us who have the courage to stand up and speak for what we sincerely believe to be the wishes of our constituents, to appear to be obstructing. If defending the rights of the people against arbitrary rule, if defending the people against not being allowed to vote in a plebiscite is to be classed as obstruction, then I am proud to be one of those on the list.
If there was anything to be gained in the interests of our country by refusing a plebiscite, I might be agreeable to some reconsideration. I have not heard any expression of objection to having a plebiscite, except the same old argument that the committee has brought in a report and we must accept it. Without a plebiscite we can only create disunity. It has already been admitted by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) that reaching agreement in parliament on the choice of a flag will not achieve national unity. I understand a quotation was made to that effect the other day and I did not hear any contradiction from the hon. member.
What we want is national unity. Let us leave the flag question to the people of Canada so that we will not create disunity. Supporting the amendment is the only true and loyal way we, as Canadians, can work in the best interests of our country. I ask all hon. members, regardless of party, not to deny the people of Canada their God given democratic rights. Let us all support the only method democracy knows as being truly democratic. Let us support the amend-

ment so that the voice of the people may be heard and that Canada can continue as a united country. I plead with the government, I plead with the members of the house to please reconsider. Otherwise I am afraid it may be too late.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should apologize for barging in on this one-party debate, but I am going to take the chance and make a few observations tonight with respect to the issue that is before the house. First of all I would like to remind the house that the position of our group has already been set forth as being a free vote-each and every one-
He said that with a straight face.
If he said it, it is true.

I am not ashamed of speaking up.

I wonder where you are going? Each member of the Social Credit party will be expressing his own point of view as he votes on this issue. So far as my observations tonight are concerned, I am expressing my own views and my own opinions relative to the matter before the house. Furthermore, lest the hon. member for Northwest Territories insists on interrupting, I am going to say what 1 have to say in far less than 40 minutes.
You never made a 40 minute speech in your life.
I could not say that for you, my friend.

Mr. Speaker, my purpose tonight is to voice my personal support for the amendment that is now before the house. Might I point out that the idea of a national plebiscite was set out by my colleague, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) on

February 27, 1964 as recorded at page 315 of Hansard, and I refer to part of the statement he made at that time:
I think the solution lies in having a committee set up that will choose perhaps four or five designs out of the some 2,500 or 2,900 designs that have been submitted, snd put thsss on 2 bsllct. They should include the red ensign, and should be put to a referendum of the people, with a transferable vote, so that each individual would choose the first, second, third, fourth and fifth in the order he preferred-
He also outlined other steps he felt were necessary or advisable in order to conduct this in a satisfactory manner. Evidently this suggestion caught the imagination of the Canadian people, and also the Conservative party, and as a result there has been a growing conviction that this would be the most democratic way of settling an issue so controversial in nature. The hon. member mentioned various steps that should be followed in conducting a plebiscite, but I shall not go into them in detail tonight because I realize I would be quite out of order in doing so.
Though, of course, the vast preponderance of correspondence from my constituency favours the red ensign, there is some which indicates the contrary, and I believe this is true of every constituency from coast to coast. Therefore I believe that in order that this question may be resolved satisfactorily or at least as satisfactorily as possible the idea of a referendum should be taken under consideration, and arrangements made for it to be held some time in the future. I think there are several reasons why such a course is advisable. We have already had an extended debate on the question of a flag for Canada and I believe we have dealt with the subject in every conceivable manner. Every angle has been considered. Controversy has raged and I believe the very fact that this debate has consumed so much time is an indication that we should submit this issue to the people and find out what their wishes are.
This matter was submitted to a committee and I am sure all of us hoped that the committee would be able to arrive at some satisfactory solution. Perhaps we were naive in thinking it could, in the light of the positions taken by the various parties before the committee was set up. But we did hope they would be able to find some compromise design acceptable to the committee and to the members of this house. The result was disappointing, in spite of the commendable work the committee did. I do not think we should detract from the excellent work of that committee. But despite its efforts it was unable to 20220-690

arrive at a design which commanded the support of the great majority of its members.
The committee has made its recommendations. It has submitted a design which has been placed before the house; but I fail to find much enthusiasm for the flag which is proposed, even on the part of those who are convinced we should have a new flag. I fail to find many who are in sympathy with the new design which has been submitted to us.
Hear, hear.

I had the opportunity of attending the commonwealth parliamentary association conference and as I walked up the lawn of the University of the West Indies I saw the array of flags and studied the red ensign in a prominent position; I tried to visualize how our flag would look had the design submitted to us been flying on that occasion. I must confess I could not get enthusiastic about the proposition. I thought it would be very anaemic and washed out in the line-up of the flags which had been designed by the other nations. Because of these various considerations I do believe this matter should be submitted to a plebiscite so that the people of Canada can voice their individual convictions-not just their views, or their opinions, but their convictions-with respect to a question as controversial as this one.
In saying this, I am not taking a new position. Some time ago, speaking on the idea of a new flag I suggested that this proposal should be allowed to lie on the table for a while to permit some cooling off time. Well, perhaps we have had that. But I also suggested that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) should give consideration to the holding of a referendum on this important issue. I am still of the same opinion and when the vote is taken on this amendment I intend to vote in support of the amendment.

I desire to speak on this amendment for two reasons. I realize that the people across this country are completely fed up with the way in which this parliament has handled the flag question. People in all walks of life and of all ages are in a complete turmoil over what is happening here in Ottawa. They are asking why this dissension has arisen over the flag. They are asking why it is necessary to have a new flag now. They are asking why the Pearson flag was changed and whether the flag proposed by the committee represents a compromise. These are the questions which people are asking their members of parliament.

Canadian Flag
Why not wait until the next election and hold a referendum or a plebiscite at the same time as the nation chooses its candidates for the federal parliament? Why is there this urgency about having a new flag now? This is the question which is uppermost in the minds of most of our people. They are tired of this flag matter; they are completely fed up with it.
We are told-or at any rate we were told a couple of weeks ago-that a general election might come at any time, even this winter. Newspapermen are saying that nowadays the west can take an election even in the middle of winter because of the improvement which has been made in the roads in the western provinces. There were confident predictions of an election at least in the spring of 1965. So why not refer this question to the people at the same time?
It has been said that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has promised he will bring in a new flag inside two years. But two years will not be up until next April and if some of the pundits are correct we may have an election by April or shortly thereafter. Why not give the people a chance to express their choice? What is wrong with a referendum? If those who advocate a new and different flag feel the country really wants it, they have nothing to lose by placing their confidence in the national choice. In this way the people would be satisfied and the government would be satisfied because they know, they tell us, that their design will win. So who would lose? What is the government afraid of? Do its supporters feel that their confidence in the new design is not well placed? This is the only conclusion I can reach-that they must have very little faith in their design. I am sure that if a referendum were held on the flag question and the Canadian red ensign did not receive a sufficient number of the votes, even the strongest supporters of the red ensign would realize that it had died a noble death, and accept the result.
There is something strange about this whole question of a flag having to be settled now. We were told we had to have a flag by July, then by November 11, and now by December 25. Why the urgency? There is something strange about this whole question. We were told first of all by the Prime Minister that he would give his party a free vote on the question. Two weeks later he took that away and said no, the government would stand or fall on the question of a new flag. The whole of the Liberal party said it was Pearson's pennant and there would be no committee. That was said at one time. However, they

went back on that; they had a committee. Then, lo and behold, every one of the Liberal members on that committee voted against the three maple leaf design that was before the house prior to the setting up of the committee. It is a shame that in this debate two or three members of the Liberal party have not stood up and explained the reason for the change in the attitude of that group. Not one Liberal member has explained this.
They are not allowed to speak.

Could they not just inform us of their reasoning? This is a place for debate, and surely we are entitled to such an explanation if they want us to accept this flag. If they have faith in their persuasive powers as speakers, surely they believe in themselves enough to be able to stand up and explain the reasoning behind the fact that one day it had to be a design of three maple leaves, with three colours, and now we are back to one maple leaf and two colours. Does it not matter to them what they have on Canada's flag? It is a symbol that is supposed to represent Canada for years and years and years to come. Does it not matter to them what it is composed of?
I would be quite prepared to accept the new flag if the majority of Canadians wanted a new flag; but one thing that bothers me, Mr. Speaker, about this whole flag question is that we have seen the government vacillate from one flag design to another with no reason or explanation as to why this has been done. We are only clear on one thing- at least I am-and that is that the government will not accept any flag that bears any relationship whatsoever to Great Britain. This is the one conclusion I can come to.

speechtext: What about the union jack?

I have always been in favour of feeling out the public on this question; I have always been in favour of trying to determine whether Canadians want a new flag. During my last speech on the flag question I was interrupted two or three times by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) who quoted from previous speeches I had made as reported in Hansard. Anyone who reads those speeches can clearly see that at page 1318 of Hansard of 1960-61 I said this:
I agree with the hon. member who proposed an amendment to the resolution.
The resolution at that time was that a national referendum be taken on a flag. I

said that I agreed with the amendment, which referred the whole question to a census. Then I went on to state what I thought should be in the census form with regard to a national flag. The other speech which I made on the flag prior to taking part in this debate was during the same year, on February 17, as reported at page 2183 of Hansard. At that time the census had already been taken, or was being taken, and I said:

speechtext:
I have just a few more words to say on this flag question and the position in which parliament finds

itself now concerning it. I pointed out last evening that I have long been of the opinion that this whole question should have been submitted to the people at the very beginning by way of a referendum or plebiscite.
Speaking to the amendment now before the house, I can only repeat my earlier contention in this regard. It was brought in initially with very little forethought. It was not even mentioned in the speech from the throne. The whole house has been continually confused as to why we are faced with the flag issue now. Away back in late June we argued that the question, if it was to come before the house, should first go to a committee. We tried then to get the question referred back to the people in the form of a referendum. We are trying once again to have this done.
I realize there is a percentage of the population of Canada which does want a new flag. I have no objection to a new flag if the majority of Canadians desire one, but it has long been my opinion that a flag is the symbol of a country that should be respected by everyone. It should not be a flag born in haste, one that perhaps represents one of the founding nations of our country and not the other, or is more favoured by one of our founding nations than the other; one that has political tinges, or anything of that order. I have long been of the opinion that a flag should be favoured by the majority of the people, who will respect it, hold it dear, revere it and serve under it proudly. I think a flag should bear some relation to the history of our country; and a flag, above all, should aid in bringing greater unity to a country. This flag and the manner in which this whole question has been handled have convinced everyone, I am sure, that it has done nothing to unite Canada but has in fact done more to disunite this country than any single piece of legislation that has been before this house for a good many years.
I have wondered why there is urgency now, why this question cannot be referred back to the people in a plebiscite. There has been much talk of an election next spring and I ask, would it not be better to settle the whole question to everyone's satisfaction at that time? If the government are so confident that the majority of Canadians want a new flag and are prepared to accept the committee's recommendation for a new flag, why is there the urgency of pushing it through now? Why not wait until an election is called and settle this question by way of a referendum? The only conclusion I can come

to is that perhaps it is a stopgap; perhaps other legislation is not ready; perhaps they want to tease and torment the country and tear the country apart.
This is what this whole debate has been doing. The country is completely fed up with parliament's action on this flag question. I am sure the opposition did its duty in representing the large number of Canadians who showed in one way or another that they were opposed to the flag originally submitted by the Prime Minister; and surprisingly enough a large number of Canadians-this has been shown by all kinds of polls that have been taken week after week-are still opposed to the flag submitted by the committee.
It was my understanding that the committee would do its utmost to bring about a compromise. In a way one might term the committee's recommendation a compromise flag, but a compromise in only one direction. They retained the maple leaf idea and did away with one of the colours. Many people have long thought that the colours red, white and blue meant something; they respected those colours. Now we have one less colour on the flag and two less maple leaves. There is nothing on it to really signify our history, to dignify our country. In my opinion there is really nothing on it that Canadians across the country can worship, respect, and to which they can pay homage.
It has been pointed out that the government, while they promised a flag in two years, did so in such a manner that only a certain part of the country heard of the promise. The two years have not yet expired, and to a great many people it is questionable whether the government has a mandate to bring in a new flag. As I have said, during the last election it might have been mentioned in some parts of the country that a new flag would be designed within two years, but there was no mention of the disappearance of our historic emblems from the flag or that it would be a completely new flag which would erase our past.
The country is completely fed up with parliament's action on this flag question. It is the government's duty to bring in the business for the house to debate. I feel it is high time we passed on to more urgent legislation, legislation which is required across the country. For example, the labour code, railway financing and rail line abandonment are matters which should be discussed, using our time in a worth-while manner instead of holding a lengthy debate on this flag question at a time when there is considerable 20220-691

opposition across the country to this flag as well as considerable doubt whether the government has a mandate to bring in a new flag.
As I said last evening, I am surprised to see government members on the flag committee willing to accept a flag design which completely erases our past. Are they sure that all Canadians are of the same opinion? Are they sure that all Canadians desire and will support the flag which has been suggested by the committee?
An interesting comment was made by Conn Smythe which I think bears some relation to the question whether or not the government has a mandate to bring in a new flag. He said:
Now, all the experts In radio and television and the press are saying people are tired of the flag issue.
I certainly agree with that.
These experts are very often wrong. Last week the Vancouver Lions proved this point.
They certainly did that.
The millions to whom the Canadian ensign means so much are not tired of the ensign, and want the flag issue settled in a democratic manner. What right has a minority government, the great number of their members never having received a mandate from their constituents, to keep on forcing the flag issue? And now that this government is under the shadow of suspicion with respect to bribery and corruption, how can they expect the people to respect a flag of its choice? Why doesn't Mr. Pearson shelve the flag issue now, get on with our national business and, at the next election, give the people of Canada a chance to vote on this issue-
It is as simple as that. This whole issue should be shelved, and at the next election it could be solved to everyone's satisfaction. I think this would satisfy practically everybody in the country.
It is with that thought in mind that I move this debate be temporarily set aside so that the many questions on the government's activities in domestic and foreign matters may be answered by the ministers, and in order that government business dealing with the labour code, C.N.R. financing and provincial-federal matters may be dealt with immediately.

I beg to differ with the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I have spoken fewer times in this debate than he has. This is my second opportunity since the resolution was introduced. I also hope to make this my last contribution.
Coming from where I do, and with my own personal ancestry, I think this matter calls for the expression of the individual's point of view. To me the flag of my country is

something more than an amendment to the customs tariff or the discussion of a redistribution bill. Perhaps I am completely different in this regard from other hon. members, but that is the way I feel. I have always indicated that I felt this question from its inception should have been approached by asking the people of Canada for a personal expression. After all, a flag which is imposed on the people will not be one which is readily acceptable. This flag is not born out of revolution. It is not a symbol of revolution. This flag is a symbol of agreement, and I think there is a clear distinction.
Many people ask why Canada could not emulate some of the new countries, or our great neighbour to the south. Their flag was adopted out of revolution. The majority of the new flags we see today have been adopted out of the granting of independence which is akin to revolution. In respect to some of them one might also question whether, if the people had been given the opportunity, they would have challenged the design of their flag.
I would have thought this matter could easily have been resolved by a plebiscite, as was suggested in another debate, so that people are not identified and we do not point the finger at this or that region. In this matter I consider that no region is preeminent; I consider western Canada just as important as central Canada, the maritimes or any portion of the country. No one has pre-eminence in this regard. Therefore the views of the people from one end of Canada to the other stand on equality. I find it passing strange that in arriving at a design for a national flag a large part of the Canadian people must divest themselves of symbols which they cherish and hold dear.
I am not making a case for any particular flag or any particular design. It is my feeling that the flag of Canada can only be that which is accepted by the people and not that which is accepted by a majority here, because respect for a flag cannot be generated by the iron heel of a dictum. Acceptability on the part of the people of Canada can only result from desire and respect.
I do not think there is any difference in the application of my argument to the Canadian flag and the Canadian national anthem. It could only be ill conceived that the people of Canada would faithfully and conscientiously sing a national anthem which they did not respect in their hearts. Only as an aside, Mr. Speaker, I find it extremely regrettable that we did not deal with the resolution

relating to the national anthem, about which I think there is general agreement, before dealing with the Canadian national flag, so the national anthem would now be settled and not be the subject of a prospective debate in an atmosphere which has now been created by a divisive expression of opinion.
The plebiscite as suggested by the amendment, to be held at the time of the next general election, whenever that may be, to facilitate administrative details, after a cooling-off period, would not generate the divisive atmosphere which some people fear. I believe that if Canadians were given a chance to express their opinions they would accept the flag chosen by the people, even though they did not agree with the choice. A choice made by a generous majority of the people of Canada I am sure would be accepted by the minority favouring a different design.
I do not intend to deal with the nature of the design now before us, though it certainly can be related to the plebiscite advocated by the amendment and is the result of a majority choice by a committee which has considered this question conscientiously. However, what may be one man's meat may be another man's poison, and I am not qualified to say to my neighbour that I am choosing a flag for him. In respect of that sort of thing I feel the people should have the right to express an opinion.
It was announced last week that we in this chamber may have to make a decision on the matter of capital punishment at some time in the future. Surely that is a matter which must be decided as a result of the dictates of one's conscience. It may be a matter that some hon. members feel their constituents should decide. Be that as it may, I think the flag question is one which goes even deeper into considerations of conscience. I think it must be concluded logically that the motives of individuals who enlisted voluntarily for service during the last war, and on other occasions, are the same motives behind the feelings of citizens for their own flag. This feeling is sometimes very inchoate and difficult to define.
I do not wish to attempt to repeat the arguments which have been made by many hon. members in this house on this and on previous occasions, but a plebiscite would provide a tremendous advantage to the members of this house in the choice of a distinctive Canadian flag. I should like to make a few remarks about this business of a national flag. We really get into deep water when we start talking about a national flag. I realize that. I think the solution lies in having a committee set up that will choose perhaps four or five designs out of the some 2,500 or 2,900 designs that have been submitted, and put these on a ballot. That will take all of us off the hook and put the responsibility where it belongs, on the shoulders of the people.
I should like to enlarge on this suggestion by saying that in addition to holding a plebiscite the votes recorded in it should be sent to a central point, preferably the city of Ottawa, for counting. In this way there would be no way of knowing in which region any particular vote was cast. There would be no way of telling who voted for a particular flag and there would be no evidence of regionalization. If this method were adopted I believe we would get a flag supported by the votes of possibly 85 per cent of the population.
The transferable ballot in a plebiscite is not something new. As a matter of fact for a

If we proceed to hold a plebiscite in that way we will get the true feeling of the people, and I am of the opinion that the result of a plebiscite would have much more permanence than the procedure we are following now because a new government could easily change the design again, and that is a point which should not be forgotten. It has been said that the youth of the country want a new flag. If so, 18 year olds and over should be allowed to vote in the plebiscite.
Some people say a new government would not follow the procedure we are following today, but I would remind the house it is the tame bull that kills the farmer. It is not hard to imagine that a new government under new leadership might wish to give the people of Canada the democratic right which is being denied to them under the procedure which is being followed today.
I am of the opinion that the whole approach to the flag question to this date has been negative. This is another reason why a plebiscite should be held. It is my sincere belief that the purpose of bringing about this debate is to eliminate the union jack from the present flag. In my view this is a completely negative approach and I am certainly not in favour of such an approach.
Those who are supporting the stand against a plebiscite may be saying: If we get rid of the union jack we get rid of crosses which stand for Christian principles; we shall eliminate them from our symbols entirely; we shall find ourselves in the position where there are no crosses in our flag, no symbols to represent the Christian principles for which we stand. Those individuals who wish to see the union jack disappear from our flag may well be saying: There will be no symbols to remind us of British justice; we are now building up for ourselves in this house and in the country a new type of justice so we do not need to rely on traditional British justice. There is our democratic origin to be considered. We know that the birthplace of democracy is the place over which the

union jack is flying. This is an emotional and a personal issue. What are we doing when we eliminate the union jack from our flag under the procedure being followed today? We are denying the people of Canada a democratic right in accordance with the traditions they inherited from Britain. Are we setting aside the democracy of old for a new type which denies people the right to say what they want in certain circumstances which involve a personal matter? This, in my view, is exactly what we are doing. We are eliminating the crosses. We are eliminating the memory of British justice; we are eliminating the memory of true democracy.
One of my hon. friends said to me the other day he did not like the idea of a plebiscite because the red ensign would win. Maybe he is right. I do not think any of us know what design would win; we cannot be sure until or unless a vote is taken on this question. I believe everybody has the right to stand up in the House of Commons and give their personal opinions. One would suspect, from reading the newspapers, that there would be many more opinions expressed from speakers on the other side of the house. In refusing to yield to the request for a plebiscite the government, according to polls, is frustrating the will of 68 per cent of the people of Canada.
I could not help recalling a television program the other night in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) used some high-sounding phrases about a code of ethics for cleansing the inner sanctum. But I want to say to him as plainly as I can that the procedure which has been followed and the action which has been taken on this flag question will make the spectre in the Department of Justice look like an angel. I am convinced that the procedure being followed today is a deplorable procedure and that the people, if denied a plebiscite, will recognize it as such when the time comes for them to cast their ballots. Of this there is no question in my mind: You cannot deprive the people of this country of the right to express themselves, because there comes a time under the constitution when the people have this right whether we like it or not. Their voices will be heard. But I do not think it is altogether wise to hold a plebiscite on this matter at the time of the election. Why should we not do this at a more appropriate time instead of on an occasion when the issue is confused by the consideration of other issues and when many people, voting as they will vote, will be depriving themselves of the opportunity to vote in
Canadian Flag
favour of some good program which an individual may have in his platform?
I believe a plebiscite is needed to satisfy the promise made to this country that parliament, which is composed of the Senate, the House of Commons and the crown, will deal with this matter. The order in council of 1945 stated it was parliament which would deal with this question. I would remind the house of some statements made by the Prime Minister as recorded on pages 4308 and 4309 of Hansard of June 15. Remember, we are about to ask the House of Commons to concur in a report. It is my view that this is where the stumbling block lies as far as parliament is concerned. This hope of settling the question in parliament is associated with the request for a plebiscite. As reported on page 4308, the right hon. gentleman says: Until such time as action is taken by parliament for the formal adoption of a national flag . . . the red ensign may be flown.
He is quoting from the order in council of 1945. Later the Prime Minister went on:
I proposed in that statement on January 27, 1960, the submission by government to parliament of a measure which, if accepted by representatives of the people in parliament, would, I hoped, settle the problem of a national flag by agreement on a distinctive design which, unlike the red ensign-a flag never given formal sanction by parliament-could not be confused with certain United Kingdom or colonial flags and which was easily identifiable as Canadian.
Note, that he said he hoped this would settle the problem. He knew that the procedure which is being followed would not necessarily do so. As for the proposed flag being distinctive, I wonder if he would like to fly the flag of Peru alongside the design we are now considering and see just how distinctive it is. Further, it is not the flag that makes a country; it is the country that makes a flag. Later on, the Prime Minister stated:
I do feel, however, that there should be a Canadian national flag which could not be mistaken for the emblem of any other country-
He was quoting from a letter he had sent out to various people. What a joke. A flag has been offered to us which is so like the flag of Peru that it is difficult to tell the difference between them. The statement went on:
-and which, by its acceptance, would be a strong unifying force in our country.
Is this what we have found out in the course of the present debate-that this is a strong unifying force? I say to you, Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Canadian Flag
Speaker, that it is anything but that. Here is another quotation:
A Liberal government will establish a distinctive Canadian flag-
He had been saying previously that parliament would establish this flag, but as reported at page 4308 of Hansard he said:
A Liberal government will establish a distinctive Canadian flag within two years of taking office.
Is this what is happening today? Certainly it is what is happening. It is not parliament that is being asked to deal with this problem, in my view. The Prime Minister is carrying out this commitment; but he is not doing what he said previously he would do. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say that we need a plebiscite to get us out of the position we are in. Parliament is the House of Commons, the Senate and the crown. I am confronted with the moral obligation which I have quoted from the pages of Hansard, namely that the Prime Minister must allow parliament-that is, the House of Commons, the Senate and the crown-to deal with this matter. I believe that the way we can get out of this dilemma is by holding a plebiscite, with the result of the vote of that plebiscite being given by the chief electoral officer to the Senate of this country so they may introduce a measure in this respect-as spoken of by the Prime Minister himself-a measure that can be concurred in by the Senate, the House of Commons and the crown. Therefore parliament would act on this question. I have heard it suggested that another order in council may be passed to annul the order in council of 1945. I say that if this happens, the whole argument has no foundation; we should not be dealing with the question at all.
I believe the question should be referred to a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate. In my opinion the Senate of this country ought to be in on these deliberations. Such a committee could choose a number of good designs including the present Canadian flag. I believe that an example of a design that could very well be acceptable under these circumstances and submitted in a plebiscite is the one suggested to me by the hon. member for Halifax. This was a very simple design in which the three maple leaves took the place of the union jack, and the union jack was placed on the shield in the present position of the three maple leaves. Nothing would be taken from the present flag, nothing would be added; only the prominence of the union jack would be 
changed with that of the three maple leaves. In my view this is one good design that could be submitted in a plebiscite. Instead of that this matter was placed before a committee that was frozen from the very beginning. As many hon. members of this house know, it was a joke around the House of Commons, after the flag committee was formed, that they knew immediately what the end result was going to be. What did we accomplish in that particular committee? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is another reason why we should hold a plebiscite on this matter and submit a number of designs to the Canadian people. The House of Commons and the Senate could provide a committee that would give us those designs, and we would therefore be fulfilling our obligation in passing them on to the people of this country in a plebiscite.
What did we do in this flag committee? We took the three maple leaves and replaced them with one maple leaf. This got the Prime Minister off the hook; it was no longer the Pearson pennant. But then the flag committee was immediately confronted with another problem; they now had the flag suggested by the members of the New Democratic party. So what happened? We folded, like a television camera, the three maple leaves into one and turned the blue bars into red. That is all we did. Basically it was the same design as that with which we started. That is all the flag committee accomplished, Mr. Speaker. In concluding my remarks I want to say that any individual in this country knows as much about what he wants in regard to a flag as does any member of parliament. But this is not true with regard to legislation that comes before this House of Commons. In the case of legislation we are able to carry out a certain amount of research-not as much as we would like to carry out, by any means-and we are able to listen to the speeches of people in the House of Commons who perhaps have more research facilities. In this way we are able to judge the matter from the experience of many members of this house who have a great deal of knowledge of the matter under discussion. But on the question of a flag, any person on the street knows just as much about the flag as you, Mr. Speaker, myself or anyone else; it is a very personal and emotional problem. Therefore I say that we should take advantage of holding a plebiscite on this question. I am also convinced that the backbenchers of the Liberal party would be doing

their leader and the frontbenchers a very good service if they would rise and support a plebiscite and take their leader off the hook.

speechtext:
In support of a plebiscite I would like to present what I consider to be the main reason for holding one. In attempting to force certain flag designs on the people the government is completely ignoring those who want to retain the flag we have had for many years, or at least some symbols from it. To be fair I would point out that one man on the government side is attempting to retain the symbols, and I give him full credit for that. We heard a very fine speech from the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) this afternoon and we realize that some hon. members in other parties are also attempting to do this.
Many speeches have been made in this debate by members from Quebec. Those members are practically all, if not entirely all, in favour of a new or different flag, regardless of the party to which they belong. I respect their views because it is obvious they are trying to present the views of their constituents. Regardless of the views of their party, these members at least have spoken for their people, and no one can quarrel with that; it is political honesty. But what about the members of the government; have they been as honest? In my opinion they definitely have not. Many of them speak, of course, from their seats; but they do not rise-with few excep-
Canadian Flag
tions-and tell us what their constituents want. We should certainly like the reasons for the abandonment of the flag which we now have for something else, or for what appears to be anything else. It does not seem to make much difference as long as we abandon the flag we have. I am sure the constituents of hon. members opposite would be very interested to hear what they have to say on this matter. It is natural that some constituents always like to criticize their member, and I do not think they should be robbed of this pleasure. But how can they criticize their member if they do not know what he thinks about an emotional issue?
It is surprising that many young people feel the need for a plebiscite, although I have heard statements to the contrary. The boy scouts magazine polled a number of boy scouts on this issue, and boy scouts are a fine example of young Canadians. The result showed that over 50 per cent of them wanted the red ensign. Over 35 per cent, I must admit, wanted the three maple leaf flag, but everyone has forgotten about it now. Less than 15 per cent wanted a one maple leaf flag.
The need for a plebiscite has been mentioned in various publications throughout the country. I should like to put on the record only those excerpts from these clippings which deal with a plebiscite. For example, the Rural Co-Op for May 12, 1964 carries the heading "Does majority or minority rule?", and in connection with the flag question has this to say:
How many quiet responsible Canadians want a new flag-brand new with no traditions behind it? Or a new national anthem? Until that fact is established all the hollering about a Canadian flag and a Canadian anthem is just that: a lot of hollering by extremely vocal persons who must have something to holler about . . .
Only a referendum can show whether a majority of Canadians want a change-or whether we are subject to rule by the loudest shouters.
Here is another clipping from the Daily Colonist, Victoria, B.C., entitled: "It's a label, not a flag". I refer only to the part which deals with a plebiscite. This article says:
The flag, which traditionally expresses our pride and our freedom, is being taken away without the consent of the majority of the people. Mr. Pearson could resolve this by a national plebiscite . . .
The flag is a basic issue and should be resolved not by an election, not by mere politics, but by a national vote in itself, for itself.
Lastly, this is a clipping from the Toronto Telegram for August 2, 1964, an excerpt from an article entitled, "Ask the people":

Canadian Flag
The voice of the people can he heard, on this issue, only through a national plebiscite.
Then it goes on to mention that the flag issue is different from a political issue.
In my opinion, the idea behind sending this problem to a committee was to obtain a compromise. But we did not get one; what we got was another label similar to the three maple leaves which was suggested at the time the committee was set up. It is my understanding that the committee had the chance to come up with a compromise which contained the symbols of both founding races. This was mentioned this afternoon. One of the three final choices bore the symbols of both founding races, but this was overlooked. That is why I say the committee did not come up with a compromise when it had the chance. I would have accepted this choice because it was a compromise. The Canadian coat of arms contains the symbols of four founding races, but this was ignored.
What do I consider to be a compromise when I speak of compromise? We have, you might say, the two extremes. We have, on the one hand, the strong supporters of the previously recommended three maple leaf flag; on the other hand we have those who support the red ensign. If we are to reach a compromise we must put something of both races on any compromise flag which is recommended by a committee, and I maintain that no symbol of the red ensign is on the flag proposed by this committee. To those who say that a plebiscite would disunite the country, I concede only that it should not show regional results. Only by showing regional results might disunity be caused. But a plebiscite would get this government out of a bad spot.
This Liberal government has shown that it does not care what is the design of a new flag so long as it does away with any symbols of our heritage. That is so obvious that this point does not need enlarging upon. The whole flag idea was brought forward last summer just before a summer recess in the hope that the house would pass it. If that had been so, of course then we would have been given a recess. Once again now, before the Christmas recess, there is the same hope. This is a typical example of the government's political manoeuvring. We are told: "Pass it, or no Christmas recess". Perhaps they have not said that in so many words, but we get the idea. This does not sound to me like real democracy in action.
The other day the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Ormiston) spoke on the question of

symbols in connection with his support for a plebiscite. He delivered an interesting and well prepared speech. There has been a tendency lately in this country to do away with symbols. The same tendency exists to do away with pleasing art. A prime example of this is the monstrosities of so-called modern art which we have in our Canadian air terminal buildings. To me this is evidence of a sick society, and this is the sort of thing which seems to get support from this government.
Why should we consult the people through a plebiscite? Who asked for a new flag in the first place? This was not the promise I heard, Mr. Speaker, in the last election campaign in my part of the country at any rate. What I heard were promises of $2 wheat. I even heard the promise of $3 wheat; that is $3 for the first 300 bushels that a farmer produces. Then there were promises of giving the country two ministers of agriculture. But I heard no promise about a flag. We sometimes wonder now how many ministers of agriculture we do have.

Have these members asked this of the eastern farmers, whose incomes are so meagre? Strangely enough, we see today the symbols of Christmas on the office doors of many hon. members as well as inside their offices, and this is very fine. But I notice that these are on the office doors of the very members who want to do away with symbols. How do they justify acceptance of traditional Christmas symbols while at the same time rejecting those traditional symbols on the flag? That certainly does not make sense in my opinion.
In conclusion I would urge the government, and particularly the Prime Minister, to give some consideration to those Canadians who

do not agree with the Prime Minister in his desire to remove the Christian crosses from our flag by Christmas.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate in order to put forward some of my views about the necessity for holding a plebiscite across Canada to decide this issue for once and for all. I am sure it is the feeling of most people in Canada that a plebiscite is the only means by which this issue can be settled. It is also my belief that the majority of the people in Canada do not have a desire to change our flag.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is the one man in Canada who, as head of this government, has a feeling that we should have a new flag, and is in a position to at least attempt to push it through the house and force it upon the people. In western Canada we often use the expression "taking the bull by the horns," and I believe that is exactly what the Prime Minister is attempting to do in forcing this change upon the Canadian people who, like the members of this party, will not accept such a change.
There is no urgency for a new flag, as evidenced by events which have taken place since last summer when the flag issue was first introduced. In June, as I remember, there was an attempt to rush the new flag design through by July 1 so that it could be hoisted at that time. I need not remind hon. members that that did not take place. The next urgent deadline was the time of the Queen's visit to Canada. The Prime Minister, and I presume government members, hoped to be able to hoist the new flag when the Queen was visiting Canada, but again that was not possible. The Prime Minister has now set a new date for the hoisting of a new flag, and is in hopes that this can take place before Christmas. I suggest one of the Prime Minister's faults in proposing this flag question lies in his continuous setting of deadlines. It must be very disappointing to him, having set two deadlines within six months, not to have at least met one of them.
It is evident by the events that have taken place in the house as a result of motions to adjourn the debate that the government members, along with the majority of other members, feel the need for greater discussion on this subject. I should like to see some government members stand in their places and tell us why we so urgently need a change in the present flag.

If we are to have a change, in order to maintain whatever unity still exists in Canada it must be the result of a plebiscite.

Invariably, many people are unhappy about the results of a general election, but they accept those results. I am sure the people of Canada would be happy to accept the feeling of the majority of the people of Canada as expressed by a plebiscite. Surely the people of Canada for the most part desire that this whole mess be cleaned up. I suggest it can be cleaned up appropriately, and in the best way possible, by holding a plebiscite, settling this matter for all time.
I should like to refer to a newspaper clipping in relation to a poll of members of parliament on the flag issue.
