And that, Mr. Speaker, is the state of affairs today. Indeed, when the Prime Minister gets out on the stump on some of these trips of discovery, he speaks of the wonderful record of this government and of how much legislation it has got through. That is when he is outside the house. Sir Wilfrid went on:
It is quite true that when we came to the first of April, supply had not been voted, and the financial year was at an end; but if supply had not been voted before that, whose fault was it? Was it that supply was demanded and was refused?
Then as reported at column 7433 Sir Wilfrid went on to say this:
Everybody knows that whenever a measure of public importance was brought to our attention we gave it our best consideration, and it was passed.
That is our position today, Mr. Speaker. Every piece of legislation this government has introduced and carried along has been passed. Indeed, we have been so anxious to get the government to produce the legislation it has not got that we have supported the adjournment of the house so the government might bring these measures forward. Then Sir Wilfrid Laurier continued:
It is true, sir, that we opposed a certain measure. It is true that we opposed the bill for naval aid. We did that	with	all	the might	at	our command; we did it	with	all	the means	at	our command under the	rules	of	the house.	Am I to betold that in the	exercise	of this power	of strenuous opposition we did anything which is not in accordance with the best traditions of parliamentary government?
Mr. Speaker, his words of 1913 come back to us today and can be applied to the present circumstances. He continued:
Sir, at all times in this house, at all times in the mother of parliaments, there have been questions upon which the minority thought it owed it to itself to offer the most vigorous opposition possible. Under the rules of the house it is expected that the two sides of the house shall carry on the business, as was stated by my right hon. friend today, and so it is generally; but there are occasions, I repeat, when the opposition or a minority owes it to itself, on account of the strong views it holds upon some public measure,

to oppose that measure with all the force at its command.
What we have done is to carry out the concepts of parliament espoused by a great parliamentarian. Then Sir Wilfrid continued and said that the remedy is not closure, that it is not the application of brute force. He said the remedy is an appeal to the people. He continued, as reported at column 7435 of Hansard:
The people, after all, are the judge and the jury. The people, after all, are the parties to pass judgment as between the government and the opposition-
Then he said:
I am sure it was not a pleasant task that my right hon. friend performed today; and, for my part, when I compare my conduct with his conduct, I am proud that I resisted all applications for closure, and that when the time came I appealed to the people, as I did on reciprocity.
Then as reported at columns 7435 to 7437 he uttered some words which are very significant. He set out the number of times when closure had been applied when there had been obstruction. Then he said that in every case the opposition was right, as it is right today.
The Prime Minister asked me why we did not abolish closure. We had the measure ready for the house but there were other matters to be dealt with. We believed in priorities in matters which deserved immediate attention. A committee on procedure was set up but did not bring in the recommendation in question. At all times we said we would not impose closure and we followed that course, although we did not in fact abolish it as we said we would. Though the legislation was ready, when defeat came to us we could do no other than accept defeat and go to the country.

speechtext: No, the Canadian flag.

This is the expression he used, our flag. Then, he looked over at us and he said, their red ensign. Was it not his red ensign, Mr. Speaker? Is it not his red ensign? This represents an amazing revelation of his thinking.
He manufactured a false claim when he used the expression that we sneered at the maple leaf. There was nothing of that kind. Many of us on this side of the house are proud of the maple leaf, but the maple leaf as an emblem is a long way from the maple leaf as the design for a flag. An example occurs to me as I am speaking. What about Ireland? Ireland established itself as an independent country after generations of turmoil and difficulty. It decided on a flag. The emblem of Ireland is the shamrock. Did they place the shamrock on the flag? The shamrock was a symbol, but when they built their flag, they made it a flag of two colours representative of the unity of their country, orange and green. Certainly, no one casts aspersions on the maple leaf. We are all proud of it as a symbol of the nation. However, there is a great deal of difference between symbolic significance and that which goes to the heart and soul of a nation, the flag that must represent the people as a whole.

Canadian Flag
I will say no more on this occasion except that we have no apologies to offer for the stand we have taken. I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will ascribe to us the same degree of sincerity which he has appropriated to himself. We believe that this flag that does not have anything to do with our heritage, with the greatness, the magnificent history of our country, will not induce unity. The imposition of this flag on the millions of people who have for generations accepted the red ensign as their flag, will cause a sense of frustration which we do not want to have within this nation.
The right hon. gentleman asked, when was Canada ever represented by the red ensign? One of the greatest cartoons that came out of the first war appeared in the April, 1915 issue of the magazine Punch, after the first gas attack at Saint Julien. it showed Canadians wounded and dead; it showed them raising the standard of Canada. Look up that issue of Punch for April, 1915, and you will find that the flag in the hands of the Canadian as he raised it, raised it with the strength that was available to him after being wounded and dismayed by the gas attack, was the red ensign.
In asking parliament to give the most serious consideration to this matter, I point out once more we are not asking something that is not peculiar to the Canadian way of life, because it has been our flag for generations. Indeed, if you read the advertising for the election of 1891, you will find that Macdonald used throughout the campaign huge placards and on every one of them was a red ensign, the only difference being that instead of the coat of arms there was the number of maple leaves representing the provinces of Canada. What we have tried to do, Mr. Speaker, is not anything to prevent parliament acting. What we have tried to do is to discharge our responsibilities in connection with the choosing of a flag which will touch this and future generations intimately and effectively, in a manner that will inform parliament, even though the majority thinks otherwise, that by taking this step it will be taking a wrong step.

I took part earlier in this debate and was able to state my views on the flag issue in ten minutes. I do not intend to repeat anything I said at that time. I just want to make a very brief appeal. I ran across a quotation the other day from a very wise author who wrote some 3,000 years ago SOme words which I

believe are appropriate at the moment. The writer was Ecclesiastes, and he said this:
To everything there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that after some 250 speeches on this issue, and I suggest particularly to my friends in the Conservative party, that the time for silence has arrived. I cannot escape the conclusion that the prolonging of this debate will make those responsible for it look foolish. This is a situation which I can contemplate with some equanimity when I see who is responsible for prolonging the debate. However I do not believe we in this house can contemplate with equanimity the fact that not only the party responsible for prolonging the debate will look foolish but parliament itself is being made to look foolish. Unfortunately, I fear it looks that way at the moment. Everything that could be said or should be said in this debate has been said. Perhaps some things have been said that should not have been said, and some things have been said more often than they required to be said, but I appeal to those members of the official opposition who are contemplating further discussion to realize the time has now come to keep silent. The time has surely come to let parliament take its responsibility.
I appeal to all hon. members to let us vote on this resolution now, so that we can get on with other important business before the house.
Hear, hear.
Perhaps the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) will not object too strongly if I now recognize the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette).

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take too much time to discuss this matter which we have been discussing for too many months, and which seems to confuse the people of Canada. It was discussed thoroughly during the first weeks of the debate on this matter, and today the same members are allowed to repeat over and over again the same old worn-out arguments which we have heard ever since the resolution was introduced.
Yesterday, and particularly last night, we heard the hon. members for Cumberland (Mr. Coates), Rbsthern (Mr. Nasserden), Vegre-ville (Mr. Fane) and Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) ask questions of the government concerning its attitude respecting the resolu-

tion on the order paper, what it would do should the amendment or the main motion be adopted, what it intends to do or will do. And all this while the government had informed the house that it intended to proceed with measures on the order paper and which should be taken up by the house before Christmas.
Mr. Speaker, it is astonishing to hear those people blame the government for giving effect to their own proposals. In fact, the establishment of a committee was proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker). When the leaders of the five parties met the Leader of the Opposition insisted that a committee be established to study the flag issue and then submit to the house a majority report.
As was stated this morning, 11 members were in favour of this report and four against it, out of a total of 15 members.
The committee was set up following representations made by the Leader of the Opposition who also called for a free vote. The Prime Minister complied with this request: a free vote was allowed. All Liberals were permitted to vote as they saw fit. The Conservatives were also free to vote as they pleased, every one of us could vote according to his conscience and in the best interests of national unity.
At that time, Mr. Speaker, mention was also made of curtailing the flag debate. Since the Leader of the Opposition disagreed, I feel he is not justified in suggesting today that any member of the official opposition was prevented from expressing his views or that of his constituents. But, to my mind, the federal parliament has never been able to see to what extent some members are wearing blinkers which prevent them from seeing the facts as they are or to realize their narrow-mindedness.
Indeed, they only see one side of the question, and refuse to look at Canada as a whole. A matter as significant as the choice of a truly Canadian flag, of a distinctive Canadian flag, is brought down to the level of their constituency and their personal ambitions.
Mr. Speaker, some people have difficulty in realizing the facts. Some attach greater importance to the symbol of our origins than to the very existence of our nation, in short, to the future of Canada.
We rightly claim and will always claim that one must have the greatest respect for his forebears and ancestors, but there is not a single member here, including the Leader of the Opposition, who would dare put on
Canadian Flag
the clothes and shoes that his forebears or ancestors were wearing 100 and 150 years ago. We must realize that we have something better to do at this time than to reduce the question of the national flag to the level of a mere political issue.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the Leader of the Opposition did not grow in the public eye when he stated here that the members of the Ralliement Creditistes have thrown themselves into the arms of the Liberals. The right hon. gentleman knows that he is wrong and that he is misleading the members of this house. And I immediately point out to the house that a proposal was made two days ago not by a member of the Ralliement Creditiste but by the deputy leader of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer).
As reported in Hansard on page 10965, he made the following statement:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege. For weeks, and even months, the House of Commons has been witnessing an unparalleled debate which is completely paralysing the business or this house and transforming it into a debating society where it is impossible to reach any decision whatsoever. Freedom of speech must be respected, but we should not act in such a way that this house be deprived of its main duty, which consists in making decisions.
Mr. Speaker, this is what we want to do at this point. And I continue:
That is why I deem that in this discussion on the flag, the whole gamut of opinions has been heard-
Including those of his party.
-and should we extend it any further, we would but prejudice the rights of parliament and the higher interests of our country.
Therefore, I believe that it is my duty to rise on a question of privilege and invite the Prime Minister-
Please note, Mr. Speaker, the words "and invite the Prime Minister."
-or one of his ministers, to give notice that he will make use of standing order 33 to have this question settled without further delay by applying the rule of closure.
We are pressing for that application, because it is impossible to bring the leader of the official opposition to listen to reason.
Is the Leader of the Opposition ready to say that his colleague from Three Rivers has gone over to the Liberals? Is he ready to repeat that his colleagues from Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), Pontiac-Temiseamingue (Mr. Martineau), Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) have gone over to the Liberals, or that they are people whom the Liberals treated kindly

during the last election campaign, or that they are people who were praised by the Liberal candidates in their respective ridings or by the government in office?
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Leader of the Opposition, on behalf of the Canadian people, to be honest in his statements and to stop playing petty politics, as he did this morning and kept on doing this afternoon.
The Leader of the Opposition knows that we do not hold the Liberals in such high esteem. We have not gone over to the Liberals. We have no intention of going over to the Conservatives either. We want to remain ourselves, and we want the Canadian people to remain themselves too, all across the country. That is why we endorse, not every policy of the Liberal party, far from it, but the stand taken by the Prime Minister and the government who want to give Canada a distinctive national flag, a flag which will be the pride of the whole country everywhere, whether it bears three maple leaves or a single one.
When the right hon. Prime Minister introduced his motion in parliament, he recommended a flag design with three maple leaves on a white background and a blue border on each side.
Today the committee decides-and the Prime Minister himself said this morning that it was the committee-in order to accept a compromise, to change the three maple leaves for a single maple leaf with red bands instead of blue bands.
In my opinion, the new design is not as nice as the first one. However, the report of the committee is now before parliament, even though the design agreed to is not exactly according to our wishes.
I for one would have preferred the flag with the red and white diagonals, with a green maple leaf, promoted throughout the country about 20 years ago by la ligue du drapeau and the Native Sons of Canada. That is the flag we were endorsing.
However, we are not opposing the new design brought in. It is not that we have changed our minds, no, but we want the flag issue settled once and for all.
Within the party of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition there are members who do not necessarily share the opinion of the committee but who are ready to accept the report as submitted to parliament. There is no question, in this case, of playing politics nor of trying to toss the issue back and forth, by saying that one party is more important than the other.
[Mr. CaouetteJ
The decision rests with parliament and, the right hon. Prime Minister said so at noon today, and not without reason: it is not the government which decides, but parliament.
The hon. member for Three Rivers said also that the chief duty of parliament was to decide. We are ready to decide and, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) said rightly a few minutes ago, it is time to stop talking, to cut off that "talkathon" on the flag issue.
When the right hon. Leader of the Opposition says that the flag issue is dividing Canada, I must say, and I know what I am talking about, that if there is a man who has spread doubts in the minds of citizens in various sectors of Canada, it is the Leader of the Opposition himself since he took up his stand on a distinctive national flag.
I happened to be in Toronto last week. I met there influential businessmen, professionals, students, people from all walks of life. Among these people, who are definitely grassroots, with whom we speak, many are disgusted with the way the flag debate is being handled at the present time in the House of Commons. And who is blamed? Not the government, not the Creditistes nor the New Democratic party, but the leader of the Conservatives in the House of Commons. Even his own followers have had enough of this obstructionist attitude, of this systematic obstruction we have seen for too many long weeks.
Mr. Speaker, our attitude-

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is naming names and naming the party. Would he name the individuals in the Conservative party that are opposed to the question he has just raised. The hon. member made a blanket statement; I wish he would nail it down.

Mr. Speaker, I did not get
the hon. member's question, but if he is asking me whether some Conservative followers are disgusted with this Conservative action in the House of Commons I will say yes, sir, because I met some prominent Conservative followers in the city of Toronto last Thursday.

Mr. Speaker, our position on the flag question is very well known. I am rising this afternoon in order to establish clearly and have it on the record that we are not devoted to the Liberals, but that we are in favour of common sense. And when there is common sense among the Liberals, we are the very

Canadian Flag
first ones to admit it, as we are the first ones to shout that they lack common sense too often, more often than they should. We know that also.
However, Mr. Speaker, on a matter as important as the flag issue now before us, we can only look at what Canada is and will be tomorrow. We are the ones who have to decide that as members of parliament; and only parliament has the responsibility to make a decision on the flag issue.
We will not let anybody sing to us the old refrain that we are rejecting the fleur-de-lis or the union jack. We will continue to have respect for the union jack and the fleur-de-lis, but we do not want those flags to represent us as Canadians. We want something typically Canadian, something which will be recognized as Canadian throughout the world, in all the countries where we will be received with our symbol, and not with the symbols of England or France.

speechtext:
He does not care what the Canadian flag is. Anything that the government will propose, he will support; that is his attitude.
