With regard to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), I am always surprised in this house that people should exhibit the colossal conceit that was shown today. Members sometimes rise in this house and say, "Everything that can be said has been said on the subject under discussion"; they contribute their own remarks for five, ten or 30 minutes and then they say the debate should come to an end, and we are supposed to bow and say, "Lord and master, thou hast spoken. Your willing servants accept your dictum".
That was the attitude taken by the hon. member for Greenwood today. Having himself spoken he said that everything had been said on the subject. That sort of colossal deceit has always astonished me in this House of Commons and I did not expect to see it in the hon. member for Greenwood.
I now want to say a few words about the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). We had expected him to speak last night but for some reason or other he had to be smoked out. Last evening, when he asked us to forgo private members' hour at five o'clock, he said "Let's get on and come to a decision on this matter before six o'clock", and I said no. I would not give unanimous consent because I said we wanted to hear from the Prime Minister, who has not spoken on this subject for six months. That is, he has not spoken here in the House of Commons, although he has said things outside the house. It was June 15 when the Prime Minister made his great speech on the flag that he then had selected and which he was putting in front of us, and then he sat silent in the House of Commons for six months.

Canadian Flag
We wanted to know, Mr. Speaker, what his position was with regard to the report of the committee, which is why we pressed him to enter into this debate. We had hoped that members of his cabinet would enter into the debate and support the Prime Minister. There is some uncertainty in the country whether the members of the cabinet are supporting the Prime Minister. Now and again under duress they confide in him and confess; but no member of the cabinet has yet risen to support the Prime Minister in this debate at this time. Earlier on, only two members of the cabinet rose to support the Prime Minister and spent their time talking of other subjects. This is a disunited cabinet, as the people of Canada are well aware now.
I have seen, Mr. Speaker, the sword swallower act on the stage. Today we saw the man swallowing act-the Prime Minister swallowing himself by going back on his determination and his promise in June of this year to give to Canada a three maple leaf flag with blue borders representing sea to sea. He has now come around to the view that perhaps that was wrong, and he acknowledges error and sees that the red bordered flag with the white centre is the flag for Canada. Give him another six months and he will change his mind again. It is because of that uncertainty that we have suggested delay and postponement on a decision on a Canadian flag. We have watched the Prime Minister in action for a year and a half, and given time he will shift his position. So we are well within our rights in discussing this issue.
The Prime Minister skirted all around closure today, and there is the threat. I was in the house in December 1951 when Mr. St. Laurent spoke much more clearly with regard to the imposition of closure and held the threat over our heads. That was in December and again we are in December. So we had the threat in 1951. It was not carried out although we were supposed to run scared; but the Conservative party in 1951 was not frightened away at all. We said to Mr. St. Laurent: "Bring on closure if you are so brave", and he shied away from it. Then in 1956 closure was applied in this house. The Conservative party did not run away from that issue either; and to the credit of the then C.C.F. party, neither did they. Now we have the threat of closure again in December 1964.
So therefore, Mr. Speaker, we have the attitude of the Liberal party. If the Liberal party cannot get its way it threatens closure or imposes closure. What is to happen later

on this afternoon? Are we going to have an announcement that closure will be applied next week? So that is the pattern followed by the Liberal party going back to 1951, 1956, 1964; and I hope the people of Canada realize that it is an autocratic, arrogant party, intent on enforcing its will on parliament and on the people of Canada.
With regard to the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas), the Prime Minister, improperly, said that this was a compromise suggestion. As I understood the hon. member for Middlesex West, he was arguing, in a very carefully given speech last night, which was concluded this morning, in favour of a meeting of minds. His argument today was this: Let us know the point of departure so that if there is to be a meeting of minds we will know what things cannot be considered and what things might be considered. So he suggested in his amendment that we have a stand-up-and-be-counted vote on the Canadian red ensign. Is this to be rejected by the Liberal party? Let the members of the Liberal party indicate in this House of Commons where they stand on the flag that has been Canada's national flag for 100 years. Let us have it down in black and white. Let them not shelter behind the committee, which is what they are doing. Why anyone should shelter behind the committee, with perhaps the determining vote in that committee being a vote cast by a member of the Creditiste party, which has no use for Canada's traditions, surprises me. Here is the opportunity for the Liberal party, man by man and woman by woman, to record their vote.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I think the hon. member has some of his wires crossed. We have use for the past in this country, but I have no use and no other party has, for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). That is where he is wrong.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: You mean South Centre.
I am sorry; I mean the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill).

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Insult me if you wish, I say to the hon. member, but do not insult other members from the city of Winnipeg. I must stand up for my hon. friend for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). We differ on a lot of points, but he is a citizen of a great city and he must not be insulted in

this house. I am glad that the hon. member who has just intervened does not agree with the leader of his party. The leader of his party wants to wipe out all history and tradition and this member does not, so we are glad to have that intervention.
The hon. member for Middlesex West was suggesting a step by step process, out in the open and not behind a committee, to see whether there can be a meeting of minds with regard to a flag for Canada. In the course of his remarks the Prime Minister had something to say with regard to his experience in war, and unfortunately used an expression which he used once before. He was speaking about the war of 1914-18, and the exact words he used were these, and I quote: "None of us saw a Canadian red ensign in those years". I interrupted and he repeated the statement. It is with regret that I refer to this, but the Prime Minister does not have to take my word for anything with regard to the first world war. I said earlier in the debate that the Canadian red ensign was seen by Canadian soldiers in the first world war. He does not have to take my word for that, because I gave evidence of others. I do not mind if he wishes to intimate that I was being untruthful earlier in making those statements. However, the Prime Minister is attacking the veracity of my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). That member has placed on the record his experience in the first world war, and has brought forward pertinent evidence by quoting a statement made by General McNaughton regarding the use of the Canadian red ensign during that conflict. I am sorry the Prime Minister expressed himself in that way, and I regret having had to interrupt him, but I did find it irritating when he repeated the statements he had made earlier which we have denied and repudiated during the course of this debate.
Let me say this, so there will be no misunderstanding. The present and former prime ministers are two Canadian prime ministers who, during the first world war, volunteered their services to this country. I respect both of them in that regard. No one who volunteered for service during the war had any jurisdiction as to where he might be sent to serve, so that question does not enter into this discussion. I have as much respect for those who served during the war of 1914 to 1918 as for those who served during the second world war, as did both those prime ministers. They volunteered for service anywhere in the world, and at any risk. If 1 raise 20220-699
Canadian Flag
an objection to anything the Prime Minister has said today I do not do so because of lack of respect for the service he was prepared to render to his country during those years.
I respect that attitude of the Prime Minister as much as I respect the same attitude taken by the former prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). These men did not stay home with the paltry excuse that they had to complete their university education, or anything of that nature. They laid their lives on the line, and by the grace of God and with good luck they survived, as did thousands of others.
I have said that the Liberal party is attempting to take shelter behind the report of the committee. This House of Commons is not obliged to accept, without question, the report of any committee, particularly a committee which is composed of less than 10 per cent of the members of this house. Incidentally, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition had suggested, as long ago as June 22, that the best way to approach a controversial subject such as the flag is through a committee. Personally I preferred a joint committee of the Senate and the house, such as the committee which considered this issue in 1945 and 1946. A larger committee should have been established rather than one restricted to 15 members. In any event, we are not obliged to accept any committee report presented to this house. I think it is wrong that the government should seek to take shelter behind a report of a committee. It is wrong for any party in this house to seek that kind of shelter.
Had the hon. members of that committee been other than the members who actually were named, I think the report would be different. Why did the New Democratic party not name as a member of that committee the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge)? Why did the Social Credit party not name as a member of that committee the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe)? That party could also have named the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) as a member of that committee. Perhaps the N.D.P. could have named the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather) as a member of the committee. The Liberals could have been represented by a member with divergent points of view by naming the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan). Had those men been named as members of that committee I am sure the report presented to this house would not be the same as the one now before us for consideration. Those men have

Canadian Flag
publicly stated their preference for the retention of Canada's history and traditions, as exemplified by the Canadian red ensign.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? When you were in power, why did you not appoint Mr. Van Horne as a member of your committees?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I cannot see any more relevancy to that question than I can in the sale of bumper stickers by the hon. minister. Perhaps he can explain the relevance to me at a later date.
A different committee I am sure would have presented a different report. The special committee was selected with extreme care, and I am sure the substance of the report of that committee was a foregone conclusion, as was the abandonment or destruction of the Canadian red ensign. Let us not take shelter behind the workings of a committee. It is nonsense to suggest that the decision of a committee, even though it has worked long hours studying a subject, is superior to the decision of 250, odd, members of this house.
The Prime Minister during the course of his remarks referred to the single red maple leaf on the coat of arms of Canada. I noted particularly his remark in this regard, and I wondered whether the Prime Minister, who served as a soldier during the war, recognized the fact, as pointed out by the members of that committee which sat in 1921, and as indicated in their brochure, that the single red maple leaf in the Canadian coat of arms was representative of the sacrifice made by the young men of Canada during the first world war. I thought the Prime Minister in referring to the single red maple leaf on the coat of arms might have made some reference to that fact. As I said before, we must either change the coat of arms-and I do not think that should be done, taking the single red maple leaf from it-or refrain from using the single red maple leaf on the flag of Canada. I do not think we would be paying a tribute to our young men who sacrificed their lives during the war by changing a symbol which has, for almost 50 years, represented that sacrifice. What has happened to the thinking of the people of Canada since that time? Is our thinking different in 1964 from the thinking of that generation of 1921 which felt that the inclusion of the single red maple leaf in the coat of arms was an appropriate recognition of the sacrifice made by 60,000 young men of a country with a population of eight million? Have we no sense or appreciation for history and sacrifice?

The Prime Minister asked why we do not embroider the maple leaf on our own national banner. That is exactly what the joint committee of 1945-46 suggested. They suggested that the shield should be taken from the red ensign and a golden maple leaf placed thereon. They in effect embroidered the maple leaf on Canada's flag. We have respect for the maple leaf in that respect. That could be an appropriate part of a flag, and it could be embroidered on the present Canadian red ensign as recommended by the committee of 1945.
Mr. Speaker, I have never objected to the maple leaf as an emblem of Canada. Rather, my objection is that it should not be the main component of our flag. Once again I suggest to the Prime Minister that this issue which has caused so much controversy, is an issue about which hundreds of thousands, and perhaps millions, of people are concerned. In view of that fact I appeal again to the Prime Minister, as others have done, to postpone this issue. I do not subscribe to the point of view, which I have heard put forward in speeches by various people, that Canada has suddenly become a new country and everything must be done differently. This is a country with a long history. If it has suddenly become a new country in 1964, those people who are talking that way will hear in 30 years from another generation that in 1994 Canada has suddenly become a new country. They will be told that a new century is just around the corner and everything will have to be different because it is new and that the older generation must be swept away and uprooted and all the symbols of the past will have to be replaced. If the proposed new red and white flag with a single maple leaf in the centre is in existence at the turn of the next century it will, of course, represent the horrible past that must be forgotten as we move into the 21st century with a new Canada. All this is just too ridiculous.
This is not a new country. This is an old country. It has centuries of history behind it, centuries of sacrifice, and we should recognize these facts. As has been mentioned in many speeches, these sacrifices were endured in warfare on Canadian soil in other years, as abroad. We also must not forget the sacrifices of the pioneers of this country who respected our flag.
Everything does not have to be new just because a few people get an idea that a new horizon has opened up. The great change in Canada, of course, as everywhere else in the

world, is in the material sphere because of the technological advances that are constantly being made. There is not much change in human nature. How can there be changes in the principles that have guided mankind? How can there be changes in our customs and traditions that are sound and have been considered to be sound over the years? Now and then you remove something which is no longer useful, but the main elements of our society carry on. Our society has been soundly based and should so continue. Some of these symbols mean a great deal to millions of people in this country.
This is a time for postponement of this issue. Set it to one side and if the people must decide it let them do so at some future date. But let it be removed from parliament at this time. Let the schools of our country interest themselves in Canadian history in a way they have never done before. As I pointed out earlier in the debate, to my knowledge the subject of the Canadian flag has never been a major topic of conversation in the classrooms of this country. Children have drawn the flag and so on, but the origin and meaning of that flag have never been discussed.
Educational circles in this country in every province can no longer ignore the Canadian flag. They have a storehouse of information on it supplied by members of this house through their arguments for and against and also by people outside the house. Let a period of time go by. Let the ministers of education and their advisers consider this matter. Let us have another look at our Canadian history books and see if something more impressive should not be included with regard to Canada's traditions. Let this be done and then, if you like, let another generation decide the question.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraiih (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have heard some 252 speeches on the subject of choosing a flag for Canada. Of the 252 speeches, 177 have been delivered by members of the official opposition.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Most of those speeches have been 40 minutes in length with some a bit shorter and a few a bit longer.
This morning we listened to a most outstanding speech by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of Canada, a speech which I am sure in years ahead, when many of us are gone from this place, will serve as an inspiration to young Canadians. In the course of 20220-6991
Canadian Flag
that speech the Prime Minister made an earnest and sincere plea for parliament to be given the right of decision on a matter that has been before the house and a committee of the house for many weeks, during which time all the speeches I have referred to have been delivered and during which time every aspect of the matter, I must say, appears to have been dealt with. The sincere appeal made by the Prime Minister was rejected summarily and immediately and, might I add, almost with contempt by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
No.
Yes.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That still seems to be the position of hon. gentlemen opposite even though since that speech was delivered we have heard a brief but eloquently expressed appeal by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) for the right of decision by parliament to be preserved as well as an appeal by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) along the same lines. In other words, speakers from two of the other three political parties represented in the House of Commons have indicated their support for such an appeal.
In the circumstances, and to prevent a mockery being made of parliament, I have no alternative but to take the action I now propose to take. I beg to give notice that immediately before the order of the day is next called for resuming the debate on the motion for concurrence in the sixth report of the special committee on a Canadian flag, presented to the house on Thursday, October 29, 1964, and on any amendments thereto, I will move that the said debate shall not be further adj ourned.
The pipe line boys are at it again. Shades of C. D. Howe.
Oh, oh.
The party is over now.
Why don't you start singing songs again, boys?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Remember black Friday.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Athabasca.

Mr. Speaker, I consider it a great honour to make the 178th speech by members of the official opposition in defence of our position with regard to Canada's glorious flag. The election

Canadian Flag
promises of the Liberal party have never been, and I trust never will be, taken as the law of Canada. We are here to make a decision. We are here to make a decision in the parliamentary way. I speak for my party 100 per cent when I say that it is our right and privilege to stand in this house and speak from our conscience and from our principles on each and every occasion that we believe it is our duty so to do.
1 have been asked by members of all parties except my own not to drag in emotions, not to parade my war effort, and I shall not do so. I speak from principle, the principle of defending those things which we hold dear and if I did not speak about those things the very rocks of Canada would cry out. The term "stubborn" is a term of derision sometimes used in trying to deflate a political opponent. However, when stubbornness is exhibited by a man of stature, whether or not he occupies the front benches of this noble house or some obscure back bench as I do, if his statements are made with conviction and sincerity, then it is a step toward statesmanship. Mr. Churchill returned to the school of his youth after some 46 years and spoke to the classes of Harrow. He had only one, small message to give them, and that message was this: When your principles are at stake you are not to desert them, never, never and again never.
Now, 178 speeches is a long way from never. However, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of this country came to this house, he came with great promise from a distinguished career in public affairs. I am sure it was the hope of the Liberal party if not the whole country, that when this man took the reins of office he would give the kind of leadership which the world and his country expected from one with such a notable career. From time to time I have stood in this house and said, I am a Canadian first and a Conservative second and, I hope, a mere politician third. This great party was largely responsible for confederation and from that day to this, December 11, 1964 we have appealed, with all the power and vehemence which we have been able to muster, to the people of Canada not to let the great experiment of confederation go down the drain.
We have been accused on numerous occasions by members of the other parties sitting in this house of being divisive in our actions. I do not see how the mere fact that I, for one, have stood and claimed I loved the flag under which I was born, the flag which I noticed outside school every

morning when I was perhaps too young to understand its significance, is being divisive. This is the flag under which I served in the mounted police for 23 years, seven of which I spent in the armed forces. I do not parade this fact in any way to establish myself as a hero, as 1 have been accused of doing by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). I merely say that this is a distinctive flag so far as I am concerned. The words "distinctive flag" of course have been used by those who would get rid of the British flag or any semblance of the British flag. I am not merely saying this because the statement appears in Hansard for this week. I refer to the extremists on the left who pretend to be more Canadian by saying they will have nothing British.
I hope that this does not include British justice because if there is one thing for which the British flag stands or the union jack quartered in our flag, it is that every citizen of this country, be he large or small, rich or poor, black or white, has equality under the law. This is what the British flag means to me, and this is what the British flag in the quarter of the red ensign has always meant to me. In case anyone thinks I am nothing but a talker I say that for 52 years of my life I have tried to make that symbol live in action as well as in words. A flag is something which we have had for many years. A flag is something which I claim we have today, by tradition and by law.
I should like to speak for a moment or two about the future. What are we going to hand on to our children, not only in the matter of a flag but in this same dual culture of which we are all proud? Where are we going to stop? As I have said, it is passing strange to me that the man who had promised to be such a great leader should not have been the first to speak in this debate, rather than third or fourth from the last. For months and months, I have sat here hoping it would not be necessary for us to appear to be filibustering. I want leadership, and I have a right to demand it from my government. The speech delivered today by the Prime Minister was perhaps his greatest speech in the House of Commons. However, I am afraid that is setting a very low standard.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You would not know, anyway.

Perhaps I would not know. I do not have a truth squad to help me. I merely have my own conscience, my own sincerity. I am speaking as a private member. By the

way, in this party, and this is one of the reasons I belong to this party, one has a right to speak as a private member. No matter how much we may disagree with our chief, never by thought or word or deed has our chief ever made his imperative views known. He has always talked to us in public and behind closed doors as the first amongst equals. This is the only attitude I will ever tolerate. I would not cross the floor of the house, but I would ask for a seat alone in the corner if this were not so. I have principles and a man who puts principles above all has the right to stand as a free citizen of this country and express his opinions on every occasion. Let my chief dare to intimidate me in any way and there would be one less member of this great party.
I do not expect members opposite to understand me. Let hon. members opposite remember that when the Hansard which contains the greatest speech ever delivered in the House of Commons by their leader is read into the pages of history, mine will not be read; but my stand will be taken now in the light of the words of that great Conservative, Mr. Winston Churchill: I will never, never, never desert the principles which I hold.
I have stood for the red ensign. It is not a party flag. It has been Canada's flag for nearly 100 years and it would be strange if anyone born in this country, of French, English or native origin, was not proud of that great banner. The first citizens of this country who signed solemn treaties with the Queen look at the red ensign as the symbol of their freedom, and if it is taken away they will feel part of their treaties has been abrogated.
There are 6,000 native Indians in my district. We are proud of them. They are Canada's first citizens, and I will find it hard to go back and explain to them why we have thrown away that symbol of peace and security which they have learned to love. When the volunteer soldiers left Canada during three wars our native people, according to their population, made the greatest contribution of any race resident in Canada. If the so-called founding races of Canada feel they are the only ones to be considered in this matter, may I point out to them we have a solemn obligation to those simple people of the soil, to explain to them why it is necessary to tear down what they regard as a symbol of freedom and equality.
I have hoped and wished in vain to hear positive arguments why a new flag should be raised on our flagpoles in place of the red
Canadian Flag
ensign. If there are positive arguments, where are they? At first when the Prime Minister presented us with his design I thought it had some merit. It contained three maple leaves, and I for one think of the maple leaf as a very dear and honoured symbol. But I want to know, why is there this negative approach?
Why is there this unanimity among certain groups in favour of tearing down the symbol we have? Why is there this strange silence on the opposite side of the house? When I believe in something I stand on my feet and say so. I make a positive contribution. If the ensign is retained I believe it will continue to be an inspiration for all classes and races of people so long as Canada remains a nation.
I make no apology for continuing the debate until I have made my point. If we do away with the red ensign we also do away with the white ensign which flies on every Canadian naval ship, and I presume we will also do away with the air force flag which flew over the airports in Britain when our great airmen, second to none in the world, helped the motherland win the battle of Britain. The men who served under these three flags, the red, white and blue ensigns, have a right to be heard.
Closure can be imposed, but far from being a great victory, far from being something to cheer about, I think it is a Pyrrhic victory. I suppose the opposition has won a small battle this afternoon in forcing us into arbitrary silence, but I wonder if they have not lost a greater battle of principle. Why is there such haste in getting rid of the flag which has served us well for 97 years? The excuse is an election promise, as if an election promise was sacred.
In the early years of the war, when the then Liberal government found itself faced with a very sticky election promise never to impose national service on the people of Canada, it held a plebiscite and approximately 87 per cent of the people voted in favour of releasing the Liberal government from its promise. In typical fashion it purported to take this as a vote of confidence, not a vote on the subject in question, which is an old trick. If the Liberal party wants to get out of this flag promise it could do the same thing, hold a plebiscite, but it has voted against doing that.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), speaking on behalf of the N.D. party just half an hour ago, begged us not to filibuster and waste the time of parlia-

Canadian Flag
ment. Yet his is the party that filibustered for two years in denying divorces to people who sought them. Apparently when one section of parliament talks it is a filibuster, and when another section talks it is a national service on a very high scale. Why should the rules not apply to everybody? Why should the rules of closure not apply to every government? Obviously the Liberals believe in closure because this is not the first time they imposed it, and the circumstances are somewhat similar to a previous occasion.
The Liberals would like to force us into an election. They would like us to make that move because they know perfectly well that this flag which represents British justice is being sadly soiled. They would like it to disappear in a red cloud with a white band around it, like a Hampshire pig.
This new design reminds me of the flag of Bolivia, but the Prime Minister did not bother to tell us why we should change our flag. He did not hurry to tell us why the single maple leaf design is superior to the three maple leaf design, and why the three maple leaf design is superior to the red ensign. When the 1945 order in council was passed the cabinet of that day were apparently unanimous in deciding we already had a distinctive flag. The question then was not to choose a distinctive flag but to postpone the need for changing the design of it.
When we marched into Holland and Belgium in the spring of 1945 and helped to restore freedom in those countries, thousands of red ensigns were brought out of the clothes closets where they had been hidden from the nazis, and every house in Holland and Belgium displayed our flag. It is passing strange that the people of Holland and Belgium should know the red ensign when they saw it while hon. gentlemen opposite say they never saw it or, if they did, they purport to despise it.
If one goes south of the line on July 1 almost as many red ensigns can be seen flying in United States cities on the borders of Canada as there are copies of old glory. The people there are proud of their long association with Canada and we are proud of our long association with them. If hon. members came to the Calgary stampede-and it would do a lot of them some good-they would see the red ensign and old glory flying side by side. Now with the change, thousands of United States tourists will not know they have crossed the border when they see the flag of Bolivia over our customs offices.

When our veterans go back to Holland they will look in vain for the flag which we associate with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: They will look for the maple leaf on the graves.

Yes, it is there, and every single soldier in each of those graves was a volunteer soldier who fought under the union jack and the red ensign. I would venture to say this to the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh), that we might well consider whether our dead sleep in peace when they think we are tearing down their flag, certainly without considering it and without being given the leadership from our government which we would expect. Even supposing we did- and I am not prepared to anticipate that day- willingly set aside our flag for any other emblem, no suggestion has been made that we will lay it away with the dignity which it so richly deserves. How are we going to pay the debt to those who are not here to defend that flag? How are we going to keep peace with those? "Lest we forget":
To you from failing hands we throw The torch; be yours to hold it high.
I appeal to this government in this regard and say, "They were speaking to you, not only to me. They were speaking to all of us who live here in freedom". They paid the price with their blood. If the people of Canada are now so delicate and so refined that I must not speak of blood or talk about the blood they gave and the sacrifice they made for us, perhaps I have lived in Canada too long. Some of my ancestors came here to be under the British flag. They could have had the so-called prosperity and freedom that exists south of the line. But I remind hon. members again that Canada was the first country in the world to abolish slavery; Canada was the first country in the world to give complete religious freedom. I am sorry that when the problem of freedom comes up again we must rely on the same old few volunteers who are sneered at and jeered at in this House of Commons of ours by those people who say our ideals of freedom are an empty dream, something out of the past.
When our friends to my left want to give dignity to what they say, they quote from the book of holy scripture. There are a good many verses in the book of holy scripture to cover this. I can give no better example than from the Ten Commandments themselves, one of which is:
Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long in the land which the Lord thy God hath given thee.

Not Marx, Lenin, Stalin, Hitler; but "the land which the Lord thy God hath given thee." I am no Jeremiah and I hesitate to bring down the wrath of Almighty God on those people who so lightly turn aside these symbols of reverence which have meant so much for 2,000 years. I will not be your judge, but I appeal to you in this regard and say that when I stand here and tell you those symbols really mean something to me, I am speaking from the depth of my heart.
Others will judge them.

I do not care whether I am hissed at, booed at or if catcalls are made from the other side of the chamber; I do not care whether there are mean threats made upon my life, as they have been made in this house. Well, Mr. Speaker, threats have been made against me before; threats have been made against me for many years and I have always tried to go ahead and do my duty. That is why I am doing it this afternoon.
If and when this House of Commons should ever come to a free vote, and if hon. gentlemen opposite ever stand in their place and take their oath and say, "Without fear, favour, affection or ill will toward any person, so help me God", on the vote, I will honour that vote. When the people in this house decide to have a change of flag I want it to be done in conscience, I want it to be done on principle; and whether the red ensign is ratified or not, or whether some new distinctive flag is decided upon-one bearing the Canadian maple leaf or three maple leaves-I pledge that I will serve that flag in the same way that I tried to serve the great, old red ensign which I love.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have said anything on the floor of the house in connection with the debate that has been going on, as has already been pointed out, for some time. In view of a recent announcement, if I am going to have an opportunity of saying a few words I should perhaps take it now. I think no one would quarrel with the right of the member who has just resumed his seat to speak with sincerity, and no one would quarrel with the fact that he was doing so. But I am glad that in his concluding remarks he did indicate that he was prepared to recognize that other members might hold somewhat different views with equal sincerity.
I would like, therefore, to address myself for just a few minutes to the amendment
Canadian Flag
which is before the house, which was moved by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas), in the light of some of the statements he made during his quite thoughtful and carefully prepared speech which was a prelude to his amendment. The hon. member for Middlesex West had a good deal to say about traditions and symbols. He paid particular tribute to the symbols of the past and his respect for them. With those parts of his remarks I have no quarrel, although I must say that I sincerely believe that the main concern of those of us in the present parliament should be more toward addressing ourselves to the symbols of the future rather than to those of the past.
I did feel that the member who placed the current amendment before us, along with some of the other spokesmen in his party, appeared to have a concept of the history of our country which in effect means that history has stopped and we are standing still where we are, or where we were 50 or 100 years ago. The hon. member for Middlesex West, however, did go beyond that which he properly should do, in my opinion, particularly when he was speaking in reference to Canadians of English ancestry. I have no objection to the hon. member for Midlesex West or any other member of the house who is of English ancestry speaking for himself; but as I listened to him it appeared to me that the member for Middlesex West was taking unto himself the right to speak for all Canadians of English ancestry.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in a speech which I will label as one of "including me out", because I am a Canadian of English ancestry who does not agree with the views of the member for Middlesex West.
He represents, as I understand it, one of the constituencies of the province of Ontario. His remarks led me to think, as I have been inclined to think rather often during the course of this debate, that much of it has taken place within the context of the limits of old Upper and Lower Canada. I happen to be a member representing a constituency in the province of British Columbia. I suppose it could be argued that I have very little right to take part in this debate because, after all, we are only Johnny-come-latelies in the Canadian confederation; we have only been in it since 1871. Sometimes I feel that some members in the house scarcely yet recognize that we have entered confederation.

Canadian Flag
That is only across the way, though.

I was born in Alberta and have lived all my life in British Columbia and Alberta, except for the months, and it begins to feel years, which I have spent in Ottawa. I am a first generation Canadian. My mother came from England when she was a small girl. My father came to Canada when he was a young lad. So I suppose it might be argued that really I have not very much right to participate in the question which is now before the house; I am only one of those "Johnny-come-lately" Canadians. I am a Canadian of English speaking ancestry who knows no other home than this Canada of ours, and perhaps for that reason I do feel I have some concern for what this country is and what it should become.
I must confess that I have something more than an academic interest in our past. History is one of my favourite subjects of study. I should like to say at once that I think most British Columbians are proud of the name of our province. We are the only province in Canada which uses the word "British" in part of its name. I have never heard anyone suggest in British Columbia that that is a name which should be changed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Wait till the Creditistes hear about it.

We are quite happy that that happens to be the name of our province; and it was the name of the British colony which entered confederation in 1871.
However, Mr. Speaker, as I listened last night to the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) quoting Sir John A. Macdonald with regard to the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway and how it was going to shorten the time to travel from London to Yokohama, and how the union jack was going to wave over these travellers all the way from London to Yokohama, I must say I should have reminded him that history is not a static thing. Indeed Canada, a nation in the full sense of the word, did not even exist when Sir John A. Macdonald was talking about this all red imperial route which was going to extend westward from London across the Pacific.
As far as I am concerned I think it is quite possible to make a logical argument that Canada came into being only in 1931, when the statute of Westminster made us an independent nation. I was a good deal younger in 1931 than I am now but I must say that

along with a great many other young Canadians at that time I was feeling my way as a Canadian. I revelled in the fact that here were we in Canada, becoming a nation in the full sense of the word. As far as I am concerned I would have become much more excited about this issue then than I am able to become now in my advancing years. That would have been the time for us to have had a flag that was Canadian and only Canadian. That would have been the time for us to have had a flag which looked to the future, which looked to history in the making, rather than to history which has gone before. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, my feeling is that for far too long have we as a nation neglected to develop a flag symbol which was distinctively and purely Canadian, which would stand for and mark that new status we had achieved as an independent partner and a self-governing nation in a new commonwealth.
I first came to this house in 1953, and at that time still very current were the rumblings of discussions which had arisen from an earlier committee of this house which had considered a distinctive Canadian flag. My chief regret is that the government of that day was prepared to procrastinate indefinitely on this subject; that the parliament of that day was not prepared to come to grips with this question and, having gone that far, to go through to a proper decision. Therefore I must say that I agree with the remarks made a little earlier by my colleague from Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), to the effect that in his view-and this is also my view-the time has come when this parliament should, after the kind of discussion and detailed consideration which has taken place in committee, pick up where the parliaments of the 1940's left off and come to a considered decision on this question.
I know that if certain actions take place which have been proposed from the government side, speeches will be limited to 20 minutes. Even though that event has not yet taken place I do not intend to prolong my remarks certainly beyond that point. But the reason I did want to get up and make a few rather offhanded remarks was to say that I wanted to be included out from that all embracing and sweeping statement of the hon. member for Middlesex West, which in effect said that all Canadians of English ancestry were being represented by the sentiments he uttered yesterday. I wanted to make this brief statement including me out, while the subject matter of his particular amendment

was before the house. Because if there is one element of this debate which has concerned me, as a Canadian, more than any other, it is the kind of suggestion which was implicit in the remarks made by the hon. member for Middlesex West, namely that somehow or other the proposal for a Canadian flag as brought in by the committee has something to do with dividing us as to whether we are Canadians of English speaking ancestry or Canadians of French speaking ancestry. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I wanted to put on the record that I am one Canadian who does not feel that way in any way at all.

Mr. Speaker, this is the second occasion since this debate has arisen in the house that I have taken part in it. The first occasion was when I spoke, not on the flag or the flag design but only on the method by which the house should proceed in order to determine the selection of a flag for Canada. Perhaps I would not have arisen again had it not been for one or two events which occurred recently, and particularly today. I believe it is a shame that the only member of the treasury benches to have risen, apart from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) today, to take part in this debate is a cabinet minister who had to move closure. The last occasion upon which this was resorted to was during the pipe line debate. Many of the same people involved in that debate are still in the cabinet. Subsequent events proved they were wrong then, and they are just as wrong this time. They have obviously not learned their lesson.
The procedure of closure has been repugnant to the sense of fair play of the Canadian people. My own personal view is that never in parliamentary debate should there be a muzzling of free debate. They will say they were forced into this by a fatuous opposition. Surely we had the right to debate this issue, especially when the government dumped their three maple leaf design and produced a new one, and in view of the fact that not one member of the government stated his position until today, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) spoke, only after being smoked out by the debate of last evening.
They will learn, Mr. Speaker, that no government can afford to take for granted that the opposition is entirely wrong in taking a stand on what it believes. In every single case, as Laurier said on one occasion, where closure has been imposed, the opposition has been justified. I am as sure as I am standing here today, Mr. Speaker, that that justification will be proved to those who
Canadian Flag
now wish to gag parliament by imposition of the closure role.
Does the Prime Minister think that a flag imposed in this way will win popular approval? I do not think so. This procedure being followed by this government is unwelcome, distasteful and unjustified, and I predict that they will live to regret it.
A flag means a lot of things to many people. A flag represents one thing to one individual and another thing to another individual. A flag to me represents one thing, and that is Canada. When the Prime Minister spoke today he said he had fought during the first world war under the union jack, and never saw the red ensign during that time. For almost ten years I served under the red ensign. I remember going to school at a place where the red ensign was raised every morning in the schoolyard. That was common practice in the west, and I think more attention should be paid to the historical traditions that were instilled in the school children in that part of the country.
This flag, instead of representing Canada to Canadians, represents a Canada betrayed. It is betrayal of the past and of our heritage, and a betrayal of parliament because of the manner in which this government has proceeded. This government has treated this whole issue contemptuously. I remember very clearly what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) said, when he was speaking about closure, which was being discussed during the past government's term of office. I have with me today an excerpt from the Ottawa Journal of April, 1962 having to do with this subject. This article was written by I. Norman Smith, and I think it might be of some use if I were to read one or two excerpts from it. The article states in part:
For some odd reason surprise is being expressed at the Liberals' eager agreement with Prime Minister Dielenbaker's move to abolish closure as a guillotine in the rules of parliament.
Any of us having even a nodding acquaintance with wrong-doing will understand Mr. Piekersgill's speech as simply that of the reformed drinker who doesn't want the stuff left in his house even for emergency. He can't trust himself.

that a house committee "consider" dropping closure. No, no, cried Mr. Pickersgill, let's not talk about it, let's drop it now.
"I believe," he said, "that no government in its senses would ever again use the existing closure rule in our book."
But apparently he could not be sure that if the Liberals got into power again they might not again yield to temptation.
And they have done so.
It is an awful thing to see a person have to acknowledge that in a given set of circumstances

Canadian Flag
he might go out of his senses, specially when that knowledge is based on past experience.
No, no, a thousand times no, cry the Liberals; take the stuff away.
What an amazing flip-flop they have accomplished.

Would the hon. member permit a question. In view of his quotation from an editorial appearing in the Ottawa Journal, would he be interested also in putting on the record what was said in an editorial appearing in the Ottawa Journal on Wednesday, December 9, to the effect that the time has come for a decision on the flag, and also makes reference to closure?

It is extremely interesting that during all the days of this debate, since the report of the committee was placed before the house, this is the second interjection by a cabinet minister who has not had the courage to get on his feet and say something during the debate. This is an example of the usefulness of the contributions that they have made. I suggest to the Minister of Fisheries that he should stand in his place and state his position as to whether or not he accepts the single maple leaf design with the red borders as accepted by the committee. I suggest to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) who has jurisdiction over all the functions of the citizenship courts in this country, that he too should rise in his place and state his position. I suggest that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), and the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) should stand in their places and state their positions. Those ministers have a very intimate reason for stating their positions on the flag issue. What have those ministers done in this regard? The Minister of Fisheries has stood up and asked an innocuous question instead of stating his position.
The course followed by the ministers during this debate has been a betrayal of even that symbol, now supported by the words of the Prime Minister, which they purport to adopt-the maple leaf. It has been dictated by a partisan advantage, particularly when one considers the very close rapport which exists among the Liberal members of that committee and the members of that committee who sit to my far left in the Creditiste ranks. In my opinion suspicions immediately occur when several Liberal members of a committee all suddenly express distaste for a design with three maple leaves which the Prime Minister suggested, when he presented it to the house on the first occasion, was the only design that had any national significance as

the national flag for Canada. I suggest that action on the part of the Liberal party was dictated by a partisan advantage, and I think that fact is clear.
If the Prime Minister feels that we are too concerned with the past, as he seemed to indicate today, then why, as he has stated, is it his intention to drag the union jack into the picture? He made an impassioned and spirited speech about the maple leaf. No one can disagree that the maple leaf is an emblem of Canada. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) said today, about the emblem of Ireland, that they do not have a shamrock on their flag. One might say the same about the eagle of the United States. It is an emblem of the United States but it is not on their flag. One could say the same thing about the rose of England. That is an emblem of that great nation but we do not observe it on their flag. The Prime Minister fails to understand the nature of a flag, and fails to understand that a flag itself is history.
The government is afraid to face the country on this issue because of their disarray and discredit at this time. So what do they do? They resort to gagging parliament as they did once before and lived to regret it. He said today that we obstructed for 23 days. The fact remains that we were right. We obstructed for 23 days, said the Prime Minister, on the basis of the three maple leaf flag. We were right. They reversed themselves and they now have a single maple leaf. They junked the three maple leaves and are now clutching to their bosoms the one maple leaf flag.
I believe that the Prime Minister missed the point. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that one of the reasons we criticized the three maple leaf design was not that it indicated a lack of any reflection of our past alone, not that it eradicated any of our past heritage and history alone, but that the government itself has changed its flag and its tune since it introduced the first resolution. The Prime Minister cannot get around this fact with high sounding platitudes. They started out with three leaves and they have reversed themselves to one. Why? The Prime Minister's speech was full of sound and fury signifying, to my mind, nothing. It was full of pious platitudes. That is the best description I can give of it.
We are concerned not with words but with what is being done. What is being done is that the Canadian people are asked to accept a partisan flag-in fact, not asked to accept, because in view of the notice given by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) a partisan flag that has already been changed

at the behest of partisan requirements is being forced upon them. I say, sir, that the Prime Minister and his government are treating parliament with contempt by shifting and changing on the flag and that they are now adding insult to injury by gagging parliament.
They talk about respecting the past but they would junk the flag embodying our Canadian history. They talk about unity and they sow disunity. At a time like this, when frictions, gaps and fissures are appearing between the two great races of this country, they have petulantly insisted on bringing the flag debate before parliament again and again and again. They have tried, with collaboration, to foist the blame on the members of the opposition for their own ineptness and inadequacies and their lack of organization.
They talk about coming to a decision and voting on the flag, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) also did today, so we can get on with the business of the country. There has never been any reason why parliament could not have been dealing with the business of the country instead of frittering away endless hours on this debate merely because of the petulant insistence of the Prime Minister that the flag issue has to be decided instead of dealing with the national labour code, the pension plan, and all of those other more important matters that should have been dealt with by this parliament. There is where the real blame lies. There is where the responsibility for leadership lies. We have been getting nothing in the way of leadership from the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister talks about change. Change is one thing and honesty is another. He has made the issue the question of change, but that is not the issue at all. We in this party are not against change. If this party were against change I for one would not be a member of it. Why does the government keep the union jack which is embodied in the second resolution and which we discarded 20 years ago? It is not a question of change. It is the kind of change and the manner in which the government is bulldozing its way to change. Have the traditions representative of a large and substantial body of Canadians the right to recognition, after having been recognized for 200 years in this country, or have they not? Apparently not, because their views are now gagged. They are cut off, they are stifled, they are throttled and they are not being heard because of the high handed and arbitrary action of the government in moving closure.
Canadian Flag
I ask the Prime Minister what happened to the three maple leaves? If he was sincere in June, is he sincere now? What changed him? He has not said a word about that nor have we heard any of his cabinet colleagues or any of the backbenchers say anything about that aspect. What gives this government the right to play games with Canada's flag? Why did they change? What gives the government the right to decide that the time has come to deprive a great segment of the Canadian people of their history and traditions? This has nothing to do with the past. These are things equally valid in the present. If they do not matter, why the feverish anxiety about remembering them?
The Prime Minister says he accepts the report of the committee and that all members of his cabinet do likewise, but that does not tell us for a moment what happened to the three maple leaves. The government will accept anything as long as it gets rid of the red ensign. The Prime Minister calls it a compromise. I say, sir, that it was no compromise. It was a deliberate scrapping of their three leaf design for partisan advantage.
It certainly was time for the Prime Minister to speak. I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) in his seat now. I think he should rise and tell us what his personal views are on the committee report. Is he in favour of the red maple leaf on the white background with the two red bars? There are other cabinet ministers here. The Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) is in his seat. Why does he not rise and state his personal views on the flag? I see the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Benidickson) completely absorbed in reading his newspaper. Why does he not rise and state his personal views?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I will vote.
I will vote too, Mr. Speaker, and I will vote against the single maple leaf because it means nothing to me whatsoever.
Shame.

There is something else I will vote against when the time comes to do so, and that is the imposition of closure in the House of Commons. I will vote against the gagging and throttling of parliamentary debate, because that is what is happening.
Another black Friday.

It is Friday again, and another black Friday, Mr. Speaker. When the Prime Minister spoke this morning it was the first

Canadian Flag
indication that any of us on this side of the house had so far as the Liberals are concerned that there was even a flag debate in progress, because we had not heard from a single minister sitting on the treasury benches. Where is the leadership to which this country is entitled?
We are working our way up.
You had better have a paid furniture invoice.

Mr. Speaker, every time I attempt to make a serious speech other members inject humour into it and it usually involves the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene).
Where, sir, in this single red leaf design is the heraldry, the history that were so eloquently described by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) in connection with the three maple leaf design that was so eloquently described by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in June when he introduced the resolution? Where has that gone? In June, the Prime Minister waxed eloquent about this design for the three leaf flag; it was the only one with tradition and history. Now he approaches the whole matter on tip-toe; the whole thing has been dumped in his lap. He is now saying, I accept the single leaf and so do all my cabinet colleagues. The fact remains, sir, this flag design was chosen by ten members of this house, seven of whom were Liberals while the other three were from the splinter groups to my left.
This afternoon the Prime Minister said, certainly, I put forward the three maple leaf design. He referred to the historical significance of it. He said also that the single maple leaf had historical significance. It is strange that this historical significance should suddenly show itself when it did not have any such significance last June when the three leaf design was introduced by him. He says, however, that the three leaves have greater significance. I suppose they have three times greater significance. The members of that committee chose the single leaf design, seven of them were Liberals, and yet we are asked to believe that it is not a partisan flag, that it is not a partisan issue. I am informed also, sir, that the Liberal members of that committee voted unanimously against the three leaf design. This afternoon the Prime Minister skated around that fact.
The fact remains, sir, that either the Prime Minister and those opposite were sincere in June when they said that only the three

leaves had the qualifications that were desirable in a national flag or they are not sincere now. They cannot have it both ways. Either they believe what they are saying now or they did not believe what they were saying then. If they did believe what they were saying last June, the only conclusion is that they changed their views to get the support of the Creditistes, the Social Crediters, and the members of the N.D.P. He injected into the debate this afternoon, and this to my mind was one of the Prime Minister's well known straw men, the fact that the report of the flag committee was a surrender to Quebec. I was sorry to hear him say this, because it only further inflames, and he must take responsibility for having done so, the French-English differences which appear in this country today. Who said, before he did this afternoon, that it was a surrender to Quebec? Whom was he quoting? Was it, perhaps, the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan)? No one on this side, certainly in the speeches to which I have listened or have read, has described the committee report as a surrender to Quebec.
I feel, sir, that it is a disgrace that Liberal cabinet ministers have not spoken in this debate. We have had to wait two weeks to find out where they stand, and we have had to learn that from the Prime Minister. I feel that cabinet ministers, in that spirit of leadership which is supposed to exist in any government, have a responsibility to see that we are informed on how they stand, what their personal views are. Having said these things or having indicated to the house partially why I intend to vote against closure and intend to vote against the single maple leaf design, I shall take my seat.

Mr. Speaker, like my colleague who spoke before me, I wish to say that I intend to vote against closure and vote against the maple leaf flag. In fact, many of us on this side wonder why only one member from that side expressed his views. I refer not to the frontbenchers as my colleague did, but to the backbenchers. Why have more of you not had the intestinal fortitude to get up and tell the people what you really think. You are going to have to go back and tell your constituents.
The other day one of the speakers in this house said that the backbenchers on the opposite side of the house looked and acted as if they were imprisoned in strait-jackets. Actually, that is the way they have looked

to us ever since this flag debate started. Today, as a result of the dictatorial action of the government, we have had strait-jackets imposed on us. I was very impressed this afternoon with the words uttered by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg), particularly when he reminded us of that poem "In Flanders Fields" by Colonel McCrae, part of which is, "to you from failing hands we throw the torch." I ask today, has that torch gone out? Have you thrown it?
I told you a few moments ago that you imposed a strait-jacket on us and we must accept it because that is the law of our country. I hope you are very proud of that. I said it appeared to us that you members on the back benches have refrained from speaking on this issue because you have been instructed to do so by your leaders. My colleague says you were threatened. I wonder what that threat was. The sole contribution that you people on the back benches have made in this debate-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; may I remind the hon. member that he should address the Chair?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am addressing the Chair and I excluded you from these remarks. The sole contribution that will go down in history that the back benches of this government have made to this loss of the red ensign for Canada is recorded in Hansard. It is interjections, interruptions, laughs, facetious questions, irresponsible points of order and privilege and ridicule. In my opinion, this major issue, this very important election promise that you people say you made-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please; the hon. member was cautioned a moment ago by the Chair that he cannot address other members of the house directly. He can only refer to them in the third person.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I will ask you, and possibly I can get an answer. We wonder why they have remained silent. We ask why they have remained silent. I am sure their constituents will ask them why they have remained silent. I know the veterans in their constituencies will ask them why they remained silent. I am sure that in future years the children of this country will ask them why they remained silent. They say it was because of a promise that they gave to the country to give the country a distinctive flag. I wonder if they are not confusing extinction with distinction by their actions.
Canadian Flag
They may well believe it when they say that this promise made must be fulfilled. I said in the house the other day that you people went out west and made one promise that was very dear to the hearts of the western farmers. You promised $2 wheat. What is going to happen to that promise? You also promised the labour people of Canada a labour code. What is going to happen to that promise?
One member of your party promised a Canada pension plan. What has happened to that? What happened to the medicare plan? What happened for the relief of those people depending on railway lines during the question of rail line abandonment? Why do you remain silent? Mr. Speaker, I hope when they answer they will answer through you, in the same manner as you asked me to ask these questions.
Is it because they have a tiger by the tail and are afraid to let go? Is that why they remain silent? Is that why they enforce closure? Is it because they have been instructed to keep silent? The people of Canada have a right to know. Certainly their constituents have a right to know why they sat silent during these days of debate except for, as I said before, interjections and interruptions.
Is it because they have no respect for the Canadian red ensign? Is that the reason they have remained silent? Is it because their constituents do not want them to speak up? The Hansard record will show how many times these backbenchers got up and spoke on this very important issue which they said must have priority above all others. They have said nothing on it. Is it because there have been other types of pressure put on them? Have they been told to keep quiet for some other reason? The country is entitled to know the answer. Are they too apathetic or too complacent, not caring whether the red ensign comes down or not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: No.

Is that the hon. member for Kootenay East? He has been on record more often in the House of Commons than most and has made the shortest speeches of anyone in the house. He makes them from a very good place, from his seat. Let him get up and tell us what he thinks about this flag. Why don't they speak?
I try to speak only once on any matter.

Yes, teacher.

Canadian Flag
Are they aware that the whole flag issue has become a red herring? The reason I say red herring is because I have in my hand The Western Producer oi December 10, which arrived just this morning. It shows a picture of a flag suggested by a certain group in the west, and I may say this is a publication which to my knowledge has never been favourable to this side of the house but is always favourable to the party that forms the government. The caption under the picture reads:
Frank Cushon of Oxbow is shown holding his "red herring" flag which he introduced to the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan farmers' union in Saskatoon last week. The design was introduced as a joke but S.F.U. delegates took it seriously and decided to send a copy of the flag to Ottawa for consideration by the House of Commons.
Why did the Liberals introduce this red herring in the first place? Is it because they needed another 60 days of decision? We could have given them another 60 days. We could have given them a recess which cabinet ministers could have spent in their offices preparing bills properly.
Was it to divert public attention from more inefficient government or was it, as Time magazine said, for spite? I do not have Time magazine with me, but it referred to the action taken by the Prime Minister after the famous Legion meeting in Winnipeg. It said they never saw a man react so fast as after the reception he got at that meeting.
The government has conveyed to the public that the decision on the flag shall be left to the judgment of members of parliament. Dealing with the judgment of members of parliament I ask, do hon. members opposite, with but one exception, agree with what Edmund Burke has said about members of parliament and their duty? I quote the following extract:
Soul-searching and attention to business are what a great parliamentarian and political philosopher of the so-called golden age of oratory believed should be principal ingredients in the life of an M.P.
Edmund Burke said in the 1770's that an M.P. should "live in the strictest union, the closest correspondence, and the most unreserved communication with his constituents."
"Their wishes ought to have great weight with him; their opinion high respect; their business unremitted attention. It is his duty to sacrifice his repose, his pleasures, his satisfaction, to their's; and above all, ever, and in all cases, to prefer their interests to his own."
Burke also held the view that an M.P. isn't elected simply to vote slavishly on every question as his electors demand. He is elected as a man of judgment on whom the electors should be able to depend. As Burke put it:
[Mr. McIntosh.)
"Your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment; and he betrays instead of serving you if he sacrifices it for your opinion."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
