subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION

speakeroldname: Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-68, to amend the Criminal Code (nuisance).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have introduced this bill on a number of occasions. In fact it is an identical copy of one that was introduced by the former prime minister, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) prior to his assuming the reins of office. I thought the bill had a great deal of merit at that time and since then I have introduced it from year to year in the hope that it will be a first step in doing something about the prevention of pollution of our waters.
The purpose of the bill is to make it an offence for the owners of industrial plants and oil refineries or other persons to discharge noxious matter into an interprovincial water thus endangering the lives, safety, health and comfort of the public.
In the first instance the bill was introduced to prevent, if possible, the pollution of certain waters that came from the province of Alberta and flowed into the Saskatchewan river.
For many years I have been very interested in the conservation of natural resources. I want to say that we can talk all we like about pension plans, national medicare plans and all the other social improvements that all members of this house desire; but unless

we maintain and improve our national resources, our standard of living in the future- and the not very far distant future-will begin to decline. All civilizations have been based on a foundation of adequate natural resources. I have been interested in this subject all my life, Mr. Speaker, and I know something about it. I have tried to do what I can in my own small way to conserve the land that I hold at the present time as a trustee for the government, pending the revolution. I have tried to do the same with the rivers and waters that flow on my property, and the forests and the wildlife. I believe I have had considerable success, so far as a private owner can under this free enterprise system. However, on that account for years I moved a motion in the house in the following words:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of calling a dominion-provincial conference on conservation, with the view to the establishment of a nationwide policy on soil, forest and water conservation and land use for Canada.
Strangely enough, Mr. Speaker, although over quite a number of years all members of the house supported this resolution in principle and gave it their blessing, shall I say, no action was taken as far as the resolution was concerned; it was talked out at the end of the usual private members' hour. On one occasion when I raised the matter the minister at that time replied. I am quoting from page 1565 of Hansard of February 27, 1956, where I said:
When speaking on my resolution last year the minister gave three reasons for not agreeing to accept it. While he supported the principles of conservation in general, he gave these three reasons for not being able to accept the resolution. First, he said that the prime responsibility for conservation of resources rests with the provincial governments. Second, he said that the suggestion for federal action should come from the provincial governments. Third, he had grave doubts as to the success of a conference called to deal with all renewable natural resources.
I want to give full credit to the former minister of northern affairs and national resources for his calling the renewable resources conference in Montreal in the summer of 1961, when numerous very interesting papers were delivered to the conference. As the result of this conference there was the establishment of the Canadian council of resource ministers, and I am glad to see, from reading the reports that I get from this council, that they are beginning to tackle this question. They have laid out a program in which the question of pollution takes a prominent part,
Criminal Code
and they are also providing for the receipt of information from other nations regarding research with respect to natural resources and their development. They are also providing for an exchange of information between the federal government and the provincial governments. I give the former minister, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), great credit for calling that conference. I think the circumstances were somewhat different then, inasmuch as the former government of Mr. Duplessis had been defeated and I believe it is quite correct to say that the atmosphere in Quebec was more conducive to calling a conference of this type than it had been in years past. I am glad to know that this council is laying down a program dealing with this problem.
I am also very glad that the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) has recognized the tremendous need for a national water management policy and has made a number of speeches on this question. I note that some time ago, through, shall I say, the vehicle of his very distinguished and good looking parliamentary secretary, he made a speech in Montreal on the question, in which he clearly indicated that he realizes what we have to do in this respect and what price the public is paying for confused policies, haphazard programs and ill planned projects. He went on to deal with the damage caused by floods; the situation with respect to shipping in some of our rivers; the depletion, often to perilously low levels, of those secure supplies of fresh drinking water without which great cities cannot exist; the virtual destruction of our once great commercial fisheries. Then he dealt with the pollution problem that is only beginning to be faced. Then he went on to deal with the slow decay of sports fishing in some areas that had previously enjoyed an international reputation; the acute shortage of water for irrigation and other purposes in farm areas; the need for water for recreational purposes, and the water required for industrial purposes. Then he dealt in a very interesting way with the fragmentation of government authority in the water resources field which, he said, "fosters a fierce rivalry and a devil-take-the-hindmost empire-building in competitive government agencies, encourages waste and duplication of effort and the taxpayers' money and which virtually guarantees an appallingly uneconomic use of water resources which, however vast, are not limitless". He then dealt with other aspects of the question and made

Criminal Code
certain proposals on how the government of the day should meet this situation. I was very pleased to see him face up to this question, because it is a very important one facing us at this time.
I want to quote briefly from an article that appeared in the October 9 issue of the Globe and Mail. It is headed, "But in the mass we're a pack of vandals". I agree with that sentiment and I could use that word "vandals" in a much wider way than possibly I should use it under the present circumstances. This article says:
One of the more certain ways of making sure that one does not run out of essential goods is to make sure that one does not waste, despoil or pollute the bountiful supplies one already has. This is a fairly straightforward fact of life which is readily comprehended by most individual humans; but it is a fact that takes an awful lot of getting through the heads of the human mass.
It is a question that is going to take a great deal of education, not only in parliament and in organizations interested in this question but in our universities, high schools and the public schools. Every one of our children going to school, regardless of their age, should have their attention directed as soon as possible to the great importance of these issues. The article goes on to say:
Canadians who appreciate a comfortable life do not stuff good food into the garbage can, smash up their furniture, yank up their rosebushes or pour the fresh cream in with the sour. They have too much respect for themselves and their possessions to indulge in such vandalism.
Yet these same Canadians, in that larger home of theirs which is the country, happily litter their parks, destroy their forests, waste their topsoil and pollute their rivers and lakes. These things are quite as essential to their well-being as their more personal possessions, are, in fact, the basic wealth from which many of the personal possessions spring. But belonging to everybody they seem, in the contradictory human mind, to belong to nobody and therefore not to be worth preserving.
I think that article very clearly states the question. As I said before, unless we do something to conserve and develop these renewable natural resources of ours as a result of management policies, our standard of living which we enjoy today and the opportunities for its possible improvement through legislation both in this house and in the legislatures of the various provinces will decline in the years ahead. There is no question of that, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I am very concerned with this particular issue. In my opinion we in this house are responsible for doing what we can to improve this situation as the result of legislation or amendments to existing legislation, and by keeping

the public informed of the seriousness of the situation.
Water is so important in life that its conservation and distribution must override the geographical boundaries of private property, counties and provinces, the political boundaries of federal and provincial jurisdictions, and the economic domains of agriculture, forestry and industry. If jurisdictional disputes prevent effective action, our heritage in natural resources will be lost by default, because above all boundaries is the supreme natural law the edicts of which are indisputable.
All that is to be done must start in the minds of citizens. "We may well ask", said John H. Storer, renowned lecturer on the natural world, in his book "The Web of Life", which I recommend to all hon. members to read, "whether man will develop understanding before he destroys himself by destroying his environment". To which may be added what was written by Myra Mannes, United States writer and commentator, in her book "More in Anger", which again I recommend members secure from the library and read, when she referred to "people who conserved their convenience at the expense of their heritage, and whose ephemeral prosperity was built on waste". The least we can do as responsible individuals is to become informed about the problems and make our voices heard in demanding conservation of our most priceless material resource, which I think at the present time without any doubt is water.
Before concluding my brief remarks I want to deal with a subject that does indicate the great value of water not only to Canadian subjects but to people in the United States and other countries. I want to refer to a statement made by the North American power and water alliance. The United States senate has appointed Senator Frank Moss of Utah as chairman of the new water development subcommittee. This subcommittee, known as NAWAPA-North American water and power alliance-has been appointed to make a study of how the waters of the Yukon, Northwest Territories and British Columbia-our waters, mind you-can be drawn down to the states of Utah, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, California and Arizona to make their deserts bloom. It is the wish of the United States senate to store this water in what is known as the Rocky mountain trench, in British Columbia. The United States senate wishes to turn the Rocky mountain trench into a huge lake 500 miles long if these schemes come to fruition; and I

mention this to indicate how concerned they are with the problem of water. The water from this 500 mile long lake would be taken by way of canals, reservoirs, tunnels and rivers to water the great American deserts of the previously mentioned six states. Perhaps even more important, these waters would be used for expansion of industries and populations in cities like Los Angeles, Phoenix, Tucson and many others.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what is happening in this question? The United States is coming to Canada with the proverbial hat in hand claiming that they are all but out of water. Is their claim genuine, or are they conserving their own water for long range future expansion? The United States knows that at the present time Canada is still very much underpopulated, and perhaps does not realize how important water will be for Canada's future growth. Senator Moss has stated on several occasions:
The era of space probes and miracle drugs has not changed man's dependence upon "the life blood of civilization". Cities and nations grow in direct ratio to their water supply. When that supply fails, they perish.
As they have in past history.
If Canada gives away all of her western water supply, can she continue to grow as a nation? Indeed, can she continue as a nation at all? Since 1940, or in the past 24 years, Canada's population has jumped from 10 million to 19 million. It is quite realistic to suppose that in the next 20 to 25 years the population could expand to 40 or 50 million. To support a population of this size we will have to turn away from a lot of uneconomical dry farms to irrigation of smaller, more productive farmsteads. If the United States plan is carried out, all the water of any importance left to Canada will be the Saskatchewan river system, as far as western Canada is concerned. But even now, before the Elbow dam on the Saskatchewan is finished, it is believed that the water supply will not be adequate to meet the present needs of Saskatchewan. That does not give us much hope for the future, unless we can tap some of the Arctic or British Columbia rivers. In all probability, we will be needing both these sources.
I could go on and deal further with this question, but in concluding this portion of my remarks I want to say that at the Canadian end of Senator Moss's project most of the rivers would have to be reversed. That is, the United States would have to make the rivers flow backwards and do a great deal
Criminal Code
of engineering miracles to accomplish that end. This plan has not been put into effect. Fortunately, I think the government of the day is aroused to the circumstances of the present situation and are determined, according to the statements made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) and his parliamentary secretary (Mr. Turner), to develop a water management policy which will protect the needs of Canada both at the present time and for generations to come.
I have dealt with this vast project, the North American water and power alliance, only briefly, Mr. Speaker, so as to indicate how important is this question of water on the North American continent and what the United States is having to do to obtain additional supplies. My bill, shall I say, takes a somewhat shallower approach to the situation than the one I have been developing, but I have used this argument to indicate the urgency of the situation and the need for the development of policy. I was very surprised to realize when I was in the committee on mines, forests and waters the other day that there has been a committee of deputy ministers from various departments throughout the years which is supposed to meet periodically and come to decisions as the result of interdepartmental consultations on various water questions which are brought to their attention. And what do we discover? We discover that at the present time the committee has not even a secretariat, and we could not get very complete information as to when the committee had met and what its decisions had been over the last few years.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, and I see you looking anxiously at me, I urge the house to consider the purposes of my bill amending the Criminal Code as a first step toward the further prevention of pollution of our rivers which flow from one province to another, or which may in the future be transferred from one province to another by gravity or by pumping. This amendment to the Criminal Code represents only a minor step, but I suggest we take that first step on that long road we have to travel.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph P. O'Keefe (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) on the presentation of this bill. I assure him that I agree wholeheartedly with the principles of it; however, I have some reservations as to its effect. First of

Criminal Code
all, I do not think a private member's bill is the proper way of doing this job and, second, that Bill C-68 is not wide enough or all embracive enough.
We quite frankly admit that and suggest that this is only a minor step in the right direction.

through in the process of using our vast store of salt water would revolutionize the world's economy. President Kennedy was right. It is a far more exciting prospect and surely a far more practicable one than landing on the moon.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to give my general support to the bill. My remarks will be brief because I see the time is getting short and I know that other members of the house would like to speak on this subject. The reason I support the bill is that at heart I am a conservationist. I think that any of us who have travelled abroad from this fair Canada, particularly those who have travelled to the Far East and who have seen the situation that exists there today, where conservation has been one of the last things the people have had in mind, have very quickly become conservationists.
I am very pleased to see that the whole matter of conservation and the whole matter of pollution are very much in the minds of other organized bodies throughout the world than the one the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) just mentioned in his speech. I have just returned from the NATO parliamentarians meeting in Paris. Although I was a member of the military committee, I noticed that the scientific committee had this matter under consideration. They were dealing particularly with the pollution of water as a result of nuclear development, but they went very much beyond that in their deliberations.
If we want to bring the matter somewhat closer to home, I would point out that in today's Globe and Mail there is an article describing how a whale was killed off the Oregon coast, off the Pacific coast from which I come, and the whale apparently had become radioactive as a result of the waste products carried down the Columbia river from the Hanford atomic plant. The fault I find with the bill, as the hon. member himself admitted, is that it does not go far enough. I should like to see the problem of pollution dealt with in a more general and broader way than is done in the bill. I think it is one of the basic requirements for the enjoyment of life that we should have clean water and clean air and that we should preserve the beauty of our countryside, including the preservation of wildlife, flora and fauna.
So far in my life I have seen tremendous changes take place in my part of the country. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, a great

period of industrial expansion is now under way in the west. I am not going to blame the industrial firms themselves. There is a statement to be found on page 823 of Hansard for February 13, 1962, which I think covers the situation very clearly. If certain things that are going on in my part of the country today are taking place, I believe it is because the companies involved are not being pressured to take action and very naturally they will do nothing until they are. I wish to read an extract from a paper prepared by Mr. J. R. Menzies, chief of the public health engineering division, Department of National Health and Welfare, Ottawa. He states in part:
Broadly speaking, the effects of pollution become a matter of general interest only when they are notoriously bad.
I am taking part in this debate today because although I do not think things are notoriously bad in British Columbia, yet they could be better and, as the hon. member has suggested, I think we must be vigilant with regard to the industrial development that is going on in my part of the country. In this bill we are dealing with the pollution of clean water. Clean water comes from creeks, rivers and lakes, and it is not only clean drinking water about which I am concerned. In my area we have a large fishing industry. The same clean water for human consumption about which we are speaking also provides the basis for a very profitable commercial fishing industry and also provides a very valuable source of revenue, through moneys expended by tourists interested in sport fishing. If we are going to keep the water clean for human consumption I think that at the same time we must give equal this commercial fishing industry and sports attention to keeping the rivers, streams and lakes clear to provide a base from which fishing industry is derived.
I have noticed that within recent years in my own part of the country, because of the method of logging, the area in which many of the small streams and lakes are located has been laid waste. This has resulted in flash floods which wash down sand and gravel into the streams covering the spawning beds with mud. I have noticed that slash is left to accumulate in the creeks and the salmon cannot get up the rivers to spawn. If they are able to spawn their fry are not able to survive, because of these flash floods tearing down the spawning beds.
When we are looking at the matter of water pollution, upon which I am only touch-

ing in view of the time element in this debate, we should look also at the matter of air pollution. I think we have a big problem. The problem is, Mr. Speaker, that no one seems to be taking a stand against the pollution of the atmosphere.
Some 20 or 30 miles north of my riding, we have a very large pulp and paper sulphite mill. When the wind and weather conditions are right there is a most unpleasant smell in the atmosphere which emanates from these plants. It may be that this is the smell of money, Mr. Speaker, but it is also something which I find simply appalling. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) will agree, I am sure, that something could be done if we were to provide a body to look after the interests of the public in connection with this type of thing. In the case of the large smelter at Trail, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company were eventually persuaded to remove from the atmosphere the poisons that were being poured out of their smelter. They only took this action under pressure. I find that no pressure is being brought to bear upon the pulp and paper company. I am sure that if there were, if there were some central organization to apply this pressure, we would long since have had this ghastly smell removed from the atmosphere.
Why is it that nothing is being done? I notice the hon. gentleman has brought forward this bill many times in the past. I have been very interested in reading what has been said, and agree wholeheartedly with it. An almost identical bill was brought before the house, as the hon. member said, by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in years past. Why has nothing been done about it? I think perhaps it is because this is a matter which obviously has federal and provincial implications. Even in so far as the federal government is concerned, who knows which department of government is responsible for looking into these matters? Is it a matter for the Department of National Health and Welfare? I suppose that it relates to both health and welfare. Is it a matter for Northern Affairs and National Resources? I think it comes under national resources. Is it a matter which should be the responsibility of the minister who has jurisdiction in the field of federal-provincial relations? I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is the responsibility of all three.
Now, in so far as conservation is concerned, since it is related to the question of
Criminal Code
pollution, I should like to cite a personal experience which I hope will be of interest to hon. members in this house and drive home to them the importance of this problem. I can recall some years ago going up a river in China, the Yangtze, and believe me this is a river that can only be used for irrigation purposes and for travel. It is not a thing of beauty. It is so polluted, Mr. Speaker, that if any westerner happens to fall over the side of the boat into the river he is immediately brought ashore and put into a hospital where he is filled with wonder drugs and kept under surveillance. This is the kind of thing that happens when you are not careful about matters of pollution.
In dealing with the matter of conservation, perhaps hon. members would be interested in knowing that this river is yellow and muddy because there has been no thought given to preserving the contours of the land, to keep the underbrush and trees growing to prevent flash floods, such as those I mentioned in my part of the country, and which there give rise to the spoiling of the salmon fishing beds. In fact, as you go up this mighty Yangtze river, when you get to within 50 or 60 miles of a town, the trees disappear. This results from the people leaving the towns to chop down the trees for firewood. When you get within 30 miles of the town all the shrubs disappear and there is nothing left but grass. This is a further evidence of the despoiling of the country for human needs. Then, the most appalling aspect of it occurs when you get within ten miles of a town and you find there is not a blade of living grass in sight. The needs of the population have required them to take the grass and the roots, dry them out and put them up in bundles for fuel. This is something which has happened in another land and it is the sight of this sort of thing which has made a conservationist out of me. It is the reason for my support of this bill.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I recommend that this subject should be brought up at the next federal-provincial conference so that the federal-provincial representatives can agree on joint responsibility for conservation and pollution. Terms of reference should be laid down for a joint board to handle all these aspects of pollution and conservation to which the hon. member has referred. The only fault I can find with this bill is that it does not go far enough.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my support for the bill which has been presented by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-

Criminal Code
ridge). This bill has been introduced before and has given rise to very interesting discussions on various aspects of the conservation policies of this country. I think the bill itself, by the very limitation of its form and the fact that it only calls for an amendment to the Criminal Code, indicates some of the complexities that arise because of the constitutional situation in this country in connection with the development of adequate conservation policies. However I feel that, since it has been introduced year after year, the hon. member for Kootenay West has been the cause of creating great interest in this subject in Canada. Certainly for this reason, if for no other, the hon. member is to be commended for introducing it.
Perhaps some hon. members are not aware of the genesis of this bill. It used to be introduced prior to 1957 by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). It may be recalled that it was due to a problem of pollution in the North Saskatchewan river, in which my former colleague, the then hon. member for The Battlefords, used to take an active part. Therefore I am a little puzzled not to see the hon. member for Prince Albert or the present hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Horner) in their places to support this bill.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) is to be commended for having taken up a good idea and having pursued it throughout the years, even without much apparent support from the hon. member for Prince Albert in the years since 1957. I hope the time may come again when that hon. member will lend his voice in support of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that this bill should pass, for reasons that have previously been indicated. It is a narrow bill and deals only with a portion of the problem. On the other hand I think the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has done the house a service by raising the problem.
One of the great things I am worried about is that the public generally does not seem to care about the problem of water pollution, and this can be overcome by discussing the matter in the House of Commons. I grew up adjacent to and have lived all my life on the shores of one of the great lakes. I spent my summers there and still do. I have become very concerned about and aware of the pollution that is taking place in the great lakes, and I would like to quote from an article which

appeared in the Financial Post on April 18 last, dealing with the extent of pollution in the great lakes area:
This is what's happening in the biggest expanse of fresh water in the world around which 25 per cent of all Canadians live and work:
On lake Erie and lake Michigan, studies made by the great lakes institute indicate that, although 60 per cent of the sewage and industrial effluents are treated before being dumped into these lakes, it is essential to treat at least 80 per cent of polluted water to restore the impure-pure balance.
There is a "dead" area of about 2,000 square miles at the bottom of lake Erie where fish and other organisms cannot live-there is no oxygen. The phenol count-refuse discharged by industries -is higher than the level recommended by the international joint commission, a body set up by Canada and the U.S.
It is doubtful whether any beach in lake Erie is fit for swimming. The turbidity and amount of dissolved salts has increased during the past few years.
The general tenor of the article is that lake Erie and lake Michigan are already polluted almost beyond repair.
The other great lakes are suffering pollution to a lesser degree, but the pollution is reaching dangerous levels. I know from friends of mine who have summer cottages on the Muskoka lakes, north of Toronto, that those lakes are also becoming polluted and their waters unfit for consumption.
There is no need to spend a great deal of time indicating the problems which arise from this. Everyone is aware of the effect on the health of people. We are all aware of the impact on our recreational facilities. There is no doubt about the impact on our natural resources, the fish in the waters and the birds that nest by those waters. There is also the impact on industry.
In short, it is a situation that cannot be allowed to continue, yet it is one we have allowed to continue. It is a man-made problem and through our lack of care we are in the process of destroying in the great lakes area one of the major natural resources of the country.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.
We are now on an amendment moved this afternoon-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: We are on private members' hour.
You are right. O.K.

At least I am glad I know where I am this afternoon.

All we have to do to cure the problem is stop pumping sewage into the water, stop adding industrial waste to the water, stop ships from dumping their garbage and sewage into the water, and stop pleasure craft from dumping sewage into the water. On the face of it, it seems a simple problem. The mechanical solutions are simple but the ways of achieving them are not. There are many jurisdictions involved. There is much study involved. Many costs are involved.
The cost of treating all sewage dumped by municipalities into the water, and which is not now treated, would be staggering and the municipalities involved probably do not have the ready funds available quickly to undertake this work.
We will arrive at a solution by discussing the matter and being concerned with the problem, and by referring it to the council of resource ministers, something which has already been mentioned. The ten provincial resource ministers and the federal minister are going to look at this problem from the national point of view and as a result of their work I hope we will reach financial solutions involved in the problem.
Business of the House
Further, I hope that when the international joint commission has dealt with the problem of great lakes water levels it will take this matter up. And before my time expires I make one further suggestion. I hope that when the committee of the House of Commons which is currently dealing with the problem of great lakes water levels has finished its study, it will inquire into this equally important problem of the pollution of these great natural resources.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-EDITORIAL IN TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAIL"

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-EDITORIAL IN TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of an editorial which appeared in this morning's Globe and Mail. I could take objection to other parts of this editorial, but I should like to refer to this part which deals with me personally, and which reads as follows:
It is Canada's misfortune that the new flag was proposed at a time when the Leader of the Opposition was a man who did not scruple to pour derision on the device it was to bear, the maple leaf. The maple leaf has had a place of honour in Canada. It speaks for Canada around the world, and marks the sleeping places of all the dead of all our wars. Yet the Leader of the Opposition and the red ensign diehards of his party have mocked the maple leaf, and now they have forced its introduction by closure.
This is the flag that is to fly above us, to express our pride of nationhood: and Mr. John G. Diefenbaker has not hesitated to besmirch it with words and now with this action.
Sir, that editorial in so far as it contains those allegations is a gross perversion of the truth. I have not risen on a question of privilege of this kind in all the many years I have been here because, after all, the press always gets the last say. However, that statement cannot remain unchallenged because my last reference to this was made on December 11 as reported in Hansard at page 11045, at which time I was referring to the Prime Minister and I said:
He manufactured a false claim when he used the expression that we sneered at the maple leaf. There was nothing of that kind. Many of us on this side of the house are proud of the maple leaf, but the maple leaf as an emblem is a long way from the maple leaf as the design for a flag.
An example occurs to me as I am speaking. What about Ireland? Ireland established itself as an independent country after generations of turmoil and difficulty. It decided on a flag. The emblem of Ireland is the shamrock. Did they place the shamrock on the flag? The shamrock was a symbol, but when they built their flag they made it a flag of two colours representative of the unity of their country, orange and green. Certainly no one casts aspersions on the maple leaf. We are all
proud of it as a symbol of the nation. However, there is a great deal of difference between symbolic significance and that which goes to the heart and soul of a nation, the flag that must represent the people as a whole.
I simply say that the suggestion that at any time I cast aspersions on the maple leaf is a falsehood and an attempt apparently to misrepresent my position as being one which I have never held, do not hold now and never will hold.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the close of the debate on Friday I had made reference to a quotation from Edmund Burke who said, and I shall read the complete last line of the quotation:
Your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment; and he betrays instead of serving you if he sacrifices it for your opinion.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has stated that in his judgment Canada needs a new flag to unite the country. Does the Prime Minister feel that he has achieved that purpose? Does he believe that by force he has given Canada the flag she needed? In my opinion force can never unite any country or any people. I regret that the flag we are going to have to honour in the future will have been imposed upon the people of Canada by force through the use of closure in this house. That is not a proud beginning for a flag which we should look up to with pride.
On Friday the Prime Minister said he had support for this flag from all parties in this house. He neglected to tell the people of Canada that there is opposition to this flag from all parties in this house. I think that fact should also be made known. Opposition has been indicated toward this design by members of every party of this house, so how can the Prime Minister say this flag will unite Canada? I do not think he has proved his point.
The Prime Minister dwelt upon that point at great length, and he seemed to be proud of the fact that he was in a position where he could use force at this time. I am sure the Prime Minister is not blind to the fact that the same disintegration of unity which has taken place in this house in relation to this question has taken place across Canada in each and every province. That same disunity does exist and will continue to exist.
On an earlier occasion I suggested that the flag issue had created more factions than have ever existed before. Before this debate on the flag issue there was not one faction which supported the three maple leaves design, one which supported the single maple 20220-700J
Canadian Flag
leaf design, and another which supported a modified version of the red ensign. I suggest, therefore, that there are three more factions which have been created in this country by the flag question and debate.
How can the Prime Minister take any pleasure from his belief that the flag issue and the adoption of the single maple leaf design will unite Canada? I suggest that the attitudes expressed during the debate on this issue confirm the suggestion that this has created more disunity in Canada than any other piece of legislation placed before parliament in the history of this country. Only after the passage of time will we know the over-all effects of this flag issue. Our constituencies are represented by people of all nationalities, yet there are now more factions supporting various proposals than there have ever been.
I regret that I cannot look upon this flag with pride, even after hearing all the arguments that have been presented to this house by members not only on this side but on the other side of the house. We regret, in fact, that more members on that side of the house have not risen to state the views of their constituents. Surely, Mr. Speaker, all those members on that side who have remained silent during all the days of this debate are not representing the views of all their constituents by so doing. They have not even expressed regret that they cannot support the opinions of certain factions in their constituencies. They have not said one word in favour of the flag that has been flying over this country for a great many years. Many of us on this side of the house would like to hear them express their opinions. We wonder why they have sat silent as they have and not uttered one word.
Actually their attitude does not affect us on this side of the house. They will be responsible to their constituents and will have to answer to them for their silence on this matter. I should like to refer to a couple of newspaper editorials. I will not read all of them, but I think they express much better than I can what I am trying to get across to the house. I quote first from the Winnipeg Tribune of May 19 last:
It is this newspaper's opinion that the timing of this flag proposal is bad.

If the main purpose is to consolidate unity it is a peculiar approach for, as witnessed at the Legion meeting, the dominant reaction is disunity.
That I believe.
Unfortunately, too, the Prime Minister's approach leaves little ground for thoughtful consideration. He asks, in effect, for a surrender of what is known for something unknown. He entertains a mystique about the price of unity which he is unable to articulate. In addition to poor timing, the method of introducing the design was odd ...
He has placed himself and his government on the record to introduce a new flag. He has rejected the proposal for a national plebiscite and insists that the issue must be decided on a free vote in the Commons.
I should like to say something more about that free vote but I do not have the time.
But then he has also added that the result would be interpreted by his government as a vote of confidence. In other words, he is prepared to fight an election on the issue. 5. It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.

On the 17th March, 1933, a member quoting a newspaper in debate was ruled out of order by the Deputy Speaker who said: "The rule is quite clear, that the quoting of a newspaper, an author or a book which reflects upon debate before the house, either directly or indirectly, is entirely out of order, because members are here to give their own opinion and not to quote the opinion of others. .. .Members may quote an article or a book stating facts, but a commentary on any proceeding or any discussion in the house, with the object of swinging an opinion to one side or the other, is out of order." Can. Deb. 1932-33, vol. 3, pp. 3103-4.
In view of the authority cited I am sure the hon. member will do his best to give his own personal opinion.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think Your Honour will agree that it is common practice in the house to refer to newspaper editorials. This is one of the most difficult areas for the Chair to rule upon. I would say that the limitation is very narrow, in that reference cannot be made to editorials which comment on proceedings in the house, and that the citation is not so wide that reference to editorials or books or articles is precluded. They are commonly cited and have been for years by members both on the government side and on the opposition side. I would say that an editorial or article which commented upon the motivation of voting or on the procedure would infringe upon the rule, but certainly there is not and never has been a rule in the house which prevents an hon. member from citing an editorial in support of his argument. This is done regularly, and I think Your Honour has ample knowledge of that.
I submit that the limitation has to do with commenting on proceedings of the house. I suggest it would be improper for an hon. member to read an editorial stating that another hon. member was wrong in his presentation of the facts. I suggest to Your Honour that the restriction on reading editorials from newspapers is a limited and not a wide restriction. Therefore I think that, with appropriate care, the hon. member should be able to proceed under these circumstances just as all hon. members have been able to do in the past.

even lengthy excerpts from editorials being allowed. However, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) said he was going to read a whole editorial. That is where I feel he is out of order.

But I am under the impression that this hon. member, not satisfied with having succeeded in bringing down closure, would very much like to be named, so that he could say, in his riding, that he was obliged to leave the house-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not know which one. However, I will dispense with that. I will say that in my opinion this issue is now creating disunity throughout the country, and there is more confusion about this issue than ever before.
The country has been told by the Prime Minister and the members of his party that if an election were held on this issue it would split the country and create disunity, and this was one of the reasons he adopted this method of implementing his desire. I say, too, that stubbornness is no substitute for statesmanship.
One writer has expressed the view that in the selection of a flag we should strive for some common understanding of what a flag is. We should understand what it means. One common understanding that has been evident from the speeches that have been made from both sides of the house is that we want to be Canadians. I believe the other day I made reference to a number of speeches from the various parties in this house who have said that we all want to be Canadians, whether we are designated now as French Canadians, English Canadians, Irish Canadians, Scotch Canadians or whatever. In fact this has been the common denominator throughout all these speeches. Can we not start from that point?
I should like at this time to ask the Prime Minister and the members of his party just what flag would be flying over Canada today, what conditions we would be living under today, if it had not been for Britain during the last two wars. This is something that I think a lot of us have forgotten. It is said that we who have supported the inclusion of the union jack as some part of our new Canadian flag should not refer to tradition. I cannot help but refer to tradition when I think of those things. If I came from French Canada or if I came from the province of Quebec I would say that those early explorers, those great pioneers who came from France

Canadian Flag
and settled in Quebec, should in some way be remembered by the people of Canada today for what they have done in creating this country of which we are so proud. Would we have a country like we have today if it were not for those people?
During this debate, Mr. Speaker, we have expressed our views as individuals. We have expressed our views as members of this party. We think we have expressed the views of our constituents. In fact some of us go so far as to say that we feel we have expressed the views of the majority of the people of Canada. We have been criticized in the press. We have been accused of obstruction, and apparently some members opposite think that is what we have been doing. I can say that I believe every one of us has spoken with conviction. We believe that as members of parliament we are using our judgment when we debate this very important issue, and the Prime Minister has said it is a very important issue. We have been debating this issue sincerely. I hope I will not again hear the suggestion that we have been obstructing on this issue.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for the time allotted in favour of the committee's report suggesting the maple leaf design as Canada's flag. I do this first of all because the flag that is being proposed is one which has been selected by a committee which represented all the parties in this house. This committee sat continuously for two months and made this recommendation under the able chairmanship of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten).
If we are dedicated to democratic principles, and I believe everyone in this house is so dedicated, then I believe it behooves us, after having expressed every shade of opinion that can be expressed on this subject, to let the democratic process take its course by bringing the matter to a vote and accepting the vote of this house. The maple leaf design that is being proposed is not a renunciation or a betrayal on our part of our Christian principles. Indeed, were we by a mere change of exterior symbols to cast off our traditions, our past, our Christian beliefs and everything that we hold near and dear, then certainly all those things would be very shallow indeed.
But, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that after this debate has ended and this flag has been adopted we, as a Canadian and Christian nation, will continue to adhere to all those things that make our country great, that make the British heritage great, that

make the French heritage great, and which indeed make our civilization worth living and fighting for. Whether we fly the union jack, the red ensign, the maple leaf flag or any other symbol we shall certainly continue to practise those liberties and respect those institutions which go far deeper than mere exterior symbols. Speaking as a Quebecker I think I should be the last person in the world to want to cast off the past and not honour it, nor to honour the British institutions that have given us our freedom, especially when the motto of my province is "Je me souviens" -I remember.
The maple leaf is a true Canadian symbol. Canadians recognize it as such everywhere, and others recognize us as Canadians by the maple leaf symbol. It is instantly recognizable and identifiable as a Canadian symbol no matter where a Canadian may go throughout the world. It is a symbol which was very much alive among servicemen during the second world war. Is it not a fact that the burial places of all those brave and true Canadians who gave up their lives are marked by a maple leaf? I recall travelling throughout western Europe at the end of the second world war and seeing that the routes which were travelled by Canadian forces all over Europe were studded with and indicated by the maple leaf, the symbol that led our forces to victory and which is also the symbol of the future.
I refuse to accept that the maple leaf can, in any sense of the word, be recognized as an exclusive or narrow Quebec symbol. It has never been accepted as such. It is an all Canadian symbol. Some have said that the maple leaf flag is a concession to Quebec. If by that is meant that it is a symbol which is acceptable to Quebec then I am entirely in agreement, because it is also a symbol acceptable to all Canadians no matter what their origins may be. But, Mr. Speaker, if by stating that the maple leaf is a concession to or an appeasement of Quebec one wants to stir up differences between the racial groups in this country, then I say that attempt is most damnable and contemptible.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The new flag is the symbol of the future because it expresses unity, that unity to which so many of us have paid lip service during the course of this debate. I believe that in the maple leaf Canadians of whatever origin or background may find something in common. I believe this maple leaf flag will express for Canadians, in their

own undemonstrative and taciturn way, the firm conviction that Canadians want to live together, work together and build a worthwhile nation.
If this distinctive flag can be accepted by the country without lasting bitterness and acrimony, then Canadians will have gone a long way to prove to the world that a nation such as ours, born in strife, diverse in its origins, speaking two languages and being the embodiment of two great cultures, can survive and prosper.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
During the course of this debate many hard and bitter words have been spoken that it would have been better to have left unsaid. It is useless, futile and, I feel, mischievous to try at this stage to assess blame in this chamber or elsewhere. But the truth remains-and it is a bitter truth-that the embers of hatred and prejudice have been fanned, and if they should continue uncontrolled they could very well lead to disaster and the end of our nation. That is why this afternoon I approved and voted for the extreme measure that is closure; because I am firmly convinced that the continuance of this debate at this stage, after it has given rise throughout the land to so many utterances born of prejudice and hatred, could only achieve its normal course, the very destruction of this country.
It may be well to look at others and learn a lesson from history. Almost 100 years ago the United States of America, our great neighbours, today's leaders of freedom, were engaged in a murderous civil war. Fortunately, and I thank God, this has not happened in our country, and I trust and believe it will never happen. When President Lincoln, in his second inaugural address, spoke to congress in Washington, his country's murderous and bloody civil war had been raging for many years. As he addressed congress his mind must have lingered on the terrible price of that useless war that had pitted countryman against countryman, brother against brother, and which had already cost more lives than any war in modern history to that date and which, in his own words, would go on to the bitter end, even if necessary until-
-all the wealth piled by the bondsman's 250 years of unrequited toil shall be sunk and until every drop of blood drawn with the lash shall be paid by another drawn by the sword.
Lincoln urged his countrymen to strive on, to finish the work that they were engaged in,
Canadian Flag
with malice toward none and charity to all, and to bind up the nation's wounds. Yes, Mr. Speaker, to bind up the nation's wounds; that is the task to which we should now be dedicated.
We have had our debate, and I believe that in order to bind up the nation's wounds-and they are deep and grievous-we must without recrimination, if defeated in our point of view in this debate, and without undue bombasity if our point of view prevails, accept the new flag when it is unfurled; because that flag will be the symbol of our country, and our country will be as great as the respect we show to the symbol that will be ours and ours alone.
If we are not mature enough to do that, if we are not big enough to forget the division that has torn us apart, then we are not even worthy to survive; but I think the immense majority of Canadians from coast to coast will accept the flag that is truly our own, and under that flag Canada will know better and greater days.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am
sure the English speaking people in this assembly, and those of English descent, are fully cognizant of the feelings expressed by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau). Thank God I belong to a party in which there can be differences of opinion. Thank God we have a liberal-minded party where those who have a different view can express that view.
Today, in the few minutes at my disposal, I want to put on record what other people throughout this dominion are thinking. I have in my hand a letter I received this morning from a mother who lost her son in the last war. Her son was named Cecil. I want the house to know what she has to say about the red ensign which is being debated here today as it has been for the past few weeks. She writes:
I feel Cecil fought for the protection of this flag and gave his young life for it.
I want to make this the theme of what I have to say here today. Young Cecil was about 22. He was the pilot of a Lancaster bomber and was shot down north of Berlin during the raids which were made on that city from bases in the British isles. His gunner was the son of a former member of this assembly. The entire crew lost their lives.
As it happens, this strikes home closely to me because Cecil Kindt, the pilot of that plane, was my nephew, and the person who

Canadian Flag
wrote to me is my brother's wife, or widow; my brother is dead. So it was this boy, in the flower of his youth, who lost his life flying a Lancaster bomber during those days when we did not know whether Britain would survive and when, as Churchill said, we never owed so much to so few. Have we forgotten those days? I hope not. But here is a mother who says in her letter to me:
I agree with your opinion on the flag situation. I feel Cecil fought for the protection of this flag and gave his young life for it.
Those among us who talk lightly about a flag and about choosing a flag or destroying a flag have never felt the emotion which those of us who have been through it feel. So I say to all those who would lightly throw the red ensign away, you are spreading disunity among the people of this nation. There is no doubt about that in my mind. Do those who talk so loudly now remember the days of conscription when recruits were needed, and when we constructed air bases in western Canada to provide the armed forces with the men who were required? We built airfields and trained people to man the bombers. Those airfields were used to train people who came from all parts of the world. We put our best efforts into this work. What was the flag which flew over those airfields? It was the red ensign. These are the circumstances which are deeply ingrained in those of us who oppose this change in our national flag.
To get the right flag, the flag which Canada needs, and make it an acceptable substitute for everything else is not an easy task. It has to be a discovery, and such a discovery has not yet been made. What happened was this. A pistol was held by the government at the head of the flag committee. The committee was told to bring in a report by a certain date. Well, they threw out the flag with three leaves, which made it necessary for them to come up with something else, and this was the flag with one leaf.
That is how we got the flag which is now presented to us. It is a political flag. It is not a flag which will unify the people of Canada. If members opposite and those who think like them cannot see the possible evil effects of their action, and follow through with the result that disunity is created in this country, the blame will rest on their shoulders.
Let me say to those who write editorials condemning the Conservative party, and those in other parties who support the red ensign, that we are expressing a point of view which is held by a large section of the people of this nation, possibly 60 per cent or more.

They have never been given an opportunity to express their views on this issue by way of a plebiscite. They never knew there would be a flag put forward consisting of one maple leaf on a white background until just a month ago.
I do not believe this is the way to choose a flag. We all know this design has come about because the committee was working under orders to produce. You cannot produce a flag which will be ingrained in the hearts of the people by following this approach. The government and its supporters are relying on having this flag approved so they can go out and sell it to the people. They will go out and support it-we will all support it, because it will be the Canadian flag. In other words it is a selling job they will be doing from now on, trusting that in a generation or two it will be as acceptable as the red ensign.
Well, I do not think this will happen. I think the disunity which will be created in this country as a result of the introduction of this particular flag will continue for years to come.
I do not believe closure should be used in order to obtain a flag. Nor do I believe that an emblem should be selected as the flag of this nation. Show me how many countries in the world, having distinctive emblems such as the shamrock, the rose, the thistle and so on, to name only a few emblems of the British isles, have chosen to place these emblems on their national flags. The people are proud of those emblems. They serve in just the same way as the maple leaf serves us. We are proud of our maple leaf. None of us has talked against it, but after all it is only an emblem. None of the countries in the British isles has its emblem on its flag. The Irish flag does not carry the shamrock, nor does the Scottish flag carry the thistle.
Therefore it is not necessary, neither is it desirable, to have a flag bearing an emblem. But when you are up against the gun and the head of a party tells a committee to bring in a report on the kind of flag we should have, it is simply imposing an impossible task upon that committee. Therefore, since the mistake in handling the matter in this way was made, the blame for the adoption of this flag and the mistake in connection with it lies squarely at the feet of this government.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the flag committee I have felt it my duty to faithfully sit in this house during the last two weeks

and listen to all the remarks which have been made by different members. However, the one thing which has upset me more than anything else has been the insinuations which have been made regarding the intelligence of the members of that committee. I have found no one has given us any credit for being bright enough, after being together for six weeks studying the flag issue, to emerge from the committee wiser than when we went in. Quite frankly, I think I can say for every other member as well as myself that we were keenly aware of our responsibilities. We were determined to be open minded. We were willing to listen to other people's opinions and to permit full participation in all our discussions. I think each one of us was ready to study the whole issue and certainly to be non-partisan.
As a westerner I think I was probably a little more conscious than were some other hon. members of the people who come from many lands to make up our country, besides those who are the descendants of our founding races. I have to admit that as a westerner I am fiercely proud of Canada. I have had the most marvellous opportunities for travel on behalf of the United Nations association through UNICEF, which travels have taken me through nine countries of Africa and South America; and every time I come home knowing that Canada is the finest land in this whole wide world.
I believe there has been in our past too little, not too much, national pride in our country. During the six weeks that I sat on that committee I was made very conscious of how little I knew of our early Canadian history, and I gleaned much in the way of knowledge from the different witnesses we heard. I wondered why this was, and one day I asked a witness when it was that we really began to teach Canadian history in our schools. To my amazement I found that this was only in approximately 1920.
It seems to me that we have all acquired an appreciation of the accomplishments of our nation's builders. I think of the missionary martyrs, I think of the voyageurs, and I think of the explorers and their extraordinary accomplishments. As I look at this whole issue now I really feel that our lack of knowledge of Canadian history, particularly our early Canadian history, is one of the causes of our growing pains today.
Now about the people who make up this country, this mosaic of Canada; I found this summer that I was really very vague about the early settlers of Newfoundland. I had
Canadian Flag
the privilege of going down there and spending a day with one hon. member going through his constituency, and it suddenly dawned on me as I read the different names of the little fishing towns built by the early settlers in Newfoundland-and I think of Portugal Cove, Bonavista, Port au Port, Ireland's Eye-and as I stopped and talked to the people in the different villages, that although confederation meant so much to them they were still very proud of their heritage.
Then, of course, we all know that the French, the English, the Irish and the Scottish are the descendants of the early settlers of what was Upper and Lower Canada and the maritimes. But at the time of confederation easterners thought western Canada was suitable only for the Indians. I believe some people still feel that way, but as a westerner I can assure them that they have a lot to learn. The fur traders were very jealous of their rights, and I think they did their best for a while to keep people out of this area of Canada; because with the farmers moving in it meant that the fur traders would have to move out. But very soon the early travellers came back to eastern Canada with stories about the rich soil of western Canada, and pioneers, intrigued by these stories, soon flooded into this part of the country and we had a new province in 1870, Manitoba.
However, the vision of a dominion from sea to sea was really only sparked at the time two British colonies, Vancouver island and British Columbia, joined together. Some people thought it was foolish to talk of a territory so far away, but with the promise of a railroad to be built within ten years a new province was added in 1871, British Columbia. This railroad was built through wild, barren land, almost bottomless swamps, muskeg, and was blasted through great mountains. This was all made possible by the Irish, the Swedish, the Italian and the Chinese individuals who had strong backs and were willing to work. It was then that the settlers poured into this vast area, coming from eastern Canada, Great Britain, the United States, Russia, Poland, the Ukraine, Germany, Austria, Hungary, Holland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, China and Japan. And there was land for all of them. Six thousand Mennonites settled on the banks of the Red river, and we will always know that this is their community when we see names like Steinbach, Stoney Brook, Rosen-feld and Field of Roses.

Canadian Flag
Then the farming Icelanders built new homes around lake Gimli, which is a beautiful place. They proved that people knowing no English and unacquainted with Canadian laws and customs could prosper in a new land if they were willing to work. With their spirit of adventure and their strong sense of freedom and attachment to their cultural heritage, the Ukrainians too have added much to our national way of life, and their contributions to community affairs have placed us all in their debt.
Let us be honest with ourselves at this time, sir. Surely today we are trying to preserve a nation in which people of many diverse backgrounds may feel at home. Let us be united by a common pride and a common dedication to the progress of Canada.
When thinking of all these other groups we must not fail to remember the first settlers of our country. As one travels west through places such as Medicine Hat, Sturgeon Creek and Yellowknife he is always reminded of those settlers. I came across a beautiful little verse the other day by Richard Huntington, as follows:
The memory of the red man,
How can it pass away?
While his names of music linger On each mount and stream and bay?
Let us not forget our Eskimos and the name that was given to them by the Indians. About a month ago there was an art exhibit in the air terminal at Winnipeg which gave everyone the opportunity of observing the skills of these people and the articles which they offer to us who live below the Arctic circle. While I was a member of the flag committee I thought of those people, and I remembered how last fall I had read of a resolution passed at the annual meeting of the chamber of commerce; and let me remind hon. members that the chamber of commerce has approximately 900 affiliates in this country. That resolution read in part as follows:
Parliament has not formerly adopted a distinctive national flag and Canadian public opinion polls continually record significant majorities favouring a distinctive national flag with the nation's youth expressing an overwhelming preference for such a flag. A distinctive national flag would be a strong unifying influence consistent with the status of whole nationhood.
For emphasis I should like to bring attention to the word "unifying" in that resolution.
During our flag committee meetings, as you have all heard so often before, we learned about flags; and when I went home to my constituency about two weeks ago someone suggested that I should wear a steel helmet. I must now state that I had no difficulty in
[Mrs. Konantz.l
explaining what the new distinctive flag was all about. It really boiled down to the fact that I only had to use two sentences to tell them that it was something to which we could give a place of honour; that the upper staff quarter of any flag is the place of honour, and that by placing the union jack in that position, which it occupies on the red ensign, we would be putting it in the place of honour. I believe the argument against the use of the union jack does not suggest any disrespect for that flag, but is made because the union jack does not represent Canada but is the official flag of the United Kingdom. It has been said over and over again that by flying the red ensign the interpretation might be made that Canada is still subject to the United Kingdom, which is denied by Canadians. So I say simply that-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? I take it that when you are talking about the red ensign you are referring to the Canadian red ensign?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am speaking of the Canadian red ensign. It is simply a matter of self respect on our part to adopt a flag which will proclaim to the world that Canada is Canada and is not subject to any other country.
When it came time for the members of the flag committee to declare themselves and vote, I voted against the plebiscite for the simple reason that I felt it would add more confusion to this whole question and would not prove to be of any use in this country. If I had more time I could give a perfect example of just how confused a group can become about what is our official Canadian flag. However, as my time is running out I am afraid I cannot go into that dissertation. I voted against the Canadian red ensign as a national flag because Canada is an independent state.
I learned from the experts who appeared before the committee that our national colours were red on white. At the time we voted for or against adoption of the three maple leaves design versus the one maple leaf design I was reminded of the Christmas day I spent in Hong Kong in 1958. We all know that Christmas is a sad day in Hong Kong because on that day in 1941 it surrendered to the Japanese. I decided on Christmas morning to visit the Sai Wang cemetery and place a wreath on our memorial. I arranged to get the wreath through our Canadian trade commissioner, and it really was a most effective one. It stood about four feet high, was circular of solid white chrysanthemums with

a single red maple leaf made of carnations in the centre.
I went to the cemetery, which is on a beautiful hillside overlooking a magnificent bay, and on my arrival there I found a little Chinese gardener in his bare feet clipping the rose bushes and cleaning up the leaves which had fallen during the night. I walked down the great stairs and placed the wreath on the cenotaph, and then wandered among the headstones on the graves of our Winnipeg Grenadiers. I had not known very many mothers who had lost loved ones who are buried there, but one thing I will always remember is that on each headstone there was a single maple leaf, and I knew that when the time came for me to vote for the one leaf design versus the three leaves design I would vote for the single maple leaf.
Surely this flag, which the committee has recommended to this house, will send out the message we all want to give to the world; that this is Canada, this is a flag which symbolizes our freedom and unity, and a flag which we will fly proudly among the flags of the 114 members of the United Nations.
Mr. Speaker, I plead with all the members of this house to put an end to this debate. Let us behave like reasonable and mature adults and bring this question once and for all to a decision. I am sure that is what our constituents expect of us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. lady who represents Winnipeg South for entering this debate even at this late hour. I was pleased to hear her say that as a member of the flag committee her heart went out to the Canadian Eskimo people, and that for that reason she was able to make a choice as to a flag design. At this time I should like to invite that hon. lady, as I have done previously, to come with me to the great treeless plains of the Canadian Northwest Territories and explain to the Eskimo people what the maple leaf symbol is all about.
Because she is a convincing speaker I was also interested that she should make a plea to us to end the debate at this particular juncture, this after her own Prime Minister and his cohorts in the cabinet had decided to invoke closure to get a new flag by Christmas if they could not do so otherwise.
I had not intended to make any more comments on this matter, but the speech of the Prime Minister and more particularly of the government house leader on Friday prompted me to put a few more remarks on the record. I was particularly interested in the frequent 20220-7011

references the Prime Minister made to the free and full debate that had gone on, and I want to put on record what he said. As found on page 11036 of Hansard he said:
Of course free and full discussion is absolutely essential to the parliamentary process-
Again, as found on page 11037 he said:
-so I hope this parliament will be given the right to exercise its fundamental duty; that is, to decide after a full and free debate.
Then that other expert on procedure, the government house leader, had this to say as found on page 11053, when he was giving notice of the closure motion with such obvious glee:
In the circumstances, and to prevent a mockery being made of parliament, I have no alternative but to take the action I now propose to take.
Let us take a look at what the Liberals mean when they say "free and full debate". I took a cue from that little Ralliement Credi-tistes member, the hon. member for Lapointe, and I made an investigation of Hansard to see how the debate had been going. Let us find out what the Prime Minister means when he says "full and free debate". If you will look at the speeches made by members of the official opposition in the 10 days the committee report has been under discussion you will find that on a total of 661 occasions members opposite and their allies in the Ralliement Creditistes interrupted those of us who were trying to make sincere speeches in the house. These are 661 interruptions where the member doing the interrupting is identified by name. If one were to include all the interjections and smart remarks by way of harassment of speakers from this party by those members who are impatient with the democratic process, the closure kids, the number of such interruptions would be well over 1,000.
I am glad the government house leader is here, because his hands are not completely clean in this regard. The shameful thing is that 98 of these specious questions of order and privilege can be attributed to the Prime Minister and other ministers of the crown. I should like to put that on the record. The government house leader interrupted the debate 18 times in 10 days with specious points of order and questions of privilege or other questions. I can see why he might have done so with the Prime Minister sitting to his right. However, the Prime Minister was only in the house to hear three speeches. But his record is not so hot, either.

Mr. Speaker, I bow to your ruling. Let us not forget that on Friday the Prime Minister was speaking to the amendment, and I am now discussing what the Prime Minister apparently means by full and free debate. I am trying to summarize the debate to date to see if it measures up to his standard. The closest the hon. lady got to the red ensign was a discussion of the Red river settlers, but none of us on this side objected to that. The government house leader interrupted 18 times and the Prime Minister interrupted nine times even though he was only in the house for three speeches. That professional interrupter, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis), interrupted 35 times on points of order and questions of privilege, and he only returned to the house from his world wide tour on December 3. Members can see the kind of record he has in this regard.
I will conclude my remarks along this line, Mr. Speaker, by stating that the ministers of the crown, those great advocates of full and free debate, interrupted speakers on this side
[Mr. Rheaume.1
of the house 98 times in the course of 10 days, and together with their allies interrupted a total of 661 times. Is this some sort of Grit definition of full and free debate?
The newspapermen of the country have a responsibility in terms of reporting this debate, but press reports have not indicated that speakers from the official opposition attempting to make their cases have been harassed and heckled. How many of these press reporters-they can live with this responsibility when the red ensign comes down-reported that 661 points of order, specious questions of privilege and other interruptions were made? The hon. member for Lapointe got up and talked about the number of speeches that had been made, and the members of the press gallery were very good about giving us the running score in that regard. We had a right to expect impartial coverage of the flag debate by the press.
Let us take a look at what a free vote means. Every member in this chamber from the province of Quebec, regardless of where he sits in the house, supports the new maple leaf flag in no uncertain terms. We know this is so. I admire and respect them for doing so, and I support their right to do so. I believe these members from Quebec have set an example that will shine forth whenever parliamentary freedom of speech is in question.
On the other hand, I have nothing but scorn and sympathy for those members who have sold out and who have refused to be as honest so far as the other side of the issue is concerned. If anyone is in doubt about how they have sold out I invite them to read the speech of the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) who described precisely how it was being done among the Liberal party members. I have talked to Liberal backbenchers myself and I know the threats that were made against them. Let it be said about them in the years to come that when the moment came to stand up and be counted according to their consciences, they chose instead to swim downstream.
In his speech on Friday the Prime Minister said to members of the opposition "Come on, let us all rally around the flag once it is adopted and help me to hoist the new flag on the flagstaffs of this country". What he was really saying was "Come on, boys, help me tear down the one we have".
