I can guarantee he will get no help from me or from anyone who thinks as I do in the process of destroying what we have had when he has not made a case for the necessity of doing so. In terms of the new one, let this be on the record and let it be clear; should a new flag be adopted for this country I will do my best to promote it throughout the far northern reaches of our country.
The northerly part of this country has known no other flag but the red ensign, because it has been only during the last few years that we have ventured that far. This will not be an easy task for me. It will be made much more difficult because my heart will not be in it. The Indian and Eskimo people in the far reaches of this country have a way of spotting insincerity. They were happy with the flag they had. For generations they have received their treaty payments, have gone to school and received their help from the mother country under this emblem.
One thing about the Indian and Eskimo people is this, Mr. Speaker. Before they change something they have to have a good reason for it. They do not discard the old ways lightly because someone has a whim or is capricious and says it would be a good thing to do. They know intuitively that the pursuit of novelty, the pursuit of change for its own sake, can lead only to social anarchy.
No one in this chamber will work harder or longer to promote loyalty, duty and devotion to whatever flag is chosen by this chamber. Nor will I, in the meantime, do anything to discredit the symbol that may be on that flag that is chosen. However, do not expect me for one second to assist in the destruction of what we have. I want to state and to emphasize, with all the eloquence I can muster, that the Prime Minister of this country can never again in my eyes and in my opinion pass himself off as a person who is willing to subordinate his personal whim to the greater and more enduring needs of this country.
The Prime Minister and his house have said "We will use closure to get a flag". They say, as they have said before, "Who shall stop us if we want to do something?" Well, I say to the Prime Minister and to his friends on the front benches, there are quite a few other things I should like to see stopped in this country before debate in this House of Commons. I would, first and foremost, like to see a stop to the highly questionable conduct

What I was attempting to say, Mr. Speaker, and apparently it was not obvious to the Chair, was not whether or not closure should have been invoked, because the house has already decided on that, but to ask why this government would be so anxious to institute closure. What is it with which they want to distract the attention of Canadians? I suggest that the new flag, the single maple leaf with which the ministry will hide its nakedness, is the reason for closure being introduced at this point.
In the short time left to me-and I do not know how much that is as there have been so many interruptions and points of order- I wish to put on the record a letter which I received today from a woman in Winnipeg. She may even live in Winnipeg South, but at any rate her name is Rose Cowan. In her letter she writes:
On May 17th this year, we were guests at the memorial service for the war dead, in Winnipeg, when Mr. Pearson, instead of opening this convention.. .with a prayer and a few dignified words, unveiled his new maple leaf flag instead, causing much disturbance and upset feelings. My husband is a veteran of world war II and both of us have lost loved ones in that dreadful fray, so we felt really unhappy. I came away with tears in my eyes, and knew then that this flag issue should never never have been brought up. It is the kind of thing which splits a country from sea to sea, and does no good at all. It is an emotional thing-and emotional things inflame. Somebody has given Mr. Pearson very bad advice.
On the basis of a letter like that from a woman who is obviously sincere, I feel that if the Prime Minister and his cohorts use closure to stifle this kind of feeling, even

if expressed by only one citizen, they are depriving that citizen of something valuable, and it would be better had they never brought this divisive issue before the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fight on the flag has been a long one, and we can see the end in sight. The amendment before us deals with the red ensign and much of the debate, as well as public comment, has been to the effect, "Why do you keep fighting on? Can't you see you are going to lose the battle? Can't you see you are going to have a new flag? Why hold up the work of parliament?" I think it is time something was put on the record to indicate exactly why we fight.
I have never been one of those who think the most important question in a fight is, how much strength have you got on your side? I think the question is, how much right is on your side? I am sure members of parliament are called honourable members because we all like to think our duty is to fight for the right, and to fight against that which we think is wrong. On many occasions we have said, and we continue to believe, that what is being done in changing our national flag is wrong, and the way in which it is being done is wrong. Therefore it is our duty to fight. I am sure the question is not how long are the odds against us, but how good and sincere is our cause. I am not concerned with whether defeat in the end is certain. I am concerned that we do not give up a fight when we are on the side of the right.
I am aware there may be a certain amount of ill feeling among certain sections of the public, and I am aware that the press has been dealing with what it calls our stubborn resistance to inevitable defeat. I am quite prepared to bear any punishment that public opinion may bring on me because members of the public fail to understand that I am not willing to give up a fight just because I may be defeated in the end.
Perhaps this is due to my Irish heritage and background. I am sure that if hon. members would only contemplate Irish history for a little while; if they would realize the years of battle, the number of lives lost, the amount of persecution, the fearful odds, the innumerable defeats, they would begin to get some comprehension of why we on this side of the house think it is an honourable thing to fight, no matter how often other hon. members may believe we should realize it is a foolish battle.

I hope my constituents will be able to look beyond the writing in the newspapers, which seem concerned only with the fact that this is a long fight. I hope they will realize it is a fight that must be carried on. I am aware that public opinion seems to have forgotten it is the government which could have broken off the fight at any time. We are in the position, I think, of being deceived that there is no honourable retreat and that if we are defeated we go down fighting.
Perhaps I am a little preoccupied with the idea of fighting and keeping on fighting because the parliament of Canada has today lost a truly great fighter. The dean of the parliament of Canada, Senator Byron Horner, died in hospital in Saskatoon today, and I am sure anyone who knew and loved him as I did knows of his long and valued service to the parliament of Canada, and knows that one of his predominant traits was to fight. He was a great and gallant fighter, and I think it can truthfully be said that we have all lost a very inspiring example, now that he has gone after so many years of service.
I am sure I echo the sentiments of all hon. members of this house when I extend to our two colleagues, the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner), our heartfelt sympathy on the loss of their father, and our sympathy to Mrs. Horner and the rest of the family. I am sure that his 32 years of dedicated service to parliament is one of the noblest and most gallant records of public service we have seen in our lifetime, or are likely to see for a long time.
I think it was when I first met him when I came to parliament that I realized how necessary it is for members of parliament to have courage. Perhaps sometimes some of us get a little too stubborn, but we are always too apt to be swayed by public opinion, by early, adverse reports in the newspapers, and by the contemplation of occasional fearful odds against us. I think I owe a deep debt of gratitude to Senator Horner because very early he convinced me that one of the greatest attributes a member of parliament could have is personal courage to stand up for what he believes.
I would like to refer to one or two comments made in the house today. I think it was the hon. member for Pontiac-Temis-camingue who mentioned the word "democracy," and the hon. member for Winnipeg South said let democracy have its way and bring the matter to a vote. There is something I believe people in this country are often

Canadian Flag
prone to forget. I do not deny that rule by majority is what is commonly thought to be the essence of democracy, but those of us who treasure personal liberty, those of us who feel we have a right to be personally indiscreet sometimes in our talk, if we so wish, realize that rule by majority is one more way of rule by force.
That is how rule by democracy came about; the masses, because of their great weight of numbers, were able to bring sufficient force to bear. I think we should realize this and remember it from time to time. I like to mention once in a while that in my opinion the crowning glory of democracy is not just rule by the majority; it is respect for the rights of minorities and for personal liberty. In this case, in this flag debate fight, I have never been convinced that the majority wants the new flag; I have never been convinced that the majority wants any new flag at this time. I have not seen enough evidence to be sure there was any public outcry or demand for a change in our national flag. I am not sure I would have chosen to continue to battle against the proposal of the government had I been so convinced.
The red ensign is a symbol which means so much to so many people in this country that I firmly believe those who wish to retain it have a right to have their views expressed and fought for. I believe that any member who wishes to speak out in defence of this right has a duty to make sure that he fights for it to the best of his ability.
My own personal view on the flag was expressed in this house two or three years ago, when I said I was not very greatly concerned; I was satisfied with the Canadian red ensign and could see no great reason for changing it, but did not think I would fuss too much if it were changed. If my attitude in this regard has altered I can only say it is because of the manner in which this issue has been handled. I am confident that the most ardent red ensign supporters could have been won over to a great extent; that most of them, if they had been properly approached and if the matter had been handled in a diplomatic way, would have been willing to make a great many concessions.
It has always seemed to me that the argument as to whether or not this question was handled properly can be settled by merely taking a look at the way in which the matter was handled in 1945-46. At that time the issue was not introduced in a political way, and the report of the committee which was set up was almost unanimous; 23 out of 24,

I think. Remember, this was at the close of a great war, at a time when we had every reason to believe that the patriotic feelings of Canadian citizens were still at a high pitch and when our people had every reason to feel proud of the contribution this nation had made in maintaining democracy and securing freedom for so many countries of the world. One would have to look hard to find any more honest expression of Canadian opinion at that time than the unbiased, soulsearching work of that committee.
This record alone is enough to explain why we on this side have fought so long and sometimes so bitterly over the different flags which the government has from time to time suggested we approve. Who can say that we are now just being stubborn? Who can say that we do not have good and sufficient reason for feeling bitter about the flag which the Prime Minister has so eloquently said should be the symbol of national unity? I wonder why we could not have allowed this question to stand for a while, even after the initial mistake had been made, until tempers had cooled, until the people had had a little time in which to get used to the idea. I for one have not been in any hurry to see forced upon this country a flag which, initially at least, can only stand as a symbol of political manoeuvring, or of political bungling on the part of the government; a proposition which obviously shows a determination to ram down the throats of the electors of this country a flag which no one even on the government benches brought forward as an idea more than a month or two ago.
I suggest that the method used in seeking the adoption of this flag cannot easily be separated from the design which has been chosen. It is not a question of what we are asking the people of this country to do. It is a question of human frailty, of human understanding and, perhaps, our understanding that Canadians are human. I am sure that most loyal Canadians when they look at the flag will not wish to remember the method by which it was brought in, the ill conceived strategy and the bludgeon used to make sure they got it. But I am sure most people will not be able to dissociate these things from the flag when they look at it. It is the eleventh hour, but I suggest to the government that the damage is not yet fatal. It is still not too late for them to put this motion aside and think it over for a while.
There is an editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune which I think should be read by other editors across Canada. No matter what else

is done, all newspaper editors in this country should try to set the people straight on what the fight is about in this house. The question is not whether Canadians should get another flag. Nor is the question whether parliament should get on with other business, at least as far as the opposition is concerned. What is causing the unease and dissatisfaction in the public mind based on the oft repeated assertion that parliament is wasting its time because the opposition is filibustering? The point is that if you have a duty to fight what is wrong, you have a duty to keep on fighting.
If the government persists in a course of conduct which is wrong, it is difficult for me to understand why the newspapers have not told the simple truth over and over again. It is that the government has control over the order of business; the government can bring in any other business which it believes to have priority at any time it wishes to do so. If there has been a day wasted, or spent, in this house, as you choose to look at it, on the flag question it is because the government chose to spend or waste that day.
When I finally get a chance to get back to my constituency I intend to make it clear to my political supporters or foes that our so-called filibuster in this house did not take place just because our party leader wanted to retain the red ensign, or because people on this side of the house wanted to talk. I intend to take my full share of credit by saying I wanted that fight kept on because I refused to quit when I felt I was on the side of the right.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising this afternoon to participate in this debate and speak to the amendment, may I say how happy and proud I am to take part in the debate at this time. May I say too, Mr. Speaker, that I have enjoyed your guidance throughout the debate and I hope you may continue to occupy the chair for a few more hours.
With regard to the amendment to substitute the red ensign, as it is commonly called, for the single maple leaf flag, may I say that I realize the hon. member who moved the amendment, the hon. member for Middlesex West, did so sincerely and proudly as a last ditch stand, fighting for something he thought entirely right and for which many of us have fought in the days, weeks and months past. I think there may also have been in his mind, and in the minds of others in this chamber, the thought that there still might be a chance for a compromise to be made.
Canadian Flag
This, Mr. Speaker, is the reason I rise once again to speak in this debate. I know it is late, and in the face of closure our hours are numbered and our debate is limited. But I still think there is some hope for a compromise, and in this connection I should like to set out my reasons for thinking this is the case.
Much has been said throughout this debate, and many people have said there is nothing new to be said. I do not pretend that I have anything specifically new to offer, but in the course of my remarks I do wish to call attention to some aspects of the symbols we are discussing under this amendment. Speaking of symbols, this is a particular time of the year when we honour certain specific symbols; it is a time when we are particularly aware of certain symbols.
Today we are facing closure in this house, this having been brought on by the government. If I may wonder a little for a moment, the other day I heard the Prime Minister emphasize the fact that his entire cabinet approved of this step. I wondered at the time whether that was so, because only a few days earlier a representative segment of the press had this to say:
Surely never again will the Prime Minister have quite the same confidence in them as he did before. The face of power, shown above, is now a partisan political face, far removed from any face that can speak for country above party.
I do not want to detail what has been said previously, but when speaking before about the red ensign I did say that when a government has the record this government has, surely the Canadian nation should not be made to accept a new flag by this means, albeit a distinctive flag which many of us have previously admitted we should like to see. To me, closure is not democratic.
As I said at the outset of my remarks, I should like to say something about emblems. Before this debate terminates, as I have said, it is still my hope that it is not too late to reach some compromise; but if not, when the time comes to haul down the flag of which so many of us have spoken and for which so many of us have fought, having received piles of correspondence from people in every area of the country, then will be the time to think of symbols.
As I said earlier, this is a certain time of the year when we are particularly prone to symbols. Some of us have wreaths on our doors. Nearly all of us embrace some symbol of this time of year, a tree or a cross. But do we forget that our so-called ties with

Canadian Flag
Britain go deeper than any symbols related to a specific country? I need not remind the members of this house or the Canadian public that the crosses on their flag are Christian symbols. So I emphasize that we should try once more to reach a compromise. Compromises have been reached before in democratic parliaments. I ask, where are those parliaments today, Mr. Speaker?
Some people have said that democracy cannot work in this way. In my opinion this is the way in which democracy must work or it cannot survive. That is what I meant a moment ago when I tried to point out that some countries in this world have forgotten about the past and even the present, and have looked only to the future, and as a result today they do not exist as autonomous bodies. I am not drawing any inferences in this regard, but I would ask the question whether, by destroying this present symbol, which is what we will do if this amendment is not accepted, we are sure we will not destroy our national unity.
If the procedure now suggested is carried forward by this house, will we be doing something to enhance national unity and the national economy? Frankly I seriously doubt that we will be doing that.
The Prime Minister is a man well noted for compromise and for his ability to settle contentious issues. Has he suddenly changed his method of operation? I followed his actions very closely when he was acting in the role of a statesman and mediator, and often commended him for the headway he was able to make. Why does the Prime Minister now, in spite of his enviable record for compromise, resort to this kind of action?
I have not been successful in finding one member in my constituency who is not willing to accept a truly distinctive national flag. I have not received one letter from an individual in Canada who is not willing to accept such a flag. Nor do I believe there is one member in this chamber who would seriously oppose the adoption of a distinctive Canadian national flag. Therefore, the only real question to be answered is, what shall be the distinctive Canadian national flag?
Many Indian people live in my constituency, and there are a great many others living in various other sections of this country. No one can refer to these people as other than truly Canadian. What do they think about the flag proposed at this eleventh hour? One need only talk to one or two in any section of the country to discover what they
[Mr. GundlockJ
think about this flag. Without relating my remarks specifically to the union jack as being the commonwealth flag, or the flag of Britain, I must state that past Canadian emblems and symbols have a different meaning for Indian people-who possess a greater degree of sensibility than apparently some of us here in this house possess-than they have for the rest of us. The Indian people remember the solemn promises made at the time of the signing of treaties, and associate these symbols with an allegiance to the Queen, the great white mother. They hold the same feelings today, and one can well imagine what they will think about a government which, by force or by any other means, tears down these symbols and casts them aside. The government should give serious consideration to the thoughts of these Indian people about the flag they intend to tear down.
Some time ago I attempted to point out that the relationship between a national flag and the feelings of the Indian people is not something which can be associated with the commonwealth or with Britain itself, but is directly related to symbolic feelings and treaties. The crosses on the flag are not merely crosses or symbols of a country, but Christian crosses which many of us do not want to see removed and replaced by a mere symbol, and I refer to the maple leaf. One can well understand what the Indian people will think about this government and this parliament in its action to remove this flag as a symbol of allegiance and promise.
I hope someone will correct me if I am wrong and the record shows otherwise, but I believe on the very first day of this debate a proposition was put forward by the Leader of the Opposition, and repeated again several days ago as a last ditch stand, in favour of compromise. Before moving to bring down the symbols which mean so much to the people of this country, I urge the Prime Minister and the government to give serious thought to the results of that action.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this historic occasion when we are debating an amendment to a motion concerning our flag it must be obvious to us all that we are under the pressure of closure. This puts a bad taste in our mouths which will remain for a considerable period of time. The Prime Minister, while speaking to this amendment now under discussion, said it was parliament's right to make a decision on this issue. I think his words were that this is an issue which the government and parliament

must decide. I should like to place clearly and unmistakably on the record our reaction to the government's procedure on this issue.
Politics involves the art of getting along, and the art of governing lies in the ability to bring together divergent groups. In this regard the Prime Minister and the government have failed the country. This issue has not been brought along in that way so that the people of Canada are united. We have all been aware of the various groups with various opinions which exist in this country, and we as a party have tried to give the right to every individual to have a voice on this issue. Having failed in that regard, by failing in our attempts to persuade the government to settle the issue by plebiscite, we commenced to move a series of amendments to the main motion in order that there may be some indication of the divergence of opinion on this issue.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that in the very early stages of this debate, in my own case on August 20 at a time when I knew there had been discussions at the leadership level as to the advisability of referring this matter to a committee of the house, four basic conditions to the sensible completion of the work of the committee were put foward. Those four issues were ignored and, as I suggested earlier during another stage of this debate, the members of that committee voted as party members. They did not make an effort to bring the main parties together, and that was a necessary ingredient to the compromise.
Now we have the amendment respecting the red ensign. The vote on the amendment will indicate to the house and to the country that there are a number of members of the house who are willing to vote for what has been our distinctive national flag for a good many years.
On that point I should like to say that a flag is meaningless until people have done something for that flag. I for one should like to give testimony to the fact that during the war I belonged to a group that did its best to make it stand out in the minds of people who were our allies and those who were our enemies that the red ensign was our distinctive flag. When I heard the Prime Minister say the other day that Canadian troops had not fought under that flag, or that he had never seen it, I wished he could have been where I was during the war.
In the latter part of the war I happened to serve with one of two Canadian squadrons in a group composed mainly of R.A.F. and
Canadian Flag
American squadrons. I served under an American general, and when you are in a mixture of squadrons doing the same type of work one squadron matches itself against the others. Some of us had served with R.A.F. squadrons, but because of the great difficulty that there was among the Canadians, Australians, New Zealanders and people from the United Kingdom it was decided to pull out of the R.A.F. squadrons all crews containing a majority of Canadians. Thus two Canadian squadrons were formed in the summer of 1944 to serve in the close support work being done by the allies for the 14th army in Burma.
I think I am right in saying that it is tough to take orders from a sergeant at any time, but when you have to take orders from a sergeant who is of another nationality, whether he be British or American, I think members here can understand how resentful we felt and how glad we were to serve in a Canadian squadron. The essence of my little anecdote is that serving as we were in the same area, crowded on a small island with all squadrons working from the same base, naturally there was rivalry among us. If you look at the official squadron records for that theatre you will find that the average tonnage per month carried by squadrons doing this particular type of work was about 3,200 tons a month delivered on objective. During the same period of time the Canadian squadrons averaged over 5,000 tons a month. No American or British squadron came anywhere near what the Canadians were doing.
Why did the Canadians do so much under such great difficulties to demonstrate that they were the best in that particular group? We did so because we knew the Americans thought they were the best in the world and told everybody about it, and the R.A.F. thought they were the best in the world and kept quiet. The only way we could show we were the best was by doing the job. So we set a record of tonnage carried to objectives that no other squadron could match.
On each of our planes was the red ensign. There was also the official roundel with the maple leaf on it, but the red ensign was carried on our planes. When we returned from operational sorties we drew up our planes in the assembly area right opposite an operations tent flying the red ensign as well as the air force insignia outside the tent. As we completed these missions each of us knew we were demonstrating to our allies that the Canadians were an effective part of the war effort, and we were trying to earn

Canadian Flag
the right tor Canadians to be recognized by their flag, the red ensign.
I have no apologies now for speaking in support of this amendment, because those of us who were emotionally involved in trying to demonstrate that this was our flag felt, when the then prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King pointed to the red ensign at the end of the war and said to General Crerar "You have made that Canada's flag", that we had been a part of making it Canada's flag.
I could go on and talk of other things of a more personal nature. In our particular group we had no defence except high flying fighters, and our orders were to use camouflage on our aircraft. In spite of those orders the Canadian squadrons painted on the sides of their aircraft the maple leaf as well as the red ensign. We did so because, with a million and a half troops on the allied side engaged in a mighty struggle with the Japanese empire, when we flew low over the troops in that area they all knew, our allies as well as the enemy, that these were Canadians who were getting through to their objective.
I well recall an occasion when the troops were advancing south down the Salween river to Rangoon. The hard pressed tank troops were without supplies and short of all amenities. A Canadian plane flew in at low level with such mundane things as big bags filled with cigarettes, dumped them on the road behind the forward element and gave the troops the chance to smoke an American or Canadian cigarette for the first time in many months. I recall too a little box story on the front page of "SEAC", the southeast Asia command newspaper, saying "Thanks, Canada". The officer commanding the tank corps said "If you had flown 10 feet lower we would have thanked you personally".
We took our flag everywhere to let those people know that it was our flag. Some of us, possibly a minority, think we earned the right for Canadians to fly that distinctive national flag with pride. It seems rather odd to me that the minute the last amendment was moved the government decided on that day to apply closure. Did they not want a debate on the red ensign so that people across the country could be made aware of the testimony in favour of that flag? The government has given us little chance to put forward alternatives.
I should like to refer to an editorial that appeared in the Globe and Mail on September 11, 1964, dealing with the question of closure. At that time the house had decided to refer

the flag question to a committee, and in approving this move the editorial stated in part:
What is more important, any flag adopted under such circumstances-
By closure.
-would have been an object of contempt and scorn.
Today the same Globe and Mail says closure is all right. What is the significance of this? It simply means that this newspaper, with no sense of responsibility to minorities in Canada, said in September that to bring in a flag by closure would lead to contempt and scorn, and today says that closure is all right.
My mind goes back once again to an event that happened before you and I were in the house, Mr. Speaker. I refer to the use of closure in 1956, when closure was applied before debate occurred. What are people going to think? In their minds they are going to associate this new flag not only with closure as it will be applied tonight but with closure as it was applied in 1956. So I checked the debates of that time. One thing that came to light at that time was that United States companies were being asked by the government to come into Canada and finance a pipe line that should have been a Canadian undertaking of great pride. The house was told that it had to get the legislation through or construction could not start right away, and that Canadians could not possibly support such a huge undertaking. So these American entrepreneurs came into Canada and set up companies so they could buy Trans-Canada Pipe Line Company shares. If my memory serves me correctly they did not even obtain them at the opening market value of the stock, $10, but got them for $8 a share.
I hold in my hand today an offer to purchase shares of common stock of Canadian Delhi Oil Ltd., which is a subsidiary company of the Murchisons from Texas, one of this group of entrepreneurs who came in and convinced the government of that day that they and they alone could handle such a great undertaking, even though when some shares were put on the market in Canada the issues were oversubscribed seven to ten times. Here, under date of November 25, 1964 is an offer to purchase which will remain open until the close of business on January 8, 1965. At this very moment this company is prepared to strip these Trans-Canada shares from its set-up and sell the balance of the company back to another

United States company. They will now be selling for more than $40 those shares which they bought for $8 because this government applied closure. This will mean that for those shares for which they paid $3.5 million they will now receive $35 million.
At the moment I cannot help but get the taste in my mouth of this graft ridden government, not being aware that it is graft ridden, coming in and applying closure on a subject like this; particularly on a day when, as everyone knows, we are honouring the eighth anniversary of the selection of the leader of the Conservative party who fought closure in 1956.
It is not only my mind that comes to this conclusion. On the editorial page of this morning's Globe and Mail there is an article by Mr. Scott Young, who tells a very interesting story. This story concerns cabinet ministers who had not previously considered hara-kiri, and asks them to consider it now. What does he say about this search for a flag? He says it has caused us to lose face in Japan, and I quote:
Partly this is because we have such plausible cabinet ministers (some days). Recent ministerial meetings between Japanese and Canadians left the Japanese with the firm conviction that what Paul-san Martin and Walter-san Gordon want, they get. So when their leader, Lester-san Bowles-san (Mike-san) Pearson said in Winnipeg last spring that he had an idea for a flag, factory whistles blew shrilly and Japan rushed to get in on the ground, or even basement, floor. They didn't make only those little auto-aerial flags, but mighty silk and nylon flags built to last as long as winds blew over the barren lands.
I learned this the other evening when Mr. Gordon and I happened to be sitting across a dinner table from one another at Massey College. He thus was absent from a night sitting in the Commons during which the flag debate was in progress. I asked if he were not afraid of missing something that he had not heard before. When he recovered from this preposterous suggestion, he said affably that he personally was having more trouble with the Japanese over our flag than he was with the Commons. The sad story came out.
Here is a report in a newspaper in our country ridiculing this flag as an effort to increase trade with Japan. Some of the members of the house, including members of cabinet, rushed out ond bought these flags. I heard that they were on sale in cities like Vancouver and Toronto for $1 each. They took thousands of suckers and high pressured them into buying this three maple leaf flag. Now they say, by closure, they are not going to get the three maple leaf flag; they are not even going to get a vote. We are going to be forced to take the single maple leaf flag.
Canadian Flag
This whole question of a flag-I have to watch my time for obvious reasons-brings me to some statements I have kept in my files for a long time. This one is from the Victoria Daily Colonist of August 8, 1964, almost five months ago:
The assumption is that the Commons will then recess-
This is after we had passed interim supply for three months instead of two at our suggestion.
-and prepare for a new session. That is, once Mr. Pearson has rammed his new flag into the statute books. He acts like a schoolmaster who won't let his form go home until it bows to his wishes.
In the present impasse that hamstrings parliament and sees it sitting through the hot months of an eastern summer the Prime Minister displays the petulence so often associated with persons of weak character. He seems to imagine that a show of authority is an indication of strength, even when a diplomatic way out of dilemma is offered him.
We offered the Prime Minister an honourable, diplomatic way to bring this matter to a successful conclusion. We would have liked to get a vote of the house on this red ensign, and we will. We would have liked other votes which would have indicated to the house that there were other suggestions by way of compromise that we think might have united the whole house, if not the whole country. However, on this very important matter we are forced to our knees by a closure vote that applies tonight. I should like to suggest to members opposite that by so doing not only have they tied themselves up with the closure imposed in 1956 but have tied themselves up with the type of action in parliament that shall ever disgrace the name of modern Liberalism.
Closure is a device that has been used in Canada several times already, but as Laurier protested and as the Leader of the Opposition protested, it was something that no government should ever use in the future. As one hon. member said when he was in opposition, it would not be used by a government that did not lose its senses. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this government has lost its senses when it imposes such a doubtful type of regulation as closure on us on such an important matter.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do
not believe there is a better example of the condemnation of the government's attitude toward the issue that is before the house than the fact that in order for the government to secure the approval it knew parliament

Canadian Flag
would give for one reason or another, whether the country as a whole was in accord with the majority view within the house, we are now debating for the last time in this parliament what our national flag should be.
It is indeed significant that at the moment we have a choice between two alternatives, a maple leaf flag that could well take on significance in the future if our nation continues to prosper and expand, and a flag that is more representative of our past than any other symbol in our nation, the Canadian red ensign. It is indeed unfortunate that we must face the fact that we are going to have to agree with the majority vote in the House of Commons as to what our nation's flag will be, without knowing with certainty the opinion of the majority of our people. Surely, sir, this is the crux of the whole matter, the fact that this government was willing to put this question forward last April or May without determining with any degree of certainty what were the views of the Canadian people with regard to our national flag.
If, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle pointed out, the government had moved in the same direction as the government of the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King did in 1945, it would have endeavoured to produce a flag by determining in a non-partisan way what the people of Canada felt the flag design should be. Had it done that we would not have seen the House of Commons become a debating society on symbols at a time when it should have been taking action that would be of material benefit to our citizens in the many areas where the government promised action would be taken.
Instead of that we saw an ill conceived, poorly handled flag design placed before the house, a design that later went into the trash can where it belonged because of the method used by the government in endeavouring to inflict it upon the Canadian people without giving them any choice in the matter. Today we are almost back where we started. We have a flag which the government embraces wholeheartedly, although there is one unique member in the Liberal party, and we still have a flag which has flown over this nation for 97 years. After almost six months of debate we are told we must now make the same decision the government asked us to make originally, without any real change in the attitude of hon. members because they are no better prepared today to speak with certainty on the views of the Canadian people than they were six months ago.
[Mr. Coates.1
When 1 a.m. on Tuesday morning comes, when the guillotine falls, when the words stop and the votes are taken, will any of us be any more certain than we were last April of what the Canadian people want in the way of a flag design? Since last April many polls have been taken. Most of them told us what the people did not want, but few of them told us what the people did want.
You may talk to an individual who will say "I think we should have a distinctive Canadian flag." But when you show him the three maple leaf design, or the present design which was agreed upon by a majority of members in the flag committee, he will say "Oh, no. I don't like those flags. I don't think that is the type of flag we should have for Canada." He does not know what he wants, but I say without fear of contradiction that there is a large majority in this nation who do not want the flag design that is now being proposed by the government. There is also a substantial group, indeed I would say the largest group, who know what they want, and what they want is the Canadian red ensign. They want no other flag, although I have always found those people quite willing either to abide by the wishes of a majority as shown in a plebiscite or to accept an alternative flag embodying the symbols of our past, the symbols of the founding races and of the contributions they made to the building of this nation.
More than anything else the problem we face in parliament today, and the problem we have faced during the six months this question has been before the Canadian people, is a problem of mishandling and mismanagement in the way this matter was placed before the country, the absolute and unbelievable carelessness of the government in endeavouring to give the people the impression that it is decisive at least on the flag issue, if on nothing else.
Members of the government have finally made a decision to bring in closure, and what a grand decision that is. I can think of nothing worse; I can think of nothing more undemocratic than to tell the Canadian people they are going to have a flag, born of division, flying from the flagpoles of this nation; for certainly when the vote is taken tonight there will be division and that division will be as indicative of the nation as it is of the House of Commons.
What will they have after the vote is taken? If the other house is kind and considerate- something the upper house in South Africa

was not-they will have a flag that is as colourless, as nondescript as any flag produced by any of the emerging nations in the world in which we live. They say the maple leaf is an emblem of the nation, and with that I have no argument. As I said earlier, it may come to mean something in the future; but for a nation 97 years of age it is a sad looking flag, produced by a sad looking government for a sad looking people, for that is certainly what they will be tomorrow morning.
The flag design, Mr. Speaker, is typical of the picture this government has produced ever since it took office. One can well understand why members opposite finally embraced it and agreed, with one exception, that it should be the flag which will fly over our nation. I think we should have been better off as a parliament and as a nation if the government had moved to set aside the whole question. Surely no one will get excited about the design now in question, and I consider there will always be a segment in this nation which will feel that the flag design chosen by the government should be replaced whenever the government is replaced. I cannot feel that any future government will find many arguments to use in opposition to the view held by many people in this country that some action should be taken to determine what the Canadian people as a whole believe should be involved in any flag which is to represent a nation which in 1967 will be celebrating its one hundredth birthday.
I regret more than anything else that a decision was made last April to move in this direction. It was known by the government that they would receive a measure of support from the province of Quebec for a flag design of this type, support which would not be available in any other part of Canada. One would have thought that in the light of other developments which are occurring and which have been occurring in the past few years hon. gentlemen opposite would have been forewarned about the type of animosity which would be created and developed by moving in this direction. It would have been more sensible to have decided that in the interests of national unity it would be better not to plant seeds of doubt in the minds of people in other parts of Canada. They should not have risked doing something which Canadians in other provinces might describe as nothing more than a concession.
I do not think the people of Quebec have much interest in whether we should have a maple leaf flag or whether the red ensign
Canadian Flag
should continue to fly from the flagpoles of this nation, so long as there is a government in Ottawa which is making an effort to solve some of the serious economic problems which face that province. It would have been much more sensible to have sought solutions to these economic problems before trying to find new symbols for this nation.
We are doing both.

You are not doing both, and the hon. member knows it. It is all very well for him to say the government is doing both, but let him tell me about one piece of legislation which has been presented to this house and which has reached any degree of finality in the last six months to deal with the problems of agriculture in his own province of Quebec. His problems are the same as those of the maritime provinces and of the area which I represent. They are problems of economics, not of symbols. We should seek solutions to these questions before getting into a fight over what the symbols of this nation should be or should not be. These are things we could all face together; we could deal with them in a united way. This is what we should have been considering and attacking since April instead of discussing maple leaves or other symbols.
When one o'clock tomorrow morning comes we shall still be faced with the same economic problems that face us today. There will be no divergence of opinion as far as they are concerned. Instead, I must resume my seat, I suppose, and see the red ensign come down-a flag which represents much of our past history-to be replaced by a maple leaf flag which may represent a great deal for the future but which represents absolutely nothing to me or to anybody else living in this nation today.

So we see, too, how simply the end of fighting might be reached. I am proud to be recorded as having spoken four times, as honestly and sincerely as I can, representing my riding on a matter of principle, rather than going down on the record as being responsible for catcalls, jeers, interruptions and objections such as we have been subjected to over a thousand times in the last ten days.
The history of this flag will go down in headlines, and I would like to repeat some of them, "The flag by July," "The Canadian flag by the Queen's visit," "The flag by Christmas," and now, "The flag by closure." I am

sure hon. members opposite can be proud of their record.
Yes, we are.
Oh, go back and be an undertaker.
Order please.
Well, stop them.
There is very little time left in this debate and I mean to ensure that each one has the proper opportunity of expressing his or her true sentiments.

Mr. Speaker, I am being accused of repetition. I ask you, is it wrong, where our country is concerned, to keep asking for reason? Is it wrong to keep asking for fairness? Is it wrong to keep asking for justice? Is it wrong to keep asking for an end to the project that is spreading disunity from coast to coast? No, Mr. Speaker, it is not wrong. This is not repetition. This should be the aim and object of all members of the house, not just those in the Conservative party.
It is wrong to have no reason.
Mr. Speaker, I hear the interjection, it is wrong to have no reason, and I sympathize with the hon. member.
To have to sit with you.

The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) rose in his place and put forward the aims, objectives and views of the government with respect to this very important matter. We had been asking him for days to do so, and we are still asking hon. members on the front benches opposite to do that very thing. The Prime Minister said he was speaking for all members of his cabinet in putting forward his views. Here was a golden opportunity for the leader of this great country to propose a plan, to put forward a compromise, to take action in a manner which would bring credit to a great statesman. Instead of seizing this golden opportunity, however, he delved into party politics to such an extent that he tried to place the blame for this political holocaust on the Conservative party.
Why could he not have left this entire measure out of partisan politics? Why did he embark on a course which plunged this country into political division? Why did he have to use our flag as barter on a partisan party platform? This is why we are in trouble today. It is sheer hypocrisy in my mind to

say this flag will bring national unity. How can it do so when there is division in this house as well as across Canada? We have been criticized for the fight we have put up in this chamber for the Canadian red ensign. If we do have a new flag let us hope that the government will be prepared to put up as much of a fight for that flag if the need should ever arise. The Prime Minister asked the opposition to join with the Liberals in putting up this glorious new flag which will mean the unity of Canada. I want to join wholeheartedly with my hon. friend from the Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) who said this afternoon that he would take no part in hauling down the red ensign. I will have no part in taking down Canada's flag. We are told we cannot have a plebiscite -that the people cannot make their wishes known. We must accept this position. This has been decided by the House of Commons. And now we have closure, so that the opposition cannot make its wishes known. Is it not a sad day indeed in Canada's history when we must have disunity in the country as a price for one man's desire for a new flag before Christmas? What a mockery of Canadian justice.
I have been criticized because I have dared to stand up and speak for the fourth time on this question. Would that I had the opportunity to speak four more times until this parliament returns to reason and sanity and allows the Canadian people to decide what flag they wish to have in the future. I am proud to be a member of a party which feels the Canadian people have the right to make Canadian decisions where the emotions of every single Canadian are involved. This is what we are fighting for, not a piece of cloth. The people of Canada will be asked to salute the flag on that flagpole and surely they should have the right to choose the flag they should salute. This is not a state; it is a democracy. We have tried, and we are continuing to try, to resolve this question in the best possible way. We have offered to compromise. From time to time we pointed out avenues along which the government could approach this question in a logical way. Instead members opposite approached this question from a partisan point of view. It was they who interjected this question into the business of the country, not us. It was they who gave it priority in the list of business to be completed by this house, not us. It was they who imposed closure, not us. Now they expect us meekly to submit to their will. We cannot do this. Representing the people I do,
Canadian Flag
I cannot accept these measures without fighting to the extent of my ability.
This is not a matter to be treated with the levity which we have witnessed. This involves the Canadian flag, and in my estimation the decision of this parliament will be final. Surely no other government in the future would dare to interject a flag question again into the work of a Canadian parliament. This is why the issue before us is so serious. This is why we must be so right in our decisions and deliberations. This is why we must be sure that what we are doing is right. I feel the government is making one of the biggest blunders any government could make because I believe that instead of unity it is actively promoting disunity in this country, as never before.
Mr. Speaker, the people will know who is responsible. It is not us: It is the government which brought this measure into being.

In the
closing hours of this debate I intend to speak only briefly because I believe there has been too much talk already. The attitude of the public as I sense it in my travels across the country and through my correspondence is simply that most people are fed up with this subject.
Whether we agree or do not agree with the method being used to close off this debate; whether we agree or do not agree with the report of the flag committee on which we shall be voting tonight, the simple fact remains that nothing positive will be gained from a continuation of this debate. There is no place in the life of our country at this time for any further rocking of the boat. After some 260 speeches in the House of Commons, most of them from members of the Conservative opposition, any further debate on this flag issue would be redundant, superfluous and unnecessary. I do not believe that after all these hours of debate one opinion has been changed in this House of Commons. I do not think it is necessary to hash and rehash the arguments which have been raised by those who hold opposing opinions.
However, I am likewise convinced that the government has handled this flag situation very poorly right from the beginning. I think it is recognized by most Canadians that that is the case.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

You have made your speech.

Canadian Flag
I was wondering how the hon. member would have handled it.

The hon. member can ask his questions when I am through. However, democratic government will never function, in fact it will not survive, if a filibustering minority is permitted to paralyse the majority. Nor, on the other hand, will it ever function effectively or survive if the government continues to stumble into and out of one crisis after another. At the present time this parliament is plagued by both situations. It is now imperative that a decision be made through a vote which will express the will of the majority of the members of this House of Commons. In my opinion, there is no other alternative at the present time.
I say that, Mr. Speaker, in spite of the fact that I feel that a flag by closure is far from the ideal. Ever since a distinctive flag was called for in the election platform of the Social Credit party it has been suggested that the problem could best be worked out through a national referendum, and we have advocated this. However, I am convinced that in the way this flag situation rests at the present time any referendum would simply serve further to divide the country. We must face up to the reality of the situation.
This is the ninth time that closure has been invoked by the Canadian House of Commons in its 97 J years of history. Six times it was invoked by a Conservative government and three times by a Liberal government. It is a legitimate and an effective tool of a democratic legislature and the parliament at Westminster uses it often.
Not in this way.

I suggest that other parliaments use it, and for the same reason it is being used now. The situation we have in the house tonight is something which can have nothing but an adverse effect on the nation as a whole, and even though we do not like it and it is unfortunate that this is the means by which a decision will be made on the flag, I can see no other alternative.
Four months late the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) suggested an all party flag committee. The resulting committee, made up of 15 members, subsequently held some 45 sittings. At the time when the names of the members of this flag committee were announced-
You were in Africa.

I suggest that hon. members in the Conservative opposition give me

the same opportunity to speak that I have given them.
Hear, hear.

At the time that these 15 names were announced it was my thought that 15 capable, honest and trustworthy men had been chosen. It was a remarkable group of individuals who represented the rest of us on the flag committee. I want to thank them for the way they went to work and for the tremendous number of hours they put in. I am convinced they did their work conscientiously, carefully and thoroughly. Their final recommendation was decided by a majority vote of ten to four, not counting the chairman. We are now considering their report, and the purpose of the motion now before the house is to enable us either to accept or reject this report. It is that vote in which we are expected to take part tonight following the vote on the amendment, which to me is contrary to the decision made by the flag committee.
As one of those who agreed to the setting up of this flag committee I am convinced that it is my own personal obligation to support the report of the committee and I intend to do so. I say this even though I personally do not prefer the design which they selected.
What would you like?

It is not a question of what I personally like. We entrusted this responsibility to these 15 men, and in view of the fact that they did submit a strong and substantial majority report I think it is our responsibility to support them. I believe this is the general opinion of the majority of the Canadian people.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that this is the opinion of Canadians living abroad, which after all is where a flag perhaps serves its greatest use, because it does represent Canadians who are abroad. I was in France and Germany in June and I spoke to many members of our armed forces. I intentionally asked them their opinion about a flag, and not one dissenting voice did I hear to the proposition that it was time that Canada, in her unique role in foreign affairs, had its own distinctive symbol. I found this opinion expressed in my recent trip to Africa, where I met hundreds of Canadians who were doing a worth-while job in the countries they were serving. They were doing a magnificent job representing our country, and once again I heard not one dissenting voice to the proposition that it is time Canada had her own distinctive flag. In

fact, I believe that the reports of the goings on in this house which have been carried by the world's press have lowered the image of Canada in the minds of a lot of people who look to Canada, a small nation, as a leader of other small nations. They are wondering just what is taking place in this house.
There is one further aspect I should like to mention in connection with this entire issue. It seems to me that the elected representatives of the Canadian people should have more concern for our country than for their own partisan or personal convictions regarding the winning or losing of a single point in debate in this house. It is our responsibility and our privilege to demonstrate to the people of the world-yes, people of diverse backgrounds who do not know unity, or have the heritage we have in Canada-that together we can solve our problems in such a way as to meet the needs of every individual in this country, and thus prove to the world that the democratic form of government is best.
A question we might ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker, is: Have we grasped the significance of our own destiny as a nation? If we have, then we should not continue focusing our attention on such an internal matter as the flag, but should be looking to much wider horizons-to the world outside.
In presenting the concept and image of unity, how much more important is it that we show that we can settle our difference in an amicable and democratic fashion? It could mean a great deal to the world if we as Canadians could set the example of solving the problems of our own country. I think this is most important at this time, and it should be remembered that it is not a flag which makes a country, it is a country and its people which make a flag.
I am convinced that the deficit picture, with which we are faced now, following these 33 days of debate, has brought us to the point where it is now our responsibility, particularly as members of parliament, to get on with the job before us which we are expected to perform. That is why my own decision is a very simple one about this debate. I believe there is only one alternative open to us, if we look at the situation objectively.
Many have spoken about the past, and let me say that I respect the past. In fact, one of the lessons I learned early in my lifetime at home is that we should respect the past and those who have been part of it, as well as the institutions for which they have fought, not only to help survive, but to perpetuate 20220-702
Canadian Flag
for us. In closing I should like to say that while that respect for the past must remain, our responsibility is to the future because we, our children and their children are going to live in the future.

Mr. Speaker, since this debate will close tonight I think it is appropriate for me to recapitulate the position the New Democratic party has taken on this question.
On June 16 when this debate was opened on the flag question I said that our party had three main objections to the proposal which was then placed before the house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). Those objections are still valid. Our first objection was toward the design which the Prime Minister proposed at that time. We said that we were prepared to vote for it because we wanted to see a distinctive national flag adopted, but that we would prefer another design.
I must say that we are pleased that the Prime Minister was prepared to send this question of a design to a parliamentary committee, and I should like to commend that committee for its work. The Prime Minister deserves commendation because of the fact that he was prepared to forgo the design he submitted to the house, and because he is now prepared to accept the design recommended by the committee. It takes a big man to adopt that position.
At least the majority of the members of this group are prepared to support the recommendation of the committee, but I am frank to say that the design the committee selected would not have been our choice. We would have preferred the design of our original suggestion, the red maple leaf on a white background with blue vertical bars denoting, as does the Canadian motto, from sea to sea. The committee voted on that design and turned it down. We live in a democracy, and no group living in a democracy can obtain all the things it wants. The committee has brought down a design, which I think is a good design and the design which ought to commend itself to the great majority of the Canadian people.
The position we have taken in this group on the flag question is that there should be a free vote. We take that view because the flag issue involves personal judgment and is a matter of one's own feeling. It has nothing to do with political ideologies or philosophies, and is not a partisan matter. One or two of our members will vote for the amendment. The majority will vote against the amendment; not because we are against the red

Canadian Flag
ensign, but because we believe that the majority of the people of Canada want a flag which symbolizes Canada's independence and Canada's role in world affairs.
I can understand those who have deep attachments for symbols of the past, since I have them myself, but I think we must recognize that Canada has moved from being a colony to a dominion, and from being a dominion to being a self-governing autonomous member of the commonwealth. As we have progressed toward being an autonomous nation, our symbols must also have changed to represent that change. We must have faith in the future of Canada, and I believe that our children's children and their children will see the day when Canada will have a bigger population and larger gross national product than the motherland which gave us birth. I think this will be one of the two great countries of the North American continent within the next century.
If we are to keep our rendezvous with destiny we must have a flag which denotes our faith in that destiny and our sense of national identity. I believe we can do this best by adopting a flag which does not constantly remind us of the things which have divided us too often in the past.
The second thing we objected to about the government's program was the method by which this whole question was brought before us. I am not going to labour that point, but I do want to say that I think the government could have saved itself and this country a great deal of heartache by sending this question to the committee in the first place without any time limit, and could have given Canadians a chance to attempt at least to work out some consensus, obtaining the support of the majority of Canadian people with a minimum of dissension and bitterness.
The report of the parliamentary committee of 1945 put forward a recommendation which, if I remember correctly, was voted for by 23 to 1. That is close to being a unanimous vote. If I remember correctly, that committee sat for 18 months. I do not think 18 months is too great a price to pay for general support for something such as a flag. The great tragedy of that period is that the flag recommended was not adopted by parliament. Had it been adopted by parliament we would have been saved a great deal of trouble during this session.
As I have said, I commended the Prime Minister on June 16, because of the fact that he picked up this thorny nettle which all his
[Mr. Douglas.)
predecessors carefully avoided. I think he is to be commended that he has undertaken this matter, but I suggest that the method which was adopted has brought a great deal more dissension and some degree of bitterness which I believe could have been avoided.
The other thing which we criticized at the beginning of the debate was the government's timing. I suggested on June 16 that by introducing this question at the time it was brought into the house the government was going to paralyse parliament and obstruct its own program. After all, there had been nothing in the speech from the throne about a flag. Early in June the Prime Minister was asked if he would outline the business for the remainder of the session and if I remember correctly he read out 38 legislative items, all of them important. Then, about the middle of June came the flag debate, with the result that we spent all of the summer months without discussing legislation. It obstructed the whole legislative program completely with the result that when this session of parliament is prorogued probably more legislation will die on the order paper than has been passed during the session. I think that is unfortunate.
When the government finally agreed to send this matter to a committee I thought the government had an excellent opportunity to redeem its mistake. It would have been a good thing to let the committee's report lie there, go on with the legislative program and let the flag wait until the end of the session or even wait until next session. But the Prime Minister, in one of his more pixilated moments on the C.B.C., promised that he was going to have a flag by Christmas. Why? It was not a matter of life or death. No one was going to suffer if the decision on the flag were delayed until January or until next spring or until next summer. What was the urgency in this matter? Many more urgent matters affecting the lives, the welfare and the well-being of the Canadian people are on the order paper that are not being dealt with because the flag has preoccupied our time. What was the hurry? What was the urgency?
Only three weeks ago I asked the Prime Minister on the orders of the day if he would agree to leave the flag debate until we had at least dealt with the national labour code, which after all affects the welfare of 650,000 workers in Canada who come under federal jurisdiction. The Prime Minister said no, that we had to deal with the flag. What we have had is one blunder after another and now

the supreme folly of all, in my opinion, the forcing of a decision by means of closure.
I am not opposed to closure when it becomes necessary on legislation whose passage means improving the lot of the Canadian people. If the Canada pension plan or the national labour code or a medicare plan or some other plan upon which the Canadian people were waiting were involved, if there had been adequate time for debate and expression of opinion by all groups in the house, and if some obstreperous minority was holding it up, I would support closure. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that closure on a flag, closure on something about which there was no urgency, closure on something which is an emotionally charged issue that touches people's lives and beliefs and faith, is a totally different thing. After all, a nation only selects a flag once in its history. Surely it ought to be allowed to take time to make that selection after due reflection.
In respect of the navy bill in 1913 and the pipe line legislation of 1956, both of which have left scars on the political life of Canada, there was at least the excuse that there was a deadline to be met, but on the flag question there was no deadline at all to be met except the deadline established by the Prime Minister's own promise that we would have a flag by Christmas. The only real issue at stake was that parliament had to conform to the Prime Minister's timetable in order to maintain the Prime Minister's reputation and enhance his vanity.
I do not mean by what I am saying that I condone the filibuster which has been carried on by the Progressive Conservative party over a long period of time. I respect their point of view although I do not agree with it. I think they had adequate time to express their opinions repeatedly, and they did so. But I think there comes a time when there ought to be a decision and I think they would have been wise to have allowed parliament to make a decision long before this. But the sad thing, Mr. Speaker, is that we have had in this parliament the spectacle of the present Prime Minister saying "we are going to have a flag by Christmas" and the former prime minister of Canada saying "you are not going to have a flag by Christmas".
What do you say?

My friend says "what do you say". I think Canadians deserve something better than this from their two major political leaders. That is what I think. I think the spectacle we have witnessed in recent 20220-7021
Canadian Flag
weeks has reduced parliament to a farce. It has been a childish exhibition that has done this country no good.
The thing that concerns me most, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure it must concern the Prime Minister, is that the two things he was hoping to accomplish by introducing this flag have been destroyed by the method which has been used to bring the matter to a decision. The first thing the Prime Minister was hoping to accomplish was to establish national unity. I do not think that the action taken today will do anything to enhance national unity.
Last week the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) and the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) were suggesting closure. I make an appeal to my French Canadian friends. I say to them very frankly that we English speaking people in Canada have too often and too long been callously insensitive to the susceptibilities of the French Canadian people. We acknowledge that and we ought to apologize for it. We ought to try to rectify it. But, Mr. Speaker, it must also work both ways. I ask the French Canadian members who are crying for closure to stop and ask themselves this question. If the committee had recommended the union jack or the red ensign and the members from Quebec had been speaking out vigorously against it, as I am sure some of them would have, would they have asked for closure or supported closure? I do not think so.
I am not one of those who thinks this flag is a concession to Quebec. As a matter of fact, I am convinced that the great bulk of the English speaking people in Canada will support this single maple leaf design. However, I would remind the French Canadian members that there is an English speaking minority, with whose views I do not concur, but I respect those views and I am prepared to fight for their right to have those views; and it seems to me that imposing closure is not likely to improve the feeling between the two founding races and is not going to promote national unity.

I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question. Does he consider that the French Canadian members are restricting the freedom of speech of the English speaking members when, after 200 speeches, they ask for an opportunity for the house to take a decision?

Well, my hon. friend ought to have more influence in stopping some of those speeches than I am likely to have. However,

Canadian Flag
I agree with him that when a debate has gone on a long time everybody gets sick and tired of it. I am suggesting when you are trying to select a flag, which you select only once in the lifetime of a nation, you will be far better to put the matter aside and let the idea become familiar, to see if you cannot find some basis upon which you can get a greater consensus than that which obtains at the present time.
I have only two minutes left, Mr. Speaker, and I want to make my last point. The other purpose the Prime Minister was hoping to accomplish by introducing this flag was to get general acceptance across Canada. I think that the government had a golden opportunity to have introduced a flag that would have given voice to Canadians' sense of pride in their country. Instead of that, we are in danger of having a flag which is going to be launched in bitterness. I hope not.
Why mention it?
The hon. member says, "Why mention it?". I fear for the reaction to a flag that is hoisted by closure.
Hear, hear.

I wanted to say that in my opinion only a government which had lost its sense of values, which had become obsessed with a political death wish, would have compounded its long list of blunders by the supreme folly of invoking closure on a measure so emotionally charged as the flag. I hope I am wrong. I hope that any bitterness or any rancour that has been aroused will be forgotten. I pledge myself and the party with which I am associated that we will not only vote for this flag but we will do everything in our power to get the Canadian people to support it-to support it as their flag. We will do all we can to get people persuaded to put any bitterness or enmity behind them and to push on to the future, to build the

kind of country over which that flag will fly as a symbol of Canada's greatness, its peace and its prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks made by the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) and to those of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) concerning the adoption of a distinctive national flag.
The hon. member who just resumed his seat said a while ago that the understanding between English speaking and French speaking Canadians must be effected in relation to-

speechtext:
