amendment. The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) now has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I have not yet had the opportunity to speak on the amendment under consideration but I feel that our party's point of view must be put forward on this last night of the flag debate.
I would say that one sentence in particular caught my attention, if not several, in the speech the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam (Mr. Douglas) has just made. He asked us to be patient; he said that a flag is chosen only once in a lifetime, that a decision must be postponed if there is not unanimous agreement in this house. And yet, a few minutes before, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam had congratulated the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for taking today a step which none of his predecessors had dared take about a distinctive national flag.
Talk of a distinctive national flag is nothing new. Henri Bourassa brought the matter up in this house in 1910 and 1911, but, at that time, they did exactly what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam proposed a while ago. The issue was put aside for lack of unanimity.

How many times, under the R. B. Bennett administration, from 1930 to 1935, did hon. Senator Pouliot say he himself had introduced, before the war, a motion for the adoption of a distinctive national flag? That was 30 years ago, and his resolution was shelved until there could be some degree of unanimity.
How many other members of this house, in 1944, 1945, every year for the last 20 or 30 years, have put forward a motion in this house for the adoption of a distinctive flag? But such a motion was never agreed to in the past on the grounds that there was not enough unanimity.
Today if the Prime Minister were to withdraw his motion or shelve it, I ask every member of this house, and particularly the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), when we would ever have this distinctive national flag?
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said that this is something which is given but once in the life of a nation, but how old must our nation be before we can fly this flag? Must we wait until we become more deeply mired in old traditions before we adopt this flag? We have been oblivious about this flag long enough. I do not approve the Prime Minister on many other points, but I do not hesitate to say that I support him unreservedly on this point, since he was courageous enough to introduce his measure, resist all pressures and maintain his intention to give the people of Canada a distinctive national flag.
Our attitude in this respect is very clear. These eternal discussions have lasted long enough, even too long, putting off until tomorrow a distinctive national flag and a national anthem for Canada, because we are convinced that such feelings reflect a true Canadianism, and we want this to become a fact.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and others before him have made a pathetic appeal in favour of good relations between English and French speaking Canadians. But how can English Canadians and French Canadians endeavour to understand each other? This understanding must work both ways.
That's right, it must work both ways.

Mr. Speaker, here is a question I want to ask all members of this house: Which of the two groups has done more toward good understanding? The English Canadian group or the French Canadian group? During the 17 years the
Canadian Flag
hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was premier of his province, during the 17 years he held that post, how were French Canadians treated in his province, with regard to the school question, as compared to English Canadians in the province of Quebec?

speechtext: Order. May I be allowed to suggest to the hon. member for Lapointe that the comments he is now making are beyond the limits of our discussion?

Mr. Speaker, if my comments are not within the ambit of this debate, then why was the matter brought up a while ago? Since I am only speaking about objections raised earlier, I think my remarks are in order. If a previous speaker was allowed to express his views on the subject, I feel I am also entitled to voice my opinion.
Mr. Speaker, understanding between English Canadians and French Canadians must work both ways, because this is essential in order to come to an agreement. It must be like the wheels of an engine on railroad tracks; they must turn in the same direction, not one in one direction and the other in the opposite direction.
What has happened since confederation? Can the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam tell me that French Canadians have not made every effort in the province of Quebec to co-operate with and understand the English element? I claim that they have done as much and even much more than the English Canadian governments in the other provinces, including the Saskatchewan government during the 17 years when the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was premier. Had he asked the French Canadians in his province if they were treated as well as the English Canadians in our province, I do not think he would have made that pathetic appeal a while ago, because I think we have done more than our share and I think we have worked for Canadian unity. If the question comes up today, it is not because we have not done our share, but perhaps because efforts have not been made for Canadian unity in all parts of the country.
Maybe there have been some extremists on one side, but there have been some on the other also. We are asked this question: Had the committee proposed the red ensign or the union jack, would you have supported it or would you not have fought to the death? In answer to that objection, I would say this: We have had it for 97 years, we have accepted it for 97 years. Today, English speaking Canadians are not being asked to

Canadian Flag
become French Canadians but to become just plain Canadians. We are prepared to fight so that each and every one of us may become Canadians. We have been lukewarm Canadians long enough, Canadians too closely connected with other countries, while we believe that Canada must be really independent, as mentioned by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
I admit that objections have been raised regarding the selection of a flag design. But when have you seen a country select a flag by means of a national referendum or a vote of members of parliament? Canada would be the first country to do this. The value of a flag does not depend on its colour, on what is on it or on its design, but on what it symbolizes. A flag represents a country where you feel at home, for that is the definition of the motherland. The motherland is where you love to live, where you feel at home. That is what a flag should represent. It is not a picture, a photograph or a drawing, it is something representing the motherland, and I have just defined what is the motherland.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that in the selection of a flag we should not pay too much attention to unimportant details, but rather try to design something which we will fly as a symbol of the motherland where everybody will be glad to live, that is in an independent Canada constituted by Canadians of different races, but races getting along with one another. And it is true that races can get along together.
Since the beginning of the debate on the flag, I had the opportunity of talking with Conservative members who rose in the house to express opinions which were flabbergasting to a genuine Canadian citizen, but when I had a friendly chat with them, understanding was possible. How is it that understanding is possible between two individuals of different races but that this understanding becomes practically impossible when one takes the floor to speak on behalf of a political party in the house? That is the whole question. To answer that question is answering the important question of Canadian unity.
When she was last in Canada, Her Majesty the Queen said that one's own patriotism should not keep one from understanding the patriotism of others.
Mr. Speaker, I quite understand that many Canadians will see with regret, even with sorrow, the red ensign lowered to be replaced by a new flag. However, Mr. Speaker, if they truly love their country, they will understand that they are saluting more than a flag, that

they are indeed saluting the country in which they live. I admit and understand the grief, the sorrow they will feel; still, emotions and feelings must not always dictate our conduct. They should rather try to look to the future of Canada, without forgetting the past, our forefathers' heritage.
We should think in terms of a great country, a country that wants to develop itself, in short a country, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said-and I agree with him on this point-which may become greater than those which contributed to its foundation and development. But, if we are to vote once in our lifetime on a flag, let us do it, at least, while we are still alive.
Mr. Speaker, we do not consider this matter as a quarrel between French Canadians and English Canadians, but we believe that the debate on the flag will have been a tremendous test concerning the future of mutual understanding and unity in Canada. It will have been a test of understanding between our Canadian citizens, in short, between the two main races which make up this country.
And if one wonders about the success of this test about the mutual understanding which may exist in Canada, there is certainly no cause for rejoicing, because we find that, before thinking as statesmen, too many members tried to play politics with this matter. Therefore, I think that the test of the flag debate is a lamentable failure and only served to point out that there was still too great a divergence of opinions in this country.
But we shall have a flag. It will be perhaps unfortunately voted in by applying closure. But if the closure rule had not been imposed, when would we have had this flag? Perhaps never, and it would have been shelved once and for all.
But, the flag once adopted by parliament, we hope that everybody will say: This is now Canada's flag, let us now work for Canada's growth and development, so that we, and the future generations can be proud of it.
This will promote throughout the country a better Canadian spirit and, therefore, a better understanding between Canada's two great races.

Today we have seen most unusual and, I believe, unfortunate developments in connection with the question of our national flag.
The amendment we are presently considering, as proposed by my hon. friend from Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) reads as follows:

That the sixth report of the special committee be not now adopted but that it be referred back to the committee with instructions to strike out in paragraph 7 all the words after "Canada" and substitute "be the Canadian red ensign."
Acceptance of this amendment would mean that paragraph 7 of the committee report would read:
Your committee therefore recommends that the flag to be designated as the national flag of Canada be the Canadian red ensign.
I do not think it will be any news to hon. members of this house when I say I have no hesitation whatsoever in favouring paragraph 7 as amended.
I wish now to refer to the speech which was made by my hon. friend from Middlesex West on Friday, because I feel he outlined in that speech the objective of every member of this house. I have no hesitation in saying he represented my views to the fullest possible extent. I quote from his remarks as reported on page 11023.
The party to which I have the honour to belong, in common with all other parties in the house, is doing, I believe, whatever it can to promote national unity in this country. Opinions may differ as to how national unity can best be promoted. There are honest differences of opinion regarding the procedure which should be adopted with this end in view. Our party has taken the stand that for the government to impose a flag by a vote of this house is not the best way to promote national unity. We have the right to present our view and to urge our view upon all hon. members of the house. We wish national unity-
In my opinion the proposition that we shall have national unity in the present circumstances, especially in the circumstances of closure, is a misleading one and the action now being taken by the government will not bring about the result which is generally desired. I wish to quote from today's copy of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald in support of this view. The writer is a distinguished member of the press gallery, Mr. Eric Dennis, and he has this to say in connection with the whole matter of national unity and what is likely to happen if the committee's report is accepted. He says:
What will be the reaction when the maple leaf flag is hoisted over the peace tower, over every federal building, every military installation, every military cemetery in which Canada's war dead lie buried, at the United Nations, every Canadian embassy abroad and at NATO, as will be required once the new banner is officially proclaimed?
Will there be the embracing of it from sea to sea which Prime Minister Pearson so eloquently pleaded for in his final speech on the issue Friday?
Will there be, as Holmes said "one flag, one land, one heart, one hand?"
Canadian Flag
The writer has certainly asked a most pertinent series of questions. In the same article he proceeds to answer them. He says:
British Columbia Premier W. A. C. Bennett already has promised that four flags will fly by official sanction over the legislative buildings at Victoria-his province's own banner, the maple leaf design, the red ensign and the union jack.
Quebec is certain to keep the fleur-de-lis flying for years to come despite the insistence of its federal representatives that it did not want even this emblem incorporated in the new Canadian flag.
It will take a good time before the red ensign comes down in the maritimes and many other parts of Canada.
And Newfoundland's Premier J. R. Smallwood has made it plain the full union jack will not be pulled down over his island.
If this is an indication of what is expected should this motion pass, and we assume it will, it seems to me the government has taken a tremendous responsibility on its shoulders.
Some members may be wondering why I should reiterate my support for the red ensign, a stand I have taken many times in this chamber. This evening my hon. friend and next door neighbour here, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Mar-tineau) quoted from Abraham Lincoln, the great emancipator. I intend to quote the same great statesman. Abraham Lincoln at one stage in his career uttered these words-they are very short but they are very potent and most pertinent to this subject. He said: "To sin by silence when they should protest makes cowards out of men". I do not propose there should be any doubt in the minds of anyone in this chamber or in Canada about where I stand on this particular question.
The recent development to which I referred a few minutes ago was this decision to use closure which would put an end to the debate on the amendment favouring the red ensign. Hon. members may properly ask: do you favour closure? I find myself saying that I do not favour closure when it has the effect of discarding a flag which has been used as the national flag of Canada to a greater or lesser degree for almost 100 years. This is one time when I do not think closure is justified. I agree with my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) that there are times, when important legislation is being held up with an ulterior purpose in mind, when closure may be justified. I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) who said that this was a time when closure was not justified, especially in view of the amendment now proposed. I do not question the advantage of

Canadian Flag
closure when used in the national interest, but in this case I think-and I say this advisedly-that the contemplated action does not qualify under the general heading of what is good for Canada.
I said in a previous speech that the changing of the flag of a country was in the same category as changing its constitution, and I repeat those words. This action should never be taken on a mere majority vote. I also said in a previous speech that changing a flag which has been in use for something like 100 years is a responsibility which should not be taken as a result of a majority vote taken of 265 members of parliament. I know there is a great deal of difference of opinion on this matter, but I think the reasons for not changing a flag without a great deal of consideration and deliberation cannot be challenged.
I am one of those who listened to the speech of the Prime Minister on Friday last most attentively, but I found myself taking exception to many of his conclusions. He quoted words attributed to Mr. Speaker Lemieux and he acknowledged they were a moving illustration of what is best in our history. But he also stated that they were an indication of how history changes and that we should not ignore the lessons of history when we support Canadian symbols for Canadian nationality. My contention in this connection is that we do not eliminate historical symbols in the process of incorporating what the Prime Minister referred to as Canadian symbols. Surely there is no need to eliminate all that is good and which we treasure in the past in order to incorporate something into our flag.
In this connection I want to quote an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette for this morning which talks about the division of the country. In speaking of this division the editorial says:
It recalls the saying of Mr. Louis St. Laurent, when he was prime minister, that he would not introduce a new flag until he was satisfied that it would do more to unite than to divide the country. To be ready to divide the house hut not the country suggests an embarrassment over the issue. Yet it remains true that in avoiding a flag election the government is acting wisely. Whether the government was as wise in getting itself into its present position is another matter.
That, Mr. Speaker, is where I say the government has made a tremendous mistake. As I have said many times, and as other hon. members have said, it is the government's handling of this whole question to which we object.

I should like to draw the attention of the house to the order in council which was passed in 1945, and I do so only to refer to the second paragraph thereof, which in my opinion is a vital paragraph. After the usual preamble the second paragraph states:
That the Canadian red ensign was employed by Canadian forces during the present war;-
That was one of the reasons for carrying into operation this order in council by which the use of the Canadian red ensign was made legal within and without Canada. That reason has stood for the last 20 years and still stands today.
What has happened, Mr. Speaker, to bring about this change? In view of the special mention which the Canadian red ensign received in that order in council, this house should hesitate for a long time before interfering with the aims and objectives of the order in council itself. According to the Prime Minister, as reported at page 11032 of Hansard he said:
It was not until 1945... that the union jack was replaced by the red ensign as an official flag for Canada. At that time we all remember that a great many sincere people in Canada opposed that change. Many who are now worried about the change from the red ensign were worried about a change from the union jack, but I think we all agree now that this was a desirable and an inevitable stage in our national progression.
I am sure everyone will agree with that; there is no question about it. But, Mr. Speaker, how can we ever justify the discarding and destroying of the symbols in our flag under which the same progression to which the Prime Minister refers has been made? Why do you throw something away under which you have made great progress, and substitute something else for it? Why should it be eliminated?
Then the Prime Minister went on to say that the order in council was made pending only a decision of the committee which had been set up at that time. I do not know how long the committee took to report; one of the hon. members who spoke this afternoon stated it took a year and a half. However, it did report following a majority vote of 23 to 1. It recommended that a golden maple leaf replace the Canadian coat of arms.
I would draw to the attention of the house the fact that the prime minister of that day, Right Hon. Mackenzie King, did not implement the report of that committee. The house never had before it a motion for concurrence in that committee's report. I am one of those who think the prime minister of that day had good reason for not doing

this, and I give him full marks in that regard.
Then in 1948, after allowing the red ensign to remain the national flag of Canada and to fly at home and abroad, Mr. Mackenzie King was replaced by Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent as prime minister of Canada. Mr. St. Laurent continued in office until 1957, a period of nine years, and Mr. St. Laurent did not change the Canadian flag. And I have no doubt that Mr. St. Laurent also had good reason for leaving it alone.
We now find this government coming into office, and one of the first things it does is to bring before the house this motion, and it does so in such a partisan way that it seems as though it is going to have a very adverse effect upon the unity of our nation. The government presented a motion for a design to this parliament last spring consisting of three maple leaves conjoined on one stem. It was presented to the house by the Prime Minister in an eloquent speech. Many speeches were made from this side in opposition to it. There were a few speeches in support of it. Many points were made in connection with it. Then agreement was reached to refer it to a committee. A majority report of the committee did not favour the three maple leaf design as approved by the Prime Minister, his government and their supporters, but recommended another design. Now the government, the Prime Minister and his supporters seem to be quite willing to concur in the report of that committee, even though that committee did not concur with the original submission made by the government to this parliament. They changed their ideas completely and seem today apparently to have lost interest. They discarded the three maple leaf design as quickly or quicker than they discarded the Canadian red ensign. They have now become enthusiastic about the one maple leaf flag. There has been a complete right-about-face which leads us properly to interpret their main intention as being to eliminate the union jack from its place on our flag. We have been using that union jack in an official capacity for almost 20 years, and for almost 100 years to a greater or lesser degree.
In the course of the Prime Minister's remarks, as they are recorded at page 11036, he said:
Unfortunately there has been a great deal of depreciation and sneering about the maple leaf as an emblem on a flag. I do not understand why hon. members opposite take that attitude toward this symbolism of Canadianism. I suggest it is unfortunate that the impression has been created in certain areas and quarters that the maple leaf is not worthy of being a national symbol of Canada 20220-703
Canadian Flag
on a flag, and I hope that when the dust of the debate has cleared away, if this recommendation carries, we will all be proud of the fact that the central feature of our flag is a red maple leaf.
In connection with the modified red ensign I should like to refer to the fact that when the committee was voting on different designs one vote related to a design which had a maple leaf in the centre. That flag had the very thing incorporated in it about which the Prime Minister said in his speech there was some prejudice. The committee did vote on a motion to support a flag with a maple leaf in the centre, with symbols of French and English heritage on either side, but that design did not carry in the committee. I mention that fact simply because it refutes the argument made by the Prime Minister that there is some prejudice against the red maple leaf as such.
Mr. Speaker, I see you nodding your head, and you have been very kind to me, so I will bring my remarks to a conclusion. I should like to refer to many other things, but I appreciate the attention which I have received from all hon. members of this house and will now take my seat.

I should like to refer to one or two things which have been mentioned earlier by preceding speakers. The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh) referred to the fact that there had been 22 days of debate on the previous resolution and 11 days debate, including today, on the present motion to concur in the sixth report of the committee. I should like to stress very strongly that the 22 days of debate took place on a resolution to adopt the three maple leaf design. The present debate is related to the one maple leaf flag. I do not understand why we should be criticized for debating this issue to the extent we have debated it, and I admit it has been rather a long debate, in view of the fact that we believe this is the most serious subject that has come before this parliament for consideration.
Certain editorials across this country have criticized us for delaying the adoption of a flag. They have pointed out that we have debated 22 days on the first flag and 11 days on this motion for concurrence. The two debates dealt with two flags, both sponsored by the government. We ask the question: Which flag does the government want? It is obvious that the government has no answer to that question.
I believe the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) said this evening that it was very important to have something overseas

Canadian Flag
which could be recognized as Canada's own distinctive national flag. I am sure the Canadian red ensign is known abroad as Canada's national flag. In relation to that which people in embassies and other places overseas think about a national flag, what do the 19 million Canadian people who live in Canada, and who might never have the opportunity of travelling abroad, think about the national flag? It is those people and their opinions about which I am concerned. I feel very strongly that we are dealing tonight with an issue which affects the hearts and souls of every Canadian. There are different points of view on this subject and I appreciate the points of view of those who do not agree with me. However, I cannot understand why we who stand for what has been Canada's national flag should be entirely deprived of any semblance of that flag on any proposed flag.
Tonight is the third time I have taken part in the debate on the flag issue. Perhaps I should receive one of the hats given out by that pinhead down in the corner; however, he is not in his seat at the moment. He took part in the debate a short time ago and I presume that he feels, having said what he did say, everything of importance has been said. As a consequence of that feeling he has left the chamber.
I make no apology for taking part again in this debate on the amendment to the motion to concur in the sixth report of the committee. I spoke first on August 24, at which time I outlined clearly my position on the flag issue. I would like to repeat some of the statements I made on that occasion, but unfortunately time will not permit me to do so. I do not back down from any statement I made on that occasion, and I state again that my position today regarding the whole national flag issue and the Canadian red ensign is as I stated it to be on that occasion.
Having sat as a member of the committee, which worked arduously for six weeks studying the whole situation, I had the honour to speak again on November 30 and move an amendment which called for a plebiscite. I do not intend to go into the pros and cons of holding a plebiscite, as they have been clearly set out on many occasions. All I can say in that regard is that the amendment was defeated, and we accept that fact. At the moment, Mr. Speaker, we are discussing an amendment moved by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) to the same motion to concur and the vote on that amendment will in effect decide whether or not we are going to continue to have the red ensign.
[Mr. Monteith.J
Those who vote against this amendment are going to vote to tear down the red ensign; let there be no mistake about that.
My main reason for speaking now at all is that we are now going to lose the red ensign which this country has known in so many emotional circumstances. I have to agree that from the sense of the house tonight this is what will happen, no matter what may be said. We know their minds are made up. They are sitting stony faced across the way. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith), the Solicitor General (Mr. Mac-Naught), the purveyor of bumper stickers- there are not too many of them on the ministerial benches at this moment-they are all going to vote us down. I know that. However, I think we should be entitled to our last plea and our last fight. I do not think we should be chastised for putting up that fight.
I am going to be very frank and say that I do not think enough has been said in the press media about where the real fault lies for the present situation. Let us say that those who wish a new flag have every right so to wish. I am not quarrelling with those who wish a new flag. I am not quarrelling in the least with those who promote it. But surely others have the right to disagree. Surely those who have grown up with and have known no other flag have a right to disagree with respect to a new flag. Surely we have the right simply to maintain what we have now. What is wrong with that?
I claim that generally speaking the press has not been fair in fixing blame on a particular party for having caused disunity in Canada. Let us face it. We certainly have greater division and disunity today than we had last May when the flag question was introduced. There is no question about that. The government, Mr. Speaker, is completely responsible for this situation. All that the President of the Privy Council does is to get up and move closure. Let him get up and make a speech as to what he thinks of the whole situation.
They are responsible for the whole situation, Mr. Speaker. Surely when they first raised this question, particularly in the manner they did, they must have realized what would happen. They could have introduced this question in a more reasonable manner. We know that. They must have realized what would happen, but they just did not care. It is the same old arrogance dating back to 1956. I should like to refer to an editorial in today's Montreal Gazette to which the

hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) referred a little while ago. I should like to read one sentence:
It recalls the saying of Mr. Louis St. Laurent, when he was prime minister, that he would not introduce a new flag until he was satisfied that it would do more to unite than to divide the country.
This is the point. You know very well, Mr. Speaker, that this whole flag question has done more to divide than to unite. Mr. St. Laurent knew that and so did his predecessor in office. They were very well aware of the situation. I should like to make one other reference. I trust I am not taking too much of the time of the house. I should like to refer to an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of last Saturday.
Order.
I do not know who yelled "order" over there, but get up on your feet and make a speech like a man.
If it was anything like yours I would sit down.
You are much better sitting down.
So are you, but you do not know it.

I should like to refer to this editorial because it accuses me as one of the Conservatives on the flag committee of having abandoned the red ensign. It reads in part as follows:
The committee rejected the red ensign. Even the Conservative members of the committee abandoned the ensign and suggested a modified maple leaf flag-
This is an absolutely false statement. Today the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) had reason to rise on a question of privilege about an editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail. I suppose I might well have got up on a question of privilege and raised this matter at that time. This statement is absolutely false. We never at any time abandoned the Canadian red ensign. When the matter was put to a vote we were defeated and after we were defeated we then tried to come up with a compromise which certainly was not acceptable either to the group across the way or to those down in the corner to my left.
I have read that there were only three choices open to the government, depending upon the viewpoint, I suppose. Some say two and some say three. The first was to abandon the plan, the second to impose closure and 20220-7034
Canadian Flag
the third to have a plebiscite at the next election. We have discussed the matter of a plebiscite and as I said earlier I am not going to pursue that subject any further. The house has made its decision on it and I am willing to accept that decision, much as I dislike doing so. As a matter of fact, I believe the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) made some reference tonight to the fact that the matter might have been best decided by a referendum. If he said that, then I accuse him of at least some ambiguity in his thinking because he did not vote for a plebiscite when he had the chance to do so.
I come back to the point that some say there were two choices open to the government and some say there were three. However, the government has made its choice and has imposed closure. I claim it has done so only to save the government's face because this vote will cause much more disunity in Canada than anything that has happened before in my memory. I am quite convinced that if the government could see its way to abandon the matter even at this late date it would do a great deal of good. I know they are not going to do so, but I just cannot say strongly enough how much good I think such an action would do for Canada.
The argument over the flag has been going on over the last several months, though I agree in a somewhat spotty manner; but at the same time I strongly believe that the only solution is for the government to withdraw its proposal so that more disunity will not be created, because that is where we are heading when the vote takes place tonight. We started out with three leaves and we spent 22 days on that flag. Now we have the one leaf design and we are on the eleventh day. This is not compromise. Let us be reasonable. Positions have hardened. Sure, the Prime Minister has said this is supposed to be an open vote. What kind of an open vote is this? Do not let us be ridiculous. He declared it was not an open vote many long months ago. The other day during the debate he suggested perhaps it could be an open vote.
Positions in this House of Commons have hardened, Mr. Speaker. There is no possibility of an open vote today. There is no doubt about it that parliament and the country must now accept an imposed verdict, an imposed flag. This is all there is to it. It is as simple as that. There are not too many members here even on the backbenches of the Liberal party, and very few on the treasury benches, who had the actual experience as I did of going through closure back in 1956.

Canadian Flag
I know the government wishes to forget that. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has indicated he would have liked to forget it. At one time he would have been willing to dispose of it. We have a new crop here today with the same mentality. They simply feel they have a divine right to rule. They will never learn.
I claim, Mr. Speaker, that this is our last stand for the Canadian red ensign, this flag which has been our country's flag for so many years, which has meant so much to practically everybody in Canada. I do not care from where they come, this flag has still meant a great deal to practically everybody. I come back now to an earlier statement I made. This government has done more by this particular manoeuvre, by bringing this whole question up as it has at the time it did, and in the way it did, to create disunity in Canada than anything else that could happen in this country. I only make a plea for those who do have some feeling for our past. I heard these views expressed by members from the other side in the committee. Could we not get together, could we not have something of the past as well as the present? I heard this view expressed. It has all gone by the board. We have nothing left that we can remember of our traditions, our heritage, part of our lives.
If this government had only waited. Sure, they ask, why do you want to wait? The Prime Minister said, what do you want to do, wait one year, two years or three years? I say, wait ten years until all the old codgers like myself are dead and gone, and then this question could be readily settled. Today it is causing a great deal of trouble. I see, Mr. Speaker, you have just received a slip suggesting that my time is up so I will resume my seat.

Mr. Speaker, as the two previous hon. members who spoke, it was my privilege also to serve on the flag committee.
I should like to take part in the final stage of this debate. First of all, I wish to state that working on the flag committee was an experience which I will not soon forget. You cannot associate yourself with 14 other members of the house for a period of six weeks, meeting two or three times a day, without gaining some knowledge, making new friendships and leaving something of yourself behind. These 14 members, Mr. Speaker, represented widely different areas of the country. They expressed their feelings and the aspirations of a cross

section of Canada. We learned to respect, if not to share entirely, our individual views. We spoke freely. I feel that I came out from the committee richer for the experience and in knowledge. I believe we all came out better Canadians.
It had been hoped and even expected, Mr. Speaker, that we should come from the flag committee with a unanimous report. It is unfortunate that we did not come out with a unanimous report. Under the circumstances, I feel that it could not be so. To insist on a unanimous decision or a virtually unanimous decision, or to insist on an 80 per cent or 90 per cent majority, in my opinion, would not be democracy; it would be a virtual minority dictatorship. I say that if only the members of this house who were elected with 80 per cent or 90 per cent majority had been allowed to speak in this debate the filibuster would have been very short indeed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we were very surprised, and indeed saddened, to hear some hon. members opposite say that the members of the Liberal party on that committee were under instructions to carry out the orders and signals received from the outside. This is not the case. Speaking for myself, I entered the committee with an open mind. I left at the door both the government's model and the red ensign. I started from scratch. My worry was not to find ways and means of preserving the red ensign. My ambition was not to impose the government design. My sole desire was to learn, to secure knowledge in heraldry, in history, and to try to end up with a design which would be technically correct, beautiful to see and truly Canadian. This is what we did.

Mr. Speaker, the task assigned to us seemed very difficult at first. But after listening to the opinions of experts in heraldry, history and economics, we soon began to grasp the essential characteristics a truly Canadian flag should have. Three basic principles were established:
1. We found that, according to the royal proclamation of King George V, in 1921, the two national colours were white and red, and in support of this first principle, let me quote from the royal proclamation itself, as it appears in this booklet published by the Department of the Secretary of State and entitled "The Arms of Canada".

A Proclamation Declaring His Majesty's Pleasure Concerning the Ensigns Armorial of the Dominion of Canada.

Now, Mr. Speaker, allow me to refer to the proceedings of the flag committee of 1945 and to quote a short excerpt from the testimony of a witness, Colonel Duguid D.S.O. an army historian of the Department of National Defence. Colonel Duguid read the royal proclamation of George V of which I have just read an excerpt and he then explained those excerpts as follows:

And upon a Royal helmet mantled argent doubled gules the crest, that is to say, on a wreath of the colours argent and gules a lion passant guar-dant or imperially crowned proper and holding in the dexter paw a maple leaf gules.
That is the full verbatim text. It may sound like nonsense but it enables anyone who understands to draw and colour a picture, complete in every detail. It resembles a doctor's prescription. It is either understood or it is complete nonsense. Cleared of confusing terms and items, and written in plain language, with argent translated as white and gules translated as red, the vital part of the proclamation would read: "The King, at the request of Canada, assigns to Canada the national colours white and red."

Moreover, on February 5, 1963, that is the very day the previous Conservative government was defeated, the following answer was given to question No. 1,449 which asked:
Does Canada have national colours and, if so, what are they?
Answer: Yes, Canada has national colours, which are white and red.
Therefore, as a first principle, the two national colours are white and red.
We also reached our decision on the basis of this second principle: the only really Canadian symbol is the maple leaf. Besides, the great majority of designs submitted to us included either one or three' maple leaves; and those designs came from every part of the country, mostly outside the province of Quebec.
The third principle by which we were finally guided to decide on the flag design is that heraldry does not allow the juxtaposition of colours or metals, that is one colour cannot be put on another and one metal cannot be put on another. Moreover, the only metals
Canadian Flag
recognized in heraldry are gold and silver, that is yellow and white.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it was a matter of applying those principles to the problem submitted to us. The conclusions can be found in the committee report, and I quote the main conclusions which were finally reached by way of elimination.
(a)	The three maple leaf design was retained by a vote of 8 to 6.
(b)	The single maple leaf design was retained by a vote of 13 to 1.
(c)	The design containing the union jack and/or the fleur-de-lis was rejected by a vote of 9 to 5.
Then, the committee had to choose between the three maple leaf design and the single maple leaf design, and another vote was taken. As we know, the single maple leaf design was retained by a vote of 14 to 0. However, it should be added that, on a last vote to determine whether or not the committee accepted finally and definitely the last design, the result of the vote was 10 to 4.
Mr. Speaker, shortly after the committee on the flag had done its work, I had the honour and privilege to lead the Canadian delegates to NATO on a visit of the Canadian military bases in Germany and then to the NATO parliamentary conference in Paris; later on, we were the guests of the Berlin government. Before leaving, I took great care to place in my pocket a model of the flag chosen by the committee. And wherever I went, I showed it to the officers, the soldiers and the Canadians in Paris. On every single occasion, without any exceptions, the servicemen, from high ranking officers to buck privates, as well as Canadians in Paris, expressed their delight with the design chosen by the committee and all were happy to have a Canadian flag.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

Certainly, as soon as I have finished my speech.
Before I left, Mr. Speaker, I met a high ranking officer in the Canadian army who told me that if the Canadian troops in Cyprus had a Canadian flag, many of their difficulties would be eliminated. In fact, in several instances the Canadian troops in Cyprus had to paint the word "Canada" on the walls which surrounded their encampments in order to avoid the shots which were intended for others. This means that the members of this

Canadian Flag
house who claim that our soldiers do not wish a new flag should obtain their information at the true source.
Mr. Speaker, I know that four members of the committee, who proved so by their vote in the house, preferred the red ensign. It is their right, it is their privilege, and I respect their intentions. But they must respect the decision of others.
I also know that about 60 and perhaps more members in the House of Commons have preference for the red ensign. It is their right and their privilege, but they must take into consideration the wishes of the other 200 members. By their persistence in delaying intentionally the adoption of a new Canadian flag,
I feel they throw our democratic mechanism out of gear, they make a mockery of parliament and they will have to answer for their actions before the people one day.
Mr. Speaker, the flag debate has been going on for 34 days. A committee was set up at the specific request of the Leader of the Opposition. This committee sat during six weeks, for a total of 45 hours. The question has been exhausted.
It seems to me the time has now come for all of us, and especially for those who have been telling us for weeks that they want to safeguard national unity, to support in this house this truly Canadian flag design and to salute it with pride when it becomes our new Canadian flag.

I just want to take time enough to ask the hon. member whether he would now answer a question. I understood him to say that while travelling overseas, showing the design which was the choice of the flag committee to high ranking officers and other employees of the Canadian government in Europe and soliciting opinions on it, he had received favourable replies from those high ranking officers. I wonder if I understood him right. Did the hon. member say he had received favourable replies from all those high ranking officers and others down to the simplest privates. Is that what the hon. member said?

Does the hon. member ask me whether all those to whom I talked about the flag and all those to whom I showed the design approved it? That is the case. They were all in favour-unanimous. I have not met a single person who did not like the model and who was not happy with it.

Such being the case, does the hon. gentleman not think that his reference to Canadian privates serving overseas in the Canadian army as "simple" is a disgraceful one and reflects a ridiculous attitude on the part of the hon. member?
The only ridiculous comment is the one we have just heard.

I realize that the guillotine of closure has been raised and is ready to drop but I rise nevertheless to speak in favour of the amendment which has been introduced whereby we would instruct the flag committee to report back in favour of the retention of the Canadian red ensign as Canada's national flag.
In rising at this time I also wish to protest against the imposition of closure by a vote of the house which does not represent the majority of the voters of the Dominion of Canada. I voted against the imposition of closure this afternoon because I do not feel that closure should be applied by a government aided by the supporters it can find elsewhere in the house when the members of parliament themselves do not command the majority of the voters behind them. We have been told there is a mandate out for a Canadian flag. There has never been a plebiscite placed before the people asking them to express their views on Canada's national flag. We are simply told we have a mandate to change the present flag.
No practical politician would desire to lay too much stress upon the mandate theory of a general election. There are men who have been elected to this house because they are residents of the ridings in which they ran. Others have been elected because they have advocated some diversion of waters in British Columbia to the prairies; others because they had promised additional authority for the Department of Fisheries. There are 265 members of this house and there are 300 or 400 reasons why they are here. There is no underlying mandate given to the 265 members to impose a flag on this nation.
When you analyse the vote and see how few have been elected on majority votes it will be realized definitely that there is no mandate. In April, 1963, the Liberal party got 41 per cent of the national vote. The Conservative party got 33 per cent, the Social Credit party 12 per cent and the New Democratic party 14 per cent of the total national vote. That does not look like any mandate to anybody on the question of a national flag. A mandate is defined as a

clear instruction, authorization or direction. How anyone can call a 41 per cent vote a clear instruction and authorization or direction is beyond my comprehension, particularly when there are scores of seats where the question of a flag was never even raised. But in August of this year, as I said in the course of some previous remarks, we were advised that the flag question had all been settled. The country had decided, and the three maple leaf flag was "it". A member of the cabinet was speaking in British Columbia when he made that flatfooted statement in August. That was the three leaf flag. In November, the same cabinet minister, speaking in the maritimes, said that 90 per cent of the country was in favour of the one leaf design. That was only three months later. What loyalty is there to suggested national emblems when you see people switching from the red ensign to a three leaf flag in August and to a one leaf flag in November? There is no loyalty there.
When it comes to the subject of closure and a free vote, three times in this house within the past two weeks we have had the opportunity of adjourning the debate to enable us to get off the flag question and proceed to some necessary government business. On all three occasions I voted for the adjournment of the debate. You know how the others voted in this house, Mr. Speaker. That was a free vote of course. Always voting the same way, but a free vote. Now, when closure is introduced we have a free vote. And notice how the vote went. It was again a free vote, of course. There was no control in that regard. I want to emphasize the fact that it was a free vote.
The statement was made in this house on Friday that although this is a minority government it is not a minority parliament. That is a very fine, mouth-filling phrase. But what are the facts of the matter? We are not a minority parliament, it has been said. I propose to give some figures which have taken me some time to analyse. I have had mathematical specialists undertaking this analysis for me. I would point out that the 129 Liberal members of this house did not receive a majority of the votes of the electorate in the ridings which sent them here. These figures have been compiled so as to include all byelections held from April, 1963 up to and including Waterloo South and Westmorland. To continue, 129 Liberal members have 2,060,000 votes behind them. The same members have 2,082,000 votes against them. The Social Credit party has nine members in this
Canadian Flag
house who were elected on the basis of 120,000 favourable votes with 166,000 votes against them. The nine Social Credit members gathered 41.9 per cent of the votes cast in their constituencies. The 18 members of the New Democratic party are here with 251,001 votes behind them and 356,879 votes against them. The 18 members of the N.D.P. in this house collected 41.2 per cent of the votes of the constituencies who sent them here. The Ralliement Creditiste, with 13 members, have 147,936 votes behind them and 168,725 votes against them. They gathered 46.7 per cent of the votes in the 13 constituencies which sent them here. I would point out that the Liberals, the Social Credit party and the Creditistes from which the closure votes came are a minority in their own constituencies, let alone a minority in the house. I have mentioned this point before and I can only mention it once again. I do not see how anyone can conscientiously support the application of closure when this government does not have a majority behind it. I am in favour of closure and it should be on the statute books; but it should only be used by a government which has an absolute control of the house and an absolute control over the constituencies for which its members sit. That is only fair and proper. When you have a majority government representing the majority of the voters, then it should have a free hand to impose objectives which it has stated to be its political intentions. But when you have a government which is only here, you might say, on sufferance without a majority vote behind them, closure should not be applied because it means that a minority of the voters in the country are applying closure to a majority of the voters in the country, which is the denigration of democracy.
I have been reading the remarks which were made in this house on Thursday and Friday last. I was absent from the house on Thursday last because I was sitting in the police court in Cooksville with the 12 taxicab operators whom the Department of Transport is persecuting-
Oh, oh.

I mean prosecuting-in connection with having picked up taxicab fares at Malton airport despite a ten year contract which the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) gave when he was minister to Air Terminal Transport without tender. We sincerely hope to get this matter on a legal and proper basis where there will be tenders for that government contract requested, and we

Canadian Flag
hope that this ten year deal can be broken. That deal is for a longer period of time than the normal span of two complete parliaments. However, we are making progress on that. We had a good time on Thursday in front of Magistrate Andrews.
Then last Friday I was out of the house and I was paired with the seconder of this motion on the flag. I could not have had a better pair, unless it had been the chairman of the committee himself, and I thank the seconder for the pair. While I was out of the house a certain statement was made. The criticism was offered that, "as a result of some kind of deal with one part of Canada, with Quebec, and that somehow this is Quebec's flag. Mr. Speaker, nothing, could be more malevolently designed to stir up division and controversy in this country. It is untrue and it is unworthy". I regret that that matter was ever brought forward and I am glad I am not the one who brought it forward.
In this regard may I refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Lamontagne), our Secretary of State, on June 13 in Toronto, which is reported in the Toronto Daily Star. The Secretary of State made this statement to the press:
The M.P. for Outremont-St. Jean conceded the new flag would be more widely accepted in Quebec than in the rest of Canada.
I wonder why, Mr. Speaker, it would be more widely accepted in Quebec than in the rest of Canada if it is not particularly desired in the province of Quebec?
Then we are told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), as reported on page 11038 of Hansard for Friday last:
If, Mr. Speaker, the absence from our national flag of symbols which to a large part of our people seem to represent early differences.. .is the absence of those earlier symbols from a Canadian flag too much of a sacrifice for the rest of us to make in the interests of unity in this country.
Who is being asked, Mr. Speaker, to make these sacrifices, and what are they being given in return? Why must one element of the community everlastingly be asked to make sacrifice, sacrifice, sacrifice in the interests of unity?
Now, Mr. Speaker, analysing the vote which took place in this house on Thursday I find that there were 45 Liberal members from Quebec who voted against holding a plebiscite. It is quite interesting to note that those 45 Quebec Liberals who voted against holding a plebiscite captured 822,230 votes in the April 1963 election, with 654,666 votes be-

ing cast against them. Where is the mandate there? Twelve of the Creditistes voted against the referendum. Those 12 Creditistes from the province of Quebec captured 133,235 votes, with 158,565 against. Five of the Social Credit members from Quebec voted against the referendum. They held 76,227 votes, with 87,600 votes cast against them. There were 99,489 votes for those seven Social Credit members of parliament when they were elected, and 118,367 votes were cast against them. With regard to the 12 members of the New Democratic party who voted against the plebiscite, there were 154,334 votes behind them and 219,089 votes against them. I give you those figures, Mr. Speaker, to show that a majority of the voters is not behind these people who have voted against holding a plebiscite.
The next question which comes up-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
-is this: Why was this question raised in the first place? There was no need to bring it up.
Mr. Speaker-
Order.

I have mentioned before, and I repeat, that on the front page of the Ottawa Citizen for March 13, 1963 there is a headline with reference to the then leader of the opposition who was running for parliament. Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was right when he said that statements made when running for parliament do not have to be put into effect once you are elected. But on the front page of the Ottawa Citizen four weeks before the election we read the headline "Pearson doesn't reject red ensign as our flag". Then follows a report by Southam News Services datelined Sherbrooke:
Liberal leader Pearson said today he had "never rejected the red ensign as Canada's flag and do not do so now".
Commenting on reports out of Winnipeg last week that he wanted to see something other than the red ensign as Canada's national flag Mr. Pearson said that he merely wanted a distinctive Canadian flag...
To reject the red ensign would mean the rejection of a British symbol, the union jack, which means much to so many people who have served and fought under it, and this he did not advocate.
That statement was made, as I say, within four weeks of the election. That statement has never been denied, and there are men sitting in the press gallery who were in

Sherbrooke, Quebec when that statement was issued to them. We cannot call them as witnesses from the press gallery, but I have been talking to them and I can identify them quite readily.
Now, I take it that the word of that speaker was to be trusted. He said on August 5 last, on a C.B.C. television network program:
I say that as one who honours the red ensign-
Therefore he will vote for its retention and not for its disappearance. Then he went on to say:
I hope that parliament will be able to decide this matter with a minimum of bitterness and rancour. I believe that when parliament does decide, the people of Canada will accept the decision of parliament.
If this parliament has a majority of the people behind it when it votes, then it is expressing the will of the people. Why does the leader of the government say:
I believe that when parliament does decide, the people of Canada will accept the decision of parliament.
I want to see a government which represents the decision of the people and the desire of the people when it votes. I do not like to see a parliament deciding something and then "believing" that the people of Canada will accept later the decision of parliament.
If we have to get rid of our old flag because of its historic connections, because it is not distinctively Canadian and not typical of this country, then why do we not get rid of our system of weights and measures? I find pints and quarts and bushels and pecks disturbing. And when it comes to gills and rods and poles and perches and acres and cubic feet, it is really upsetting. This does not belong to Canada. This is an English system, so why not have a purely Canadian system? Why do we bother with the English language?
Why do we speak in the English language? Why do we not get a language of our own? Why do we stick to the use of the French language, it does not belong to us? The French language belongs to France and the English language belongs to England. Let us have a language of our own.
I say, let us stick with the red ensign if we are proud of our history. Surely there is not one member of this house who would not say that the majority of the people of Canada believe as we do. When we vote let us vote in a manner to indicate our support for the retention of the red ensign, within the next two hours.

Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to follow the hon.
Canadian Flag
member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) who has just made a very eloquent address, in spite of the fact he is a member of the Liberal party. If we read the weekly report to the weekly press by the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Francis) we might be led to believe that the hon. member for York-Humber will be run out of the party if he continues to express himself with that intestinal fortitude, which is not possessed by other members of his party. I congratulate that hon. member and take my hat off to him.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the address of the leader of the N.D.P., the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). The Indian bands in my constituency very often honour individuals by making them members of the band and giving them names which relate to their characteristics.
I am sure if that hon. member were honoured by the tribes of my constituency they would name him "Chief Two-Voice Tommie", because he spoke for us and against us; he combed the Liberals against the grain; he took a crack against the Conservatives hoping to create a vacuum, with the idea that he and his party in the long run would become the benefactors. In the long run I think the people of this country will understand that he is still preaching socialism.
I did not intend to speak during this debate.
Hear, hear.

But I intend to speak now, so you need not applaud too hastily. I hesitated to take part in this debate because I felt it was moving in the direction of an Anglo-Franco dialogue, becoming louder as the time passed. It was creating disunity, I admit, but it was started by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) who was bound and determined that this flag should be placed foremost on the list of things to be done by this parliament, above important pieces of legislation. It was my feeling that a member who was of neither French nor English origin should act like a good neighbour when a common law husband and wife are fighting, and stay out of it.
I felt like staying out of this debate, but I was prompted to take part by the impressive speech of that sweet young lady, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Konantz). She made a tremendous impression upon me, as I am sure she did on this house.

Hear, hear.

Canadian Flag

You perhaps will not applaud after you have heard the rest of what I have to say.
That hon. member discussed the history of Canada, told us about Mennonites, Germans, Ukrainians and Icelanders, but she did not tell us under what flag these people came to this country. She very deftly skirted around that fact.
She informed us that she was a member of the committee that studied the flag issue. I know how the Liberal members of that committee voted. The Prime Minister did not make any announcement to the members of his party as to how they should vote, and I do not suggest that the Liberal members were told how to vote. However, they knew what the Prime Minister wanted.
The Prime Minister during his outright speech in this house said, among other things, that there must be just one national flag. We do have another resolution on the order paper and, although I am not allowed to discuss it or even mention it, I should like to know why this debate is a two flag debate.
The Prime Minister also said that he had agreed to a compromise. I agreed with the Prime Minister when he said that the three leaf design was more attractive than this one maple leaf caricature which we now have before us. I agreed with him when he said that the three maple leaf design was a more attractive and beautiful flag than the design chosen by this committee. I support the amendment which, if adopted, would send this issue again to the flag committee.
We should give some consideration to the red ensign under which those people referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg South came to this nation. Those people were guaranteed certain freedoms-freedom of speech, freedom of religion-as well as British justice and fair play.
They were guaranteed there would be no closure.
They were guaranteed there would be no closure, yet we certainly have closure in this house.
Your time has expired.

During the 30 days of this debate, which I admit is a rather long period of time, few if any of the members who continually interrupt us have had guts enough to stand up on their feet and ask questions. All we have heard them say is "order, order" and "question, question". When I have completed my speech I will be glad to answer

any questions, but I have the floor at this time.
I am pleased to know that there is one member on that side of the house who has the courage to stand up, but as far as those members who shout "order" and "question" are concerned, I must state that I am ashamed of their attitude and ashamed of this government and those who support it. I think the people of this country should be made aware of the fact that the members on the government side of this house have been glued to their seats, nailed to their seats, pinned to their seats, and by whose orders? They have been pinned to their seats by the orders of a man who, by the actions of some of his ministers, has been forced to send out a code of ethics. That man does not happen to be in the house at this time, but I suggest that if the division bell rings he will be here posthaste to vote for this flag which he suggests is the only one for this nation. He is the man who has said that he has compromised in accepting the one leaf design recommended by the committee rather than the three leaves design. Of course a member of parliament cannot make or take bets on the actions of the House of Commons, but I would bet that if the Creditistes, Social Crediters and members of the N.D.P. had not committed themselves to supporting that man, the right hon. gentleman who leads the Liberal party would not have pushed this flag through. Am I right in that or not?
He knows he has a majority in the house but he does not know whether he has a majority in the country, and the hon. member for York-Humber has said so plainly. I had an over-all majority over my three opponents of over 50 per cent. Yet I do not say I have a mandate. I am expressing my own opinion. I know the feelings of a lot of people. The government has no mandate but a majority has been guaranteed to these people who want to bury the past.
There is another matter I should like to bring up, the question of the founding races. The subject of the founding races is beginning to wear pretty thin. I too have studied Canadian history and I am not a member of either of the founding races. I am one of those who Mr. Rene Levesque says have to become either English or French or-well, I am not going to say the rest. But, Mr. Speaker, out of me and the likes of me and all those mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Konantz) you can make darn good Canadians but you cannot make English or French people out of them

but only good Canadians. The founding races?
It was a marriage of convenience. I would say it was a common law marriage of the conqueror and the conquered. You might as well admit it. You cannot rewrite history, and I have studied Canadian history as much as you people have.
What of the conquerors? Most of them were United Empire Loyalists who came here after the revolution when the United States broke off from England. They wanted to live under the British flag. What did those in Lower Canada want? They were afraid that if they ever joined the United States they would be absorbed as the French have been absorbed in Louisiana, where there is no trace of the French language or culture. I do not know about the religious part of it. So it was a marriage of convenience, a common law marriage and the two parties are fighting today. Who started the fight? Not the English speaking segment of Canada at all, Mr. Speaker. That is the way I see Canadian history.
The hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) said this was the last chance. I believe this will be the last time I will ever speak in favour of the red ensign. It will be the last time I will have the opportunity of doing so, and that applies to all other members.
Let us vote.
Oh, yes, I know you have got a guarantee that others will vote with you.
You were a Conservative once.
He does not know any better.
You have said you never voted Liberal until you ran as a Liberal, Harry.
Order, please. The Chair would like to hear the interesting historical summary.

Mr. Speaker, I know there are people in this country and many of the members across the way and to the left of us who will cheer when they pull down the red ensign. It will become a foot wiper in the same way as some have already wiped their feet on it in certain parts of Canada.
Oh, oh.
Yes, that has been proven.

That is a stupid thing to say.
Canadian Flag
That has been reported and never denied. There will be many foot wipers and some will cheer when the red maple leaf goes up.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.

I am going to tell you this, Mr. Speaker. I like to see a man get up and say something instead of yak-yaking and hiding behind somebody else. We have heard that for 30 days. The Liberals have been glued and nailed to their seats. I wonder why? I do not know. I think the man who established the code of ethics for the whole cabinet must have established one for the whole party. That is perfectly all right. That is his business. But, Mr. Speaker, there are going to be many people in this nation who will have heavy hearts. They are going to be sorry to see the ensign come down.
You hope.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, if any of these members of the Liberal party want to get up and ask me questions that is fine or if they want to speak after me I will be glad to give them part of my time, but they have not got what it takes.
The guts.

There are many who are going to have heavy hearts. Many are going to be sorry. We are not Africans, Mr. Speaker, and I am not insulting the Africans. I feel that if this parliament in its wisdom or ignorance, shall I say, adopts this flag, and I include the Senate and His Excellency the Governor General, I too will have to salute this flag. But I have one thing about which I am proud, Mr. Speaker. Two years ago the province of Manitoba enacted a provincial statute making the red ensign the provincial flag. I asked the premier of the province what he would do if the federal government relented and accepted the red ensign. He said, "Then we will just repeal our enactment". I do not think Mr. Roblin is happy. He would have been glad to repeal that act. I know where his sympathies lie. I know where Mr. Thatcher's sympathies lie and Mr. Manning's.
Mr. Smallwood.
Mr. Smallwood too. Many people will look upon the hauling down of the red ensign with heavy hearts. I speak with emotion because emotion is natural for
Is the house ready for the question?
Question.
All those in favour of the amendment will please say yea.
Yea.
All those opposed will please say nay.
Nay.

In my opinion the nays have it.
And more than five members having risen:
Call in the members.
I declare the amendment lost.
Mr. Speaker, I was paired. Had I voted I would have voted against the amendment.
Is the house ready for the question?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we enter the last and dying hour of this debate I consider it a privilege and an honour to participate once more in our discussions as the House of Commons reaches a very historic stage in the establishment of the flag which will be flown in Canada. A few days ago I had the pleasure, as I have this evening, of making a contribution to this debate regarding one of the amendments which was then before the house. At that time I laid before me on my desk four, five or six prominent daily newspapers from across the two main provinces of Canada, and I indicated the importance of their headlines for that day. None of the headlines made any reference to the flag debate which was taking place in the house at the time. There was a sinister warning made on that particular day to me and all Canadians by the reference to those things which are unsatisfactory in our Canadian political life. Those references had a bearing, in my opinion, on the words I used on August 12, the day I first participated in this debate. It is not my intention this evening to be as lengthy as I was on that occasion, but because of the close association of that warning with the words I used at that time, and the close association between the situation as it existed at that time and as it exists tonight, I should like to quote from that speech of August 12, at which time I quoted from a book known
Canadian Flag
as "The Fight for Canada" by W. Wood, with reference to the time Canada was a colony of France. I said:
We find that Vaudreuil was "-a liar, a backbiter, and a pettifogger, utterly unfit for his great position; and the best excuse that can be made for him is that he was almost as great a fool as a knave."
Dealing with Bigot it says:
"He deliberately set to work to create universal destitution in order that he might requisition help from France and make his commission on it."
Is there not a comparison to be found between the situation which existed at that time and the situation which exists today?
The government has chosen a very inopportune time to suggest that it has the right to present a national flag for Canada under existing circumstances. I think this is particularly true when one considers what might have been done during the long summer months, during the months of the fall, and during the months of the winter, to the greater advantage of the people of Canada than a debate such as we have had on a flag issue.
I think also of the situation which has faced the eastern farmers, and what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) has said about that situation. That situation has grown worse at least in the area which I have the honour to represent. The Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) stated that the farmers of eastern Canada were in a very sorry state so far as their economical situation is concerned. Many of my colleagues, as well as myself, have pleaded with the Minister of Agriculture to do something about this situation. What was his answer to this plea? It was simply that if we just keep quiet everything will look after itself. He stated that we were not rendering the farmers of eastern Canada any service by mentioning the situation. I guess this house did not do them any service by fighting this flag battle, because while we were debating the national flag issue the Minister of Agriculture forgot about the growing protest on behalf of the eastern Canadian farmer. Surely this house could have rendered some more beneficial service to the people of Canada than has been rendered them during the course of this debate.
I believe this night is an historic one. We are approaching Christmas, that season hallowed by the Christian world. I believe Canada is a Christian country, and that Christianity is part of our heritage. I believe that Christianity is representative of our way of life and, as I said on August 3, I960, Christianity as brought down to us through English common law also forms a part of the laws

Canadian Flag
of this country and the laws of the United States. I quoted an authority at that time, Mr. Speaker, and that authority is still the one to which I refer in support of my argument today.
The purpose of my brief speech this evening is this. An hon. member who spoke earlier in the course of this debate made a very earnest and passionate appeal, and speaking as to the other side of the question he said that the adoption of the flag now before us for consideration would not have application in Christian heritage. He said the flag would have no application to those things we cherish in our legal structure, or our institutions.
When I returned home last Sunday and, as is my custom, I attended church service with my wife and family, the man who preached the sermon impressed on me very emphatically that the times in which we live are changing. He said that Christianity was not keeping pace with the increase in the population of the world. He said that all churches which regard themselves as Christian churches were tending to adopt Christianity as an easy thing, and treating it just like a club, rather than a religion. He said there was a tendency by this mode of life to remove symbols, such as the cross, from Christianity. He went on to say, as I indicated this evening, that if we remove the cross as a symbol of something which we who call ourselves Christians believe in, we are actually denying our Christian heritage.
Mr. Speaker, I deplore the fact that all Canadians who find themselves in the situation with which we are faced tonight will grieve the denial of our Christian heritage under the flag which is proposed to be flown over Canada. I feel as sincerely about this as anyone who takes a different position.
As I present my point of view to the house tonight, I am not unmindful of the contributions which were made during the world wars, and while my contribution was insignificant, one of my colleagues lies beneath the ground somewhere in Holland. He died as a result of being shot down.
