With all sincerity I do not think we will ever live down the fact that we are removing something which men who have given their

lives, honoured as part of Canada's Christian and democratic heritage.

Mr. Speaker, on September 2 I took part in the proceedings of this parliament in order to express my views in the controversial Canadian flag debate.
Let me say first of all that, in my opinion, a distinctive flag is not an extinctive flag. I wonder why Canadians of my province who, in many respects, show so much faithfulness to their origins, have ceased to believe in the mission assigned to them by Providence.
Unfortunately, I fail to understand why, in considering this delicate matter of selecting a flag, they admit so readily that the fleur-de-lis should disappear from our flag, even from our mind, and forever. Perhaps they agree with the remarks made last Thursday night, December 10, by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) who stated this, as reported on page 11023 of Hansard:
X understand the feelings of our friends. They are quite willing to forgo any symbolism of our French heritage in Canada provided they can, at the same time, eliminate all the symbolism of the British heritage in connection with our country from our flag.
On second thought, those words seem to me strictly true. I knew before that the hon. member was living in an aura of wisdom. This reminds me of King Solomon's characteristic touch when he offered two women, who were quarrelling about the possession of a young child to cut the living child in two. The true mother then preferred yielding her child to seeing it die before her eyes. I leave it to each of you to draw his own conclusions from this excerpt of the book of wisdom.
Of course, I am in favour of a Canadian flag, but a single flag, representing, or comprising the symbols of the union jack and the fleur-de-lis, with a green maple leaf.
On this last point, I must say this. The hon. member for Vegreville, Alberta (Mr. Fane), this noble representative of a riding where 40 different nationalities are living together in harmony and who, moreover, has received a third mandate with an absolute majority, insisted upon the inclusion of a green maple leaf. I thank him for this.
Are you aware that a red leaf maple tree does not mean much to a maple sugar producer? I myself am a maple sugar producer,

so I have a knowledge of the facts. The good varieties of sugar and syrup maple trees have green leaves during the spring as well as in summertime; in the fall, the leaves take a yellowish colour, the same as that of ripe wheat, then they fall and return to the soil. The red leaf maple tree may be lovely to look at, but that is all that can be said for it, as far as its practical value is concerned.
In proceeding with my investigation on this point, I noted on page 11038 of Hansard in the left hand column, words that in my opinion, come from a true diplomat- from the Prime Minister's lips-about the maple leaf for our flag, and I quote:
-it has become so deeply a part of our symbolic history. This is especially true when the other symbol of our past, which has appeared on our flags in the past, the union jack, is to be recognized in another way.
There is the core of the problem. I want to dispense with any comment.
Quite often I find I am asking myself questions; it seems I am looking at myself and at everything around me, and I have the feeling that we are at the crossroads.
At this time those nations who yesterday celebrated their independence with glee are plunged into days of agony. They thought that they must at all costs rid themselves of imperialists, Belgian imperialists, Dutch imperialists, French imperialists and British imperialists. Was it a decision based on a common desire to thwart materialism, injustice and hatred in order to follow in the path of love? I do not think so, Mr. Speaker.
I think it was a day of victory for facility, for licence, for materialistic forces over moral forces. In that regard, everyone of us has a responsibility, because we are interdependent in this world.
But however, is it necessary to insult our Queen, Her Majesty Elizabeth II, to declare our eagerness to lead the good fight against the abuses of capitalism, against famine, leprosy, nakedness and against corruption in the public service, sure symptoms of our despicable selfishness? No, no, no.
Those who know me are not surprised to hear me give such a testimony in this house today.
In the tradition of my family, I learned that in two different periods, several Ouellets gave their lives serving the king of France, here in Canada in the province of Quebec, and then later under the regime recognized by the Paris treaty, and today I want to be worthy of my ancestors. I recognize that England did make some errors

in her colonial policy. I think, however, she did her best for us, French Canadians. In any case, we had not been spoiled by France.
In fact, each of us believes he is invested with undeniable powers, or at least with a fair possession of a political and legislative power.
Mr. Speaker, if our loyalty towards the French Canadians rests on the contempt or persecution of anything that is not French, whether it is toward the members of this house or of the other place, or elsewhere, then we put justice and charity on the rack.
I have always believed that when love and hate meet and face each other, victory goes to love. Our Canadian political history teaches us lessons to remember and, as a member for the county of Rimouski, a county which is inscribed in the golden book of Canadian democracy, here is why.
Indeed, we all learned that one day Sir Georges Etienne Cartier was elected in Manitoba, in the constituency of Provencher, Sir Wilfrid Laurier in Saskatchewan, in the constituency of Prince Albert-they are glorious, the constituents of Prince Albert-and before that, Robert Baldwin was elected by acclamation in Rimouski. These facts are on the record and do honour to us.
At present I am saddened when I see that at the very moment when there is a rift in the structure of the communist bloc, free men are destroying themselves by despising the principles they had cherished until the advent of a contagious materialism.
Before I take my seat, I must say that I believe in the future of Canada-a future resting on a glorious past where men and women with different languages and customs erected a country which history has already recognized as unwilling to die.

I wish my hon. friend would allow me to deliver my speech in my own way, because I am coming to those various matters. He has brought up these two points, so perhaps I should deal with them now.

In so far as the first point is concerned, it was raised in the early days of the debate and I answered that at the time. There has been no change since that time. I said then, and I repeat now, that naturally when a resolution of this kind was before the Canadian parliament the Queen, through the high commissioner in London, was informally apprised of the fact that this resolution was before parliament. Her advice was not sought. It would have been quite unconstitutional to ask for her advice on a matter which had not yet been decided upon by the Canadian parliament. If I had done that I can imagine what my right hon. friend would be saying today. He would be accusing me of dragging the crown into politics. What we did, as a matter of courtesy, was to inform the Queen of the action or the proposal that was before the Canadian parliament, and indicated to the Queen that if that proposal were accepted she would be asked to take the necessary constitutional action, as Queen. This cannot be done, of course, until parliament has declared itself.
In so far as the second question is concerned, the question of a commonwealth flag, that was not mentioned at the prime ministers' conference at all. It did not come up in any way, shape or form, nor has it come up in any commonwealth meeting since of which I am aware. I have made informal inquiries of certain commonwealth leaders as to whether it may be practicable to consider the possibility of some emblem which would be common to all states of the commonwealth. However, it is quite impracticable at the present time and may be impracticable for a long time to come because of the very nature of the states within the commonwealth. There are monarchies in the commonwealth, are monarchies that recognize the Queen of England, the Queen of Canada or the Queen of Australia. There are republics in the commonwealth. But surely, in this day and age, it is not either wrong or unusual to have emblems flying in a country which denote different forms of association of the people of that country with different international or national organizations.
I believe, therefore, it is logical and desirable to retain in this country an emblem of our association with the other members of the commonwealth. Even though it is not a commonwealth flag, it is a flag which would denote Canada's association with the commonwealth. I will try to explain later why I think the royal union jack is the most logical and best emblem for that purpose.

At the moment this is the only constitutional link, the only formal constitutional link, between the various members of the commonwealth, through the Queen. There is no other formal link. I remember very well when that link was first constitutionally recognized. In earlier days before the commonwealth achieved its present organization, it was not necessary because all members were linked by their allegiance to one queen. They were all monarchies inside this association.
In 1948, at a commonwealth conference which I had the honour of attending, the commonwealth was faced with the problem of trying to absorb within its association a republic, a state which owed no allegiance to the Queen and was republican in character. The commonwealth has proved itself, over the years, to be a very adaptable institution indeed. It was able to accommodate itself to this alteration in constitutional structure in one of its members by a formula which has been found to apply to all the new members of the commonwealth since, most of whom are republics. This was done by the official communique of the conference which included this sentence, and this is an important sentence because it does indicate why I believe the union jack is the right emblem for commonwealth association.

I believe the majority of Canadians wish to have a Canadian national flag which cannot be mistaken for the flag of any other country, and the majority of the members of this house certainly decided that last night. I also believe, Mr. Speaker, that the vast majority of Canadians wish to recognize our membership in the commonwealth and our allegiance to the Queen as head of that commonwealth, as we do to her as Queen of Canada.
Some will argue, and indeed I think my hon. friend took the position this afternoon even though his amendment does not seem to me to support that position, that we do not need any special flag to provide such recognition or that, if we do, the union jack is the wrong flag for the purpose. As I have already indicated, I would disagree with that position both

in regard to the need and the nature of the flag denoting the relationship, and I would like to point out that other members of the commonwealth, that we call the older members of the commonwealth, have made provision for this recognition. The Australian flags act of 1953, section 8, provides:
This act does not affect the right or privilege of a person to fly the union jack.
There is no requirement, but there is a recognition of the desirability of maintaining that emblematic association which we provide for in our recommendation. In the statutes of South Africa while South Africa was a member of the commonwealth-this does not apply now because she has withdrawn from the commonwealth-there was in volume 2, chapter 2, section 7(1) (a) the following:
The flags of the union shall include the union jack to denote the association of the union with other members of the group of nations constituting the British commonwealth of nations.
It is interesting in this connection to recall some words used in this house by a man who passionately advocated a distinctive Canadian national flag, without the emblems of any other association on that flag. I am referring to Mr. Bona Arsenault, who is now a member of the government of Quebec. This is what he said in 1946 when he was passionately arguing in this house for a distinctive national flag. On March 21, 1946, as recorded at page 154 of Hansard for that date he stated:
All nations of the world at all times have used different flags for different tactical purposes...
Since Canada is a member of the British commonwealth, united to her sister nations under the constitutional authority of the same king, I cannot very well see why anyone in this country could reasonably object to the full-sized union jack being officially recognized by this parliament as the official symbol of our partnership in the commonwealth, the finest example in history of mutual friendship between nations and one of the strongest means of maintaining peace in the world in these trying days.
Mr. Bona Arsenault, a very good Canadian nationalist in the right meaning of the word, went on to say:
Too much is involved to try to put forward any sort of narrow nationalism in the face of the distressful conditions that we find in the world today. Not only should we help to maintain the British commonwealth of nations, we should have a commonwealth of all the nations of the world based on the same principles of mutual friendship and collaboration.
We also believe in that, Mr. Speaker, and on occasions in this country, indeed over this building, we fly the blue flag of the United Nations as well.

I believe that the most fitting emblem for this association is the royal union flag, the flag of the Queen, the flag of the monarchy since it was first established in the seventeenth century, the flag which is peculiarly identified with the monarchy and, as such, identified with the commonwealth because the Queen is the head of the commonwealth.

We discussed the two resolutions and we said "No, we do not want two flags". I am not alone, and was not alone in the committee, in that view.
However, I would just like to say one or two things following on what the Prime Minister has said. I believe he was a little off the beat. I must say that I hate following him in a speech because many of the points he puts forward I find rather difficult at times to follow from the point of view of sense. I have stated that the committee believed we should have one flag and one flag only, and I believe this change in government thinking is just one more attempt to wipe the Canadian red ensign right off the face of the map. Their last minute substitution of the royal union flag just does not bear any merit at all.
The Prime Minister had a great deal to say about the royal union flag and the reason for our using it, which he said is historical. The royal union flag and its predecessors in England and those countries comprising Great Britain were always the Queen's flags, the Prime Minister said, and the royal union flag was the flag for the whole of the country.
If my recollection is correct, out of the mouths of the witnesses the Liberals called in the flag committee there is no question at all but that the royal union flag and its predecessors were not the flags of the country. The royal union flag was a distinct naval flag for use at sea only; it was not supposed to be used even on land bases. However, after a great many naval victories it became a very popular flag and through usage, tradition and the fact that the British people liked to fly it over their own home base, it became popular. It became popular first of all not by edict, any parliamentary reference or anything like that, but because it was flown over the homes and was finally popularized to the extent that the government made it the flag of the country. This is my recollection.
I would like to draw an analogy between that and the Canadian red ensign. After drawing the analogy I would only point out that the Canadian red ensign, our present Canadian flag, is the flag we should have if we are to have two flags. That is why I seconded this amendment. The Canadian flag that we now have-the red ensign is still our flag- has flown in this country since its beginning in 1867. It was the first flag to fly on any flagstaff over our government buildings, and it stayed there until a Liberal government in 1904, for some reason or another, hauled it down.
But that did not kill the red ensign. It came back and-we all know its history from a legislative point of view-has been Canada's flag since that time, and is still until an act of this parliament changes it. During

I must say at the beginning that it is a flag which I did not want to see changed in any way, shape or form, and I fought for it in committee until such time as we had a vote on it and our red ensign was turned down. I should like now to touch upon the history of the use of the Canadian red ensign in Canada. Many people feel that this flag was created overnight. The usage of this flag has been responsible for its acceptance. It was not adopted as a result of some parliamentary whim of a Liberal government some time after 1904, when it was taken down. It was again adopted as the Canadian flag after serious consideration; and what it meant to the people of those days it means to the people of Canada today.
If we want a change then I will agree to such a change, but to make my position absolutely clear in this regard I must say that the committee from the beginning intended to select one flag for Canada and one flag only. The resolution passed by the committee included the word "only" in association with a national flag. Obviously we were thinking of two flags, one to be the national flag and a second to show our allegiance to the Queen and our membership in the commonwealth. Many arguments were presented to the committee in this regard, but as far as I am concerned the word "only" means, only one flag for Canada.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has suggested that we should show our allegiance to the Queen and our membership in the commonwealth by the adoption of a second flag. Surely we do not need a second flag to show our allegiance to the Queen. Other commonwealth countries have not adopted flags to show their allegiance to the Queen or their memberships in the commonwealth. Throughout our history we have demonstrated time and time again our allegiance to the Queen.
Canadian Flag
If we adopt, as our final choice, the one red maple leaf flag as our national flag, that should be accepted as our flag for all purposes.
The only other argument in support of the adoption of a second flag is that it will show our relationship to the commonwealth. Canada has shown leadership in commonwealth studies, and has done a great deal to further commonwealth relations. We have never been backward in doing so. Therefore do we need a second flag to exemplify our commonwealth relationship Do we need a flag other than the red ensign to show our allegiance to the Queen?
The Prime Minister stated that the vast majority of Canadians desire a second flag, and indicated that the evidence supported his statement. I have never seen any evidence, certainly none was presented to the committee, that supported that argument. Has any member ever talked with an individual on the streets of the cities of Canada and heard that individual state that we need another flag to show our allegiance to the Queen and our relationship to the commonwealth?
For the reasons I have stated I was, from the beginning of the committee meetings, opposed to the adoption of a second flag. In this regard I should like to support the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) who said that the Prime Minister was despicable in his remarks about the speech made by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming).

speechtext:
Whatever the circumstances, the votes taken in the committee were to remain secret, and it was certainly not proper for the Prime Minister to indicate what took place.
The Prime Minister rather scathingly attacked the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton,

who said that two flags were not necessary. I suggest he attacked him in this way because of his proposed amendment, which does in fact suggest a different flag. In actual fact the reasoning behind that amendment lies in the knowledge that the votes on the flag issue now being taken in the house are not consistent with the votes taken on the same issues at the meetings of the special committee. Adoption of the red ensign was defeated by the committee, and that is a matter of record. Following that defeat we did not turn our tails and scurry home but attempted to find a solution to our problem by the adoption of a modification of the red ensign. When that attempt was thwarted, we tried to select a flag which would incorporate emblems symbolic of the contributions of the two founding races of this country. I have used that same analogy today.
It is perfectly obvious that the government is being supported by members of other parties in this house in its desire to approve two flags. Now that they have taken a stand we are asking them to consider, instead of the royal union flag, Canada's flag of the past, her ensign. It is rather interesting to note what happened in the committee as set out in the report. In the third paragraph there is the following:
It was moved "that the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to provide that the Canadian red ensign may continue to be flown as a symbol of Canada's membership in the commonwealth of nations and of her allegiance to the crown". An amendment was moved to substitute the words "royal union flag, generally known as the union jack" for the words "Canadian red ensign".
Then the votes are set out. One can read this easily and quickly, but any member who was on that committee knows that there was a wealth of time and words behind the final adoption of the recommendation in the seventh report of the flag committee. Members of the house should consult their own members who were on that committee to find out just what their attitude was.
We had the distinct impression that word had come down from Joey Smallwood that if a recommendation for the royal union flag was not made he would be offended and would continue to fly it anyway. That is what we thought. We expressed that view and we were laughed at. I would say to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) that he should sit down and consult with the Liberals who were members of that committee because as I said a great deal of time was

spent and many words were uttered in that regard.

There was a lot of emotion on the part of the Liberals, and I will leave it at that. I do not want to go on at length at this time. I think I have made clear the basis of the recommendation of the committee that there should be only one distinctive national flag. I believe 1 have made my feelings very clear on the matter, as did the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) who moved the amendment. As I have said, we could not understand why there was a change right at the end.
I respect the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) because he was a distinct asset to that committee, but I know he will recall the argument that preceded the recommendation for one national flag. I have put forward my argument why we should not have two flags and at the same time why we have now moved an amendment for a second flag. I say that if Canada has a flag today which is hers through tradition and general usage it is the Canadian red ensign. In seconding the amendment I wish to emphasize the fact that if we are to have a second flag for the two distinct purposes that have been set out, to express allegiance to the crown and our commonwealth affiliation, then there is one flag in Canada today that does so to a T, our present Canadian red ensign.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the amendment to the motion for concurrence in the seventh report of the special committee I should like to begin by suggesting that in spite of some of the arguments that have been made it is completely clear in my mind that there is a distinction between the flag adopted by the vote early this morning and what we are considering now. I think the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) outlined this very well when he said that the committee had decided, as contained in their report, that only one national flag would be adopted. Paragraph 5 of the sixth report of the special committee, subparagraph (b), sets out the position clearly in these words:
Your committee considered the following motions: ... (b) The adoption of only one national flag -motion carried 14 to zero.
So there is no confusion whatever, Mr. Speaker. It is clear that the committee's decision was for only one national flag and that
Canadian Flag
that flag should be the single red maple leaf on a white background with two red bars.
I want to say, as is recorded in Hansard and in Votes and Proceedings, that I did not support the recommendation made by the committee to the house, but the consensus of the house has now been taken and so far as I am concerned I intend to accept and respect the decision made by the House of Commons respecting Canada's national flag.
There is one other thing I think we should be clear about and that is that this house and, indeed, parliament as a whole, does not have the right to create a commonwealth flag. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) pointed this out. I believe we have the right to designate a symbol of our allegiance to the commonwealth and to the crown. The Prime Minister argued that if we are going to do this it would be proper for us to select the royal union flag as that symbol. So far as I am concerned, that may be an argument but it is not conclusive from the point of view of ruling out all other symbols that could in fact serve for this purpose.
It is my personal opinion that the flag that is designated as being suitable for the purpose of displaying our allegiance to the commonwealth and to the crown could in fact be some other symbol than the royal union flag. I believe that the Canadian red ensign, which contains the royal union flag as part of its composition, with a distinctive Canadian content would in fact be a more appropriate symbol. As I have just stated, the Canadian red ensign has the royal union flag on it but there is also the Canadian coat of arms in the fly, and in my opinion this is a preferable symbol for the purposes suggested in the seventh report.
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton moved the amendment now before us and it is coincidental that the hon. member for Danforth indicated he was prepared to move essentially the same amendment. For your information, Mr. Speaker, I have written out before me a similar amendment. It was, therefore, just simply a matter of time and who was recognized first.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to go on at length about this matter, except to say that the sixth and seventh reports of the committee are matters of free votes within our party. There may be other members of our party who wish to express their own individual views respecting this matter. So far as I am concerned, I am ready to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming). I hope that we can

Canadian Flag
have unanimous consent in this house to accept the amendment. The reason I say that is contained in the last sentence of the amendment moved by the hon. member in which it is stated that the committee, for such purpose, be revived.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that under the rules of this house it is not proper for this house to amend a committee report. If we do not accept a committee report and we have some suggestions for changing it, then under the rules that amendment must contain instructions to the committee when the report is referred back. Of course, for such purposes, the committee must be revived. If there were unanimous consent in this house, however, I believe we could save a great deal of time by asking for that unanimous consent and amending the seventh report of the committee by substituting the Canadian red ensign for the royal union flag. Then, we could get on with dealing with this matter and perhaps complete it during this sitting. I appeal to the members of the house on all sides to accept this amendment unanimously so that it would not be necessary to revive the committee and we could get on with other government business.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after sitting for six weeks on the special flag committee, which was also instructed to study a proposal similar to the amendment proposed today, I had then decided not to support the motion along those lines, for the adoption of a flag identifying us as a member of the commonwealth or as an associate member of the British commonwealth countries, if that flag were to be the union jack.
I rose earlier to say that I was the only one to vote against it at that time. I must point out again today that in this matter, I am speaking for myself. Everyone is free to speak as he sees fit. I am convinced that to refer the matter again to the committee would be to no avail and would delay everything.
The amendment which has just been introduced tends to substitute the red ensign for the union jack. I think that it is a trap. We have just voted last night in favour of a distinctive national flag. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, we have sweated hours and even days to arrive at last night's result. As a member of the committee, I can even say that the selection of such a flag brought tears in the eyes of many. Those members of the committee who are in the house this after-

noon could confirm my statement. They worked industriously and with all their hearts.
I am wondering today why we must choose a flag to show our allegiance to and our association with the British commonwealth of nations. Did we not adopt last night a distinctive national flag which, in due course, will become official? That flag could very well represent us at all times and in all circumstances.
I fail to understand also why the Canadian government is obliged to choose a flag to show our allegiance to the commonwealth. If the commonwealth wants a flag to identify its member nations, it should choose one.
It is true that we are free to do so, but it is very difficult to find any sense in all that.
We now have a flag-a flag that we got with great difficulties. Everybody here and outside the house knows that. I think that the single maple leaf flag will be quite appropriate to represent our country within the commonwealth. Because of what this flag means, of the eagerness displayed to get it, of our pride in flying it, because also of the sincerity of the Canadian people as evidenced by that symbol we chose last night, I think that this emblem would be quite appropriate to represent our country within any organization. In closing, I say that it is not necessary to have a second flag, one is enough to represent Canada. Let us hoist that flag, telling ourselves that it serves all purposes and that we are entitled to fly it in any circumstances, as it was adopted by parliament. It is true that we are also a member of the British commonwealth of nations.
But it is not so much the interpretation that could be attributed to it when it will be hoisted across the nation. It will not be hoisted only to show that we are a member of the commonwealth, but as a national flag, and some will defend it as such. It will then be absolutely false.
One must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that this flag hides legitimate feelings which deserve to be defended with the greatest ardour, the greatest unity, as it is a national flag. On the other hand, today we are presented with a flag which has so many ties for some groups across the country that it is intended to impose it as a second flag, a second class flag, to impose it simply to show our allegiance to the commonwealth.
The best sign of allegiance-and we can never say it enough-is a national flag, the

one we adopted yesterday; and when I heard, with my own ears, the anthem sung yesterday, I saw what emotions the adoption of this flag had given rise to.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot reveal how the vote was taken, but the matter was studied and discussed in the committee. I must abstain from revealing how the other members of the committee voted after these negotiations, but I adopted a position in committee, I maintain it today and I shall defend it tomorrow.
I did not approve the choice of this flag in the committee, and I will not support it today; my colleagues can follow the dictates of their conscience, but I for one oppose the second motion. This does not mean that I can be expected to support the other, for when the second comes, I will adopt exactly the same attitude. For, in my opinion, one national flag is sufficient to represent us anywhere, anytime.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words must be those of congratulation to the hon. member for Vic-toria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) for presenting in a highly competent and capable manner an argument that should find great merit in the eyes of the government, since he was proposing that the government adopt as our commonwealth symbol a flag over which we have some right and jurisdiction.
If nothing else was learned from the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the interjections during it there is one definite lesson, that we in this country have no right to ask the people of the United Kingdom to provide us with their flag for use as a commonwealth symbol. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, we have every right and justification to propose the Canadian red ensign as that symbol.
In my speech yesterday I listed the reasons that I felt the flag design which was adopted by vote early this morning would not be satisfactory as a national flag. Already we see some of the justification for the argument I made then, an argument which was made by many other hon. members on a number of occasions. The flag design adopted last night is not capable of conveying an association with any other country which belongs to the commonwealth because it does not contain within it those symbols which are inherent in the red ensign, a flag capable of being both a national and international flag in indicating our association with our com-
Canadian Flag
monwealth friends and the contribution Canada has made over the years to the building of the commonwealth of nations.
Despite the conviction displayed by the Prime Minister in his speech in supporting the recommendation of the flag committee, the design recommended by the committee is not at all as satisfactory as the Canadian ensign would be in representing our commonwealth association. He presented in a most illogical argument a degree of gobbledy-gook unsurpassed during the last flag debate and, in my opinion, not surpassable in the present debate.
Last Friday the Prime Minister made a high sounding speech indicating his views on why we should adopt a new flag. I did not agree with the arguments he made then, nor do I now, but I admit he made a significant contribution to the debate. But his speeches earlier this morning and this afternoon have added nothing to any feeling of respect for him and the office he holds, principally because of the attitude he adopted and the method which he used in endeavouring to get his points across.
One of the most interesting portions of his speech this afternoon was that in which he admitted for the first time that the Canadian red ensign was our national flag. Until he said that I had always held the impression, according to statements made by the Prime Minister, that we did not have a national flag and that what he was endeavouring to do was produce one. Now, all of a sudden, after the vote has been taken and a new flag chosen, we discover through the mouth of the Prime Minister that the Canadian red ensign was, according to his mind, all the time a national flag.
The Prime Minister attacked the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton in a most despicable way. He laughed at the hon. member and told him how illogical he was. If the hon. member was illogical in any way it is because of the illogical procedure of the government in endeavouring to produce a second flag for the Canadian nation. What the hon. member was trying to do, as we in the official opposition have tried to do on so many occasions during the life of this parliament, was put forward arguments which he hoped would make sense not only to the Canadian people but to other members of the commonwealth. Since I have been in this house the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) has displayed a devotion and dedication to the betterment of the Canadian way of life which is a credit not only to his

Canadian Flag
constituency and to his province but to this nation. He is not the type of man who should find the Prime Minister deriving great joy and benefit from deriding the remarks he has made in putting forward a cogent argument with regard to an illogical recommendation on the part of the government.
Why should the Canadian red ensign not be the flag which represents our association with the commonwealth? What better flag could be flown from the flagpoles of this nation to portray our association with that great body? I cannot think of anything of which Canadians would be more proud than the knowledge that this house had at last found a place in this country for a flag which has meant so much to so many for so many years. As I said yesterday, I appreciate that this new flag may in days to come acquire something of the meaning which attaches to the Canadian red ensign today. But it does not have that meaning now. If we are to do anything for this new flag in the hope that it will become an acceptable symbol of this nation, we should produce alongside it, since the government desires two flags, one which is steeped in the history and traditions of this land, one which means so much to those who have lost loved ones in two world wars, one which means so much to the builders of this nation. I point out again that this is a flag which incorporates in it the union jack; it has in it the stuff of which the commonwealth is made, especially the British tradition which is so important and which has played so large a part in the development of this nation of ours. Surely the fact that the New Democratic party and the Social Credit party find a degree of merit in this amendment which they could not find when it came to the selection of a unique national flag should be an indication to the government that it would be wiser and saner to accept this proposal by my hon. friend from Victoria-Carleton and have it adopted, without the degree of debate and rancour associated with the vote which was taken early this morning.
I am not interested in debating at great length the value of a second flag to this nation. I am not interested in debating whether we should have one, two, three or four flags flying from the flagpoles of this country. But I am interested in seeing some common sense used, if we are to accept the second flag, in the selection of that flag. We as Canadians can find many more reasons in favour of the adoption of the Canadian red ensign than can be found in favour of the adoption of

the union jack. It is true there was a time when the union jack was used as widely in this nation as was the Canadian red ensign. There was probably a time when Canadians did not know whether the union jack or the Canadian red ensign should be the official flag of this nation. But that time has long passed.
If anything was achieved by the debate which has just ended it was that great bodies of Canadians in all parts of this nation were convinced that the Canadian red ensign has been the flag of this country ever since 1867. A great many of them for many years hence will continue to fly it and to respect it. They will still consider it to be the flag of Canada. What more logical step could this parliament take than to adopt it, thus recognizing the feelings which are held, and deeply held, by so many people in this country today? For many Canadians it will not be easy to move from the Canadian red ensign to a red maple leaf flag. If we were to adopt the Canadian red ensign as our commonwealth symbol it would at least give these people an opportunity during the period of transition to fly the flag they want to fly, knowing that it still had some meaning in this country.
Nothing which the Prime Minister said today convinces me there is any justification for accepting the union jack rather than the Canadian red ensign. I believe there are many other members in this chamber who remained unconvinced by what the right hon. gentleman had to say. I believe that in his own party there is less acceptance of the union jack than there is of the red ensign. After all is said and done, after votes have been recorded and after a new flag design has been adopted by this house, I remain convinced that there are many members of the Liberal party who feel great devotion for the Canadian red ensign. They do not want to see it hauled down from the flagpoles of this nation. They feel deeply about this. Now, at this moment, they have an opportunity to do something about it by urging the Prime Minister and his colleagues to accept the amendment which is before the house, thus ending this flag question so that we may go forward to deal constructively with the material and economic affairs of this nation which the people who sent us here wish us to deal with as prudently as possible.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to enter into the debate on this amendment at this time, but rather to speak on the main motion. However, after listening to some of the

speeches of this afternoon I feel I should enter into the debate. I am perhaps one of the last of the members of the flag committee to speak during this flag debate. First of all I would also like to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for appointing me to the committee. It was not a task that I asked for but it was a task I was happy to carry out, not only for the Prime Minister but in my view for Canadians across this country.
I found on that committee, together with the other members of all parties, close friendships and close associations of mind although we differed in certain respects. I found that apart from our differences in certain respects we could always be friendly and sociable. I am happy therefore that this committee gave me an opportunity to know some members of this house somewhat better. I disagree with some of the remarks that have been made with regard to the Prime Minister's speech. I think the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) used the words, in connection with that speech, "insulting" and "despicable". He also suggested that some things had been said with derision. I am sure the Prime Minister did not intend to be insulting or derisive. I knew the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton before being appointed to the flag committee, and during the meetings of the committee and before that time I always had a great deal of respect for him, although we were of different minds on this subject. I thought he would be the last to suggest that the remarks of the Prime Minister should be taken in this vein and used against him.
Certain remarks have been made in this house with respect to the decision of the committee regarding one national flag as contained in the sixth report of the committee. It is true that the report stated that a vote was taken on one national flag for Canada but, as the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) pointed out, during the committee meetings it was made very clear and all members of the committee knew very well- and I was also one who raised this question -that although there was to be a vote on one national flag for Canada it was to be without prejudice to the committee dealing with a flag symbolizing our connection with the commonwealth of nations and our loyalty to the Queen. I challenge any member of that committee to deny that as a fact.
My views on a national flag were well known in the committee and are known in my constituency. I wanted to speak in the debate on the sixth report of the committee,
Canadian Flag
but circumstances prevented my so doing. However, I have no hesitation in making my views known with respect to the seventh report of the committee. I respect the views of the hon. member for Danforth and the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois). The hon. member for Danforth at all times -he stated this in the house and I am sure he will not think I am taking too much of a liberty in stating it again-supported the Canadian red ensign as being the flag symbolic of our commonwealth association. That view was always held by the hon. member for Danforth. Although I assume that when the vote was taken he may have voted for the union jack, I believe he did so reluctantly because he was always for the Canadian red ensign being the flag designated for our commonwealth association.
The hon. member for Megantic was also opposed to any kind of flag symbolizing our commonwealth association. I respect completely this hon. member's view. However, Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to draw attention to the remarks made in committee by the mover of this amendment, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, and the seconder, the hon member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh). I am sorry they are not present at the moment. I would point out that the remarks made in the committee, when the proposal was put forward that there be a flag symbolizing our commonwealth connections and our loyalty to the Queen, should be discussed by hon. members opposite, as a loyal opposition which sincerely believes that the Canadian red ensign should be the flag designated to symbolize our commonwealth association, with the mover and seconder of the amendment, because the views they propounded in the committee were exactly opposite to those they are now propounding.
I can understand the views of those who believe the Canadian red ensign should be the flag designated for this purpose. I also, being honest with myself, held that view and I held it, I might add, somewhat strongly. But then I kept looking into the matter further, when it was brought to my attention that perhaps it should not be designated as the flag for commonwealth purposes. In addition, Mr. Speaker, the views expressed by the Prime Minister today helped me to see why it should not be so designated. In fact a question was asked by, I believe, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), "Were they Liberals who moved both motions?" The answer was yes; the hon. member for Leeds admitted that he

Canadian Flag
was the one who moved the amendment designating the union jack as the commonwealth flag, and another Liberal member moved the original motion that it should be the Canadian red ensign.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why did the Prime Minister change his mind?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of that either. Perhaps the hon. member should 
have directed his question to the Prime Minister when he was here today.
The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) stated that the Prime Minister had said today that the Canadian red ensign was the national flag of Canada, and of course we have heard a great deal on that subject. The Prime Minister has stated on many occasions, and I support him, that the Canadian red ensign was originally intended to be used as the national flag of Canada until parliament ruled otherwise. That argument has been repeated here on many occasions.
I am of neither French nor English stock, although I was born in this country. My grandparents were immigrants to Canada, and I am thankful that they came here rather than somewhere else. My wife is of English and Scottish descent, so I do not know what my children could be called. In any event we have too many hyphenated names around here as far as I am concerned. Perhaps my children should be referred to as English-Scottish-Italian-Canadians. However I have always considered them to be strictly, only and always Canadians, and I feel very strongly about this.
Many individuals have suggested that in my point of view I am overlooking British history. Many individuals living in my riding, who are of English speaking and U.E.L. stock, do not take exception to the flag adopted this morning. I can give the names of some of these people, who would not be opposed to my doing so, but I will not do so at this time.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member laughs, but I suggest that he knows many individuals of the same type who live in his riding.
As I suggested, many people have spoken to me harshly because they feel I have forgotten British tradition, and British jurisprudence in law. I would be lacking in respect for, and ignoring those principles I learned at university if I were to forget either British tradition or the tradition and culture of my own family, and I say with a great deal of reluctance that those who would do so are neither true to themselves, their consciences or anyone else.
I am in favour of a flag which denotes our commonwealth relations and our loyalties, if you will, to the Queen. I am not in agreement with those hon. members, such as the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), who suggests that because there is something missing in the one national flag

which we have proposed we feel the need for a second flag. Anyone who feels that the symbols on a flag represent feelings that can be lost when those symbols are replaced does not hold true feelings for that which the flag represents. I suggest such individuals have never held dear to their hearts those things represented by a flag, if they can believe that such things can be lost by a change in the flag.
The members of the Conservative party who sat on the special flag committee saw fit to absent themselves during two votes. On the first occasion the vote concerned the adoption of the Canadian red ensign as representative of our commonwealth relationship. The second occasion was on an amendment that the flag to indicate that relationship should be the union jack. If their feelings were so strong in this regard why have they adopted a different attitude at this time? Why, having taken the attitude they took in the committee, do they now in this house propose an obviously illogical amendment?
The royal union flag, commonly known as the union jack, still flies in many areas of this country, particularly in Ontario. One has only to look at high schools, elementary schools and public buildings to observe the union jack. Why should the union jack not continue to be flown in this country? I am sure that it will not cease to be flown because of the adoption of this amendment. I am sure the Canadian red ensign will not cease to be flown as the result of the adoption of the flag which we voted on early this morning.
I do not suggest for a moment that we should attempt to stop the citizens of this country from flying either of those flags. However, there is nothing at all wrong with flying the union jack in this country as an indication of our allegiance to the crown and our membership in the commonwealth, particularly when it is flown by the government of Canada and those citizens of Canada who will continue to fly it, in any event, on appropriate occasions. I do not profess to know all of the occasions on which the union jack should be flown. I have always felt that the Canadian red ensign is a beautiful flag, and I still feel that way. I do disagree with those who suggest that the Canadian red ensign imparts a specific Canadian message, but that does not mean I disrespect the feelings of hon. members who think otherwise.
We learned from experts who appeared before the committee that the red ensign came to us from the British admiralty, and that as a result of usage it was adopted by order in
Canadian Flag
council as the Canadian national flag in 1945, at which time it was stated that it should continue to be the Canadian national flag until a future parliament decided otherwise, and adopted a distinctive flag. I cannot accede to the argument that we can fly the Canadian national flag proposed now by the government while at the same time fly the Canadian red ensign with the Canadian coat of arms.
I went along with the suggestion to substitute the union jack for the Canadian red ensign because I felt very strongly and sincerely that the Canadian red ensign should not be placed in a secondary position, as a flag representative of our commonwealth relations. I think the amendment to the motion now before us deals with this suggestion in even stronger terms than I have used.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will be through in a moment and I will be glad to answer anything then. The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh) stated in his speech that he saw no evidence in the flag committee that there should be other than one national flag. I have already given my view on that and it is substantiated by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott). I put out the challenge that this is not so, that there was always the qualification that it would be with no prejudice to the committee discussing the matter at a later date.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) stated today, I felt during the debate on the amendment that to be consistent with their views and with the views of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary they would have moved an amendment to delete altogether the recommendation made in the seventh report of the committee. I do not wish to put forward to members opposite that they should not have changed their minds. Of course they should. We all have the liberty and the freedom to do so, but I felt I should try to clarify some of the things that were said during the debate on this amendment.
If the amendment should carry, my own personal feeling is that I am quite prepared to continue respecting the Canadian red ensign not only as the flag designated to represent our commonwealth association and our loyalty to the crown but as a flag which I admit and have always stated has some history in the development of this country. It

Canadian Flag
has some history. I disagree that it should be our national flag but I am not one who has ever said that it has no history whatsoever.
I will conclude my remarks now and wait to speak on the motion itself, if we get to it. Before sitting down I will accept the question that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) may have had.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I will reserve my question and answer the hon. member in a speech I hope to make later today.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso) was labouring at some length the question of the logicality or otherwise of the position taken by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) when he introduced the amendment. He appeared to be rather puzzled by it. I should like to say at once that I find nothing illogical about the fact that this amendment was introduced by the hon. member for Vic-toria-Carleton. I can understand the preoccupation of the hon. member for Hamilton West, having been a member of the committee, with the ins and outs of all the votes that took place, but it seems to me that those in the official opposition who have spoken so far *on the proposition now before us have made it quite clear that in the first instance they would have preferred a single flag without any other arrangement, that that single flag should have continued to be the red ensign and that they reserved their position on the second proposition in the committee and abstained for that quite logical reason. However, when the decision made by the house last night is given full effect it will result in the removing of the red ensign from the Canadian scene in any official sense, and it is logical that the official opposition should now seek to propose the amendment that is before us.
I say at once, Mr. Speaker, that I do not share their line of reasoning in this respect. I made a public statement in my own constituency when the original resolutions in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) appeared on the order paper. I said that while I did not necessarily agree with all the particulars contained in those resolutions I personally liked the idea of Canada having a national flag of a distinctive maple leaf design and I also liked the idea of having a flag which would be a symbol of our relationship with the commonwealth and our allegiance to the Queen. That has been my position ever since.
I have not participated in the debate since it began except briefly for a few minutes the

other day, but I have a few things I should like to say with reference to the amendment now before us, which I may say I support quite strongly. I listened rather carefully to the statement made by the Prime Minister earlier this afternoon and I must say I was a little surprised that, after having been so reticent about participating in the earlier discussions, he should suddenly launch himself to the forefront at such an early stage of the debate on this motion.
When the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) spoke earlier he urged that some of the members of the Liberal party, who he feels have an attachment to the red ensign, should do some urging of their leaders to reconsider their position and to consider supporting the amendment. In my view the hon. member for Cumberland is suggesting a rather circuitous route. So far as I am concerned I appeal directly to those members of the Liberal party, in the light of the declaration that there will be a free vote, to show their attachment to the retention of the red ensign for the particular purposes suggested in the report of the committee, namely as a symbol of our association with the commonwealth and of our allegiance to the crown.
My assessment of the Prime Minister's arguments was that they were embedded purely in the ancient principles of heraldry. He had some authorities and I am not going to quarrel with the correctness of the views of the authorities he cited. But I am going to suggest that with regard to the question of the kind of flag symbols we are going to have there are considerations which are of more vital and vibrant importance than strict adherence to all the principles of ancient heraldry. As a matter of fact, I think we have already ploughed a little new ground in this connection by the action the house has already taken in connection with the other motion. I am not suggesting that such considerations should be entirely ignored and in my view they are not entirely ignored in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton which my colleague, the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott), indicated he would have been prepared to move had it not already been proposed. I feel that the original suggestion brought forward by the flag committee ignores the very thing which was symbolized in the earlier report of the committee, namely that history is not a static or a dead thing. This report of the committee ignores the fact that the British empire and the British commonwealth is something which is living, evolving and mov-

ing on into the future which I, for one, hope will be as splendid as it has been in many respects in the past.
At the conclusion of his remarks I asked the Prime Minister whether or not the Canadian government had consulted with or made any attempt to ascertain the views of the government of the United Kingdom in respect of the proposal that we might adopt the royal union flag as the symbol of our allegiance to the commonwealth. I did so specifically because of my feeling that, while at one time we were in effect under the umbrella of the United Kingdom, we were an extension of it, since 1931 that has not been the case. We are, in fact, an independent nation even though we owe allegiance to the Queen who is one in person with the Queen of the United Kingdom. It would have been simply a matter of courtesy, in my view, apart from anything else, before such a proposal as this were placed before the Canadian parliament, at least to have had some sort of assurance that the government and people of the United Kingdom were willing and happy that we should do so. At least we should know if they are unhappy about it.
The Prime Minister's arguments concerning the origination and derivation of the royal union jack may be quite sound and logical from a historical point of view. I am not going to enter that argument or attempt to set myself up as any authority in this connection. I do suggest that, for all practical purposes, the union jack is the flag of the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland. We should recognize that fact. I do not know whether or not any other members have heard reports similar to those I have heard from people returning to Canada from the United Kingdom in recent weeks and months. I have had it reported to me that at least some people in the United Kingdom, when they read their newspapers, were rather disturbed by the fact that at this late date we Canadians apparently were trying to steal their flag. I have no way of knowing how widespread that sentiment may be in the United Kingdom. Apparently it has come as quite a surprise to at least some people in the United Kingdom to discover that Canada, who they thought had asserted her independence quite some time ago, still considered that, somehow or other, she was under their umbrella or tied to the apron strings of the mother country. I gather they were inclined to be just a bit resentful over the fact that we had taken action which led to the establishment-I think we all agree it was in
Canadian Flag
large part under the leadership that came from Canada-of the commonwealth of nations, as free, independent nations associated with one another, and yet apparently still desired to keep the United Kingdom flag rather than be willing to fly our own.
In support of the amendment, I may say that I feel there would be no quarrel on the part of anyone in the United Kingdom if we were to select what has been our flag since 1945 officially, with its union jack in the corner and our coat of arms, as a symbol of our association with the commonwealth. We may continue to use it freely in that sense. We have other associations in addition to those we have within the commonwealth. For an example, we are a member of NATO. Let me take a hypothetical situation. Let us suppose we wanted a flag which would be, in some measure, a symbol of our association in NATO. Would we think of proposing a resolution in this house that would make the stars and stripes the symbol of our association in NATO without asking our cousins in the United States whether or not they were agreeable to this idea? Perhaps the parallel is not exact. I would agree that perhaps the royal union flag has heraldic implications that the stars and stripes has not. Nevertheless, if you consider the logic of things in this day and age, I suggest that really there is not much practical difference between suddenly deciding we are going to adopt officially in this parliament, for our own purposes, the flag of the United Kingdom, and suddenly deciding we were going to adopt for certain purposes and usages, the flag of the United States of America.
I really have not much more to say, Mr. Speaker, except that I do feel when we look back on all that has taken place in this house and throughout the country since the question of a Canadian flag came to the fore, the difficulties that have been encountered, and if we take into account all the factors that are involved in terms of healing some of the wounds that were referred to last night, then it would be the part of wisdom for this-parliament to retain in a permanent and honoured place the red ensign that many Canadians have come to know and to love. Apart from any other considerations, apart from the fact that I find the symbolism of the Canadian red ensign very appropriate for our association in the commonwealth, I believe these considerations should not be lost from sight by members of this house in reaching a decision on the committee report which is now before us.

Canadian Flag
I appeal to hon. members opposite in particular to consider these things before they come to a decision. All of us in this house claim we have the right to vote freely and have been given the right to do so by our party leadership. We should consider all these elements before we decide to reject out of hand the amendment which is now before the house. My only real association with the red ensign in conjunction with the commonwealth was during the period I was in attendance at the commonwealth parliamentary conference in Kuala Lumpur some time ago. I must say that there are situations when we, as the senior member of the commonwealth, find that the position of our flag in the array of commonwealth flags is right next to that of the United Kingdom. This is a symbol which I feel most Canadians would accept equally well. It is in keeping with the traditions that have been built around this particular emblem which first had official recognition in this country. It is a symbol which I would hope would be more acceptable in the eyes of many people of French speaking ancestry than one which is purely and simply a symbol of the United Kingdom, a country which I honour and respect and to which I have a strong sense of emotional attachment that sometimes puzzles me because I have never been there. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I think here is an area in which we can move toward a unity of feeling and understanding, things which may be lost if we insist on implementing the report of the committee.
For these reasons I would appeal to other hon. members of the house to join with those of us who have already indicated our support for the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, several weeks ago, I had no intention of speaking on a distinctive national flag for Canada. But I certainly intend to discuss the recommendation contained in the seventh report of the committee concerning the desire of the government to have a flag representing the agreement between Canada and the commonwealth.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso), who so ably dealt with the procedure adopted by the committee, showed how difficult it is for members who did not sit on the committee to understand the ramification of the votes. How much more difficult it must be for the Canadian people in general to follow the proce-

dural implications of all the votes that were taken.
As I set out on my few brief remarks this afternoon may I say to you, sir, that everything I have to say in a historical context, and every other context, relates to the amendment before the house and the desire of the government to have a flag representing Canada's co-equal position in the commonwealth.

Mr. Speaker, I always thought that it was not quite proper for a member to speak in too great details about the history of his own electoral riding in the House of Commons. But allow me to recall some historical facts concerning Brome-Missisquoi, the electoral riding I now represent in this house.
Some 75 years ago the population of Brome-Missisquoi was approximately 75 per cent English speaking and 25 per cent French speaking. Today, in 1964, the percentage is exactly the opposite: 75 per cent French speaking and 25 per cent English speaking.
Mr. Speaker, you can undoubtedly notice by my accent that English is my mother tongue, but today I have the honour of representing a dominantly French Canadian population in the House of Commons.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Today your riding is 75 per cent Liberal and 25 per cent Conservative.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is not true, and I am glad the hon. member for Lotbiniere made such a remark, because I am going to answer him in a few minutes. I am quite pleased- [Text]
-I think hon. members will soon realize why I am happy that the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) made such an interjection because he thinks-

-because the government proposed a distinctive flag, that the Liberals will necessarily obtain votes in the next election in the province of Quebec. That is not necessarily so.

speechtext: We will get the Liberal vote, that's for sure.

speechtext:
We in Brome-Missisquoi understand the true historical fact that two great races founded the glory and the strength of Canada. Today this approach also includes many citizens who, since the time of confederation, have come to Canada to join

the two historic founding races in building a stronger and greater nation.
I know, as I begin my observations, that I am going to repeat myself but I am sure you, sir, will see that these keynote remarks, these introductory remarks I make, are definitely to be related to the amendment before the house and the government's desire to have a commonwealth flag. I cannot do it without referring to the historic background of my riding and to the present situation in it.
Although we are dealing with something that has national significance I think there are times when we can speak in some detail of our ridings, more especially when one speaks of Brome-Missisquoi where we truly understand, where the two great founding races live side by side in harmony and understanding, where we understand-and it is not an intellectual proposition-the positive attributes of unity in diversity are something deeply believed in and felt. That is why I found it very difficult to take the floor of the house and speak one way or the other during the debate on a distinctive national flag; but it will soon become apparent to the hon. member for Lotbiniere why I am on my feet now.
[Translation\
I have a good answer to the question put to me by my hon. friend a few minutes ago.

I feel, sir, that in relation to the problems of national unity and confederation, when we talk about the necessity for mutual understanding and bonne entente, and better understanding, we are not nearly positive enough in underlining the positive and glorious aspects of unity in diversity.
I think that in most organizations it is unfortunate that a 90 per cent area is the problem area and a 10 per cent area is the area of rich opportunity. This has been true in questions relating to national unity. Unfortunately we spend an inordinate amount of time on the 90 per cent problem area and typically ignore the 10 per cent area of pure opportunity. I hope before this debate is over, whether we are on amendments or subamendments, whether we are speaking of a commonwealth flag or a distinctive flag, I hope from now on in this house and outside it we will talk about the 10 per cent area of rich opportunity in relation to the problems of confederation and national unity.
Ten years ago I was speaking with one of my good friends in Montreal and I made remarks rather like those I am making in the house right now, and he said, "Oh, Heward,
Canadian Flag
how boring. Can't we take it for granted we are united and strong and go ahead and deal with the bread and butter economic issues that are really facing this nation?" "Well," I said, "I suppose you are right, we can." But I think today as we deal with this subject, whether it is a distinctive flag or a commonwealth flag, that we cannot take such a thing for granted. Especially in the House of Commons we must show real leadership and discuss positively subjects which lie in the area of national unity, federal-provincial relationship and confederation. Now that we have a distinctive Canadian flag I hope we shall get on to discuss the real, bread and butter economic issues.
The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) suggested in the course of his intervention, and I am glad he made it, that because the government had proposed what the Prime Minister described as a non-political flag, and because of what has happened in the house in the last 24 hours, the Liberals would be elected automatically in the province of Quebec. I would simply point out that in 1962 there were some who felt that because of the introduction of simultaneous translation services in this chamber, bilingual cheques and that sort of thing, the position of the Conservative party in Quebec might be helped. Well, I think the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Choquette) -

-Mr. Caouette and the Creditistes have certainly given proof to the contrary in 1962. [Text]
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that I am straying from the subject of the amendment to some extent. But speaking directly to the amendment and to the question of a flag representing our association with the commonwealth, we must concede, now, that there is no fleur-de-lis in the distinctive flag or the proposed commonwealth flag. I say this without any rancour whatsoever. I am not saying it is what I want and I am not saying it is what the people in my province want. Certainly, whether the choice, now, is to be the union jack or the red ensign there will be no fleur-de-lis in the proposed commonwealth flag.

speechtext: It is in the red ensign.

speechtext:
It is in the red ensign but not, I think, in the sense we were considering during the original debate. I know that much of the Prime Minister's argument was technically correct-not all of it, by any means. But who in the world would suggest that it is

possible to explain technicalities from the Atlantic to the Pacific on an issue so emotionally charged as this? I am convinced of one thing. I am convinced that while we on this side of the house had a free vote, no matter what was written or said across this land, the same could not be said for members on the other side of this chamber.

speechtext: Order, please. Would the hon. member kindly resume his seat. I am sure he will permit the Chair to bring to his attention the rule that he cannot reflect on a vote of the house.

speechtext:
I was not speaking on a past vote. I was speaking of a vote on the particular amendment which is before us.
I know there will be laughter from the other side at what I am about to say. But had the party to which I belong formed the government-I cannot say when we would have brought a flag, or flags, before the house for approval, or even if we would have proceeded by bringing a flag or flags before the house at all-I am convinced of one thing: We would have brought in one distinctive flag for one united Canada. There would have been no doubt about it. I realize I am speaking very frankly and forthrightly. My party, collectively and as individuals, has often made mistakes in the province of Quebec. But we have never made the mistake of dividing and ruling, as members opposite have done. That is why I left the Liberal party. I left the Liberal party because of resolutions such as we have before the house today.
The Prime Minister can try to tell us this is not a two flag resolution. He can go into technicalities. He can squirm. But he knows as well as I do that members in his Quebec caucus have stated this will be interpreted in Quebec as a two flag resolution. A party which is sympathetic to an associate state, a party which has never said the same thing inside the province of Quebec as it has said outside that province, now pleads with us to keep this question of a commonwealth flag above politics. I am not scared of the Prime Minister. He is an honourable man who wishes to do everything possible to unite this country. What I am scared of are his lieutenants such as the hon. member for Lotbiniere, who think they can wave a flag and forget the economic issues and attempt to poison the minds of the people in the province of Quebec against the party to which I belong, telling them: Here is your flag; we are going to be elected automatically. No matter what

the Prime Minister says, this is a two flag resolution.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: We can go for two weeks on this subject.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Like his right hon. predecessor, a great Canadian, Louis St. Laurent, a man I respect as I respect the present Prime Minister, a man who did much to unite and help this country, the present Prime Minister does not know what the old guard of the Liberal party is like in the province of Quebec. We have noted the utter surprise of the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan). He could not understand why his party is doing what it is doing. At the same time we notice this other attitude expressed by the members from the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I will tell you why the government is following its present course. It is because the party opposite has never said the same thing in the province of Quebec as it has said outside that province. While the Prime Minister would like to keep this whole matter out of the political arena, through gross ineptitude people who wanted to vote for a distinctive Canadian flag were forced to do it by reason of closure and today we are forced to move into an area-

speechtext: Would you answer a question?

I will answer later. On this side of the house we have always said we want a united Canada under one distinctive flag. But no matter what members opposite say, this proposal now before us will be looked upon in the province of Quebec as a two flag issue. Their colleagues from Quebec will soon tell us how it will be regarded in many sections of this country. No amount of technical explanation, no amount of weasel-ling in and out will explain that away.
Make sure of one thing. Members opposite have come up to me and said, jeeringly: "Heward, you cannot vote against report No. 6; think what would happen in Missisquoi county, which is mainly French speaking." Again, members have approached me and said in the same tone: "Heward, you cannot vote against report No. 7. Look what will happen in Brome county".
