subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Try to make sense. You have just said the opposite thing. Make up your mind.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I want to make one thing very clear. Yesterday I made my position unequivocally clear both in English speaking and in French speaking Canada. Members of my party did not in all cases agree with me, but we were allowed to vote in such a way as to express our views. Since I was a college student I have always stood for one united Canada under a distinctive flag without a fleur-de-lis or union jack in it. I was allowed to vote that way. Were you allowed a free vote over there? Are you going to be allowed a free vote on this seventh report of the committee?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Sure.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Not on your life. Through gross ineptitude you have plunged, like the Liberal party has always plunged, a delicate question of national unity, federal-provincial relations and confederation right into the heart of partisan politics. Mr. Speaker, I am proud of Canada's co-equal position with other members of the commonwealth in the commonwealth of nations. I am proud, as every member of this house is proud, to recognize the presence of the crown in Canada. Enough said. But when I voted yesterday for a distinctive Canadian flag, I voted in the name of all the citizens of Brome-Missisquoi, English speaking and French speaking; and we did not need this cynical approach that is being brought forward today, namely a two flag resolution.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Let us hear about the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned at six o'clock I was talking about my riding of Brome-Missisquoi, and I pointed out that most of the citizens of Brome were English speaking while most of my electors in Missisquoi were French speaking.
I also wish to point out that when I voted for a Canadian flag last night, I voted for a distinctive flag for a united Canada. And when I voted for a distinctive Canadian flag, I voted on behalf of my English speaking and French speaking fellow citizens in the riding of Brome-Missisquoi.
Concerning the seventh report of the flag committee, I must tell the members of the government that as the member for Brome-Missisquoi and speaking for all the voters of that riding, we do not need a flag for Brome and another for Missisquoi.

Mr. Speaker, I simply wish to say that I intend to do everything possible during this debate, with a sense of responsibility, to make sure that every Canadian will recognize that, as far as those who support this party are concerned, this is a one flag resolution. Because of the actions of the present government there is a definite feeling among the people of this country that this is a two flag debate. That is the situation, whether we like it or not, in spite of the appeals for unity that have been made by members of this party to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
A number of Liberal members from the province of Quebec, as well as from other parts of Canada, have told me that the situation with which we are now faced is not indicative of a Quebec phenomenon but

rather of a Canadian phenomenon. I believe that a great number of people in this nation feel that the government, as the result of this motion for concurrence, is proposing two flags for Canada. As far as my constituency is concerned, the government is proposing one flag for Brome yet another for Missisquoi.
Hon. members perhaps will remind me that yesterday I voted in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag and I did so because I believe in one flag for one united Canada. Hon. members opposite do not like to hear this side of the debate, because it is in this area that they are going to find themselves in difficulty. No matter how many errors the party which I support has made inside and outside of this House of Commons during the flag debate, and no matter how many technicalities the right hon. Prime Minister discusses, we believe in one flag for one united Canada.
Just before we adjourned at six o'clock I explained that, because this is an emotionally-charged issue, we in this party have exercised a free vote, and we will continue to exercise a free vote in respect of each phase of this flag issue.
In reference to the amendment now before the house, I plead with members opposite to make sure that their whip is off when they vote. It is not good enough for them to say that the whip is off, yet stand as a group and vote as a group, because the people of this country cannot be fooled about this issue. Action of that kind on the part of Liberal members of parliament does not represent a free vote.
We in the Conservative party believe that no matter what distinctive flag is selected, it should be the only distinctive flag for Canada.

I am not speaking with the authority of my party but I know in my heart of hearts as I stand here that while we Conservatives may have a rough time in the province of Quebec we voted yesterday, no matter how we vote on this motion, in terms of thinking of one distinctive flag for one united Canada. Sir, as a member from the province of Quebec I am not willing to stand here and listen to the pontifications of the leadership of the Liberal party in the House of Commons and then go back to the province of Quebec and face the villainous type of partisanship we are going to see on this kind of issue.

There must be give and take in this sort of thing. Because of the actions of the Liberals in and out of the house there is great danger no matter what we do here. Let us not have this unnecessary confusion. If you are not plunging the whole matter into partisan politics, why do you sit there and sneer and yell? Where is the give and take? Let us recognize the fact, as I said before six o'clock, that neither of the two traditional parties, the Liberals or the Conservatives, can truly call themselves national parties any more. I recognize that with our corporal's guard from Quebec we are no longer a national party in the great sense of the word, but with your corporal's guard from west of the lakehead neither are you.

I have listened with perhaps more than usual attention to the remarks of the hon. member because in many ways the constituency of Brome-Missisquoi and the constituency of Verdun are very similar. Like the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi I represent French speaking Canadians and English speaking Canadians in great numbers. Like the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, as he said earlier today, my decision on how to vote on the flag was a very agonizing one as I struggled to reconcile the different factors and to come up with a vote which I thought was in the best interests of my province and all Canada. Despite the sincerity which I sensed in the remarks of the hon. member, I resented deeply any implication on his part that my vote then, and my vote in the future on this seventh report, will be motivated by anything other than my own desire to do what is best for my constituency and for my country.

I believe the hon. member said for the two flag resolution; it is a question of semantics, I think. I say this in all sincerity that my vote for a new, distinctive flag and my vote for the union jack as a symbol of membership in the commonwealth are votes made out of sincere conviction. As a matter of fact, I believe that this action will finally restore this flag to a place of distinction in this country. What has been the role of the union jack since the red ensign has taken prominence? What, specifically, has it stood for other than some symbol of that particular country that was the mother country of so many of us? At least, by this action of parliament, if the motion passes, the union jack will once again have a proud place in our country, in our future events.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi made an issue of the fact that we will get confused with a new flag and a union jack. As a great Canadian, as the good Canadian I happen to know he is and also as a good Quebecker, I wonder what the hon. member might do this Saturday or next Saturday when he stands at the ceremony for opening a new road under the fleur-de-lis flag of Quebec? Does he turn his back on it or does he not recognize it for what it is, a symbol in the province of Quebec to be used on occasions where it cannot be confused with the red maple leaf or the union jack? The same thing happens to members of other provinces. The province of Quebec is not the only province with a provincial flag of its own. Other provinces have provincial flags. Certainly, they have a place in this country. There is no need for any confusion.

We will have occasions in Ontario, Newfoundland, Quebec and the other provinces, upon which the maple leaf, the union jack and the provincial flag are all displayed in a position of prominence. What amounts of intelligence is necessary to distinguish between them, to understand why they are there? So, Mr. Speaker, much as I appreciate the remarks made by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi and his sincere sentiments toward the province I respect and love, I resent the fact he said that our party has spoken with two voices in that province. This, again, was an unfair remark when it comes to national unity. On four occasions in his remarks to the house the hon. member paraphrased the remarks of Brutus when he praised the Prime Minister, then accused him of having two voices, one for Quebec and one for the rest of the country.
I know the hon. member thinks very highly of the French. However, I ask him if he would get up in his riding this Saturday and read some of the things that have been said in the heat of battle in this house during the flag debate? Would he read the statements of one member that the symbol of French Canada is the red maple leaf, a statement which was based on a letter written in the 1800's? Of course he would not. He would be ashamed to do it and so would I. I am sure there are many good Canadians on your side of the house who stand and make an impassioned plea for a point in which they believe. I can forgive any speech in this House of Commons if it is made sincerely and it reflects a man's true feelings, and I include the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) as long as they are made with sincerity. This is his prerogative. If I vote sincerely for the resolution which will make the union jack a symbol of our membership in the commonwealth, I do not want the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi or any other to be imputing motives for my vote. I will have no problem in going back to my constituency, which resembles the constituency of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, and explaining to those people that there is but one flag, the new red maple leaf, and one symbol of our membership in the commonwealth of nations.
In conclusion I would like to say on behalf of the French speaking members, not only on this side but on that side, that many of us thought the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) was a classic in tolerance and I sense it made a lot of us a little bit ashamed,

perhaps because it was in complete contrast to much of the bitterness and hate that has permeated this house for too long.
I know the French speaking Canadians Of my own party are free to vote as they wish, and because of their cultural and other traditions, because of the fact they are the first to admit they do not have the strong ties with the British isles that we do, if they are willing to vote for the union jack let nobody here interpret it as an effort of the whip, as an effort of party discipline, but rather as a symbol of these French speaking Canadians willing to subjugate their natural desire for what they think is in the best interests of Canada.

To recognize in our statutes the union jack as one of our own flags, even if only in certain circumstances, constitutes an encroachment, it seems to me, upon our Canadian sovereignty, inasmuch as the union jack is the flag of the United Kingdom and its colonies. Canada has been an adult and sovereign country since the Statute of Westminster. I find it unacceptable that we should support the motion respecting the union jack.

amendment does not mean a vote against the union jack, but in favour of maintaining the red ensign. Therefore, I would rather abstain from voting.

The reasons invoked by the government in support of the union jack could also apply in favour of the tricolour because, for an important part of our people, it carries the same meaning as the union jack does for another section of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure many of us must envy the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) who says he has no difficulty and will have the courage to vote on this ques-
[Mr. Deputy Speaker.)
tion. I am sure we are all aware of that old expression, "Fools rush in where wise men fear to tread". Those of us who have some conception of the depth of feeling and compassion in the nation and how important these questions are to so many people who are, rather like myself, perhaps just a little puzzled as to why this nation needs two flags, are just a little hesitant about how we should vote on this question. The question in my mind is not clear. Because the hon. member may think that is because there is such a limitation on my thinking power I will reserve my right to the opinion that he who cannot even see the difficulties is not likely to give us much valuable advice on how to handle them.
I did think the remarks of the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) were worthy of some comment and note, and they do highlight what I think is the most important aspect of this matter that we can discuss; that is, the mental attitude of the members, our state of mind when we consider this question. Certainly much has been said by the hon. member for Verdun about the sincerity of members taking part in this debate and he made much of that point. We all know that there can be very sincere mistakes, but there can be a lack of understanding or a willingness to take a stand on so few facts that it is difficult to comprehend that it can reasonably be called honest. I think many of us have varying standards by which we feel that we must acquaint ourselves with the problems involved in a question before we can really call ourselves sincere when we venture an opinion.
In my view, while I do not want to make this just an exercise in semantics, sincerity means more than a mere belief, because of ignorance, in a certain thing and standing in this house and saying it. Certainly sincerity calls for the responsibility of knowledge, for acquainting oneself with the facts as well as trying to give honestly the opinion one has formed. I may be just a little bitter or perhaps a little suspicious, or perhaps I have learned a lot from watching the Liberal party over the years; but when the hon. member for Verdun says he does not think anyone in this house would want to get up and talk about the flag unless he was absolutely sincere I think he perhaps pinpointed for us the reason why so few Liberals took part in the flag debate. I suggest this does not exactly go along with his comment that while he may have been speaking for himself, it was not because the whip was on. I suggest that

if he is asking us to consider as worth while his opinion that all members of the Liberal party are like himself in that regard, then he is indeed naive. I have seen nothing to indicate, in the actions of the government supporters, that there was anything approaching what I would call sincerity with regard to this problem.
Certainly anyone in this house who listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when he said what this flag was supposed to stand for, the unity it was supposed to bring to the nation, why the flag had to be distinctive, and then looked at the same time at the order paper and the resolution which is before us to bring in a second flag, can only come to the conclusion-this is what it indicates to my mind, at least-that this is an admission on the part of the Prime Minister that the flag adopted by this house last night is very hollow when it comes to symbolism.
1 suggest to the Liberal members of this house that they will have the same task as the rest of us, if we are to have a new flag that must be honoured and accepted. I ask seriously the question: When there is before us this present resolution, which cannot signify anything but a complete failure of the flag that was adopted last night to be symbolic, how are we going to sell last night's flag? I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that I am very perturbed at the question now facing us with regard to a second flag, particularly since we now have an amendment that the red ensign be substituted for the union jack if we are to have a second flag. I am aware of the depth of feeling and attachment to the red ensign of so many Canadians. I am sure every member in this house knows that there is a good percentage of the population of this country who as long as they live will neither forgive nor forget the tearing down of that banner to which they have become so attached. If I thought for a little while that perhaps the transition period while older people get older, young ones grow up and the attachment to the red ensign fades and those people gradually die out, so that a decade or two or a generation or two from now all that feeling may have faded away and the new flag will be accepted as symbolic of everything that the two flags are now supposed to stand for, I suppose I should feel a little better about it. But I cannot see how we hope to generate that feeling toward the new flag, if it is really to become the flag of this country, when we find it necessary to have a second flag flying when we want to really express something.
Canadian Flag
How can we build up this flag and say that the flag adopted in this house last night is a Canadian flag, if we are going to start at the outset by saying that it does not stand for anything and we must have another flag to fly when we want to express ourselves as Canadians? It becomes even more incomprehensible to me, Mr. Speaker, when I note that they want to have the union jack, not the red ensign, as Canada's second flag. These are the people who have put so much emphasis on the word distinctive and have said they want to fly a distinctive flag on special occasions. They have now put forward the union jack in place of the red ensign, which has signified Canada for 100 years, which is the only flag that is really distinctive of Canada today.
Meeting the arguments of my hon. friends opposite, who say they find on the red ensign the symbolism of the union jack repulsive and have rejected it because they have taken it as a symbol of colonialism and it has some unhappy memories connected with it, surely they are not going to suggest that the union jack does not have those same objections. As well as that, the union jack does have the disadvantage that it could not by any stretch of the imagination be called distinctive. I am really seriously interested in seeing some member on the government side get up and straighten out my thinking on this question or explain their own, because certainly on the record so far there is no logical explanation for this proposal.
This brings me back to where I started in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, namely to the question of sincerity. The hon. member for Verdun may be very sincere in his remarks on this question. Again I say that if he is sincere about himself, I can accept that; but when he asks us to accept his opinion of the rest of his party I find it just a bit difficult to swallow.
Most of us on this side of the house are convinced that there is only one reason why the union jack is being presented to this house by this report of the committee. That reason is that Joey has said: Give us the union jack or else. That statement does not seem to surprise or upset many of the members on the other side of this house. Perhaps that is because they sit in their places obeying the party whip slavishly on all scores.
On many occasions it has been embarrassing to me that the members in this house have shown such little unanimity. Perhaps I envy the members of the Liberal party because of the effect their party whip has on

Canadian Flag
them. He seems to be able to drive them like a flock of sheep in any direction he wishes them to go. On the other hand, perhaps it is better to be a member of this party where the men are men and not trained seals.
In seriously considering the flag issue we must also think of the state of mind of the members of the Liberal party. I have attempted to understand their feelings. I have listened to the remarks made by hon. members opposite in an attempt to figure out what is taking place. Many times in this chamber the kind of remark made by the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) has been repeated. He has invited us to forget all about our feelings on the matter of this flag, has suggested that we begin again without recrimination and leave politics out of the question. Every time the Grit party is successful in achieving something by its dirty tricks, the members of that party immediately begin talking to us in that manner. Last night they voted in favour of the sixth resolution of the committee, and by their remarks and attitudes have indicated to us that the Liberal whip managed to get to them, lining up their vote. Yet today-and he did not even wait until today-their leader played the cheapest trick I have ever seen played in this house. Even last night he said, vote with us now. That is a most contemptible performance on the part of a prime minister, and I suggest to the members on that side of the house that if they wish to consider the flag issue on a level above politics, let them first stop those dirty, Grit, political tricks. Put an end to their purely political lines of approach, and do away with all their pious platitudes. Let them depart from the level of hyprocisy we have observed on that side of the house month after month.
The flag issue is a serious one, and I suggest that members on the other side of the house should have some regard for the welfare of this country. Once they have accomplished their purposes in adopting the flag proposed by the sixth resolution of the committee as the national flag of Canada, by dirty political methods, let them now for God's sake refrain from political trickery in respect of the union jack. Is it necessary that they continue to divide this country, and to continue with their Grit tactics which are based on the concept of divide and rule?
While I realize that the government must satisfy Joey's desire on the flag question, I would ask members on that side of the house how far they intend to go with their Grit political methods. How much consideration

do those members have for that political party in preference to the general welfare of this nation? My suggestion at this time is that if any member on that side of the house wishes the flag, voted upon early this morning, to become revered as a national symbol, standing for the unity of this country, he must stop now in his attempt to adopt a second flag. Two flags can only mean two sections of this country, and that is one sure way of continuing the division of this nation. Surely a thinking person in this country, even a member of the Liberal party, will realize that the manner by which the flag issue has been introduced to parliament can do nothing but add to any division which exists in this nation.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if the members on that side of the house wish to have something of significance on a flag which is represented by the red ensign, as a result of more than 100 years of usage in this country they should give the people of this country a fighting chance to adopt such a flag. I implore them not to push the union jack on the people of Canada as an added reminder that even in the Liberal party the members do not believe that their flag is symbolic of this nation. They must be aware of the fact that the flag they have chosen is representative of pressure from Quebec and from Joey Smallwood, and that the maple leaf in the middle stands for what is left of the country. They must be aware that the flag indicates their belief that this nation is treated by the Liberals as a club. There is symbolism in that flag they have chosen, and it is this: The bars on each end separated by the big red maple leaf represent the two parts of the country divided by the Liberal party.
I am not sure whether I should vote for our amendment, but I know that I feel that, if we must have a second flag, it should be the red ensign rather than the union jack. I am unable to comprehend how any hon. member of this house can come to any other conclusion. As I have said, over the months I have come to understand some of the attitudes expressed in opposition to the red ensign, but it has been my feeling in that understanding that the opposition was directed more toward the union jack than the red ensign. If we are going to have a second flag, the flag suggested by the government is in fact that part of the red ensign which is most objectionable, and that part which many people have felt should be replaced. I think that objection was the basis of the move by the government to introducing the new one red maple leaf or Canadian distinctive flag to parliament; That being so I cannot understand government members who

support the union jack rather than the red ensign. If those members who object to our commonwealth ties and our allegiance to the Queen are honest in their feelings that we should have a second flag for Canada, surely they must realize that it is the union jack which has been associated with colonialism. Of the two flags, the one which symbolizes colonialism, I suggest, is the union jack.
Mr. Speaker, I should be very pleased if some hon. members opposite, particularly those representing French Canadian constituencies, would enlighten me as to some of my difficulties. I should like some hon. members of the Creditiste party, who are so determined to rid the country of the union jack, to explain their approach to this flag question. If we must have a second flag, I have no hesitation in voting for the Canadian red ensign in preference to the union jack, and I shall certainly vote in favour of the amendment. However, I am afraid that the amendment might carry, in which event I would have voted for a second flag for Canada which I think is silly.
I should like to understand one thing about the way the flag committee worked. I realize how the Liberal members tried to mislead the committee by proposing a vote on the question as to whether the committee preferred the three maple leaf design to the one maple leaf design. Following that vote the Liberal members of that party were quick to suggest that the vote had been unanimous in favour of the one maple leaf design, but that is not a true picture. I suggest that a vote on the motion and amendment before us now is similar to that vote. Most of us have some difficulty in this regard. I think an honest member on the government side, who has seriously thought about the flag issue in relation to the events of the past several days, would vote for the red ensign in preference to the union jack as the second flag for Canada. I had sort of hoped that both resolutions would be withdrawn completely. I really think that if there is hope of the flag we adopted yesterday becoming what it must, for the good of this nation we must defeat this resolution completely, and I hope we do.

Mr. Speaker, I think we have been led to believe that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickers-gill) is not an admirer of Mr. Stursberg. I would say that in this as in other things I do not share his point of view. It is not for us here to discuss Mr. Stursberg, but he does happen to be a man who has a very high reputation not only in Canada but abroad as a highly qualified student, scholar and commentator.
It is interesting that in this country of ours, which people sometimes say is dull and lacklustre, we have spent so much time on a flag. I suppose no country in the world has ever discussed a flag for as long as we have been discussing the question and now to add to the infinite variety we are beginning a discussion on two flags. Who says that Canada is not an interesting and different country?
Yesterday it was a new flag; today it is an old one. I think that the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) has through his amendment sought to improve a situation which was made far from glorious by the action of the committee, as indeed by the action of the government earlier in its two flag resolution. There has been some reference made to the flag which was discussed previously, a matter on which I made one speech, and I expect this speech to be my last on this one. I am not now, Mr. Speaker, nor have I ever been one of those who are so adamant against the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag without the symbolic representation of any other country. Had we on this troubled occasion had a distinctive flag introduced in an appropriate way which would not have torn and disturbed our country and which was a flag of interest and of beauty, I would have had no hesitation in supporting it. Therefore when I endorse the amendment of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton I am not waging any rearguard action on behalf of the Canadian red ensign.
I think the hon. member has given a big assist toward resolving the situation in which we found ourselves by reason of the introduction of that first embarrassing, unhistoric and almost ludicrous exercises in dual flagdom. There are many reasons why it is difficult to support the committee's seventh report as it

now stands. In one case there is some uncertainty as to the use of the royal union flag, the union jack. We are not clear when it would be used. On a visit of the sovereign the royal Canadian standard would be flown. On a visit of the prime minister of another commonwealth state it would be highly questionable whether the union jack would be flown because that individual would not be a head of state but a head of government. Indeed, if any flag were flown would it not be the flag of that particular commonwealth country?
As some of my colleagues have mentioned earlier today, it seems that this second flag diminishes the role and the symbolic value of the national flag. One might ask: Are there any occasions on which Canada is not a member of the commonwealth? Are there any occasions when Canadians do not bear allegiance to the crown? Therefore you have the problem of flying a flag on given occasions to demonstrate certain facets and facts of our national life which are in existence at all times. This is one of the problems that troubles me.
To go further with regard to the matter of the symbolic representation of flags, a flag should reflect, reveal and symbolize Canada in all its facets, international and otherwise, The flag of Canada should demonstrate that we are a member of the commonwealth, of NATO and of the United Nations. A meaningful flag should demonstrate all the aspects of Canada and all the things for which it stands in the great international world. It stands for great things in that world, and we can and should be proud of it.
We have before us the matter of a second flag, and we must take some action upon it. We must vote. However, the suggestion that such a flag be the union jack is a most regrettable and improper suggestion. It is a presumption upon the United Kingdom, a great and friendly country. It is a symbolic denial of Canadian history and the growth that has been made in this country from colony to nation. I do not ever suggest that one political party has a monopoly on virtue or has uniquely contributed to the development of this country. However, the thing that makes me proudest of the party to which I belong is that all down through the years it has been a great commonwealth party, and within that commonwealth has been the great champion of freedom and independence for this country. I ask why the flag of the United Kingdom should be chosen for commonwealth representation? Why

should it not be the flag of Australia, or any other commonwealth state?
Through the efforts of the great Sir Robert Borden, and his efforts will be admitted by everyone, we put into action the dream of a commonwealth of autonomous communities, in no way subordinate one to another. The United Kingdom has been a great and friendly power, an ally, a country which has brought freedom to many parts of the world. It does not, however, hold any position of prominence in the commonwealth of nations. I think it is a disservice to history to suggest that this country, the United Kingdom, has a role in the commonwealth greater, juridically, constitutionally or otherwise, than other commonwealth states including our own. This is a backward step. I do not suppose it was a deliberate step toward colonialism. It reminds me so much of Mackenzie King's suggestion that the British government should intervene in 1926, just shortly before he went all over the country on the phony constitutional issue.
Where in the seventh report of this committee do we remember the work of Borden, do we remember the great commonwealth conferences in which Canada took the lead, do we remember Meighen, do we remember the Statute of Westminster, do we recall that throughout the years this country led the way within the commonwealth and, as the senior dominion, was the champion of freedom within the commonwealth in so many ways. This commonwealth is one of the greatest political institutions of modern time. If we are to have this second flag, Mr. Speaker, let it be one which has something unique in its representation of Canada's role in the commonwealth, a role of which we can be very proud. Someone said earlier today that we used only the union jack in this country until 1945. This was not the case. The ensign was used in this country long before 1945. My colleague from Calgary North (Mr. Hark-ness), during his participation in the earlier debate, showed a poster used by Sir John A. Macdonald in 1891. The slogan then was, "The old flag, the old policy and the old leader." The flag was not the union jack, it was the red ensign in 1891. The ensign signifies not subservience, not colonialism, but it signifies independence and it signifies monarchy. It signifies, too, that the monarchy is a Canadian institution. Monarchy is not confined to the United Kingdom. When the Queen is in this realm, she is the Queen of Canada.
Canadian Flag
We have developed a unique and wonderful country here in the new world, retaining the values of the old and I hope the virtues of the old, too. If we must have our second flag, let us try to retain something which symbolizes Canada in the commonwealth.
Perhaps a more practical point, Mr. Speaker, we can predict that regardless of what the other place does in respect of the red maple leaf flag, millions of Canadians will continue to fly the Canadian red ensign for many years. Why not let the practice of these Canadians be given some official status? Do not let us in these difficult times, times which have torn a nation and wrecked parliament, exacerbate the difficulties by asking Canadians to turn in their red ensigns and buy red maple leaf flags and buy the flag of the United Kingdom at the same time. The flag of the United Kingdom is not the flag of Canada. I think it is presumptuous of us to be passing legislation relative to the flag of another great country.
If we put ourselves in a situation where, on occasions, we officially raise to the top of the flagstaff all over Canada for Canadian purposes a union jack, we have just retraced history to those days when we were a colony of Great Britain. Great Britain was a great mother country but this land, Canada, was not without its difficulties in relation to London. The stories of some of our statesmen indicate, I think, that they had to press vigorously for the kind of independence to which we were entitled. It is a meaningless and regrettable thing, after all these years, after the ensign had been sanctioned by custom and then certified by law, after the passage of years and generations, that we should move back to the flag which flew over us in colonial days. If this is to be something meaningful, this second flag, our other face to the outside world or perhaps only to the commonwealth, I hope that the government, which has in so many things been able to change its decisions and alter its directions, will accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming). As a Canadian who loves the commonwealth and admires Britain, but who is a Canadian nationalist first before being a lover of Britain, I would not want to have to vote against this report incorporating, for Canadian purposes, the flag of another country. I do not think this is an exercise any of us would wish to engage in, and the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), in the wisdom and good judgment which he always brings to public matters, has provided an

Canadian Flag
opportunity for unanimity on this matter at least.
Heaven knows, we have had enough trouble over the first flag. Let us be sensible about the second. Let us underscore our history a bit. Let us not do that which those in future generations will consider a bit ridiculous and wonder how the champions of independence within the commonwealth should, in 1964 or 1965, suddenly decide to go back to a flag of their colonial past, to take from one of the members of the commonwealth its flag and make it, for peculiar and limited occasions, our flag.
This thing is going to be difficult to rationalize. I do not know who suggested it. I have not the slightest idea who has the power in the Liberal party. I do not particularly care, but I have an idea that it might be from a part of the country that has not had the long tradition of dominion development that Canada as a whole has had.
I do not want to speak with partisanship but I say this is a great mistake. It is a backward step. It is one which will embarrass many of us today and the whole country tomorrow. I would commend to the house and the government the sensible, soundly historically based amendment of my colleague from Victoria-Carleton.

"Contrat d'adhcsinn": A contract where all the terms are set out in advance by one of the contracting parties without the other parties having any say in the matter.

Therefore, membership in the commonwealth, as stated in the report of the committee, would mean entering into a contract with another country where the contract would stipulate in advance all the terms on which we, who are becoming a member, would have nothing to say.

There are none, so why should Canada do so? Are we in such a hurry to give ourselves this flag in anticipation, now that we have decided to have one, whereas, since confederation, we Canadians have been refused a distinctive national flag?
Mr. Speaker, what are the other countries which, under the same circumstances, and through parliament, had members who are responsible to the people vote in favour of a flag as a symbol of their membership in the commonwealth? There are none.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the union jack is not the flag of the commonwealth and has never been. It has always been the flag of England, the flag of the British empire, but it is not the flag of the commonwealth. On the other hand, the Prime Minister admitted himself that it is not the Queen's flag, but the flag of royalty. Every attempt was made to make us Canadians distinguish between the Queen of England and the Queen of Canada, in order that we should accept the latter.
Today they want us to assimilate British royalty with Canadian royalty, in order to have us adopt the union jack. They have always tried to make two different things out of Queen Elizabeth II: on the one hand, she was the Queen of England, and on the other hand, the Queen of Canada. I even recall that, to make us understand, they tried to compare her to the Holy Trinity: only one God, but three persons, three distinct persons. We were told, I do not know for how long, that she was the Queen of England, but not the Queen of Canada; that it could be the same person, but not the Queen of Canada; that those were definitely two different things.
And now, today, they would have us accept once and for all what they have always maintained in Ottawa: this royalty united into one person, the Queen of England and the Queen of Canada, the same royalty. They then go on to say that, since the union jack represents the flag of royalty, we must have the union jack in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, when we took the oath of allegiance, it was to the Queen of Canada and not to the Queen of England that we pledged our loyalty, so that should a conflict arise between the various countries of the commonwealth, should we have to fight one against

Well, we no longer accept it.

The United States did not, at the same time, impose their flag upon the United Nations; the latter chose a truly distinctive flag. Today we are asked to approve the British flag to symbolize Canada's "appurtenance" to the commonwealth.
Several Liberal members, and especially those from the province of Quebec, will admit that I am perfectly right.
This afternoon we heard the Prime Minister of Canada quoting Bona Arsenault to add weight to his thesis; I must say that, at that point, he could not rise to the occasion if he had to resort to Bona "la pitoune" Arsenault, of Quebec. His argument must have been very weak indeed if he had to quote him. If he can quote that passage, why then does he not accept his statement according to which the C.B.C., in Montreal, is infiltrated with communists? Oh. No. There are protests among the members of the Liberal party, because Bona Arsenault is a man who changes his mind as often as he changes his shirt, and he must change his shirt quite often because he changes his mind often too. Is the Prime 
Minister so short of quotations that he feels he has to quote Mr. Bona Arsenault? I would say, therefore, that his argument is very weak indeed and even sophisticated.
I never heard such a series of sophisms as I heard this afternoon to try and make us adopt this flag. We have been told: It is the flag of royalty; the Queen is the head of the commonwealth, therefore, we choose the union jack.
On the other hand, it is also true that the royalty is not recognized in all the commonwealth countries. Royalty is not recognized in Ghana or in India. Yet, the Queen is recognized as head of the commonwealth.
Then, Mr. Speaker, it is not the royal flag that is needed but the flag of the Queen of Canada and, in my opinion, the best flag for the Queen of Canada would be the national distinctive flag we have chosen yesterday, as it will be the one that will really symbolize royalty in Canada.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me a question?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have but ten minutes left.
Time has come for Canada to assert herself in the world. A year ago I found out at the United Nations that the Prime Minister was not treated like a chief of state but rather like a servant in the United Nations because, as we were told, only the chiefs of states are entitled to a special seat. But the Prime Minister was not entitled to the "blue seat treatment", since the chief of state of Canada is the Queen of England. Then, let us give the Prime Minister of Canada an opportunity to become the real head of state of Canada and to be considered as such at the United Nations.
Mr. Speaker, for all these reasons, because we believe we are perhaps the most Canadian of the Canadians, we object to the union jack becoming the symbol of the commonwealth, as well as to the red ensign. When the commonwealth chooses a flag accepted by all the countries in the commonwealth, then we shall accept it, not by a vote in this house, but by custom, and that will be all. Until then, we accept only one national distinctive flag, namely the one we chose yesterday, the maple leaf flag, and we shall accept no other, let alone the flags of other countries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
May I be permitted to call attention to the ceremony that took place this afternoon on parliament hill when a good many people, under the patronage of the Societe historique de Boucherville, paid tribute to two great Canadians, the Hon. Robert Baldwin and Sir Louis-Hyppolyte Lafontaine.
Sir Louis-Hyppolyte Lafontaine died 100 years ago, and it was 50 years ago this year that a joint monument was erected on parliament hill to those two great politicians.
Mr. Speaker, we could not let this occasion pass without recalling that Sir Louis-Hyppolyte Lafontaine and the Hon. Robert Baldwin were those who made the strongest stand to obtain for us what is called today a responsible government.
One could recall also that the first step taken by Lafontaine on entering parliament was to make a speech in French to ask for equal status for the French language in parliament. If, today, we can make speeches in our mother tongue in this house, we owe it to Lafontaine and Baldwin.

speechtext: Has any penitentiary employee been provided with a blackjack or other similar truncheon, club, or weapon and, if so, in which penitentiaries were such weapons so provided, in which areas in each such penitentiary, and has any such employee ever had occasion to use such a weapon and, if so, what are the details thereof?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliameniary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PENITENTIARY EMPLOYEES PROVIDED WITH WEAPONS
speechtext:
1. Custodial officers of the Canadian penitentiary service were issued with regulation billies at the following penitentiaries: Dorchester penitentiary; St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary; Manitoba penitentiary; Saskatchewan penitentiary; British Columbia penitentiary.
2.	Such weapons were provided for employment in areas as follows: (a) Dorchester penitentiary, to the officers assigned to the dissociation and segregation areas (b) St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, to the officers assigned to the dissociation and segregation areas (c) Manitoba penitentiary, to the officer assigned to the dissociation area (d) Saskatchewan penitentiary, to the officers patrolling ranges after the closing of the prison (e) British Columbia penitentiary, to all custodial officers employed at the penitentiary.
3.	Custodial officers had the occasion to use such a weapon under the circumstances described hereunder:
(a)	Dorchester penitentiary, there has only been one such incident during the course of the last year. Two inmates were exercising in the dissociation area, when they began to fight with one another. The officer supervising the exercise attempted to intervene and break up the fight whereupon one inmate turned on the officer and attempted to attack him. The officer drew his billy and struck the inmate one blow. The inmate desisted immediately. The injury was not serious, the inmate did not require hospitalization and received immediate first aid to a slight cut on the back of the head.
(b)	St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, on one evening in 1963, in cell block No. 1, one inmate set fire in his mattress and cell equipment. The three officers on duty went to remove him from his cell as the inmate appeared to be unconscious. The officers carried the inmate to a table, and while two officers were looking for the stretcher in the same building, the inmate suddenly stood up and attacked the third officer, reaching for his neck or his face. One of the two first officers came back rapidly and used his billy on the inmate's head.

The blow was sufficient to stop the attack, however, the inmate was not unconscious. He was escorted to the hospital for check-up. He was not seriously hurt.
On another occasion in 1962, two inmates returning from the exercise period attacked the three guards escorting them and five other inmates to the isolation cells. One guard was hit on the head, suffering a serious cut which kept him away from work for a period of two months. Another guard suffered a broken right hand.
The guards were not able to reach their billy and one of them had to use a shovel to free the guard who had been hit on the head. These two inmates had attacked the officers by using one bench and one brush handle and were inciting the five other inmates to participate, in order to take hold of that building. These inmates were sent to the criminal court and were sentenced to one year consecutive.
4.	In all other cases of attacks by inmates against custodial personnel, such attacks numbering to 23 since 1962, the guards have used their bare hands to overcome inmates using knives, crowbars, soft drink bottles or broken pieces of furniture. Nineteen officers have suffered injuries, varying from slight contusions to 100 per cent permanent disability confirmed by the provincial labour department work accidents compensation board.

subtopic: CONTRACT OF C.N.R. PRESIDENT
speechtext: Pursuant to the provisions of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act 1936 (later amended by Canadian National Railways Act 1955), Mr. Donald Gordon was appointed president of the Canadian National Railway Company by its board of directors, such appointment being approved by the governor in council, effective January 1, 1950. The appointment is not for any specified term, but in accordance with the statutes the chief executive officer holds office "during the pleasure of the directors". subtopic: DEATH OF MAPLE TREES
DEATH OF MAPLE TREES
speechtext:
1.	Has the government any statistics respecting the dying of maple trees during the past several years?
2.	Has any study been undertaken to counteract maple decline and, if so, with what results?

subtopic: DEATH OF MAPLE TREES
speechtext:
1.	A conspicuous dieback of maples has occurred in recent years throughout southern Ontario. Sample plots have been under surveillance for several years by the Department of Forestry and these show that the condition is restricted to exposed trees along highways, secondary roads, and streets in urban areas and does not extend into natural stands of maple. The severity of dieback varies from year to year and between areas but observations in 1964 show that a high proportion of the roadside trees are in various stages of decline at locations in the lake Erie, lake-Huron, Lindsay, and Tweed forest districts.

2.	Studies to date indicate that a number of factors are involved including: drought, chemicals used along highways to control dust, ice, and weeds; low winter temperatures when there is deficient snow cover; and the age of trees. Studies are in progress to determine the relative importance of these factors. Once this is established, appropriate means of prevention or treatment can be developed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: EFFECT OF INSECTICIDE PHOSPHAMIDON ON WILDLIFE
speechtext:
1. Yes, Dr. C. D. Fowle, head, department of biology, York University, Toronto, carried out surveys for the Canadian wildlife service on the use of phosphamidon in New Brunswick in 1964. Dr. Fowle has submitted a preliminary report, the contents of which were presented to the interdepartmental committee on forest spraying operations on October 27.
2.	The data obtained by Dr. Fowle indicated a marked reduction in bird song and activity and in numbers of birds seen following the spraying of phosphamidon at the rate of one half pound per three quarters of a United States gallon per acre. Numbers of dead and sick birds were found by the investigators as well as by residents of the area; however, some of the sick birds recovered.
3.	The government regarded the use of phosphamidon in 1964 as experimental. Results of the 1964 experiments suggest that phosphamidon applied at the lesser rate of one quarter pound per three quarters of a United States gallon per acre or phosphamidon plus a penetrant applied at one half pound per acre do not seriously affect bird or fish populations. The governmental agencies responsible for assessing the effects of forest spraying operations in New Brunswick are presently considering the 1965 program; however, no decision has yet been made.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DRUG MANUFACTURING COMPANIES
ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DRUG MANUFACTURING COMPANIES
speechtext:
Do regulations administered by the food and drug directorate of the Department of National [Mr. Deschatelets.l
Health and Welfare, the Department of Industry or any other federal agency control the establishment of new drug manufacturing companies and the sale of their products and, if not, is consideration being given to the inauguration of a licensing system making the registration of such firms mandatory?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DRUG MANUFACTURING COMPANIES
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Industry is concerned there are no regulations that control the establishment of new drug manufacturing companies or the sale of their products and the department is not aware of such regulations administered by other federal agencies. No consideration is being given by the Department of Industry at the present time to the inauguration of a licensing system.
There are no regulations administered by the food and drug directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare which control the establishment of new drug manufacturing companies. However, drug manufacturing facilities and control, as well as the drug products, are subject to the requirements of the Food and Drugs Act and regulations. Certain injectables, such as liver extract injectable and insulin, listed in schedule C to the Food and Drugs Act, and other products such as living vaccines for oral or parenteral use and antibiotics for parenteral use, listed in schedule D to the Food and Drugs Act, may only be manufactured by the manufacturer to whom a licence has been issued.
Consideration is being given to a system under which it would be mandatory for all pharmaceutical manufacturers to supply the food and drug directorate with a list of all the drug products which they manufacture.

We are now considering the motion for the adoption of the final report of the flag committee constituted by unanimous decision of the house. Mr. Speaker, in spite of the Conservative amendment, I believe we should ask ourselves two questions:
1.	Does our country need this second standard, emblem or symbol of our membership in the commonwealth of nations and our fidelity to the Queen of Canada?
2.	Would the union jack or the red ensign or something else be a more proper symbol?
The first spontaneous reaction of many people is to ask why we should consider the adoption of a second flag now that we are on the verge of having a distinctive national flag, particularly in view of the following facts.
Canada is recognized as a self-governing and independent country and we are steadily on the way to achieving nationhood; our central government, in co-operation with the ten provincial governments, has agreed upon a formula to amend our Canadian constitution, a fact which should soon lead to its repatriation; and, with the growing pains we are going through at the present time, we witnessed the development of a Canadian spirit
which a better dialogue, at the federal-provincial level, has definitely promoted.
In short, we become better Canadians, we are more concerned with the future of our country, with Canadian unity, without for all that forgetting our origins, even though they have much less importance in this country.
I would venture here to quote from two articles published in the Montreal Star on December 15. First, here is the conclusion of an editorial headed: "Enough is Enough". I quote:

What this country has wanted is a flag. The particular design was not that important. What it has got after 97 years is a flag, and we should be proud of it. A new generation with new ideas has taken over. Mr. Pearson has shown himself a contemporary figure.

The second item is by Peter Newman, of the same newspaper. It is headed: "Transfer of Power", and I quote:

The debate which marked a turning point in the evolution of our nationhood: The transfer of power from one generation of Canadians to the next.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose that to all intents and purposes we

should be celebrating the birth of our new flag. Now that some of the dust has settled and the house has returned to a more friendly frame of mind, I wish to say that I think we have a flag, a distinctive Canadian flag; and as I promised in six earlier speeches, that new flag will have my unqualified support.
It has never been my practice to stand up one day and recommend something, and then overnight change my mind. I hope I will not be considered as being stubborn or narrowminded. I believe in principle; I believe in being consistent, and I shall try to be consistent today. I am one of those who have always believed that one country needs only one flag. But of course I am here to represent the great district of Athabasca and to vote yea or nay on every subject that comes before the house.
I should like always to be able to decide between right and wrong. I would like to have clearcut principles, but on this subject I find the question proposed to me is something like this; which of your brothers would you like to murder, your brother Ted or your brother Walter? I do not believe in fratricide; therefore I cannot say which of my brothers I prefer to murder. As I am a lawyer some people may say this is legal jargon, and if they wish it explained I shall relate it to the question before the house; which of two designs, among second flags, do I want? The answer to that is very plain.
For this great country of ours, this young and virile nation, we need only one flag, but I am forced by principle to vote yea or nay between two designs which I do not want, now that the main question has been settled. How does a man vote on principle when he is presented with this problem? I shall vote when the time comes, but first I believe we are here to discuss the principles behind the whole issue.
As I have said, I accept the new national flag. I hope every citizen in Canada will rally to it whenever their services are needed. Here again I will be consistent. I have tried to serve the glorious old red ensign well, and I shall try to serve Canada under this new flag so long as I draw breath. But that is not the problem before us today. We are forced to vote on a two flag proposition, no matter what you call it. You may call it a one flag proposition if you like, but we are asked to sanctify or give legal acceptance to a second flag proposed by those very people who said the new national flag would be so representative of the whole nation, would be so distinctive that no person in the world could
Canadian Commonwealth Flag possibly make a mistake when seeing it flying at the mastheads of our ships, painted on the fuselages of our airplanes, or waved by children on parade.
I hope this is so. I hope that as the years go by the citizens of Canada, men and women, young and old, will serve this new flag with the same distinction with which they served the old one, until 100 years from now it will be truly loved and revered, not as a mere empty act of parliament but as one of the symbols of our nation.
I have never criticized the maple leaf as a symbol of Canadian unity, but I have asked that we recognize those other symbols of our past. There are some people who scream to get rid of anything British. I am not thinking of anyone in particular, but it has been said in this house that all vestiges of British colonialism must disappear. I happen to be of British blood. I have a great respect for British justice and their sense of fair play, and even for their colonialism which is classed as the finest the world has ever seen. No other empire in the history of the world gave so much of its strength and brains to develop other countries and set them free.
After Canadians showed in no uncertain fashion on the battlefields of Europe, particularly in world war I, that they had grown up, the old lion was mighty proud of her cub. Punch magazine of that day produced a wonderful cartoon showing the old lion lying inside her cave watching this great, mighty young lion striding forth to become independent and free. At no time in history has the mother of parliaments denied those necessary, and perhaps slow, steps required to bring a colony to nationhood. This is why I revere the British flag. I also revere it because it is something more than a mere symbol of empire. As has been said in this house on numerous occasions the flag of Britain, the noble union jack, is nothing more or less than the combination of three great Christian crosses.
I disagree with those who say we should do away with all that is old and revered just to have something new. There is no education without history, without rehearsing the folklore, the poetry and the great literature of our forefathers, both French and English. We said that we wished to retain in our Canadian flag those vestiges of our past. We did this in no small way. We did this in no petty, partisan way. We had a free vote, at least in the party to which I belong. I am not here to cast aspersions on any other party. We are a positive party. We are a building party. We do not recommend anything in this party of

Canadian Commonwealth Flag ours which in any way tears down the achievements or the beliefs of any other people. We oppose that which is negative but we do not turn down anything that is positive. We are the builders, and now that we have a new flag I appeal to each and every hon. member to put away any acrimonious feelings which may have been felt and to build for the future. Let us have a new dynamic program of building in Canada. Let us eliminate poverty in Canada. When I say we have a new flag, I wish something more to go with that flag. There should be real equality in this country-equality for every man, woman and child, economically as well as in matters concerning religion and race. This is a program we must carry out. I do not expect we shall have to resort to socialism or anything connected with it in order to put this program forward.
I come from a race of pioneers, from a race of adventurers-gamblers, if you will, if you call it gambling to get into a leaky ship, cross 3,000 miles of stormy sea and walk into the bush with nothing but a gun and an axe. I do not think that spirit is dead in Canada. That is why I am able to accept this maple leaf flag as a symbol of those who stepped out into the hardwood forests of Ontario as pioneers and settlers. When pioneering in the east was finished, my grandfather went further west. When my grandfather was at Lac la Biche the flag which flew over his fort looked a great deal like the Canadian red ensign though, in fact, it had the letters H.B.C. in the corner. He was law and order. He was priest, educator, businessman. He was everything in that part of the country. And he did not hold his position because the people were afraid of him. At the time of the rebellion they allowed him to walk out unscathed because he was a man of honour. These same native people loved our red ensign and I am sure that in time they will learn to love the maple leaf flag. If necessary, they will fight for it as they did for the red ensign in three great wars. I am going out to sell them the idea of Canadian unity. But even more important than this idea of Canadian unity I should like to bring them economic equality and economic freedom so that they will no longer be mere wards of the government; so that each and every one may grasp the one thing which, I hope, our race has given them-the idea that a man can stand on his own two feet and make his way in the world. Then, I hope, they will be willing to fight, if necessary, for all those things
TMr. Bigg.]
which a generous nation has put within their grasp.
We cannot call ourselves generous today. Yes, we can pat ourselves on the back and say we have seen the birth of a new flag. But that new flag is like a child, innocent of reputation. Let it not be a foundling child. If members opposite believe in it-and they have commended it, if only by their silence- let them work to establish it. I should not say they did not have the opportunity of a free vote. I would hate to think any Canadian would do anything at any time to prevent his voting freely on such a subject. It took us 2,000 years to get this free vote and I will be the last to suggest that any member of the party opposite would dare give up this heritage. If he did, the men who died at Vimy Ridge and in the battle of Britain must have died in vain. Even now they speak to us when they say:
To you from failing hands we throw The torch; be yours to hold it high.
If ye break faith with us who die We shall not sleep, though poppies grow In Flanders fields.
These are words which should not be forgotten. This is part of our British heritage.
I do not think it is necessary to fly any flag alongside this new democratic flag we have chosen to prove that we are, in fact, a nation, or to prove that each and every one of us is dedicated to that new nation. If the introduction of this new flag, the one and only symbol of our national pride, represents Canada's birthday, let us not sully it by pretending it needs to be bolstered up. Surely those who wanted a distinctive flag should be the first to say, now that we have a distinctive flag: The House of Commons voted on this flag, and now we have it. I who come of British stock will be the first to say we need not shore it up except with our devotion, our acts and our imagination. We shall go forward and build in the northern half of the North American continent the greatest nation which ever flew any flag.
Some say we need this second flag to show equality in the commonwealth. We do not need any flag to show equality in the commonwealth. The nations of the commonwealth look to Canada for leadership. All through the years they have looked to us for leadership and we have shown that leadership. This is why we are not afraid, now, to launch out on our own; this is why we have cut the umbilical cord. This is why we now have a Queen of our own, and she is a Queen of our own choosing. We are not trammelled

here. Any person in this house can preach in favour of a republic if he wishes. But I will not; I will be consistent in that. Australia and New Zealand know that we are first among equals. That is a good phrase. That is what Canada is in a position of leadership within the commonwealth; she has never asked for a special place but she has earned a place in front because she is marching down that great road at the end of which all men will have equality, dignity and those economic advantages which we ourselves have found in this land of ours. Let us have no more talk about marking our association with the commonwealth by a flag.
We had a beautiful and distinctive one, in my opinion; and if you will bear with me, Mr. Speaker, because I do not see any other occasion on which I could say this, I have a suggestion to make with regard to it. I think that one of these days, perhaps Vimy day or on July 1, 1965 we should set aside the whole day to honouring this great red ensign of ours and to honouring the boys who served it so well. I would suggest that our great Governor General, General Vanier, should be given the privilege of laying our red ensign where it belongs-in the peace tower, where the names of those who gave their lives are graved in stone or written in letters of gold. As long as one stone stands on another and as long as we honour these men the flag will remain there as a lasting tribute to their love and devotion-the great old flag they served so well.
If we are to have a flag to show we are a member of the commonwealth, why not a special flag to show we are a member of NATO? I think the members of NATO know Canadians will be there, should the defence of western Europe make it necessary. Why should we not be asked to approve a special flag to show our membership in the United Nations? I may say that had I been in the committee which was concerned with choosing a flag I might well have suggested designs which would have shown our devotion to the United Nations-I do not know whether any were put forward or not. I think our contribution in money and in devotion to the idea of one united world might well require that we take the lead and incorporate in a new flag the United Nations banner and, in this way, let Canada be the first to recognize the brotherhood of man. But we have chosen otherwise in democratic conclave, in committee meetings. I have never been of the opinion that a committee was the best way of proceeding. I would much have pre-
Canadian Commonwealth Flag ferred that we should have discussed this matter for as long a time as was necessary and then come to a conclusion in the house. I cannot understand how we could expect 15 men chosen by parties to sit behind closed doors and decide something which we could not decide here. Nevertheless, the committee did come up with this report. We have had a debate in the house, and we have a new flag. Surely, if we thought a committee could do it, we must say they have done it.
They have made that decision. We abdicated our decision to that committee and they came out with a report and gave us a flag. They must have given us a distinctive flag, a flag to serve under and love, and one which requires no bolstering up. I am quite sure this is what the committee intended to do, because the first time the question was raised they voted 14 to 0 for this very proposition. I am not going into the motives behind their change of heart but I suggest that on that occasion they showed their true principle, which is the principle that I suggest again should lie behind this whole question.
I must get back to the proposition before us, Mr. Speaker. The amendment is, of course, a method of trying to get a little more reason out of what I consider to be an entirely impossible proposal, namely that we should have two flags. However, if we must have two flags and are back again between the devil and the deep blue sea, I suggest that the red ensign of Canada is far and away ahead of any other flag, if we must have a second, distinctive flag for our country. I am going to have to vote, and I am quite sure the people of Athabasca want me to vote on this question; they want it settled as quickly as possible. However, we cannot settle things as important as this as quickly as some people may desire, because every member of this house certainly has as much right to speak on the subject as I have. I do not think I am trying to make cloth out of old rope; I am trying to be positive. I suggest that nothing can be gained by weakening the position of our new flag and it is my hope that when I try and celebrate, as I hope to do, the new flag for our great nation we shall not be torn between that flag and a second choice of any kind. I am sure many hon. members will vote in favour of the red ensign as a second flag-I know members on both sides of the house are going to do so- but this will only be Hobson's choice.

Canadian Commonwealth Flag
I have great respect for those sections of the country which have a particular love for the old union jack. Newfoundland has not been long in the dominion, just since 1949. I hope that the way we have treated Newfoundland is appreciated and understood. We have offered them full partnership in our family. I believe nobody will deny that we have tried to be generous to them. I think we can appeal to the people of Newfoundland and say that if they feel wounded because we have turned down the idea of a secondary flag, it is because we have tried to build this country of ours into a great, united nation. I know that when the people of Newfoundland get together with those people in Canada who are not of British stock they will love them as I do, and will not forget their British heritage but will put this question in its proper perspective and put Canada first. Let us put our sentimental attachments, our family devotion, on one side and put Canada first, not only today but for ever.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman).

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to rise today to speak on behalf of the red ensign as a symbol of Canada's relationship with the commonwealth. I would like to take a moment to express my appreciation to the voters of Waterloo South for having accorded me the honour of electing me to the House of Commons as their representative. I would also like to take this opportunity of expressing my appreciation to all members of the house for their very kind and friendly reception. I hope it may continue.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am also extremely proud that I have been here on an historic occasion and one which will no doubt be long remembered by Canadians. I think the decision this house has made will be remembered long after the bitterness is forgotten. I am very proud to have participated in voting for the new Canadian flag. I think it is a good flag. Like most people, when I first saw it my feelings for the red ensign obscured the affection I might have had for the new flag; but every day as I look at it, it becomes more vital, it becomes stronger. I can see a united Canada in this flag and I am pleased and proud to have been able to vote for it.
[Mr. Bigg.)

Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, Waterloo South is an English speaking riding. It has very strong United Empire Loyalist roots; its people are proud and hard working; it is the home of the Highland Light Infantry of Canada, a great regiment with many battle honours; it has four branches of the Canadian Legion, all of them doing extremely well; and it is proud of the red ensign. I have followed this debate with great interest and great emotion, as hon. members will understand. I have spoken to many people in Waterloo South about the flag, and their feelings regarding it. I think the people in Waterloo South recognized very early that Canada needed a new flag, a flag that would not be hyphenated, a flag that would not say "French Canada", "English Canada" or any other Canada, but only one Canada. I believe this parliament has accomplished that; we now have that flag.
The people in Waterloo South could have waited for a flag. They could have waited, because they were most reluctant to transfer their loyalty from the ensign that they love to another flag which they will learn to love. But I think it should be recognized by many of the members of this house that we could have waited. There are other members of this house who could not wait. We recognized that fact and as good Canadians we said they had real, just grievances and we were prepared to meet those grievances. I refer to the grievances of French Canada. I believe we have shown our willingness to do this. We now ask those French Canadian members of this house to recognize, much as we understood their feelings and the justice of their cause, that we have very strong and real feelings for the ensign.
We have heard them say that if another flag is necessary and there was a flag representing the world, this is the flag we should accept and honour rather than one which only recognizes our commonwealth relationships. When that day comes and that flag is ready to be accepted, a flag that represents the brotherhood of man, the universality of all people, I will be one of the first to vote for it if I am fortunate enough to be here. But until we reach that point it must be recognized that we do have a flag that means a great deal to us, a flag we have given up voluntarily on behalf of Canadian unity. I think that flag should be retained in our affection and on our flagpoles as a symbol and sign of our relationship with the British commonwealth.

It is my opinion and my feeling, and I think the feeling of many members of this house who voted on this matter, that if the red ensign is retained as a symbol of our relationship with the commonwealth, that connection with the past will go a long way toward recognizing and accepting the new flag. I would ask whether those members in this house who were so willing to ask for a new flag-and I was one of them-would be equally as willing to recognize the affection in which we hold the red ensign? If they are, then when the vote comes they will have an opportunity to heal the wounds, and we may yet reach a unanimous decision on the retention of the red ensign.
