I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, it would not. Our members who are away today want to vote on the amendment which we proposed yesterday; that is the point I am making. We were prepared to do this last night, but as I mentioned, last night there were two members of the Liberal party who were anxious to get the floor, which happened to be given to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). So I just wanted to make it clear, in view of all the accusations that we have had over weeks and months that we are trying to delay the business of the house, that that is not the case, and it is

Canadian Commonwealth Flag certainly not the case today. I want that thoroughly understood. However, this does not hinder me from discussing the present situation, the work of the committee, the report it made, and some other matters which I will deal with as I go along.
I notice that in its seventh report-and this has been dealt with by others-the committee started off with the proposition that the second flag to be proposed for Canada should be the Canadian red ensign. Last night the information was given to us that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deach-man) proposed that motion in the committee. Certainly as far as our members on that committee were concerned, if there had to be a second flag this is the one they favoured. Then along came the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) and reversed the position by putting before the committee an amendment which is almost word for word the resolution on the order paper which was put there six months ago. So the committee was put right back in the position which the government took six months ago. The hon. member for Leeds reversed the suggestion of his colleague for Vancouver Quadra.
Our committee representative, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), explained the position of our members on that committee and why they abstained from voting. First of all, they were of the opinion that only one flag was to be chosen. Second, when it became evident that the committee was not going along with that idea but was going to propose a second flag, they said this was just ridiculous and they were not participating in that vote in the committee. I thought that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was unfair to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton in ridiculing him the other night, or yesterday, when the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton was explaining his position as of the present moment, as contrasted with his position in the committee.
I ask, as members of the committee asked, what was the reason for suggesting that there should be two flags officially sanctioned by the parliament of Canada? When did we have to indicate by means of a special flag our allegiance to the crown? Have we not in all the years of Canada's history shown our allegiance to the crown by our activities both in war and in peace as citizens of this country? As members of parliament we swear allegiance to the sovereign. Must we now carry around a flag indicating that allegiance? It strikes me as being rather ridiculous.


What is the weakness in the proposed flag that does not show allegiance to the crown? There must be troubled consciences on the other side of the house in the Liberal party in that they must realize that the flag which they proposed and which at this present moment has not been accepted as the national flag of Canada shows only allegiance to the Liberal party. That is all it shows at the present time. It has not been accepted by parliament. It has not been authorized by the crown.

speechtext:
-by the Liberal party shielding behind the committee has serious weaknesses. It does not show, according to the Liberal party, our allegiance to the crown. It does not show our membership in the commonwealth. I say it is not even distinctive because it closely resembles the flag of Peru with the colours red, white and red. The main difference is that the proposed Liberal flag has a larger expanse of white, but at a distance it will be hard to distinguish it from the flag of Peru. So it is not distinctive. The great search for a distinctive flag has failed. At a distance the maple leaf will not show up any more clearly than the coat of arms or diagram on the Peruvian flag.
It is much less distinctive than the present Canadian national flag, the Canadian red ensign. In the United Nations, in NATO, in the commonwealth, where flags are flown and where it counts to have a distinctive flag, the 20220-7111
Canadian Commonwealth Flag Canadian red ensign is unmistakably Canadian. It spells out the word "Canada" which we have heard about from the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) and from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). The message of Canada is spelled out right now by the present Canadian red ensign. You can examine the flags of those nations in the commonwealth, in NATO and in the United Nations and you will see that is true and that it cannot be mistaken. It stands out very clearly.
I suggest that because of these weaknesses in the flag proposed and forced on this country by the Liberal party they have tried to come up with something else that will satisfy various elements in this country, and they are suggesting to us in the seventh report of the committee that we have a second flag. The committee is suggesting that that flag should be the union jack and we are suggesting that it should be the Canadian red ensign. We would have preferred to have a flag chosen for Canada that would have incorporated the very emblem which the Liberal party now says must be shown somehow or other in Canada, namely the union jack. We would have preferred that. We wanted a flag that represented something of our history and our traditions. We wanted the union jack on it. We also wanted the fleur-de-lis and the maple leaf on it, and we have said so time and time again. If such a flag had been proposed we would not now require a second flag to show our membership in the commonwealth or our allegiance to the crown, or another flag that would convey some other meaning. But our suggestions were not accepted.
As I mentioned in an earlier speech, and I am not going to repeat what I said, we were wrong. I admitted I was wrong, along with hundreds of thousands of people in Canada, in thinking that a compromise was possible incorporating the symbols of our past history. This was the initial mistake that we made months ago. This initial mistake was carried on right down through the work of the committee. I sympathize with our members who were on that committee because they conscientiously and seriously thought that a compromise could be effected incorporating the union jack and the fleur-de-lis, as well as the maple leaf, in our flag.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is a rather sad period in our history when we have to consider two flags for this country because the flag proposed by the Liberal party fails in its purpose. We have to select another flag for the reasons they have advanced. We would have preferred, as I said, one flag;

Canadian Commonwealth Flag but faced in the house with this juggernaut of the Liberal party supported by their associates, chiefly the Creditistes, we find ourselves in a situation where another flag is going to be selected by the House of Commons. Under those circumstances, then, we have to make a choice. Our choice is the preservation of the Canadian red ensign. This is the reason our amendment has been placed before the House of Commons.
I noticed that when the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) was talking, he quoted from some newspaper or other to the effect that the particular design of the flag is not of importance. This is Creditiste doctrine: Anything at all on the flag; it does not matter what is on the flag. I am surprised that the hon. member who spoke a little while ago should have quoted with approval that sentiment from some newspaper or other. Then he talked about the emergence of a new generation. I do not know which generation the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) represents. He represents an older generation than the one to which I belong. Is he a member of the new generation that is going to be in evidence in Canada now for the next 30 years? I think not. However, we hear from the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry that a new generation is now taking over. Well, who is leading this new generation-the Prime Minister of Canada? When I belonged, many years ago, to the new generation a person of his age appeared to me to be very senior indeed.
I suggest, sir, that we are going to be in difficulty in the future with regard to the two flags. Where are they to be flown? Are they to fly conjointly? What flag will be on the peace tower? Is it to be this new flag imposed by force on the Canadian people? Will we see the Canadian red ensign pulled down from the peace tower and this other flag run up which has not behind it the majority opinion in this country? The Prime Minister has said, and I could quote his exact words, that the majority of the people in this country favour a new flag. He said, as recorded on page 11148 of Hansard, that he believed the majority of Canadians wished to have a Canadian national flag which could not be mistaken for the flag of any other country. Then he picks one that looks like the flag of Peru. How does he know the majority of Canadians want this flag? Nobody knows that. We have not had an opportunity to find out, and that is the very thing to which I object. Do the majority of the people in

this country want the Canadian red ensign pulled down from the peace tower, the greatest shrine that we have in this country? This is a shrine to which hundreds of thousands of visitors come every summer as we have seen, year after year. Every public building in this country will have the Canadian red ensign pulled down, I suppose. I do not know what will be done with regard to the schools, province by province. I do not know what will be done in the court rooms of this country. What will be done in the citizenship courts? The red ensign comes down, does it, and perhaps the new flag will be put up in its place?
What happens in so many of our churches in this country in which we have deposited Canadian flags of another era representing the sacrifices of the people in wartime? Are those flags to be taken down now and replaced by this new flag? Well, the ramifications of this are not known yet to the Canadian people. We have never been a flag conscious people. We have not been saluting our flag every day. Now we are becoming flag conscious and we are going to be confused with the multiplicity of flags in this country.
I have been distressed during the course of this debate by the evident intent of the Liberal party to destroy the red ensign. I have been distressed by the references we have heard from some corners of this house to the fact that we, in the Conservative party, are not real Canadians. The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire)-I regret that he is not here, although if he were I would be interrupted every other minute-stated the other day, as recorded on page 11186 of Hansard, that they are perhaps the most Canadian of Canadians. We have had suggestions from that corner of the house that just because members of the Conservative party have supported the Canadian red ensign they were not true Canadians. We, they say, are second class citizens and represent a declining minority in this house. This is the position in which we have been placed because we have fought the proposal of the Liberal party.
Now, I do not know how you determine between a real and an unreal Canadian. I do not know why the member for Lapointe and his friends consider they are more Canadian than we are. How do you become this? I thought we were attempting to recognize in this country that there was no distinction among Canadians by race, class or creed or anything else. I thought we were

all Canadians, all honouring our country, all anxious to work tor the benefit of our country and all of us honouring the crown. Why do we have to be divided into first class citizens and second class citizens? The hon. member for Lapointe and some others are going to find it very difficult indeed to relegate us to an inferior position. We will do our part, as we have done in the past, for Canada.
There has been a great deal of bitterness in the course of this debate. We are asked to forgive and forget. We saw the spectacle just the other day-though it seems longer it was only on Tuesday morning-of the Prime Minister asking not to have a vote, to all join together in favour of the flag which his party put out.

I did not think I was reflecting on the vote, Mr. Speaker. I have known nothing in the history of the world that corresponds to this action-the imposition of a flag on a country without the will of the people behind it. This has only been done by a foreign conqueror. speechtext:
Before addressing myself directly to the question before us I should like to refer to the remarks made by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman) who spoke effectively, briefly and from the heart in a way which moved us all. I am sure the good wishes of all members of the house go to this new representative of an historic riding.
My friend the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) during his speech a little earlier in this debate talked about consistency. I would point out that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and a number of us who had the privilege of serving on the flag committee like to think that we have in fact been consistent. A number of years ago it was the policy of the Liberal party as, indeed, it was of other political parties, that a distinctive Canadian flag be adopted. During a general
Canadian Commonwealth Flag election in 1963-I am referring now to Liberal party policy-party literature was distributed in my own riding. Under the heading "Positive Canadianism" were these words:
The new Liberal government will submit to parliament a design for a flag which cannot be mistaken for the emblem of any other country.
These words also appear:
The union jack will be flown on appropriate occasions as a symbol of our membership in the commonwealth.
I would point out that in the sixth report of the flag committee we recommended the adoption of only one national flag. The vote was 14 to 0. I stress the word "national" because this word was used repeatedly in the course of our committee discussions. I think it is entirely consistent with the first purpose set out in the policy of the Liberal party-namely that we adopt a flag which cannot be mistaken for the emblem of any other country; in other words, a distinctive national flag.
Subsequently in the flag committee there was a motion to the effect that the government be authorized to take such steps as might be necessary to provide that the Canadian red ensign may continue to be flown as a symbol of Canada's membership in the commonwealth and of our allegiance to the crown. This was moved by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman). I did not share this view, and I may say that within our committee and within party groups throughout the process of the six weeks deliberation a number of different viewpoints were expressed from time to time. I myself moved an amendment substituting the words "royal union flag generally known as the union jack" for the words "Canadian red ensign". This amendment carried by a vote of 7 yeas to 2 nays with 5 abstentions-and the members of the official opposition have indicated they abstained on the vote. The motion as amended then carried by a vote of 8 yeas, 1 nay with the same 5 abstentions.
I think therefore that the position we have taken as a party and the one I have taken personally is a position which has been entirely consistent. Perhaps it would be helpful to explain why I moved an amendment against the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, to substitute the royal union flag for the suggested Canadian red ensign. I think it is clear that in the sixth committee report, the report which on Tuesday was adopted by this house in convincing

Canadian Commonwealth Flag fashion, what we did was establish a national flag clearly distinguishable from the flag of any other country. I do not pay particular attention to comments with respect to its similarities to other flags; I can assure hon. members that the committee spent six weeks considering this matter very carefully. Incidentally the design finally approved was suggested as early as March, 1964, by a former lieutenant colonel in the army, a man with seven years historical training at Oxford; he is a Canadian with an exceptional academic background.
Why would it be inappropriate at this time to approve an amendment respecting the Canadian red ensign as the flag to denote our relation with the commonwealth and with the Queen? I think it is perfectly clear we wanted one national flag, not two; and the Canadian red ensign is, after all, the "Canadian" red ensign. If we brought this flag back now all we would be doing, in effect, would be to create two national flags.
We have heard a great deal of argument, particularly from the official opposition, that two flags are a mistake. I think it would be wrong certainly to have two national flags. However, I am not against several flags for different purposes. I think that is entirely proper. The hon. member for Athabasca referred to the flag of the Hudson's Bay Company. Many old companies have their own flags. The provinces have flags, in several cases, and a number of municipal corporations have their own flags. We know there is a NATO flag which occasionally flies here in Ottawa and elsewhere over our various headquarters. And there is, of course, the United Nations flag which, I am glad to say, flies over some schools in Brockville. This is a sign of the times. Flags serve various purposes. But surely it is our purpose to have one national flag. Many years ago we obtained permission to use the red ensign by an admiralty warrant granted on the 2nd day of February 1892. I have studied the communication that was sent to Evan MacGregor by the under secretary of state, colonial office, dated February 2, 1892, where they answer the query as to whether it would be possible for a warrant to be granted empowering ships of Canadian registry to fly the red ensign of the royal navy defaced with the arms of the dominion. Although there were strong objections to any defacement of the traditional sea flag, as a result of strong representation from Canada permission was in fact granted. May I read to the house the significant words 

of the admiralty warrant of that date. It says:
Whereas we deem it expedient that Canadian registered vessels shall be permitted to wear the red ensign of Her Majesty's fleet with the Canadian coat of arms on the fly thereof.
We do therefore by virtue of the power and authority vested in us hereby warrant and authorize the red ensign of Her Majesty's fleet with the Canadian coat of arms in the fly, to be used on board vessels registered in the dominion.
Perhaps because I was raised as a boy in Quebec city and spent a good deal of time, as a young fellow, on the water I have always been led to think that the merchant service flag is a sea flag. If anybody has any doubt in this matter I suggest that they read the important text "Flags of the World" edited by H. Gresham Carr, in which he sets out the various countries of the commonwealth that use the red ensign for specifically that purpose. I am not going to take any more of the time of the house to dwell on that aspect of the matter. However, Mr. Speaker, may I raise the question as to the proprieties, in contrast to the Canadian red ensign, of using the union jack for the specific purposes which have been set out in this report. May I refer to correspondence respecting the flag to be flown on land by British subjects. A letter was written by John F. Stedman of Ebenezer, Saskatchewan, Canada, March 11, 1911, to the secretary of His Imperial Majesty, King George V, in effect asking what flag was appropriate for Canadians to fly. The answer was given by L. Harcourt in a letter addressed to His Excellency, Right Hon. Earl Grey, G.C.M.G., C.G.V.O., etc. May I read to the house the substance of the communication which came from Downing street under the date May 21, 1912. This communication is to the Governor General, His Royal Highness, the Duke of Connaught and of Strathearn, K.G., K.T., K.P. It says:
I have the honour to transmit to Your Royal Highness a copy of a letter from Mr. G. S. Hodgins in regard to the flag which should be used by private persons who are British subjects.
2. I should be glad if you would be good enough to cause Mr. Hodgins to be informed that the union flag is the national flag of Canada as of all other parts of His Majesty's dominions, and may be flown on land by all British subjects: and that the red ensign, with the arms of the dominion of Canada in the fly, is intended to be used only by Canadian merchant vessels.
X have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your Royal Highness's most obedient, humble servant,
L. Harcourt.

Perhaps my hon. friends on the opposite side will suggest that this is a little out of date, but I would point out to them that those members on the government side of the house who have been interested in this important matter for not only some weeks or months but indeed years have gone into this question rather thoroughly and have been advised by a great many authorities to which we referred that the union flag is an appropriate flag in these circumstances for any subject of Her Majesty anywhere in the commonwealth of nations. It is perfectly true, as certain hon. gentlemen have indicated, that in recent years it has become popularly thought of as the flag of the United Kingdom, but this is not legally its status.
May I give the house the view of a knowledgeable Canadian, Alan B. Beddoe, O.B.E., who served for some years as commander in the navy and has done a great deal of research on this subject. His views are expressed in this way:
In the first place, the so-called "union jack" Is actually a "royal badge", usually applied to a banner or flag, or as an "augmentation of honour" to certain coats of arms...It is today one of Her Majesty's personal badges. It is not, as is erroneously thought by many, the flag of all British people everywhere, in spite of its long and unauthorized use in this way. Since its advent on January 1, 1801, no permission has been given by the crown for the public at large to display it, except by King George V in 1933, when His late Majesty declared that the "union" might be flown publicly on the national day and on the King's birthday, the national day in this case being St. George's day and St. Andrew's day. The "union" is not the national flag of the United Kingdom, as many are prone to believe, for the simple fact is that the United Kingdom has no national flag. England has one, and Scotland, but not the U.K.
This is perhaps a purist view, but we are hearing here the opinion of a recognized authority on the matter. However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to something that has come to us under the hand of Sir Anthony Wagner, Garter, Principal King of Arms, under date May 26, 1964. After all, he is Her Majesty's highest heraldic authority; it is his responsibility to offer advice on these matters. I think that what he says here tends to confirm in general what we have read in various flag texts as, for instance, the Observer's "Book of Flags'', wherein it is stated that the union jack now is commonly used as the flag of the United Kingdom and a flag of the commonwealth of nations. Sir Anthony Wagner puts it this way:
The difference between the arms of England and the St. George's cross, or between the present
Canadian Commonwealth Flag royal standard and union flag is not a difference of ownership, but a difference in the uses to which they are applied by the sovereign to whom they alike belong.
One sometimes sees a distinction drawn in this context between the sovereign and the nation, on the lines that the royal standard is the sovereign's flag but the union the nation's. Such a distinction is alien to our constitution. For us the sovereign is the representative of the nation and the nation has and can have no flag but the sovereign's.
That is the view of Sir Anthony Wagner namely that the union flag is the flag of the sovereign. I listened carefully to my friend the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) last night and I thought he made a very logical and compelling address on this matter. I think one might reasonably contend that we do not need any symbol of commonwealth association to prove our loyalties to this commonwealth family of nations, and indeed the flag which we have selected as our national flag is a perfectly appropriate banner and will always be so regarded as an indication of the devotion of loyal Canadians, to the sovereign of Canada.
A few minutes ago we heard a respected privy councillor in this house who had served in world war I, and I believe in world war II as well, speaking feelingly with respect to symbols of the past. I am not in his age group; I am perhaps in between being old and being young. I am sure that for my children the Canadian flag alone would be quite adequate, but I believe there are many Canadians who will want this other symbol, the union jack preserved. Certainly in our churches, Legion halls and places like this there will be a great wish to preserve some precious symbol of this association which we value and treasure.
In conclusion, I would point out this interesting fact relating to flags authorized in war. On June 3, 1963, question No. 142 asked the government:
What flags, or flags, were flown by the armed forces of Canada in world war I and world war II, and upon what authority?
The answer with respect to world war I is quite categorical: "The Canadian army flew the union jack." I am quite prepared to concede that there may have been occasions when other flags were flown, but this was the official answer. With regard to world war II the answer was:
The union flag (jack) which was the flag officially prescribed in king's regulations and orders, 1939, for the Canadian army until superseded by the Canadian red ensign.
Hon. members will, of course, recall that on January 22, 1944 the Liberal government

Canadian Commonwealth Flag made provision for the Canadian red ensign to be flown by all units of the Canadian army serving with the forces of other nations.
So, Mr. Speaker, this is surely not the case of tearing down the Canadian red ensign. I am sure that we have enough wisdom and reverence for the past that at commemorative ceremonies and at places hallowed in the memories of those who fought in world wars I and II we will drape both flags at appropriate sites of remembrance. But as a continuing recollection of our British associations, of which we are so proud, I am sure that many of us will be very happy-certainly the people in Leeds constituency, which is a noted United Empire Loyalist community, will be-about flying with our new Canadian flag the old union flag of our sovereign. I think that in my constituency the union jack will always fly, and I am sure in other parts of Canada this will be so, as well.
I know we have heard expressions from certain members which indicate that this would not be acceptable to them. However, I would ask my good friends from the province of Quebec, who are not on this side but on the other side of the house, those not sympathetic to this view, to remember that being generous is the only way to build this nation. I think the French speaking people in Canada are as generous, as understanding and as sympathetic as any of us. Perhaps this is one of the characteristics of an ethnic minority. Perhaps they are more sensitive, more kindly, and more understanding of the feelings of others. So in order not to perpetuate two national flags I would ask hon. members to vote down this amendment and be prepared to show a generous support for an ancient banner, which has been described by Sir Anthony Wagner and the authorities to whom I have referred as being a royal badge.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak in this debate, and our group had agreed not to delay further the discussion on the amendment proposed by the Conservative party concerning the red ensign.
But after the Conservative leader told us that we must absolutely continue this debate until at least six o'clock, I would like to take a few minutes to state once more the views

of our party concerning this amendment which was moved by the Conservatives.
First of all, I thought that after such a long fight to obtain a distinctive national flag the government would rest after such a painful labour without making a mess of everything and giving new headaches to the house with its second resolution, by endeavouring to have us accept through the back door a second flag for Canada.
Everyone knows our views on this matter. Every time we spoke on the flag issue, we plainly stated that we wanted only one distinctive national flag for Canada.
That is the fight we led throughout. We were accused of supporting the party in power in order to ensure the success of that idea. We did not accept anything, either from the party in power or from any other group. We merely defended the views of our constituents, the views of our province, and we finally accepted the opinion of the majority of the house, and we were very happy in doing so. I must congratulate the Conservative members who accepted the vote; I heard some this afternoon say that they accepted the decision of the majority, and I am happy to congratulate them for that.
I sincerely hope that this new flag will bring complete unity in Canada from one ocean to the other. I deplore that the Prime Minister and his government have brought forth this second resolution which was disapproved during our discussions on this second resolution dealing with a second flag, under the pretext that it would show our membership in the commonwealth nations.
In this respect I believe that the Conservative amendment does not make any more sense than the proposal of the Prime Minister concerning the adoption of the union jack, while the Conservatives propose the red ensign. Where is the difference between the two?
The union jack would bring back the memories of the colonialism we rejected in 1945 after the developments which then occurred. I congratulate those men who then set aside the union jack in order to adopt a new flag which was accepted at that time-namely, the red ensign. Today, there are those who would bring us back to the days of colonialism. We refuse to accept this.
The Conservative party offers us the red ensign which has been flying over Canada for the last 24 years. I am not ready to admit that the Conservatives are really wrong. As a matter of fact, I believe that the red ensign would more adequately represent our membership in the commonwealth than the union
Canadian Commonwealth Flag jack, since the red ensign, if it were approved, is, at least, a commercial flag, and would therefore stand for our commercial and military union with the other commonwealth countries. Neither would I say that the Conservatives are wrong in comparison with the Liberals, because I think that even if parliament were to accept the Conservative suggestion and retain the red ensign, that flag would be more acceptable than the union jack.
The red ensign, which was accepted in 1945, has just been put aside by parliament -which does not mean that we spurn it, nor indeed, the union jack-because this country is entering a new period of evolution in order to grow and attain a new status in the eyes of the world.
We were glad to accept this evolution, as were the parliamentarians of 1945 when they accepted the red ensign as a symbol of a new evolution in Canadian politics. We were very pleased with this evolution. We always worked in that direction, and we supported the government with all our might so that the single red maple leaf flag might become a reality throughout Canada.
Now, it has become a reality, and we are proud of that. I congratulate all members of the House of Commons who now support the decision of the committee, for I am not ready to say, as some claim, that this is a government flag. No, far from it. This is the flag of the committee specifically appointed to choose a design. We have agreed with the committee proposals to the effect that we accept this design.
Therefore, it is not the flag of one party in particular. It is the flag that stands for the national concept. We represent here the Canadian nation as a whole, the people of all provinces. We have had a majority vote and, as in all sound democracies, we must accept the wish of the majority, and this was accepted by most. I find there are but a few exceptions, people who have probably been in politics too long to keep pace with the evolution now taking place. That is somewhat the impression I get from those who are telling us today: we do not accept this flag.
I blame those old people who lack the required flexibility to get behind our new nation, which has taken a real step towards an evolution that will prove beneficial to the Canadian people.
As I said, if the house could accept a second flag to show our membership in the commonwealth of nations-I am saying if
11254	HOUSE OF
Canadian Commonwealth Flag parliament could accept, could order-because I believe that parliament does not have the necessary powers to dictate anything to the commonwealth of nations, no more than this parliament has the power to impose a flag on NATO or the United Nations-it is up to the council of the commonwealth of nations to select an emblem for itself, and if and when they do make a selection we will accept it as we have accepted all the emblems of the organizations to which Canada belongs.
I have yet to see this parliament refuse to accept the emblem of the organizations which Canada has voluntarily and deliberately joined. When we reach the stage where such a decision should be taken, when all commonwealth countries will have decided upon a flag, no matter if it is the British flag, the red ensign or another one, it will be up to them and not to us to make such a decision, for we are not even entitled to decide upon such a matter. Why then is the Prime Minister and his cabinet so bent on doing something which we are not empowered to do? What strikes me and startles me is to see our governors so determined to take the place of others and decide for them while they are only associated with other countries composing the British commonwealth, countries who have to decide for themselves what emblem they should have.
I am not against an emblem representing all commonwealth countries or the commonwealth partnership. And I am also very proud to see the United Nations flag. We accepted it without the slightest action on the part of parliament, just as we do not need any legislation in order to accept the emblem for all commonwealth countries. I maintain that it does not rest with the Canadian parliament to choose this emblem.
I heard my friends opposite suggest that the union jack has always been considered generally as the flag of the commonwealth of nations. I would ask them to show me at least the resolution carried by all commonwealth countries which have agreed to recognize the union jack as the emblem of the commonwealth. If they are able to show it to me, I will be the first to follow them; but if they are unable to do that, we will maintain that the union jack represents England, which is our ally within the commonwealth. If, one day, it is decided to choose an emblem for the commonwealth, we will support it willingly, without need for regulations or laws. We will willingly support the decision of the commonwealth, as we accept


the decisions of all the associations of which Canada is a member.
Mr. Speaker, in short, we do not support the Conservatives' amendment, not because it is weaker than the government's resolution, because in itself, the Conservatives' argument is stronger, but mostly for this reason: if the government lacks the power to propose the resolution, it also lacks the power to legislate on the amendment. The decision is not up to the government. We shall not support the amendment nor the resolution for the same reasons, because we feel that it is the responsibility of the leaders of the countries within the commonwealth of nations to select their own symbol. It is in that light that we consider the situation.
As for the second reason, to indicate our allegiance to the crown, we claim that if the Queen of England remains the queen of that country under the folds of the flag of England, why then would the Queen of Canada not remain the Queen of our country under the folds of the distinctive Canadian flag? Why again take a flag from our English friends to show the allegiance of Canada to their Queen? If the union jack can represent the allegiance of the English people to their sovereign, I maintain that our flag can indicate our allegiance to the Queen of Canada. Why was it chosen, if it is unable to represent us?
Mr. Speaker, this is all I wanted to say about the Conservative amendment and, for the above-mentioned reasons, we will not support the amendment nor the resolution which should never have been introduced, because it only spreads more confusion.

As a member of the house, as one who admires those members who use another tongue than mine, as one who has lived in peace and amity with them all my life, and will live on in that spirit for the remainder of the years which the Lord may give me, I, in all sincerity, in a question involving as much emotion as patriotism and in a question which, as the hon. member for Megantic said, did bring tears to the eyes of the members of the flag committee-and I can assure you it brings tears to the eyes of many citizens of the Dominion of Canada-wish to make a request.

The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) has been frank enough to state publicly on the floor of the house that he will not be voting on the amendment. Now we are into a situation where speaker after speaker has referred to the union jack as a foreign flag. They refer to it as the flag of England. They refer to it as the flag of Great Britain, and others refer to it as the flag of the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland. We who love the two flags that have flown over this country in the past, and which are still unfurled to the breeze, ask those of our compatriots in the house who are so wholeheartedly in favour of the one maple leaf flag, which the House of Commons has declared to be the official national flag of Canada and which will be so honoured in the future by all citizens, to abstain from voting and allow us who love the two old flags and hold them so dear, to make the decision to show which shall be the flag demonstrating our allegiance to the crown and our membership in the British commonwealth of nations.
I have never asked any favour of any man. I find it hard to ask a favour tonight but I would remind you, of the words of Burke, who, when speaking on the subject known today as conciliation with America said:

Mr. Speaker, it is not my desire to hold up in any way the proceedings in the debate on
Canadian Commonwealth Flag this amendment, but I did not speak in the debate on the first part of the flag question and I think I might be permitted to say a few words at this time.
I have been distressed at the perseverance of some members of the house in their abusive attitude towards the fairly chosen selection of the flag committee which was approved by the house the other night. I thought, therefore, I would speak for a minute or so today. I do so, though my remarks do not represent the ripened fruits of meditation; I have not had the opportunity to give much time to the consideration of exactly what I would say. Nevertheless there are certain views I would express.
For Canada I see shadows, clouds and darkness if the efforts of some to divide this country are not abandoned. I can understand that in the highly emotional atmosphere which existed during the first part of this flag debate feelings could easily carry one away. But now we have come to the second part of the resolution we should, I think, all attempt to take a broad view of the situation, and seek to reach a decision on a suitable second flag to mark our commonwealth connection with singular unanimity and enthusiasm. It seems to me unfortunate that the house should appear to be divided on the question of whether the union jack or the red ensign would best serve our country for this purpose. While I am of Irish descent myself I do not accept the proposition that any member of this house holds any higher regard for our historic relationship with the British isles and with Britain. In Nova Scotia, which is my province, we have always been closer to England than have some other parts of this country because of our geographical proximity, because most of the inhabitants of our province are of British descent and because of our close and historic trade ties. Joseph Howe, whom I will quote later in my remarks, said more than a hundred years ago that loyalty to our British connection is, in Nova Scotia, an enduring sentiment. And I think it remains an enduring sentiment today some 120 years after his remark was made.
I am quick to admit I would have had difficulty in voting for the selection of a totally distinctive and new Canadian flag if the union jack was not also to be recognized by this legislation. I was in this position: I felt we did need a distinctive flag, one which could not be mistaken in any part of the world for the flag of another country, but at the same time all my background and

Canadian Commonwealth Flag all my Nova Scotian sentiment favoured the reflection in some symbol of this country of a continuing connection with our mother country. I believe that the union jack which has been selected as the symbol of our commonwealth connection serves this purpose admirably. In these circumstances I felt I could vote for the selection of a distinctive flag. I believe most Nova Scotians would agree with me that we should have some symbol of our association with the commonwealth. I also believe that many Nova Scotians agree there is a need for a totally distinctive Canadian flag. In this regard I would quote the words of the hon. Robert L. Stanfield, premier of Nova Scotia, for whom I have great respect, although he is not of the same political faith as myself. Speaking on April 6, he said:
Surely, however, it is not necessarily patriotic for me to insist that something I value highly must be adopted as a national symbol if it is objectionable as a national symbol to a large number of Canadians. Surely the Canadian thing for us to do is to find symbols which are mutually acceptable. Let us emphasize what we have in common. Surely we could have a national anthem and a flag which unites Canada.
Those were the words of the premier of Nova Scotia and while I do not dare speak for him I should be surprised if he, like many Nova Scotians, did not feel there is a place for a commonwealth flag, a flag which does show our tradition and our history.
In the course of a few minutes I will deal with the question whether that role is best fulfilled by the union jack or by the red ensign. Let me say that the selection of a distinctive flag is another step, although an important one, in the development of our nation, even as the change from the almost universal use of the union jack to a partial use of the red ensign was an earlier step. I had the opportunity of spending four weeks in the British House of Commons last spring in connection with the commonwealth parliamentary association and I came back from that visit with, if anything, even stronger feelings about our association with Britain than I previously felt. I treasure our relationship with the mother country and I do not accept the view that the use of a distinctive Canadian flag will in any way lessen those feelings or dishonour our relationship.
Let us now consider why we should choose the union jack rather than the red ensign. In the first place, the red ensign has been the Canadian flag since 1945 when it was adopted by order in council. The union jack has been the flag recognized as the symbol

of the empire, and subsequently of the commonwealth, across the world from a much earlier date than that. The selection of the union jack would, I suggest, perpetuate our association with the British isles. The red ensign is a variation of that flag. I have no strong feelings on the question of whether the red ensign or the union jack should be the commonwealth flag. But on balance, after weighing the arguments in each direction, I have no difficulty in making my choice in favour of the union jack. If we wish to retain a symbol of all our past, of all the years of our past, what better symbol could there be than the flag which flew here on this hill in 1867, long before the red ensign had come ashore? At that time the union jack was the flag which reigned in Canada, as it was for a large part of our history. So if we are to choose a symbol of our past, why choose something which is a symbol of only part of our past? Why not designate the flag which flew at the time of confederation-a flag which to this day is used in my province, I would say, more widely than is the red ensign. I think the same is true of the other maritime provinces.
The red ensign, though of more recent vintage, deserves honour and respect. But even the words of the order in council at the time it was adopted show that it was to be of a transitory nature. On the other hand the union jack has always been flown in this country. It was under this flag that British justice and British culture spread across the world creating the political climate under which free nations such as Canada have been able to grow and prosper. I think it more fitting that the union jack should be selected as the flag symbolizing our ties with the commonwealth. The hopes and aspirations of the people who founded this federation were fulfilled under the union jack.
These are the few words I wanted to say on this subject today, Mr. Speaker. In common with all members of this house, I am sure, I am extremely grateful to the many Canadians who took the time and trouble to write to us during the months the flag question was topical in this nation, to express their views and help us in reaching our decisions. I received many letters on this subject. There were many letters that favoured the selection of a totally new flag, many that favoured the retention of the red ensign, many that favoured other designs. With regard to those who wrote to me in favour of the red ensign or the retention of a flag that

contained the union jack, I hope they will in time see, as I honestly feel, that we are right and that their purpose and desire to not tear away the ties of history is best expressed by the adoption of the union jack as the commonwealth flag; but that as a great and growing nation of citizens of many races we need and badly need, a flag which will be recognized in all parts of the world as nothing but Canadian.
Speaking of the people who did write to me on this subject and specifically those who favoured the red ensign. I know that many of them, as is the case with many of my good friends on the Conservative side of the house, had strong, honest, sincere and deep feelings on the matter. On the day we had the flag vote, I received from a friend of mine, with whom I grew up from early boyhood, a telegram which read:
It is not right that the red ensign which is treasured and loved by so many Canadians throughout the country should be taken from us.

In this morning's Gazette it is announced that yesterday the Prime Minister sent a memorandum which was read into the record of the Dorion commission. As it appears in the Gazette it reads as follows:
Mr. Pearson's memo filed with the inquiry said:
During the evening of November 23 and the morning of November 24, I learned for the first time of the details of the allegations and of the contents of the R.C.M.P. report into the Rivard case.
As I told the house on November 24, I had not known until that day of the alleged involvement of my parliamentary secretary in this matter.
The member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) then asked me whether I was informed and, if so, when, of any of the other circumstances of this case prior to these matters being brought to the attention of the house November 23.
My answer on this point should be clarified. I made it clear that I first learned of the contents of the R.C.M.P. report shortly before the justice estimates were introduced November 23.
However, the Minister of Justice had informed me earlier, on September 2, that there were allegations of bribery involving the executive assistant (Denis) to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration: that these allegations were denied by the official in question: that they were being investigated by the R.C.M.P. upon the instructions of the Minister of Justice and with the knowledge, of course, of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; and that the person in question had been sent on leave while the investigation was taking place.
Clearly those were the full and appropriate measures at that stage and they had been taken promptly. I was, therefore, content to wait for

Question of Privilege
the R.C.M.P. report oi which, as I have already stated to the house, I was informed on November 23.
This statement is not, in my mind, a clarification but rather an admission that the information given to the house on November 24 was incorrect. I point out, Mr. Speaker, that had the correct information been given -that the Prime Minister was aware of the charges against Mr. Denis on September 2- I, and no doubt many other members, would have had further questions to ask him, and the whole course of the debate would have taken a quite different direction.
Not only has the house been misinformed and affronted in this way, but it has been further affronted by the Prime Minister not having made his new statement here, as he could have done at any time on a question of privilege rather than sending it in the form of a memorandum to the Dorion commission.
A further question of the Prime Minister's position vis-a-vis the House of Commons arises from the point of how long ago he realized he had made a misstatement to us, and thus how long he continued to leave us in ignorance as to the true facts.
This is a case, Mr. Speaker, which I think you should take under advisement.

speechtext: May I ask, is this on the same subject?

subtopic: MR. HARKNESS-REPLIES BY PRIME MINISTER TO QUESTIONS IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I had intended to raise this matter on a question of privilege, but in view of the fact that the hon. member for Calgary North was the member whose questions were answered and he was directly affected by the replies, I was quite willing to give way to him. I am now rising on a question of privilege regarding the unsatisfactory nature of the answers we have received.
I think my point of privilege can be dealt with in two parts. The first is that the answers of the Prime Minister are completely unsatisfactory. The questions which were asked on November 24 by the hon. member for Calgary North had nothing to do with whether or not the Prime Minister was aware of the charges contained in the R.C.M.P. report or any of the allegations contained therein. Nor had it anything to do with information regarding the involvement of his parliamentary secretary. Those two questions had been answered the same day but prior to these answers. The three questions which were put in succession by the hon. member for Calgary North, as reported at page 10429 of Hansard, had to do with whether the Prime Minister had been informed "about any of the other circumstances". The answer of the Prime Minister was clear and succinct. First of all he said he had been informed only shortly before the justice estimates came before the house. His second reply was:
-I think I was informed on the day before his estimates were brought before the house.
In view of the statement of the Prime Minister to the effect that when he gave that reply he had forgotten that on September 2 these matters had been revealed to him, it would seem to me that if on November 22, the day before the estimates were brought to the house, the Minister of Justice had informed the Prime Minister that he had the R.C.M.P. report in his possession and that it contained serious allegations regarding certain persons, surely that would have refreshed his memory about the conversation which had

Question of Privilege
taken place on September 2. Therefore I find it extremely difficult to understand how the Prime Minister on November 24 could make the categorical assertion that he knew nothing about any of the other circumstances regarding the Rivard case until the day before the estimates were introduced in the house.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that this is completely at variance with the statement filed by the Prime Minister with Chief Justice Dorion. This statement is attached to a letter which, if I may quote in part, says:
I had hoped that before now I would have been able to make a short statement on this aspect of the matter to the House of Commons, but the procedural situation made that impossible.
I hope that very shortly the procedural difficulties will be removed, but meanwhile I am attaching to this letter a copy of what I had hoped to say before now, as I think you may wish to have it before the inquiry opens tomorrow.
Yours sincerely,
L. B. Pearson.
The memorandum which is attached is dated December 14 and is entitled "Statement by the Prime Minister". It is in the following terms:
This is my first opportunity to report to the house on the judicial inquiry which, as I mentioned three weeks ago on November 24, would investigate allegations that had been made concerning possible bribery and improper pressures in relation to the extradition case involving one Lucien Rivard.
The relevant paragraphs, Mr. Speaker, are these:
The member for Calgary North then asked me whether I was informed and, if so, when, of any of the other circumstances of this case prior to these matters being brought to the attention of the house on November 23.
My answer on this point should be clarified. I made it clear that I first learned of the contents of the R.C.M.P. report shortly before the justice estimates were introduced on November 23. However, the Minister of Justice had informed me earlier, on September 2, that there were allegations of bribery involving the executive assistant to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; that these allegations were denied by the official in question; that they were being investigated by the R.C.M.P. upon the instructions of the Minister of Justice, and with the knowledge, of course, of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; and that the person in question had been sent on leave while the investigation was taking place.
My first point, Mr. Speaker, is that if the statement which the Prime Minister filed with Chief Justice Dorion is correct, then the statements made by him on November 24 as reported at page 10429 of Hansard are incorrect, and the house was consequently mis-

led by the Prime Minister regarding the statements he made at that time.
My second point of privilege is that the Prime Minister has had over three weeks in which to refresh his memory and make a correction in the House of Commons. It is not correct, as he says in his letter to the chief justice, that the procedural situation made that impossible or that there were procedural difficulties which he hoped would be removed. Mr. Speaker, there were no procedural difficulties, because any member at any time can rise in his place on a question of privilege. As a matter of fact, during the past two weeks several members at various times have risen on questions of privilege. There was nothing to prevent the Prime Minister from correcting this matter and correcting his statements of November 24. If he found that his memory had been defective with respect to the replies he made to the hon. member for Calgary North he could at any time after his return from his trip west have risen in his place and told the house that he had been in error, and set the matter right.
We take a very serious view of the fact that the Prime Minister made no such statement in the house, and for a period of over three weeks made no attempt whatsoever to correct what was obviously a misstatement of fact. Instead, the Prime Minister sent a statement to the chief justice, which he said he hoped to make in the house when the procedural difficulties were removed. It is only today, when a question of privilege has been raised, that the Prime Minister has seen fit to make an explanation to the effect that his memory had failed him when he was replying to the questions asked by the hon. member for Calgary North.
Therefore I think the members of this party cannot accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary North that this be referred to Your Honour. With all due deference, sir, I feel that this matter must be referred to the house and to the proper committee appointed by the house for that purpose. This is a matter which the house must determine. If the house feels, as I do, that it was misled by the Prime Minister in answers which he gave on November 24 to the hon. member for Calgary North, the house must determine that and the house must say so. If on the other hand the house is satisfied with the explanation which the Prime Minister has given or by any further elaboration which he may care to make to the committee on privileges and elections, then at that time the house can make a determination as to whether or not

the house was misled by the Prime Minister, and decide if that was due to either an unwitting or an intentional action on the part of the Prime Minister.
I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher):
That the statements made In the House of Commons by the Prime Minister on November 24, 1964, concerning his knowledge of the matters referred to in order in council PC. 1964-1819, as amended by order in council P.C. 1964-1820, be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections for consideration in the light of statements made by the Prime Minister in his letter of December 14, 1964, to the commissioner appointed under the terms of the said order in council and in the statement enclosed with the said letter.

subtopic: MR. HARKNESS-REPLIES BY PRIME MINISTER TO QUESTIONS IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Before accepting the motion, Mr. Speaker, you must first of all determine whether there is a prima facie case of privilege. If you do accept the argument that there is a prima facie case of privilege, then of course the substantive motion which has been made is in order. In so far as we in this party are concerned, we believe that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Calgary North is a good one, that is that you take this matter under advisement.
If, in your determination, you are able to satisfy yourself that there is a prima facie case of privilege, then of course you can allow the motion that has been moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. It appears to us at this stage that there is a prima facie case of privilege. We believe the house will determine this matter eventually, but that it ought to go to a committee so we can have the facts all assembled.
We know this whole matter is now under investigation by a judicial inquiry set up by the government, known as the Dorion commission. I believe the determination of whether or not the house has been misled can be brought out by cross checking the evidence that will come out in this judicial inquiry against the dates and the statements that have been made in this house. Then the committee will be able to decide whether there has been a misstatement of the facts in this house or whether there has been an honest lack of memory.
So far as we are concerned, Mr. Speaker, we would support the suggestion that this matter be referred to a standing committee of the house, and I believe the Prime Minister has already accepted this procedure.

subtopic: MR. HARKNESS-REPLIES BY PRIME MINISTER TO QUESTIONS IN HOUSE
speechtext:
There is a motion before the house now, and perhaps I can say a word about it. As I understand the rules, if any
Question of Privilege
member of this house makes a charge that a member of this house has deliberately deceived the house, that is a matter which must be investigated and the hon. member making the charge takes the responsibility for asking for the investigation before a committee. If a charge is made it must be investigated, and the hon. member making the charge takes the responsibility for that. Under the circumstances now, I do not know whether the hon. member is making such a charge. It must be a charge that I deliberately deceived this house. If that is the charge it certainly should be investigated.
The hon. member has said two other things. He said that two or three weeks ago I should have made the kind of statement I have now made as a question of privilege. The hon. member obviously does not give much credence to my statement that I believed the right way to do this was not as a question of privilege, which if I had raised it would have been tantamount to admitting that I had deceived the house, but by making a statement on motions which could be replied to by hon. members of the house. This is what I intended to do at the first opportunity, notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman has said.
Another point the hon. gentleman made was that I discussed the matter with the Minister of Justice on the morning of November 24 and he must have informed me of the earlier talks. He does not accept my word when I say I was not informed by him of any of the antecedents of this matter. He does not have to accept my word, but I repeat that is the truth, absolutely.

subtopic: MR. HARKNESS-REPLIES BY PRIME MINISTER TO QUESTIONS IN HOUSE
speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I cannot allow the Prime Minister to put words into my mouth. What I said was that when the Minister of Justice, according to the Prime Minister's own statement, informed him on November 22, the day before the estimates were brought into the house, that he had in his possession a report from the R.C.M.P. alleging certain wrongdoing on the part of certain persons, surely that must have refreshed the Prime Minister's memory that he had discussed this matter with the Minister of Justice on September 2. subtopic: MR. HARKNESS-REPLIES BY PRIME MINISTER TO QUESTIONS IN HOUSE
speechtext:
The hon. member may find it difficult to understand, but I am telling him the facts. When the Minister of Justice spoke to me, it was to the effect that a report had been received, and what it contained. I had

Question of Privilege
no thought of the earlier discussion at all. He can accept that statement or not, but I am making it as a statement which is true. I would remind the hon. member that, as I said in my first statement, this was a conversation on an airplane coming back from a constitutional conference, the kind of statement which could easily be put in the back of a prime minister's mind when he had other things in his mind during that week, and especially when it was a matter that was now in the hands of the minister and the R.C.M.P. I was informed I would be given the results of the investigation when the minister felt they were complete. This is the story, and it is the absolute and complete truth.
I might have made an error in not getting up on a question of privilege, but I thought it would be better to make a statement under motions. I apologize if that error was made. If the hon. member wishes to charge me with deceiving the house deliberately, he should do so and certainly the matter should go to a committee.

subtopic: MR. HARKNESS-REPLIES BY PRIME MINISTER TO QUESTIONS IN HOUSE
speechtext:
I have to decide whether there is a question of privilege. Dealing first with the argument of the hon. member for Calgary North, I should like to cite Beauchesne, citation 104, subsection (2), which reads:
It has often been laid down that the Speaker's function in ruling on a claim of breach of privilege does not extend to deciding the question of substance whether a breach of privilege has in fact been committed-a question which can only be decided by the house itself.
It seems to me, therefore, that it is not part of my function, as was suggested, to take all this into consideration, and I do not propose to do so. Furthermore, the hon. member did not finish up with a motion either to refer this to a committee or asking for some penalty, and without some specific motion it seems to me it was a general statement and not necessarily a question of privilege. Then we had a long explanation from the right hon. Prime Minister, and up to that stage it seems to me it was more in the nature of a grievance than a question of privilege. Then the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam rose and moved the motion which I have before me.
In that connection I should like to call to the attention of the house a ruling by Mr. Speaker Michener which is very much in point. The ruling appears in the Journals of the House of Commons of June 17, 1959 and I referred to it in the house on October 30, 1964. I do not propose to read the whole ruling but just to cite one key sentence. These are the words of Speaker Michener:

In my view, simple justice requires that no honourable member should have to submit to investigation of his conduct by the house or a committee until he has been charged with an offence.
On reading and studying the motion moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam it seems to me there is no specific charge set out in it. The words are too vague. If the hon. member wishes to make a specific charge there is a proper way to do it, to stand and bring a specific charge.
Here we are dealing with a misstatement, not a question of privilege. There must be a real accusation made against, in this case, the right hon. Prime Minister, and there must be something in the charge which shows the misstatement, if it was a misstatement, was made with intent, with purpose. There is no specific charge, and in view of the ruling of Speaker Michener and of what I have said, in my opinion there is not a prima facie case and therefore no question of privilege.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, December 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Batten that the seventh and final report of the special committee on a Canadian flag, presented to the house on Thursday, October 29, 1964, be now concurred in, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Flemming (Vic-toria-Carleton).

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SEVENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned yesterday at six o'clock I was saying that we, in this corner of the house, have or would have no objection to the seventh report of the flag committee being considered again so as to suggest to the government to propose the union jack as the commonwealth flag to all member countries of the British commonwealth of nations.
Several members mentioned yesterday that the Canadian parliament could adopt this flag, since Canada is a member of the British empire or of the British commonwealth of nations.
Now, that flag is not recognized at all as the flag of the empire or of the British commonwealth of nations, but rather as the flag of a country, namely England.
I wish to repeat that we hold nothing against the traditions represented by the union jack or the red ensign. We have nothing against what either of these two flags represent, far from it. On the other hand, the people of Canada wonder why our country

should have two flags. Ours will be the only country in the world, in similar circumstances, to have two flags; a Canadian national flag and another to prove its membership in the commonwealth of nations.
Mr. Speaker, surely we need no flag other than our own Canadian flag to indicate our co-operation with the other members of the British empire. We would have no objection either should any province decide to adopt the red ensign as its provincial flag, if it wishes to do so. We would have no objection to that, but Quebec does have a provincial flag, and it is not trying and never tried to impose it on the federal parliament or any of the other Canadian provinces. We would not attempt either to impose to anybody our provincial flag which symbolizes our origins and our traditions which are essentially Canadian, because everybody knows that Canada was first discovered in 1534 by Jacques Cartier. Therefore, at that time our allegiance was to France. But today we would not impose or try to impose French symbols on the Canadian people as a whole.
We have seen other provinces besides Quebec adopt a provincial flag. For instance, British Columbia and Nova Scotia adopted a provincial flag, and Saskatchewan adopted one yesterday. If Alberta decided to adopt a flag similar to the red ensign or the union jack, we would have the greatest respect for such a decision.
Unfortunately, such is not the case: Attempts are made to force a second Canadian flag on us. And we are sorry to say that this project of the Prime Minister or of the government to adopt a second flag for Canada is bringing about unfortunate reactions in certain parts of Canada.
Reading in the press yesterday and this morning that hon. members from Ontario and other provinces were threatened because they voted for a distinctive national flag, we wonder what has become of our truly Canadian civilization, what has become of that civilization we wish to set as an example for several nations in the world, when things get to the point where hon. members are threatened because they vote for a true Canadian symbol.
Mr. Speaker, we deeply regret the doings of these people who make threats against hon. members, be it against members of the Liberal, Conservative, New Democratic, Social Credit or Ralliement Creditiste parties. I think the Canadian people have reached such a degree of maturity that our country,
Canadian Commonwealth Flag Canada, can be held up as an example to other countries, and even to certain countries which are members of the British commonwealth of nations at this time.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved by the Conservatives and included in the second part of the resolution, to the effect of changing the union jack for the red ensign, faces us with a choice, to use the words of some hon. members.
Now, we of the Ralliement Creditiste have said loud and clear, not only in the province of Quebec but also in Ontario, and I even said so in western Canada, that we would support the adoption of a distinctive national flag, but not two Canadian flags. That statement met with the approval of English speaking and French speaking people as well, and today the Conservative amendment does not imply a choice to the effect of changing the union jack for the red ensign.
Let me tell you how we will vote on this amendment and on the main motion. We have the greatest respect for what the union jack and the red ensign represent, but we still stick to the ideas set forth several months ago to the effect that Canada must have one flag and not two flags, and that it can belong to the British commonwealth of nations with its distinctive Canadian flag and nothing else.
Mr. Speaker, the proposal for the adoption of the red ensign forces us to make a choice, and the stand we have taken is evident. We are in favour of one flag and against any plan for the adoption of a second flag. The Conservatives would like to give us the red ensign as a second flag and the Liberals want to give us the union jack as a flag indicating our allegiance to the crown and our membership in the British commonwealth of nations.
Mr. Speaker, we agree neither to the amendment of the Conservatives, nor to the main motion, and we will be against any plan and any amendment or subamendment which would force upon us a second flag, whatever it may be.
We want to remain authentic Canadians from coast to coast and I think that England and all other countries of the British commonwealth of nations will respect us even more if we appear before them with a Canadian symbol representing Canada in this British commonwealth of nations.
Mr. Speaker, those are the few remarks I wanted to make on the amendment now before us as well as on the main motion that we will probably discuss this afternoon.

Canadian Commonwealth Flag
Out stand is clear and I will sum it up this way.
The distinctive national flag is adopted. We have voted for that flag not because we had something against one or the other, but because we have voted as real Canadians, not as French Canadians.
We shall vote against the Conservative amendment and against the main motion.

speechtext:
One hon. member says
"Shame". Sir, my position was known to all the members of this House of Commons; my position, I believe, was known to the people of Canada because of the symbolic gesture which I made to indicate that no flag should be raised on parliament hill that was not the flag of Canada since it had not been approved by the House of Commons. My position being known to all the members and all the people of Canada, and some 270 speeches having been made, what more was required to be said on either side of the question? When I had the opportunity of expressing my hope, I voted for the red ensign as the distinctive flag of Canada. When that motion was defeated, we then had to face the vote on the recommendation of the special committee of the House of Commons, a special committee representative of all parties, and having lost what I really wanted, then as a democratic member of a democratic House of Commons I accepted the majority democratic position of all parties in this House of Commons and voted for the new flag. I make no apologies for that.
Now, sir, we have a further question in front of us, and that is what you may call a second flag, a flag introduced on the basis of the fact that, in addition to a national flag, we should have one that will demonstrate the relationship of Canada within the commonwealth, as a part of the commonwealth and of our allegiance to the peoples and countries that were the founders of our country.

I disagree completely with the recommendation of the committee. I cannot understand how the committee reached their conclusion. It is to be a flag that demonstrates our relationship with the commonwealth. How you demonstrate your relationship with the commonwealth by a flag which is wholly and solely outside of Canada, I cannot understand.
The amendment is reasonable; the amendment is understandable. The amendment is the only position that the members of the House of Commons can take in support of the committee if they want a second flag which demonstrates Canada's position within the commonwealth. This flag is, should be, and must be the red ensign. This morning I made once again a special study of the facts to insure that my information was correct, and I think it is.
Let us take the union jack, strictly as the union jack, and we find that is not a flag which demonstrates the relationship between Canada and the commonwealth. It is the flag of the United Kingdom. However, I should like to put this to the members: Take the red ensign, and what is it? It is a combination of the union jack and the Canadian shield. Why is it, sir, that no matter what constituency or province one comes from, there are so many in this house who ignore the Canadian shield. We have the union jack on the red ensign. We have the union jack which we, in Canada, share with other commonwealth countries in what is sometimes termed the staff side of the flag or the jack side of the flag or, if you want to be particular, the canton No. 1. So, on the staff side, the jack side, the canton No. 1, is the union jack, which represents not only the United Kingdom but the commonwealth because it is common to all the commonwealth countries. On the red ensign also, Mr. Speaker, you have the Canadian shield.
Now, sir, a few weeks ago this was explained in heraldic terminology. I am afraid too many have forgotten the heraldic terminology of the Canadian shield. On the red ensign, the Canadian shield is symbolic of Canada. This shield has maple leaves on it, which everyone agrees are symbolic of Canada. It also has emblems that go back to ancient times, ancient times of the peoples and countries who have founded and built this country. You have the couchant lion or, if the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) were here, he would refer to it as the heraldic leopard. We know that it came over from France and was the emblem on the flag of

William of Normandy. Ever since, from 1066, it has been incorporated in the heraldry of Great Britain and of the British kings. On the shield of Canada you have the red lion rampant on a golden field, which was the emblem of the Scottish kings and came to Scotland from ancient Ireland. Then, you have the harp, an emblem on our Canadian shield which is equally ancient and was taken into Ireland many centuries ago. You have the fleur-de-lis on the Canadian shield, which is well known as the lily of France and held a proud place in the arms of British kings proclaiming the French ancestry of the sovereigns from, to put it politely, the distaff side of the house. About the time the fleur-de-lis was removed from the royal arms of the United Kingdom it began to appear in the heraldry of Canada and it has been there ever since.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these emblems on the Canadian shield represent the early pioneers who were instrumental in laying the foundation of our country, Canada. We must remember that the emblems on the Canadian shield, with all their heraldic meaning and early history, were incorporated officially in 1921 because the Canadian government requested King George V to prepare a new coat of arms for Canada. It was in response to the request of Canada in 1921 that the royal college of heralds laid down what we now know as the coat of arms or the shield of Canada.
In view of all the foregoing, in view of the fact that the House of Commons has established what is termed a national, distinctive flag, I say it seems only suitable that the second flag which demonstrates our understanding of the past, recognizes the ethnic groups that founded Canada, demonstrates our history of the past, our allegiance to the past, our recognition of the pioneers who came from many countries and made Canada great, our recognition of our membership in the commonwealth, should be one on which you have the union jack on the staff and the coat of arms on the fly. On that one flag we have Canada with its history and origins, and with its membership in the commonwealth of nations.
Sir, how can anyone argue against the red ensign in such a matter? How can anyone say, with our understanding of the commonwealth, that the second flag shall be the flag of a country outside Canada? The real living proof of our membership in the commonwealth and the real living proof of our knowledge of history and ancestry demand
